## The Treatise of Saddanīti

## Saddanīti-suttamālā

## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa

## 1. Sandhikappa

Following this (the forms completed by roots), the divisions of Sandhi, Nouns, and so forth, together with the Suttas, will occur according to the order of the exposition. In this exposition, "salakkhaṇo sandhināmādibhedo," the Sutta is called "Lakkhaṇa." There are many names for Sutta: Sutta, Lakkhaṇa, Vacana, Yoga, Ārambha, Sattha, Vākya, and Yatana.

Those students who are skilled in the various divisions of Sandhi, Nouns, and so forth,
And who, being possessed of great power of wisdom,
Apply themselves specifically to the desired Three Piṭakas,
They certainly attain the various essences of the sublime meanings.

Those students who are not skilled in those divisions (of Sandhi, Nouns, etc.),
Even though they always exert great effort,
Because of their intense confusion regarding words,
They certainly do not find the essence desired in the Three Piṭakas.

Therefore, for the benefit of students at the beginning,
I shall explain the divisions of Sandhi,
Which is a method uniquely and wonderfully arranged, such as the prescription of designations (saññā),
And is a well-constructed method in accordance with the Pariyatti Dhamma.

This exposition, "salakkhaṇo sandhināmādibhedo bhavissati," has been stated. In that exposition, as well as in the verses beginning with "ye sandhināmādipabhedadakkhā," the benefits and faults have been shown. In showing those benefits and faults, the promise was made: "sandhippabhedaṃva pakāsayissaṃ" (I shall explain the divisions of Sandhi).

In that promise, why is Sandhi shown first? Because the function of Sandhi (joining words) is desired in all instances, just as salt is desired in all curries, and just as a minister who manages all affairs is desired in all royal duties. Therefore, among the divisions such as Sandhi, Nouns (Nāma), Case-relations (Kāraka), and Compounds (Samāsa), I shall first show the divisions of Sandhi before Nouns and others.

Wishing to show the divisions of Sandhi, I shall first show the arising of sound (sadda) that has reached the state of a letter (vaṇṇa), along with the prescription of designations and so forth. Only the sound produced by the mind (cittaja-sadda), which has reached the state of a letter and is dependent on the body and the element of space (ākāsa-dhātu) which is the path of the wind, is called "Sadda" (in the context of Pariyatti). Sound produced by the seasons (utu) is not "Sadda." This mind-produced sound does not arise in the whole body. Some sounds arise in the chest, some in the throat, and some in the head. Thus, they arise in these three locations. Specifically, the voice of the Blessed One...
2:
In that promise, the function of Sandhi is desired in all instances, just as salt is desired in all curries, and just as a minister who manages all affairs is desired in all royal duties. Therefore, among the various divisions such as Sandhi, Nouns (Nāma), Case-relations (Kāraka), and Compounds (Samāsa), I shall first show the divisions of Sandhi. While showing the divisions of Sandhi, I shall first show the arising of sound that has reached the state of a letter, along with the prescription of designations and so forth. Only the sound produced by the mind, which has reached the state of a letter and is dependent on the body having the various space elements as the path of the wind, is called "Sadda." This mind-produced sound does not arise in the whole body. Some sounds arise in the chest, some in the throat, and some in the head; thus, they arise in these three locations. Specifically, because the physical basis of the Blessed One's voice has been purified by the merit of perfections (pāramī) such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla) fulfilled for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, when it arises starting from the navel, it is like the voice of Mahābrahmā, undisturbed by bile, phlegm, and so forth, being pure and endowed with eight qualities. Thus, the mind-produced sound arising in those three locations reaches the state of a letter by striking the five bases of articulation (ṭhāna) known as the throat, palate, top of the tongue, teeth, and lips. When one thinks and reflects, "I will say this," the mind-produced earth element (cittaja-pathavī-dhātu) arising in various parts of the body strikes the karma-produced earth element (kammaja-pathavī-dhātu), and thus sound is born. It should be understood that this sound reaches the state of a letter by striking the five bases of articulation through the power of the striking of these two elements. In this Saddanīti treatise, I shall state the Suttas, making some with commentary (vutti) and some without.

1. The forty-one sounds starting with 'a' are called Vaṇṇa. In the Buddha's word (Pāḷi), the forty-one sounds starting with the letter 'a' are called Vaṇṇa. What are those Vaṇṇas? They are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o; ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ. They are called Vaṇṇa because meaning is expressed or spoken by these sounds.
3:
What is the purpose of the designation 'Vaṇṇa'? It is for the lack of confusion and the successful accomplishment of tasks in Suttas such as "ho dhassa vaṇṇasandhimhi."

2. Those (Vaṇṇas) are also called Akkharā. Those forty-one sounds starting with 'a' are called Akkharā. For what reason are they called Akkharā? Because of the sense of being imperishable (akkhaya) and the sense of not being harsh (akkhara). That which reaches destruction or wanes is called "khaya." That which is harsh or hard is called "khara." These Vaṇṇas, although they exist in the five paths of the knowable (ñeyyapatha)—namely, formations (saṅkhāra), variations (vikāra), characteristics (lakkhaṇa), Nibbāna, and concepts (paññatti)—they do not reach destruction, nor do they wane; they remain clearly manifest successively. Even when they revolve in extremely subtle and profound symbolic concepts, they do not reach harshness or hardness; being extremely soft, they do not become harsh by the power of meaning. Therefore, they are called "Akkharā." The intended analysis (viggaha) here is: they are called Akkharā because they do not perish (na kkharanti). The meaning is that although they are only forty-one in number, even when they reach the infinite meanings to be expressed, they are not exhausted. What is the purpose of the designation 'Akkharā'? It is for the lack of confusion and the successful accomplishment of tasks in Suttas such as "akkharato kāro" and "akkharānaṃ sannipātaṃ, jaññā pubbāparāni ca." From here on, because of the desire for brevity, I shall not state the purpose of designations such as 'Sara' (vowels).

3. Among those (Akkharā), the first eight are called Sarā. Among those letters starting with 'a', the first eight letters are called Sarā. They are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o. They are called Sarā because they reach the state of being heard (sara-nti). Or, they are called Sarā because they cause the consonants associated with them to reach the state of being heard. However, the etymologists (neruttikā) say, "They are called Sarā because they shine by themselves (sayaṃ rājanti)."

4. Among those vowels, the first, third, and fifth are called Rassa (short), having a duration of about a blink of an eye.
4:
(They) are called rassa (short). What are those rassa? They are: a, i, u. In this context, the word 'mattā' refers to a brief moment, described as the closing and opening of the eyes. Indeed, the duration it takes for a healthy person to blink once is the measure of one mattā for the rassa vowels. They are called rassa because they are recited in a short duration.

5. The remaining vowels with two mattā are called dīgha (long). Among the vowels, those other than the rassa that have two mattā are named dīgha. What are those dīgha? They are: ā, ī, ū, e, o. They are called dīgha because they are recited in a long duration. This meaning has been stated in the Vinaya Commentary: "Dīgha refers to those starting with 'ā' which are to be recited in a long duration. Rassa refers to those starting with 'a' which are to be recited in half the duration of that (dīgha)." [Vin-a. 4.247]. Since letters do not have physical shapes, their long or short nature cannot be found through shape, but can only be found through the duration of pronunciation.

6. The remaining letters with half a mattā are called byañjana (consonants). All letters starting from 'ka' which remain after the vowels and have half the mattā of a rassa vowel are named byañjana. What are those byañjana? They are: ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ. The 'a' sound included in 'ka' etc. is for the purpose of pronunciation. They are called byañjana because they make the meaning clear (manifest) by depending on a vowel as in "dhī, bhū, go," etc., or by depending on a group of letters together with a vowel as in "buddho bhagavā," etc. Teachers proficient in grammar (Saddhammaneruttika), however, say, "They are called byañjanas because they produce (manifest) the vowel." Those who know the Vedas say, "They are called byañjanas because they follow the vowels."

7. The consonants starting with 'ka' and ending with 'ma' are called vagga (groups). Among those consonants, those starting with 'ka' and ending with 'ma' are named vagga. What are those vagga? They are: ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Among those groups, the first is ka-vagga, the second is ca-vagga, the third is ṭa-vagga, the fourth is ta-vagga, and the fifth is pa-vagga.
5:
There are five kinds of groups (vagga). They are called vagga because they proceed or occur in divisions of five each. Alternatively, they are called vagga because they are known to exist in divisions of five each. Furthermore, the word 'vagga' has the meaning of a collection or assembly; thus, they are also called vagga in the sense of a collection.

8. The letter heard after a vowel as aṃ, iṃ, uṃ is called niggahīta. The sound that occurs and is heard after a vowel as aṃ, iṃ, uṃ is named niggahīta. For example, in passages such as "I was once a fisherman's son in a fisherman's village," the bindu (dot) that occurs after the three rassa vowels should be known as niggahīta. That niggahīta is called so because, in the usage of the Dispensation (Sāsana), it is taken and pronounced depending on a rassa vowel. Alternatively, it is called niggahīta because it is uttered with a nasal sound by restraining the articulation points (karaṇa) with the mouth not fully open. It has also been said: "Niggahīta is that which is to be spoken with a nasal sound by restraining the articulation points, without releasing them, and with the mouth not fully open." [Vin-a. 4.247]. In this context, 'niggahīta' is the term used in the Sāsana. In grammar treatises, however, they call that niggahīta 'anusvāra'.

(a) 'a' and 'ā' are called avaṇṇa.
(b) 'i' and 'ī' are called ivaṇṇa.
(c) 'u' and 'ū' are called uvaṇṇa.
(d) Only those pairs of avaṇṇa, ivaṇṇa, and uvaṇṇa are called savaṇṇa (similar vowels).
(e) 'e' and 'o' are called asavaṇṇa (dissimilar vowels).
(f) Vowels called savaṇṇa are also called sarūpa (similar in form/sound).
(g) The remaining six vowels relative to avaṇṇa etc. are called asarūpa (dissimilar in form/sound).
(h) For the letter 'e', the other seven vowels are called asarūpa.
(i) Likewise, for the letter 'o', the other seven vowels are called asarūpa. In this context, 'e' and 'o' are called 'asavaṇṇa' because they do not have vowels with the same articulation points (karaṇa) as themselves, and...
6:
...because they do not have the same sound (suti) as other vowels, they receive the name 'asarūpa'. Vowels such as avaṇṇa, however, receive the name 'savaṇṇa' by virtue of being pairs, and receive the name 'asarūpa' in relation to other vowels. However, they do not receive the name 'asavaṇṇa' because they have the same articulation points.

Among those savaṇṇa and asavaṇṇa, 'savaṇṇa' means vowels having the same articulation point (karaṇa), or vowels having the same place of origin for the letters. 'Asavaṇṇa' means vowels not having the same articulation point, or vowels having different places of origin for the letters. In this context, the word 'vaṇṇa' should be understood as expressing the articulation point (karaṇa). Accordingly, the root is found as: "vaṇṇa in the sense of vaṇṇa-kriyā (articulation), vitthāra (extension), and guṇa-vacana (quality)." The place of origin for letters such as the throat is called 'karaṇa'. Indeed, it is called karaṇa because letters are produced (pronounced) there. Thus, vowels with the same articulation point are savaṇṇa, and those with different articulation points are asavaṇṇa.

'Sarūpa' means those with the same sound (suti), and 'asarūpa' means those with different sounds. In this context, sound (suti) is expressed by the word 'rūpa'. Hearing is called 'suti', and that hearing belongs only to sound (sadda). The sound that is heard manifests the meaning, and the word 'rūpa' also has the meaning of manifesting. Accordingly, the root is found as: "rūpa in the sense of rūpa-kriyā (manifesting)," and there is the derivative definition: "rūpayatīti rūpaṃ" (that which manifests is rūpa). Therefore, sound (suti) is expressed by the word 'rūpa' which denotes the meaning of manifesting. For this reason, it is concluded that vowels with the same sound are sarūpa, and vowels with different sounds are asarūpa.

9. A dīgha (long) vowel is called garu (heavy). Examples: ā, ī, ū, bhū, dhī, mā.

10. A rassa (short) vowel followed by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga) is also called garu. Examples: vatvā, gantvā, yassa nakkhamati.

11. A rassa vowel preceding a niggahīta consonant without a vowel or a consonant with a 'takhon-hlwar' (virāma/pure consonant) is also called garu. Examples: sukhaṃ, isiṃ, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.

12. A rassa vowel is called lahu (light). Examples: a, i, paṭhati, vadatu.

13. A rassa vowel not followed by a conjunct consonant is also called lahu. Example: yassa na khamati nu.
7:
14. Among the five groups (vargas), the first and third letters are called sithila (soft or unaspirated). They are k, c, ṭ, t, p and g, j, ḍ, d, b.

15. The second and fourth letters are called dhanita (hard or aspirated). They are kh, ch, ṭh, th, ph and gh, jh, ḍh, dh, bh.

16. A sithila letter is called aphuṭṭha (uncontacted); a dhanita letter is called phuṭṭha (contacted). Grammarians state that the group letters are phuṭṭha, and y, r, l, v are īsaphuttha (slightly contacted). However, teachers proficient in the Sasana state that only group letters possess the qualities of phuṭṭha and aphuṭṭha. In this regard, according to the view of the Sasana teachers, whichever letter among the groups touches the place of articulation (ṭhāna) in a soft manner, even though it is contacted, it should be understood as aphuṭṭha (uncontacted) because it touches softly. If understood this way, there is no contradiction in their doctrine.

17. The first and second letters, along with the letter 's', are called aghosa (unvoiced). They are k, kh, c, ch, ṭ, ṭh, t, th, p, ph, and s.

18. The third, fourth, and fifth letters, along with y, r, l, v, h, and ḷ, are called ghosavanta (voiced). They are g, gh, ṅ, j, jh, ñ, ḍ, Ḏh, ṇ, d, dh, n, b, bh, m, and y, r, l, v, h, ḷ. Grammarians also desire the voiced quality for the anusvāra, known as niggahīta. However, teachers proficient in the Sasana desire for that niggahīta only the state of being free from both voiced (ghosa) and unvoiced (aghosa) qualities.

19. Speech uttered in connection with the following word is called sambandha (connected). For example: "Anāthapiṇḍikassārāme", "Nārahatāyasmā ambaṭṭho".

20. Speech uttered by separating the words is called vavatthita (separated). For example: "Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme", "Na arahati āyasmā ambaṭṭho".

21. Speech uttered with an open mouth without restraining the instruments of articulation (karaṇa) is called vimutta (released). For example: "Dhammaṭṭhitatā, dhammaniyāmatā", "Kusalā dhammā".

## Thus ends the Mūlasaññāvidhāna.
8:
Now, the rules for the recitation of letters (Sikkhāvidhāna) will be presented—

22. In some places, the letters 'e' and 'o' occurring before a conjunct consonant should be recited as short (rassa). For example: ettha, seyyo, oṭṭho, sotthi. Why is it said "kvaci" (in some places)? Because in instances such as "Mañce tvaṃ nikkhanam vane" and "Putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja", they are recited long despite being before a conjunct. In some treatises, the instrument (karaṇa) is called the place of articulation (ṭhāna), but in this treatise, the distinction between ṭhāna and karaṇa should be understood.

23. Letters arise due to the place of articulation (ṭhāna), the instrument (karaṇa), and the effort (payatana). There are five places of articulation, starting with the throat (kaṇṭha). Including the nose (nāsikā), which is the place for the niggahīta and ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m, there are six. Including the chest (ura), which is the place for the letter 'h' when combined with the group-final nasals and y, r, l, v, ḷ, there are seven.

(a) The instrument (karaṇa) refers to the middle of the tongue and so on.

(b) The effort (payatana) refers to the specific exertion in recitation, such as saṃvuta (closing) and so on.

(c) The vowels 'a', 'ā' (avaṇṇa), the ka-group consonants, and the letter 'h' are gutturals (kaṇṭhaja).

(d) The vowels 'i', 'ī' (ivaṇṇa), the ca-group consonants, and the letter 'y' are palatals (tāluja).

(e) The vowels 'u', 'ū' (uvaṇṇa) and the pa-group consonants are labials (oṭṭhaja).

(f) The ṭa-group consonants, the letter 'r', and the letter 'ḷ' are cerebrals (muddhaja).

(g) The ta-group consonants, the letter 'l', and the letter 's' are dentals (dantaja).

(h) The letter 'e' is gutturo-palatal (kaṇṭhatāluja).

(i) The letter 'o' is gutturo-labial (kaṇṭhoṭṭhaja).

(j) The letter 'v' is dento-labial (dantoṭṭhaja).

(k) The niggahīta is nasal (nāsikaṭṭhānaja).

(l) The group-final consonants (ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m) are produced in both their respective places and the nose.

(m) The letter 'h' combined with y, r, l, v, ḷ and the five group-final nasals is pectoral (urasija). The letter 'h' alone (without a conjunct) is only guttural (kaṇṭhaja).
9:
According to the usage in the Sasana, the letter 'h' combined with ñ, ṇ, n, m (excluding ṅ), and likewise with y, l, v, ḷ, should be known as pectoral (orasa). The letter 'h' alone is only guttural (kaṇṭhaja).

This is true. Examples such as taṇhā, nhā, asumha, muyhate, vulyhate, as well as avhito and rūḷhī, exist in the Sasana.

(n) The middle of the tongue is the instrument (karaṇa) for palatal (tāluja) letters.
(o) The area near the tip of the tongue is the instrument for cerebral (muddhaja) letters.
(p) The tip of the tongue is the instrument for dental (dantaja) letters.
(q) For the remaining letters, their respective places of articulation (ṭhāna) are themselves the instruments (karaṇa).
(r) The closed recitation of the letter 'a' is called saṃvuta.
(s) The open recitation of the seven vowels starting with 'ā', and the letters 's' and 'h', is called vivaṭa.
(t) Vowels are called supports (nissaya).
(u) Consonants are called supported (nissita) letters.
(v) The order of letters is established by the sequence of the five places of articulation and the supports, etc.

In this regard, I shall state this summary verse:
The order of letters is spoken of according to the sequence of the five places—throat, palate, tip of the tongue, teeth, and lips—and by the distinctions of support (nissaya) and so on.

## Thus ends the Sikkhāvidhāna.

Now, the definition of auxiliary terms (Upakaraṇasaññāvidhāna) will follow.

24. Preceding, following, and so on, are the auxiliaries for the operation of sandhi (euphonic combination). They are: preceding (pubba), following (para), elision (lopa), augmentation (āgama), conjunction (saññoga), disjunction (viyoga), moving to the following (paranayana), inversion (vipariyaya), modification (vikāra), and reversal (viparīta).
10:
(a) The letter uttered first is called 'preceding' (*pubba*).
(b) The letter uttered later is called 'following' (*para*).
(c) The disappearance of an existing letter is called 'elision' (*lopa*).
(d) Even when the meaning is appropriate, the non-use of a word is also called 'elision' (*lopa*).
(e) The arrival of a new letter from elsewhere is called 'augment' (*āgama*).
(f) The union of two or three consonants into one without an intervening vowel is called 'conjunction' (*saṃyoga*).
(g) The separation [of a consonant] from a vowel is called 'disjunction' (*viyoga*).
(h) Making [a consonant] one with either a vowel or a consonant is called 'carrying over' (*paranayana*).
(i) The inversion of the order (above/below or front/back) of letters is called 'metathesis' (*vipariyaya*).
(j) The change into another letter and its simultaneous association is called 'modification' (*vikāra*).
(k) The change of consonants into vowels or other consonants, and the change of vowels into other vowels, is called 'transformation' (*viparitata*).

25. 'O' is called 'inverted' (*viparita*). Alternatively, because the word '*ava*' is inverted, the letter 'o' has the name *viparita*. For example, as in saying '*ovadati*' for '*avavadati*'.

26. The letter 'u' also has the name *viparita*. Because the letter 'o' formed with the word '*ava*' is inverted, the letter 'u' also has the name *viparita*. For example, as in saying '*uññātaṃ*' for '*avaññātaṃ*' and '*ūhato*' for '*avahato*'.

## Thus ends the Chapter on the Definition of Auxiliary Terms (Upakaraṇasaññāvidhāna).

Now follows the definition of words (*pada*) and so forth.

27. A sound that expresses meaning, whether it ends with an inflection (*vibhatti*) or not, is called a 'word' (*pada*).

A sentence, which is of four kinds, is obtained only through words. Those sentences are called *gajja*, *pajja*, *geyya*, and *kaccha*.
11:
Among those three (*gajja*, *pajja*, *geyya*), a sentence composed of a sequence of words in prose (*cuṇṇiya*) only is called *gajja*.
A sentence composed in the form of verses (*gāthā*) is called *pajja*.
A sentence composed by mixing verses and prose is called *geyya*, because it contains verses.
The language of treatises such as the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*), which is free from those three types like *gajja*, is called *kaccha* by the wise.

In those treatises categorized as *gajja* etc., ancient scholars understood *sandhi* (euphonic combination) to be of three kinds: vowel (*sara*), consonant (*byañjana*), and mixed (*vomissa*).
It is also understood as three kinds by way of vowel, consonant, and *vutta-sandhi*.
In another way, this *sandhi* is shown to be of four kinds.
Namely: vowel-sandhi (*sarasandhi*), *niggahīta-sandhi*, vowel-consonant-sandhi (*sarabyañjanasandhi*), and common-sandhi (*sādhāraṇasandhi*).

Ancient teachers presented these *sandhis* without destroying the ten perfections of consonants like *sithila* (lax) mentioned in the Vinaya Commentary, avoiding faults such as [incorrect] letters, and demonstrating the perfection of sound, the perfection of meaning, and the delightful perfections of meter (*chanda*) and ornament (*alaṅkāra*); for the sake of preserving the meter in verses and for ease of recitation in prose.

In the Dispensation of the Buddha, these three kinds of *sandhi* serve to distinguish between what precedes and what follows, etc. Therefore, I have explained the distinction of preceding and following, etc., in this treatise.
Furthermore, in this context, *sandhi* is also desired to be of two kinds in brief: word-sandhi (*padasandhi*) and letter-sandhi (*vaṇṇasandhi*).
12:
Among those two, examples like "*tatrāyaṃ*" should be shown as *padasandhi*. Examples like "*သာဟု ခတျာ*" (*sāhu khatyā*) should be shown as *vaṇṇasandhi*.

In *padasandhi*, the splitting of preceding and following words is understood. In *vaṇṇasandhi*, only the sequence of preceding and following [letters] is obtained.

The wise should first perform the *sandhi* operation of the preceding and following. The operation to be done on the following vowel should be performed later, and then they should be joined.

28. One should separate the consonant from the vowel. That consonant should be placed before that vowel. In that *sandhi*, just as a task to be done with a sword cannot be accomplished if the sword is covered by its sheath, the *sandhi* operation cannot be accomplished if the vowel is covered by a consonant. Therefore, in the domain of *padasandhi* such as "*tatrāyaṃ*", one should split the words as "*tatra ayaṃ*"; and in the domain of *vaṇṇasandhi* such as "*sāhu ekasataṃ khatyā*", one should establish the word forms as "*sādhu ekasataṃ khattiyā*" and then separate the consonant from the vowel. That consonant should be placed before that vowel. (Example: *tatrāyaṃ*).

29. A consonant without a vowel should be carried over to the following letter. The consonant to be carried over, which is without a vowel, should be moved to the following letter. This is the simultaneous occurrence of both preceding and following. [Examples:] "*tatrābhirati miccheyya*" (for elision), "*etadavoca*" (for substitution), "*nayime bhikkhū*" (for augment). What is meant by "to be carried over" (*netabbaṃ*)? In examples like "*akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ*" and "*buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi*", although there is a following vowel, it is not "carried over" because it is separated by the formation of the letter.

## Thus ends the Chapter on the Definition of Terms and Conventions (Saññāparibhāsāvidhāna) in the Section on Sandhi (Sandhikappa) of the Saddanīti.

Now follows the rules for vowel-sandhi (sarasandhividhāna).

Here, *sandhi* is the joining of words and letters without an interval. It is a word formed by union (*saṃhitapada*). The joining of vowels, or joining at the following vowel, is called vowel-sandhi (*sarasandhi*). In this context, the *sandhi* accomplished by means of substitution (*ādesa*) and elision (*lopa*) of vowels is called *sarasandhi*.

30. Preceding vowels undergo elision because of a following vowel. Only vowels undergo elision because of a following vowel. This is the *vutti* (commentary). One, two, or three vowels undergo elision because of a following vowel. This is another *vutti* that clarifies the meaning. (Examples: *rājabhaṭo*, *yassāsavā*, *yassindriyāni*, *yassīdisā*, *ajjuposatho*, *ekenūnāni*, *yassete*, *mamodanaṃ*). These examples are cases where the letter 'a' is elided when followed by vowels starting with 'a'. (Other examples: *kāmattha*, *māvuso*, *cāturitthiyo*, *sabbītiyo*, *tadā uṭṭhahi*, *nāganāsurū*).

30. Preceding vowels undergo elision (disappearance) when followed by a vowel. Only the preceding vowels undergo elision because of the following vowel. This is the *vutti* (explanation). One, two, or even three preceding vowels undergo elision because of the following vowel; this is the *anuvutti* (supplementary explanation) which clarifies the meaning.

This is the illustration of eliding the vowel 'a' (*akāra*) when followed by vowels such as 'a', etc.

"Nānādisaṃ yanti" (They go to various directions). "Vissāsaṃ eyya paṇḍito" (A wise man should not abandon effort). "Sace uppādo heyya" (If an arising should occur). This is the method where two preceding vowels are elided simultaneously because of a single following vowel.

"Na maṃ puna upeyyāsi" (Do not let me approach again). "Ajjheyyāsi" (Should recite). This is the method where three preceding vowels are elided simultaneously because of a single following vowel. Together with these two methods of double and triple elision, sixty-six methods of preceding vowel elision should be known. There is no other method of preceding vowel elision found in the Pali Canon apart from these sixty-six. In those examples, "Nasi rājabhaṭo" is analyzed as "Na asi rājabhaṭo". In the word "yanti", the letter structure is "yā a anti". Here, three vowels are obtained in sequence. In the word "upeyyāsi", the letter structure is "upa i a eyyāsi". Here, four vowels are obtained in sequence. In that regard, I shall speak this verse—
15:
“Vowels are elided when followed by vowels; one, two, or even three (vowels may be elided). This is stated with reference to Sandhi (euphonic combination) involving roots. Therefore, the wise should understand this, which destroys the doubts of listeners. ‘Nasi rājabhaṭo yanti’ etc., are examples of ‘eyya’ and ‘heyya’. ‘Venti’, ‘lanti’, ‘disā bhanti’, ‘santi’, and ‘panti’ should also be understood. ‘Ajjheyyāsi’, ‘upeyyāsi’, etc., are also examples.”

31. When there is a dissimilar vowel, the following vowel is elided in some places. (Examples are:) Dīpo, kaṭiṭṭhi, cakkhundriyaṃ, yassadāni (of whom now), saññāti (as perception), chāyāva (like a shadow), aphalā hoti'kubbato (for one who does not act according to good speech, the benefit is in vain). Other examples should also be combined accordingly. Among those examples, ‘dīpo’ should be analyzed as ‘di āpo’; it is called ‘dīpo’ (island) because the water flows in two directions. Why is ‘vā’ (optionally/in some places) said? To indicate that in cases like ‘pañcindriyāni’ (the five faculties), the following vowel is not elided even though there is a dissimilar vowel.

32. The similar vowel following the vowel of the prefix ‘pa’ is elided in some places. (Example:) In ‘udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avinduṃ’ (they found much water in that sandy courtyard), it should be analyzed as ‘pa āpaṃ’. In ‘nālaṃ kabaḷaṃ padātave’ (unable to take a mouthful of grass), it should be analyzed as ‘pa adātave’. Why is ‘vā’ said? To indicate that it is not elided in cases like ‘pādātave’.

33. The vowel ‘i’ of the word ‘iti’ following the vowel ‘i’ is elided in some places. (Example:) In ‘iti ca danti ca’, it should be analyzed as ‘i iti ca’. Why is ‘kvaci’ (in some places) said? To indicate that it is not elided in cases like ‘i iti saddo’.

34. After the preceding vowel is elided, the following vowel—whether similar or dissimilar—becomes a dissimilar vowel (e, o) in some places. By virtue of proximity of articulation, only the i-group and u-group become ekāra and okāra respectively. (Examples:) ‘Bandhusseva samāgamo’, ‘ate'va me acchariyaṃ’ (it is extremely wonderful to me), ‘jinerita’ (the method taught by the Buddha), ‘māluteritaṃ’ (fallen due to being struck by the wind), ‘nopeti’ (does not reach), ‘udakomiva’ (like a water wave), etc. Why is ‘kvaci’ said? To indicate that it does not become a dissimilar vowel in cases like ‘tathūpamaṃ’ and ‘vāmūru’ (my wife with beautiful thighs).
16:
The method taught by the Buddha is like (leaves) falling due to the wind. An Arahant who has reached the end of the Vedas (the goal of knowledge) no longer reaches designations (such as Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, etc.). It is like a wave that has arisen. Why is ‘kvaci’ said? He taught the noble Dhamma with such a simile. You have indeed abandoned my wife, who has thighs as beautiful as a golden plantain trunk.

35. After the following vowel is elided, the preceding vowel becomes a dissimilar vowel (asavaṇṇa) in some places. (Examples:) Munelayo, rathesabho, sotthī. They should be analyzed as muni ālayo, rathī usabho, and su-itthi. One is called ‘rathino’ because he has a chariot. One is called ‘usabho’ because he is like a bull among the warriors stationed in chariots. It means a king who is like a bull among chariot-warriors. Why is ‘kvaci’ said? To indicate that it does not become a dissimilar vowel in cases like ‘ucchuva’.

36. After the following vowel is elided, the preceding vowel becomes long (dīgha) in some places. By virtue of proximity of articulation, short vowels (rassa) become similar long vowels (savaṇṇa dīgha). (Examples:) Buddhānussati, saddhīdha, vūpasamo. Why is ‘kvaci’ said? To indicate that it does not become long in cases like ‘desesi’.

37. Except for the letter ‘a’ and the word ‘ikkha’, a vowel preceding a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga) does not become a dissimilar vowel or long. After the preceding vowel is elided, the following vowel that precedes a conjunct consonant does not become a dissimilar vowel or long, except for the letter ‘a’ and the word ‘ikkha’. (Examples:) Lokuttaraṃ, yassindriyāni, saddhindriyaṃ. Why is it said “except for the letter ‘a’ and the word ‘ikkha’”? To allow it to become a dissimilar vowel or long in cases like ‘saññāvāssa vimuyhati’ (the perception of one who hoards wealth becomes confused) and ‘upekkhati’ (he looks on closely).

38. There is no elision of the vowel ‘ā’ preceding the word ‘iva’, and because there is no such elision, the following vowel ‘i’ is not changed to the dissimilar vowel ‘e’. (Examples:) Latāva, patināva.
17:
39. *Avaṇṇassa citiṃhā*. There shall be no elision of the a-group (a, ā) preceding the word ‘iti’, nor shall the following vowel ‘i’ be changed to the dissimilar vowel ‘e’. Examples are: ‘sumedho sujāto cāti’ for ‘sumedho sujāto ca’, ‘saññāti’ for ‘saññā’, and ‘rājāti’ for ‘rājā’.

40. *Hoti kesañci matena*. According to the opinions of some teachers who speak by adopting methods from Sanskrit texts, there are procedures that we have prohibited. Examples are: ‘lateva vātābhihatā’ (like a vine struck by the wind), ‘patinevakāminī’ (like a woman not separated from her husband), ‘ceti’ for ‘cattāri lokuttarāni ca’, ‘guṇeneti’ for ‘kenaci guṇena’, and ‘pabbajjeti’ for ‘pabbajje’. However, such methods do not exist in the Pali Canon.

41. *Na mā dā vā smā tra ṇhātvādīnaṃ saralope ayyaññagghassussānamakāro dīghaṃ*. After eliding the preceding vowel which is a part of words such as na, mā, dā, vā, smā, tra, ṇhā, tvā, etc., the vowel ‘a’ which is a part of the words ayya, añña, aggha, assu, and assa becomes long, even if it precedes a conjunct consonant.

Examples are: ‘nāyyo so bhikkhu maṃ nippāṭesi’ (that monk is not an honorable one; he did not take me along). ‘nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya’ (one should not desire the suffering of one another). ‘kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ’ (they are not worth a sixteenth part). ‘nāssudha koci bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamati’ (no one here approaches the Blessed One). ‘nāssa corā pasahanti’ (thieves cannot oppress him). ‘māyyo evarūpamakāsi’ (venerable sir, do not do such a thing). ‘māssu kujjhi bhūmipati’ (may the king certainly not be angry). ‘tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjanti’ (at that time, they yoked the black ox). ‘kadāssu maṃ assarathā’ (when will you remember me?). ‘taṃ kudāssu bhavissati’ (when will that matter come to be?). ‘satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyya’ (or he should seek a weapon-bringer). ‘tasmāssa hoti saṃvaṇṇanā’ (therefore, there is the commentary of that text). ‘tatrāssa karaṇīyaṃ natthi’ (therein, there is no duty for that monk). ‘katvātra’ (having done in this place). ‘taṇhāssa vippahīnā’ (craving has been abandoned by him).

42. *Sassa kvacantatthānaṃ*. After eliding the vowel of the word ‘sa’, the vowel ‘a’ of some words like ‘anta’ and ‘attha’ becomes long.
18:
Sāntevāsiko (one who lives with internal defilements), Sātthaṃ (endowed with meaning), Sātthikā dhammadēsanā (beneficial Dhamma teaching). Why is the word "kvaci" (in some cases) used? It is to prevent lengthening (dīgha) in instances such as: Vanantaṃ (to the forest), Satthō bhaṇḍaṃ ādāyagatō (the merchant went taking his goods), etc.

## 43. Tēmēpabbatyādīnamēssayō vinā yēkārēna.
Excluding the word "yē", the final "ē" vowel of words such as tē, mē, and pabbatē shall be changed to the letter "ya" in some cases when followed by a vowel. For example: "Tyāhaṃ ēvaṃ vadēyyaṃ" (I would say thus to them). "Adhigatō khō myāyaṃ dhammō" (I have indeed attained this Dhamma). "Pabbatyāhaṃ gandhamādanē" (I live on Mount Gandhamādana). "Kyāhaṃ" (Who am I?). "Kyassa byappathayō assu" (What kind of words would that monk have?).

Why is the word "kvaci" used? It is to prevent the substitution of "ya" in instances such as: "Tēnāgatā" (they did not come), "Puttā matthi" (sons exist for me), etc. In this context, one might ask: "Why say 'excluding the word yē' (vinā yēkārēna)? Are there not many other places to be excluded?" True, however, great teachers such as Buddhapiya, the author of Rūpasiddhi, desire to change the "ē" component of the word "yē" into "ya" to use it as "yyassa". This is stated to refute that view. In the Pali texts, since there is no special pronunciation with a geminate sound as in the word "uyyāna", the word "yyassa" with a double "y" cluster does not appear; only the word without the cluster appears. Indeed, in the Chakkanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the following text is seen:

"That fool who performs evil deeds, knowing his own misconduct, suffers like a poor man who, having taken a loan, is distressed while consuming it. Thereafter, sufferings born of remorse and mental distress follow him, whether in the village or in the forest, wherever the remorse arises."

In this verse, only the word without the cluster appears. In the Commentary (Atthakathā) as well, "yassa vippaṭisārajā" is explained as "yē assa vippaṭisāratō jātā". In this lemma (ulliṅgapada) also, only the word without the cluster appears. Similarly, in various Suttas: "yassa tē hōnti anatthakāmā", and "yassu maññāmi samaṇē", and "aññaṃ itō..."
19:
"...yābhivadanti dhammaṃ", only the word "ya" without the cluster appears. In that context, "yassu" should be analyzed as "yē assu", and "yābhivadantī" as "yē abhivadantī". To show this distinction, we have said "excluding the word yē".

44. Ka kha ta tha da na ya sa hānaṃ vōdudantānaṃ.
The final "ō" and "u" vowels of words ending in the letters ka, kha, ta, tha, da, na, ya, sa, and ha are changed to the letter "va" (vakārādēsa) in some cases when followed by a vowel.
Example: Yāvatakvassa (yāvatakō assa) - The body of that Great Man is of such an extent. Agamā nu khvidha (khō idha) - Has the young Māṇava always come here to this Venerable Gotama? Cakāpāthamāgacchati (cakkhupātaṃ āgacchati) - It comes into the range of the eye. Sitaṃ pātvākāsi (pātu akāsi) - He manifested a smile. Yatvādhi karaṇaṃ (yatō adhikaraṇaṃ) - Because of which non-restraint of the eye-faculty. Vatthēttha vihitaṃ niccaṃ. Dvākārē (du ākārē) - Having bad causes, forms, or manners. Anvāgantvāna dūseyya (anu āgantvāna) - Having come to the house, he would destroy it. Yvāyaṃ (yō ayaṃ) - Which person. Svāssa hōti (sō assa) - That effort of trading becomes according to his wish. Svāgataṃ tē - Welcome to you. Bavhābādhō (bahu ābādhō) - Having many illnesses. Lavhakkharam (lahu akkharaṃ) - A light syllable.

Why is the word "kvaci" used? To prevent the substitution of "va" in instances such as "kō atthō", "atha khō ēsa", etc. Why is the word "anta" (final) used? To prevent the substitution of "va" in instances such as "savanīyaṃ", where the "u" vowel is not at the end of the word but is only a part of the syllable. By specifically listing the letters ka, kha, etc., it is clear that the "ō" and "u" vowels of the group consonants (vagga) ga, gha, ca, cha, etc., and the non-group consonants (avagga) la, va, ḷa, do not change to "va". Therefore, in instances such as "mahāyāgō āsi" and "yāgu atthi", the "ō" and "u" vowels do not change to "va".

45. Na parēpi sarē hētudhātādīnumussapāvacanē ca.
In the Pali Canon (Pāvacana) and in the ancient Commentaries, the "u" vowel of words such as hētu and dhātu shall not be changed to "va" even when followed by a vowel.
Example: Hētutthō (meaning of cause), Dhātutthō (meaning of element), Hētindriyāni, Khandhadhātāyatanāni, Hētuatthō, Kattuatthō, Kattutthō, and so forth. However, according to the view of some teachers, forms like "hētvatthō", "dhātvatthō", "pañcadhātvādiniyamā", and "katvatthō" may exist. "Api su khalvāsēsiṃ" (khalu ahaṃ āsēsiṃ) - Indeed, I have yearned. "Assō..."
20:
"...khalvābhidhāvati", Citragvādayō (citragu ādayō), Bhvāpānalānilam (bhū āpa anala anilaṃ), Madhvāsavō (madhu āsavō), and such words occur. However, when it comes to the Dispensation (the Pariyatti Sāsana), only the form "madhāsavō" occurs.

46. Atipatītīnaṃ ti caṃ.
The "ti" syllable of the words ati, pati, and iti changes to "ca" in some cases when followed by a vowel. (Example:) Accantaṃ (ati antaṃ), Paccakkhāṃ (pati akkhaṃ), Iccētaṃ (iti ētaṃ). Why is the word "kvaci" used? To prevent the substitution of "ca" in instances such as atiodātaṃ, patiuttarati, and itissa muhuttampi.

47. Itissa tisaddabyañjanōpi.
The consonant of the word "iti" which is the "ti" sound (the tya cluster) also changes to "ca" in some cases when followed by a vowel. In this rule, "tisaddabyañjana" refers to the "tya" consonant cluster. (Example:) Iccatra (iti atra). Why is the word "kvaci" used? To prevent the substitution of "ca" in instances such as "sutā ca paṇḍitā tyamha".

48. Dvisandhītisaṅkhēpē niccamikāralōpō na yattha caṃ.
In an instance where the substitution of "ca" for "tya" does not occur, if it is understood as a place where double or triple combinations are possible, the elision of the "i" vowel is mandatory. When the consonant of the word "iti", which is the "ti" sound (the tya cluster), does not reach the substitution of "ca" in a context of double or triple combinations, the elision of the "i" vowel in that usage is always mandatory; the "i" vowel never remains in its own form. This is the nature of the Buddha's word known as the Māgadha language. Thus, the non-conjunction of the "tya" cluster together with the "i" vowel of the word "iti" exists. Therefore, the word "ityatra" does not exist in the Buddha's words or the Commentaries. This rule should be understood as a restrictive rule (niyama sutta). Examples of this restrictive rule are: "sutā ca paṇḍitā tyamha", "sutā ca paṇḍitā tyattha", "ñātō sēnāpati tyāhaṃ", "yaṃ paṇḍitō tyēke vadanti lōke", "manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti tyādinā", which are the mentioned eight factors. Among those examples, in the usage "paṇḍitā tyamha", when the procedure is performed by breaking the words as "paṇḍitā iti amha", it becomes the context of sandhi called double or triple combination.
21: 49. When the 'e' of the word 'eva' follows, the 'i' of the word 'iti' and the 'i' of other words are changed to 'va' in some instances. For example: "itveva coro asimāvudhañca" (Thus the thief discards the sword and the weapon), "vilapatveva so dijo" (That bird is indeed lamenting), "isigilitveva" (Only as Isigili), "samantapāsādikātveva" (Only as Samantapāsādikā). Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? To prevent the change to 'va' in places such as "icceva" (thus indeed).  50. The 'dha' of the word 'idha' following the word 'eka' must always be changed to 'da' when a vowel follows. For example: "ekamidāhaṃ bhikkhave samayaṃ" (Monks, I, at one time). Why is "ekasmā" (from the word 'eka') said? To prevent the change to 'da' in places such as "evamidhekacco", "idhāhaṃ bhikkhave bhuttāvī assaṃ". Here, one might ask: "In the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, it is stated that in the word 'ekamidāhaṃ', 'idā' is merely a particle and means 'ekaṃ ahaṃ'. If so, why is it said in this rule that 'dha' is changed to 'da' by the power of the word 'idha'?" To answer that question: In this rule, for the sake of generating expertise in word derivation for the wise, it is said that 'dha' is changed to 'da' by the power of the word 'idha', based on the process of word formation. In the commentary, however, when 'ekamidāhaṃ' was spoken, because the sound of the word 'ida' is heard, without considering the effort of word derivation, it is said that 'idā is merely a particle' based on the mere sound according to the Ariyan usage (Māgadha language).  51. The preceding 'i-vaṇṇa' (i, ī) becomes 'ya' in some instances when a vowel follows. For example: "byākāsi", "byākato", "byañjanaṃ", "byākaraṇaṃ", "paṭisanthāravutyassa", "dāsyāhaṃ para-pesikā ahuṃ" (I was a slave-woman who was a servant to others). Among these examples, the word "byākāsi" should be analyzed as "vi ā akāsi". "Vi" and "ā" are prefixes (upasaggas), and "akāsi" is a verb (ākhyāta). This word is capable of expressing the meaning "he spoke" by the power of the prefixes "vi" and "ā". In the word "byākato" also, the word "kato" is...
22: ...the word "kato" is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning. Here also, among the three vowels standing in sequence, it should be understood that the following 'ā' is elided because of the non-homogeneous 'i'. Why is "navā" (optionally) said? Because of examples such as "gacchāmahaṃ", "muttacāgī anuddhato", "tassa puṭṭho viyākāsi", "akkharānaṃ viyañjanaṃ".  52. When a vowel follows, the 'e' of the word 'eva' becomes 'ri', and the preceding vowel becomes short in some instances. For example: "yathariva vasudhātalañca sabbaṃ" (Just as the whole surface of the earth is), "tathariva guṇavā supūjanīyo" (In that same way, one who possesses virtue is worthy of great worship). Why is "navā" said? To indicate that this change and shortening do not occur in "yathā eva" and "tathā eva".  53. When a vowel follows, the 'ga' augment (āgama) is added to the end of the particle "putha" in some instances. For example: "puthageva" (separately indeed), "puthagayaṃ" (this person is separate). Why is "kvaci" said? To indicate that the 'ga' augment does not occur in the usage "putha eva".  54. When a vowel follows, the 'ga' augment is also added to the end of the word "pā" in some instances, and the final vowel of that "pā" becomes short. For example: "pageva itarā pajā" (If even a king does not deviate from the Dhamma, what need is there to speak of other beings not practicing according to the Dhamma?). Why is "kvaci" said? Because it does not occur in "pā eva".  55. When a vowel follows, 'o' is changed to 'u'. For example: "manunñaṃ" (that which greatly pleases the mind).  56. When a vowel follows, the augments 'ya', 'va', 'ma', 'da', 'na', 'ta', 'ra', 'la', 'ha' occur in some instances. For example: "nayimassa vijjāmayamatthi kiñci" (There is nothing to be done by science for this hermit), "yathayidaṃ cittaṃ" (Just as this mind is), "tivaṅgikaṃ" (having three factors), "lahumessati" (it will arrive soon), "samaṇacalalo" (an Arahant who is steady and unmoving), "dubhato vanavikāse" (the forest groves on both sides), "sammadeva" (only rightly), "attadatthaṃ" (one's own benefit), "ajjadagge pāṇupetaṃ" (from this day forth as long as life lasts), "ciraṃ nāyati" (he comes after a long time).
23:
Does not come from here. "Monks, because of which," "Monks, therefore in this world." "One should associate only with the virtuous." "Like a mustard seed on the point of a needle (not sticking)." "The six higher powers (Abhiññā)." "The six sense bases (Āyatana)." "Being well upright." "Well-arisen." "It is thus," "It is not thus." Why say "vā" (optionally)? "This accomplishment of merit has such great power."

57. Abhissabbho. When a vowel follows, the final vowel of the word 'Abhi' is changed to 'abbha'. (Example:) It has been greatly spoken; he greatly ascends.

58. Adhissajjho. When a vowel follows, the final vowel of the word 'Adhi' is changed to 'ajjha'. (Example:) They have greatly come; he greatly carries.

59. Te na vā ivaṇṇe. When the vowels 'i' or 'ī' follow, the aforementioned changes of 'Abhi' and 'Adhi' to 'abbha' and 'ajjha' do not occur in some places. (Example:) It has been greatly desired; it has been greatly spoken. Why say "vā"? (Because it does occur in some places, e.g.:) It has been greatly spoken; he is greatly released from debt.

60. Ti ca caṃ. The letter 'ti' of the words 'ati', 'pati', and 'iti' does not change to 'ca' in some places when the vowels 'i' or 'ī' follow. (Example:) A great group of seers; it has been greatly spoken; it has greatly become (or) the past; it has become manifest; thus it is; this much.

61. Dvinnamākārikārānamettaṃ tyādīsu. When the 'ti' and other suffixes follow, 'ā' and 'i' are replaced by 'e'. (Example:) "Thus he comes forward," "This charioteer Sunanda comes." Why say "ākārikārānaṃ"? (Because it does not happen if it is not 'ā' and 'i', e.g.:) "Depending on the cause, the result arises from this ignorance, etc." Why say "tyādīsu"? (Because it does not happen if 'ti' etc. do not follow, e.g.:) "When the sun sets behind the sunset mountain."

## Thus ends the section on Vowel Sandhi in the Saddanīti.

62. Sarā pakatī byañjane. When a consonant follows, vowels remain in their original form (natural state). (Example:) "Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind." "Heedlessness is the path to death." "The Arahant who has crossed the four floods has reached the other shore (Nibbāna)."
24:
63. Kvici sare. When a vowel follows, some vowels remain in their original form. (Example:) "Who can disentangle this tangle (of craving)?" Why say "kvici"? (Examples where they do not remain original:) "Having come to this life," "This mango tree was formerly (endowed with color, scent, and taste)."

## The section on the natural state of vowels is finished.

Now follows the section on Consonant Sandhi --
The combination of consonants, or combination in consonants, is called Consonant Sandhi (Byañjana-sandhi). Alternatively, sandhi achieved through the substitution, elision, etc., of consonants is called Consonant Sandhi.

64. Sarā byañjane dīghaṃ. When a consonant follows, some vowels become long (dīgha). (Example:) "To one who clearly sees the Dhamma." "Thus should a sage wander in the village." "Patience is the highest austerity, endurance." "Those taints are abandoned for him." "It is for him." Why say "kvici"? (Examples where they do not become long:) "Tyajja", "Tyassa", "Svassa".

65. Rassaṃ. When a consonant follows, some vowels become short (rassa). (Example:) "He is called a 'Bhovādi'." "He is as he is by virtue." "Whatever sacrifice or offering is made in the world." Why say "kvici"? (Example where it does not become short:) "Sammāsamādhi".

66. Lopaṃ tatrākāroca. When a consonant follows, some vowels are elided (lopa), and in the place of the elided vowel, the letter 'a' (akāra) is substituted. (Example:) "He is virtuous." "This is the Dhamma." If the examples "Sa evattho", "Esa attho", "Esa ābhogo", "Esa idāni" were mentioned in this rule, they would belong to the domain of Vowel Sandhi. Therefore, those examples are not shown here. The reason is that in this context, only sandhi caused by a consonant is intended to be shown.
25: The name "Byañjana-sandhi" is intended because the meaning of junction of consonants or junction among consonants is possible. Why is "kvaci" said? In "so muni" and "eso dhammo" (to prevent vowel elision and 'a' substitution). 67. Parassa dvittaṃ ṭhāne. When appropriate, a consonant following a vowel should be doubled (dvitta). A consonant following a vowel becomes doubled when there is a suitable occasion. Examples: "Idhappamādo", "pabbajjā". Why is "ṭhāne" (in the appropriate place) said? In "idha modati" (to prevent doubling). 68. Vagge ghosāghosānaṃ savagge tatiyapaṭhamā. Within the five groups (vaggas), voiced (ghosa) and unvoiced (aghosa) consonants are doubled as the third and first letters of their respective groups. Within a group, preceding voiced and unvoiced consonants following a vowel become doubled as the third and first letters of their respective groups respectively when appropriate. Examples: "Paggharati", "eseve cajjhānapphalo", "yatraṭṭhitaṃ nappasaheyya maccu", "viddhaṃseti", "vibbhamati". Why is "ṭhāne" said? In "daḷhaṃ gaṇhāti thāmasā" (to prevent doubling). From this rule on doubling onwards, in Consonant Sandhi, word-splitting (padaccheda) is not applicable in the context of letter-sandhi (vaṇṇa-sandhi); because there is no junction of two words, only the sequence of letters is obtained. 69. Saralopo ya ma na rādīsu vā. When letters like ya, ma, na, ra, etc., follow, the preceding vowel is optionally elided if appropriate. When letters like ya, ma, na, ra, etc., follow, the vowel of the letters standing immediately before is optionally elided when appropriate. Examples: "Ārāmarukkhacetyāni", "atthetthekasataṃ khatyā", "opupphāni ca padmāni ca", "nisnehamabhikaṅkhāmi", "nānāratne ca māṇiye", "kriyacittāni vīsati", "klesavatthuvasā pana". Why is "vā" (optionally) said? In "khattiyānaṃ ekasataṃ" and "padumāni pupphanti" (to prevent vowel elision). Why is "ṭhāne" said? In "Suppiyo paribbājako" (to prevent vowel elision). 70. Yathāpāvacanaṃ vidhi. The procedure occurs according to the Pali scriptures (Pāvacana). In this treatise, procedures like substitution (ādesa) and so forth occur only in accordance with the Pali scriptures.
26: 71. Animittopi vā dīghādi. Procedures like lengthening (dīgha) and so forth occur in some places even without a cause (nimitta). (Example:) In the place "nadīstatehiva sahā", the lengthening in "sahā" is merely a phonetic variation. It is the same in the place "nacāpi apunappunaṃ". Why is "vā" said? Because lengthening does not occur in "dukkhajāti punappunaṃ". Here, one might ask: "By looking at the Pali sequence 'nadīstatehi va sahā, gaṅgāpañcahi sāgaraṃ', the 'a' of the word 'saha' reaches lengthening because of the consonant in the second foot; so why is it called lengthening without cause?" In the Pali scriptures, sandhi or compound (samāsa) procedures are not performed between the first foot and the second foot, or between the third foot and the fourth foot. (Except for the sandhi procedure of the simplification of a conjunct consonant caused by eliding a vowel after a niggahīta.) Therefore, it is said here that lengthening occurs without cause. 72. Ho dhassa vaṇṇasandhimhi. In letter-sandhi (vaṇṇa-sandhi), 'h' (hakāra) is substituted for 'dh' (dhakāra) according to the Pali scriptures. (Example:) "Sāhu dassanamariyānaṃ", "ruhiramassave". Why is "yathāpāvacanaṃ" (according to the Pali scriptures) said? Because if 'dh' were substituted with 'h' in the word "dadhi", it would not be in accordance with the Pali scriptures. Why is "vā" said? Because the 'h' substitution does not occur in places like "sādhāvuso" and "maṃsampi rudhirampi ca". From this rule onwards, the term "yathāpāvacanaṃ" applies to all rules. In some rules, however, the terms "vā" or "kvaci" apply as appropriate. 73. To dassa. 't' (takāra) is substituted for 'd' (dakāra). (Example:) Tathāgato, sugato, kusīto. 74. Ṭo tassa. 'ṭ' (ṭakāra) is substituted for 't' (takāra). (Example:) Dukkaṭaṃ, pahaṭo. 75. Dho tassa gabbhokkamanāsannasatte. 'dh' (dhakāra) is substituted for 't' (takāra) when referring to a being about to enter the womb. (Example:) "Gandhabbo ca paccupaṭṭhito hoti" (A being about to enter the womb is also present). Why is "satte" (regarding a being) said? Because in places like "maggo gantabbo hoti" (the path should be traveled), where a being is not intended, 't' is not substituted with 'dh'.
27:
...A being who is near death, a being who has reached a destination, or a being who is destined to reach a destination, stands before [the next life]. Why is it called "satta"? Because the traveler will go. This is stated to show that the substitution of 'dh' for 't' does not occur in such words.

## 76. Tr-o tt-assa.
The letter 'tr' occurs in the place of the double 't' (tt). Atrajo (a son born of oneself), khettajo (a son born in the womb), vatrabhū (Sakka, who excels others through conduct), gotrabhū (one who experiences the lineage, or the mind/knowledge). However, in words such as "attajaṃ attasambhavaṃ putto māsakhettaṃ", the substitution of 'tr' does not occur due to the authority of the Pāḷi text.

## 77. K-o g-assa.
The letter 'k' occurs in the place of the letter 'g'. Hatthūpakaṃ (hand ornament), sīsūpakaṃ (head ornament), kulūpako (a monk who frequents a family), khīrūpako (a suckling calf). In some places, words such as hatthūpagaṃ also exist.

## 78. L-o r-assa.
The letter 'l' occurs in the place of the letter 'r'. Mahāsālo (one with great wealth), palipanno (sunk all around).

## 79. J-o y-assa.
The letter 'j' occurs in the place of the letter 'y'. Gavajo (a gayal), or it also exists as gavayo.

## 80. B-o v-assa.
The letter 'b' occurs in the place of the letter 'v'. Sīlabbataṃ (the practices of cows or dogs), nibbānaṃ (Nirvana).

## 81. K-o y-assa.
The letter 'k' occurs in the place of the letter 'y'. Sake pure (in one's own city).

## 82. Y-o j-assa.
The letter 'y' occurs in the place of the letter 'j'. Niyaṃputtaṃ (one's own son), or it also exists as nijaṃputtaṃ.

## 83. K-o t-assa.
The letter 'k' occurs in the place of the letter 't'. Niyako, or it also exists as niyato. Sumitto nāma nāmako, or it also exists as sumitto nāma nāmato (a person named Sumitta).

## 84. C-o t-assa.
The letter 'c' occurs in the place of the letter 't'. Bhacco (one who is supported/nourished), or it also exists as bhatto.

## 85. Ph-o p-assa.
The letter 'ph' occurs in the place of the letter 'p'. Nipphatti (completion), anantaṃ sabbatopaphaṃ (Nirvana, which is a landing place from all sides).

## 86. Dr-o d-assa.
The letter 'dr' occurs in the place of the letter 'd'. Indriyaṃ (sense faculty), dudradāmā (a coin named dudradāma), bhadro or bhaddo (goodness).

## 87. Gh-o kh-assa.
The letter 'gh' occurs in the place of the letter 'kh'. Nighaṇḍu (a dictionary/thesaurus).

## 88. D-o j-assa.
The letter 'd' occurs in the place of the letter 'j'. Pasenadī (a king who conquers the army).

## 89. Paññattipaññāsānaṃ ñ-assa ṇṇ-o.
The letter 'ṇṇ' occurs in the place of the letter 'ñ' in the words paññatti and paññāsa. Paṇṇatti or paññatti (designation). Paṇṇāsaṃ or paññāsaṃ (fifty).
28:
90. The word 'pañca' in the word 'pañcavīsati' should be substituted with 'paṇṇa'. There are forms such as paṇṇavīsati or pañcavīsati.

91. The letter 'n' should be substituted with 'ṇ'. Examples are paṇidhānaṃ, paṇidhi, and paṇipāto.

92. The letter 'ṇ' should also be substituted with 'n'. There are forms such as taluno or taruṇo. There are illustrations such as "he laments pitifully (kalunaṃ paridevayi)" and "they spoke pitiful words (karuṇaṃ giramudīrayuṃ)".

93. The letter 'd' should be substituted with 'dh'. There is the form kammāsadhammaṃ.

94. The letter 'y' should be substituted with 'v'. There are forms such as āvudhaṃ or āyudhaṃ.

95. The letter 'y' of the word 'āyu' used in a designation should be substituted with 'v'. There is the form dīghāvukumāro. Why say "in a designation"? To prevent the substitution of 'v' in places such as "May this young boy be long-lived (dīghāyuko hotu ayaṃkumāro)".

96. The letter 'l' should be substituted with 'ḷ'. Examples are sīhaḷo and garuḷo.

97. The letter 'k' should be substituted with 'd'. There is the form sadatthapasuto.

98. The letter 'm' should be substituted with 'p'. There are illustrations such as "a man who has been away for a long time (cirappavāsiṃ purisaṃ)" and "like a mahout holding a hook to a rutting elephant (hatthippabhinnaṃ viya aṅkusaggaho)".

99. The letter 'p' of the word 'vanappati' should be substituted with 'm'. There are forms such as vanampati or vanappati.
(a) Alternatively, when the word 'pati' follows, the letter 'a' of the word 'vana' should be substituted with 'aṃ'. There is the form vanampati.

100. The word 'vi' and the letter 'v' should be substituted with 'p'. There are forms such as pacesesati or vicesesati, and paccapekkhanā or paccavekkhanā.

101. The letter 'p' should be substituted with 'v'. There is the form kāvaṇyaṃ.

102. There is also the transformation of mentioned and unmentioned consonants into other consonants. By this rule, hundreds of other illustrations such as jalābu and sannisīva should be established. Among those illustrations, jalābu means...
29:
Having established the word 'jarāyu', when the letter 'r' is changed to 'l' and the letter 'y' is changed to 'b', the form 'jalābu' is accomplished. It is called 'jalābu' because it reaches decay and destruction; it refers to the placenta (afterbirth) that wraps and covers beings dwelling in the womb. In the word 'sannisīva', having established the word 'sannisīda', when the letter 'd' is changed to 'v', the form 'sannisīvo' is accomplished.

103. The letter 'mūka' of the word 'mukha' following the word 'eḷa' is changed to 'g'. (Example) Eḷamūgo.

(a) Alternatively, it remains as the letter 'mūka' of the word 'mukha'. (Example) Eḷamūko or eḷamukho.

104. The clusters of 'ty' and 'dy' become the double 'cc' and double 'jj' respectively. (Examples) Jaccandho (jāti-andho - one who is blind from birth), yajjevaṃ (yadi evaṃ - if it be so), hīnajacco (one of low birth), "one does not become an outcast by birth", yathābhaccaṃ (yathābhūtyaṃ - the state as it really is), paṇḍiccaṃ (paṇḍityaṃ - the state of a wise person), kukkuccaṃ (kukkuccayaṃ - remorse/worry), seat, water for drinking and use, water for washing feet (pajjaṃ), sohajjaṃ (suhadaṃ - the state of a good friend), vajjaṃ (speech to be spoken), dajjaṃ (thing to be given), "the rivers are thought to flow". Furthermore, other forms such as jāti-andho, yadi evaṃ, hīnajātiyo, paṇḍityaṃ, paṇḍiccayaṃ, kukkuccayaṃ, and nadiyo are also seen. In places such as "I am your son", "one should be of a friendly disposition", "then he makes an acquaintance", etc., the doubling of 'cc' by this rule does not occur.

105. The letter 'n' of a cluster is changed to niggahīta, and in the place of 'ty', a single 'c' occurs. (Example) Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ.

106. In the place of 'thy' and 'dhy', the double 'cch' and double 'jjh' occur. (Examples) Bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ (true speech), whether it be true or whether it be false, bojjhaṅgo (factor of enlightenment), dummejjhaṃ (the state of one without wisdom), "excluding the practice along with the factors of enlightenment (one does not see happiness)", bojjhā is the same status as the word bodhiyā. In places such as "grass, creepers, and medicinal plants/deities", the substitution by this rule does not occur.
30:
107. In the place of the *ttha* letter group, the *ṭṭha* letter cluster occurs. *Aṭṭhakathā* or *Atthakathā* (Commentary). The nature of oppression of the Truth of Suffering (*dukkha-sacca*), the nature of being conditioned by causes (*saṅkhata*). (Giving) rice to one who desires rice. One should listen attentively. In some places, it does not change (to *ṭṭha*), as in the words "*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*" and "*attharaso*."

108. In the place of the *kaya* letter group, the *kka* letter cluster and *jja* letter cluster occur. *Nepakkaṃ* (mature wisdom/mindfulness). Mahānāma the Sakyan king. Because it is this thing of a physician (medicine), it is called *bhesajjaṃ*. Furthermore, other variant forms such as "*Sakyā*" and "*Sākiyā*" are also seen.

109. In the place of the *caya* letter group and *jaya* letter group, the *cca* letter cluster and *jja* letter cluster occur. *Paccati* (cooks), *pavuccati* (is said). *Palujjati* (is destroyed), *bhojjayāgu* (edible gruel).

110. In the place of the *laya* letter group, the *lla* letter cluster occurs. From *vipari āso* comes *vipallāso* (perversion/distortion), from *vipari atthaṃ* comes *vipallatthaṃ* (distorted meaning/destruction), *pattakallaṃ* (appropriate time), *kosallaṃ* (skillfulness). In some places, it does not occur, for example: *sumangalyaṃ* (the state of being a good omen).

111. In the place of the *vaya* letter group, the *bba* letter cluster occurs. *Vedhabbaṃ* or *vedhabyaṃ* (widowhood).

112. In the place of the *sya* letter, the *ssa* letter cluster occurs. *Porissaṃ* (manliness/effort), and the variant form "*porisiyaṃ*" is also seen. In some places, it does not occur, for example: *ālasyaṃ* (laziness).

113. In the place of the *gya* letter, the *gga* letter cluster occurs. *Dobhaggaṃ* (misfortune or the state of misery in the lower realms). In some places, it does not occur, for example: *odagyaṃ* (exultation/elation).

114. In the place of the *pya* letter, the *ppa* letter cluster or a single *pa* letter occurs. *Appekacce* (some people), *appekadā* (sometimes), *sāruppaṃ* (suitability/appropriateness). *Dīpā* means "those covered with panther skin."

115. In the place of the *ghya* letter, the *gha* letter occurs. *Veyyagghā* means "those covered with tiger skin."

116. In the place of the *ṭya* letter, the *cca* letter cluster occurs. The state of one who is diligent and making effort is called *veyyāvaccaṃ*. In some places, it does not occur, for example: *pāribhaṭyaṃ* (the state of a nurse/child-minder).
31:
117. Both the letter *nya* and the letter *ṇya* become *ñña*. For example: from *āni-āyo* comes *aññāyo* (the Noble Path), *ākiñcaññaṃ* (the state of being without possessions or the sphere of nothingness), *gelaññaṃ* (sickness), *sāmaññaṃ* (recluseship). In some places, it does not occur, for example: *āṇaṇyaṃ* (freedom from debt).

118. The letter *bhya* becomes *bbha*. For example: *osabbhaṃ* (the state of a bull/excellence).

119. The letter *mya* becomes *mma*. For example: *opammaṃ* (the state of a comparison/simile), *sokhummaṃ* (the state of one who is subtle).

120. Among three consonants, one identical consonant is elided. For example: in the sentence "*maceesi ekasataṃ khatye*" (freed one hundred and one kings), *khatye* is formed from *khattiye*; and the form *aggāgāraṃ* (fire-hall). Why is it said "identical"? To show that in the place "*evampi titthyā puthuso vadanti*" (thus the heretics speak much, even though it is wrong), there is no elision in *titthyā* because the sounds are not identical.

121. In the view of other teachers, the consonant following the prefixes *u*, *du*, and *ni* undergoes gemination (doubling) with an identical consonant. For example: *ukkāsi* (coughs), *uttāso* (terror), *dummano* (depressed), *dukkaraṃ* (difficult to do), *nissoko* (sorrowless), *nikkaṅkho* (doubtless).

122. In a cluster of aspirated (*dhanita*) letters, the preceding consonant becomes an unaspirated (*sithila*) letter. For example: *uṭṭhito* (stands up; *ṭṭh-ṭṭh* becomes *ṭ-ṭṭh*), *ugghāti* (removes/opens), *dubbhasitaṃ* (badly spoken words), *dubbikkhaṃ* (famine), *niddhano* (a poor person), *nibbhayaṃ* (fearlessness).

123. In a cluster of unaspirated (*sithila*) letters, the following consonant sometimes becomes an aspirated (*dhanita*) letter. For example: *nikkhamati* (goes out; *k-k* becomes *k-kh*), *nipphatati* (the lid falls off), *nittharaṇatthāya* (for the sake of crossing over), and the form "*sohmi etarahi kantāraṃ nitthiṇṇo*" (I have now crossed the difficult wilderness). Why is it said "sometimes"? To show that it does not occur in places such as "*taṃ ve nappasahati māro*" (Mara cannot oppress him) and "*uttaranti mahānadiṃ*" (they cross the great river).

124. In a heterogeneous cluster, one consonant becomes assimilated to the other. For example: from *pari-esanā* comes *payyesanā*, from *nābhiyo* comes *nabbho*, and *osabbhaṃ*.

125. When a consonant follows, in some places, the word *jāti* is substituted with *jacca*. For example: *jaccabadhiro* (or *jātibadhiro*—one who is deaf from birth), *jaccajaḷo* (or *jātijaḷo*—one who is foolish from birth). The mention of "when a consonant follows" in this rule is to show that in places like *jaccandho*, it is accomplished by another rule because a vowel follows. Although some forms in this text could be accomplished by previous rules, they are mentioned again to make the students very skillful by showing various methods and to show that these rules are continuous like rainwater; therefore, this should not be considered a fault of redundancy (*punarutti*).
32:
In words such as "jaccandho," the substitution of the word 'jāti' to 'jacca' does not occur even when a vowel follows, as indicated by the rule "ne lakkhaṇa." In this treatise, although some examples are established by previous rules, they are stated again to produce supreme proficiency in the listeners by showing variations in methods, and to demonstrate that the rules are continuous like rain (pajjunna-gatika). Therefore, it should not be understood as the fault of repetition (punarutti-dosa). This is because a treatise (Nīti) is beautiful only when explained in various ways. Furthermore, as this work is the Saddanīti, which carries the True Dhamma in the Dispensation (Sāsana), it is explained in various ways. Thus, it should be noted that there is no fault of repetition.

126. Avasso. In some places, the prefix 'ava' is changed to 'o' when a consonant follows. (Example:) Those covered by the shell of the darkness of ignorance (onaddhā). Admonishes (ovadati), the end (osānaṃ), the final end (vosānaṃ). Why is "kvaci" (in some places) said? It is to prevent the change to 'o' in words like 'avasussatu' (let it dry up) and 'avasānaṃ' (the end). Why is "byañjane" (when a consonant follows) said? It is to prevent the change to 'o' when a vowel follows, as in 'avayāgamanaṃ' and 'avekkhati' (looks at).

127. Evaṃ khvantare viyassa byā. The word 'viya' situated between the words 'evaṃ' and 'kho' is changed to 'byā.' (Example:) Venerable Sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way (evaṃ byā kho). 'Evaṃ byā kho' means 'evaṃ viya kho' (in this very way/just like this).

128. Vācāya byo pathe. When the word 'patha' follows, the word 'vācā' is changed to 'byo.' (Example:) Byappatho. 'Byappatho' means 'vacanapatho' (the path of speech). Speech itself is called 'byappatho' because it is like a path for others who follow the example.

129. U byañjane puthassanto. When a consonant follows, the final vowel of the particle 'putha' is changed to 'u.' (Example:) Puthujjano (worldling), puthubhūtā (become many). Why is "byañjane" said? It is to prevent the change to 'u' in the phrase 'putha ayaṃ' (this person is separate).
33:
130. Kvacokārāgamo. In some places, the augment 'o' (o-kāra) occurs when a consonant follows. (Example:) A Saṅgha of monks numbering more than a thousand (parosahassaṃ). May you live for a hundred autumns/years (saradosataṃ). Why is "kvaci" said? Because the augment 'o' does not occur in places such as "Come and look at this world" (etha passathimaṃ lokaṃ) or "This world has become blind" (andhībhūto ayaṃ loko). Teachers, however, also desire the augment 'ga' along with 'o'; they cite as an example: "It is still too early (atippago) to wander for alms in Sāvatthī." This is our preference. The word 'pago' should be understood as a particle synonymous with the word 'pāto' (early). Therefore, the commentators said: "'Atippago' means very early."

131. Napuṃsake taṃsaddādīnaṃ niggahītaṃ byañjane nissaraṃ takāraṃ so ca sassaraṃ dakāraṃ kvaci gāthāyaṃ. In verses, when a consonant follows, the niggahīta of neuter words such as 'taṃ' etc. in some places becomes a vowelless 't' or a 'd' accompanied by a vowel. (Example:) May that which you desire be fulfilled for you (tadate). For a brahmin, this is not even slightly better (etadakiñci). Here, 'taṃ te' is analyzed as 'tadate,' and 'etaṃ kiñci' as 'etadakiñci.' Why is "kvaci" said? Because it does not change to 'd' in places such as "That victory is not a good victory" (na taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ) or "This is the supreme blessing" (etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ).

132. Adhissa jjho. In some places, the prefix 'adhi' is substituted by 'ajjha' when a consonant follows; this substitution should be understood as occurring only in verses. (Example:) He dwelt ruling the house (agāraṃ ajjha so vasi). It is analyzed as 'adhi so āvasi.' There, the meaning should be stated by connecting the word 'ajjha' with the word 'āvasi,' according to the Pali usage: "If he dwells ruling the house" (sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati). The Blessed One's Pali has diverse and wonderful methods.

133. Addho bhūmaye pare. In some places, the prefix 'adhi' is substituted by 'addha' when followed by a consonant derived from the root 'bhū.' (Example:) One who is oppressed/overcome (addhabhūto).
34:
The form 'addhabhavati' exists. "Monks, the eye is oppressed (by birth, etc.)" (addhabhūtaṃ). "What overcomes all?" (addhabhavi). "Name overcomes all" (nāmaṃ sabbaṃ addhabhavi). Why is "kvaci" said? It is to show that the substitution to 'addha' does not occur in places like 'adhibhūto' and 'adhibhavati.'

## Thus ends the section on Consonant Sandhi in the Saddanīti.

Now follows the section on Mixed Sandhi (Vomissa-sandhi) --

The junction of vowels, consonants, etc., that have become mixed is called Mixed Sandhi. Indeed, the sandhi achieved through the substitution (ādesa) and elision (lopa) of vowels, consonants, and niggahīta is called "Vomissa-sandhi." This same Vomissa-sandhi is also called "General Sandhi" (Sādhāraṇa-sandhi) because it encompasses many procedures through substitution, elision, inversion (viparita), etc., of vowels, consonants, and niggahīta. Likewise, it is also called "Metrical Sandhi" (Vutta-sandhi) because it is performed in verses to preserve the meter (chanda) or the rhythm (vutti), and in prose (cuṇṇiya) for ease of pronunciation through elision, augment (āgama), etc. Although these three types of sandhi are mentioned separately by name, they should be understood as being included within Vowel Sandhi and Consonant Sandhi.

134. The letter 'e' (ekāra), upon reaching a verse, in some places becomes 'a' (akāra) or 'i' (ikāra). (Example:) We have performed your task (akaramhasate). (The deities) showed respect (okkantamāsi). Here in these winter and summer months (idha hemantagimhi su). Why is "kvaci" said? It is to show that even in a verse, in some contexts, 'e' does not become 'a.' Why is "gāthaṃ" said? It is to show that it does not occur in prose, for example: 'hemantagimhesu.'

135. A geminate consonant (saññoga), upon reaching a verse, in some places becomes simplified (visaňñoga). (Example:) The killing of sons is indeed painful (puttānañhi vadho dukho). One experiences various suffering (vividhaṃ vindate dukhaṃ). I was cooked in hell (nirayamhi apaccisaṃ). Why is "gāthaṃ" said? It is to show that it does not occur in prose, for example: 'dukkhā vedanā.' Why is "kvaci" said? It is to show that even in a verse, in some places, the gemination is not removed, for example: "Being bitten by a snake is not called painful" (na dukkhaṃ ahinā daṭṭhaṃ); "Formerly, I was restrained (in giving)" (ahaṃ pure saṃyamissaṃ).
35:
136. Asaññogo sasaññogo ca. A non-conjunct consonant, when occurring in a verse (gāthā), sometimes becomes a conjunct consonant. (Example:) "Dhammo pāpeti suggatiṃ" (The Dhamma leads to a happy destination). Why say "gāthā"? (Example:) "Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno" (He reached the happy heavenly world). Why say "sometimes" (kvaci)? (Example:) "Ito bho suggatiṃ gaccha" (O deity, when you pass away from this human world, go to the happy heavenly realm).

137. Kvaci sare byañjane vā paṭi patissa. In some instances, the prefix "pati" is changed to "paṭi" before either a vowel or a consonant. (Example:) "Paṭaggidātabbo" (A fireplace should be given), "Paṭihaññati" (He is oppressed). Why say "sometimes"? (Example:) "Patilīyati" (He shrinks back), "Patirūpadesavāso ca" (Living in a suitable locality is a blessing).

138. Niggahītaṃ vagge vaggantaṃ vā. When followed by a group consonant (vagga), the niggahīta sometimes changes to the final consonant of its own group. (Example:) "Dīpaṅkaro" (Dīpaṅkara Buddha), "Dhammañcare sucaritaṃ" (One should practice the Dhamma well), "Lokassa saṇṭhiti" (The stability of the world), "Tanniccutaṃ" (That Nibbāna is without deviation), "Saṅghasammato" (One agreed upon by the Saṅgha). Why say "optionally" (vā)? (Example:) "Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu" (That deed done is not good).

139. Le lakāraṃ. When followed by the letter 'l', the niggahīta sometimes changes to the letter 'l'. (Example:) "Asallīnaṃ" (Not shrinking), "Paṭisallīno" (Secluded), "Paṭisallāno" (Seclusion), "Sallakkhaṇā" (Careful observation), "Pullingaṃ" (Masculine gender). Why say "optionally"? (Example:) "Āmisaṃ labhati" (He receives material things).

140. Ña mehe. When followed by the letters 'e' or 'h', the niggahīta sometimes changes to the letter 'ñ'. (Example:) "Paccattaññeva parinibbāyissāmi" (I shall attain Nibbāna individually), "Taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi" (I will ask about that very matter here), "Evañhi vo bhikkhave sikkhitabbaṃ" (Thus, O bhikkhus, you should train yourselves), "Tañhi tassa musā hoti" (For that is a lie for him), "Saññito" (Endowed with benefit). Why say "optionally"? (Example:) "Evameva tvampi" (Even so you too), "Evametamabhiññāya" (Knowing this matter thus), "Evaṃ hoti subhāsitaṃ" (Thus it is well-spoken), "Pamāṇarahitaṃ hitaṃ" (Immeasurable benefit).
36:
...Inspire faith. Knowing this matter thus. Thus it is well-spoken. Immeasurable benefit.

141. Ye saha. When followed by the consonant 'y', the niggahīta together with the 'y' sometimes changes to the letter 'ñ'. Example: Saññojanaṃ, Saññogo, Saññuttaṃ. Why say "optionally" (vā)? (Because it does not happen in some places) Saṃyogo, Saṃyuttaṃ.

142. Napuṃsake yatetehi do sare pāyena. In the neuter gender, the niggahīta following the words 'ya', 'ta', and 'eta' is generally changed to the letter 'd' when followed by a vowel. Example: The hermit Bāvarī said that word (Yadabravi). That very object (Tadevārammaṇaṃ). The Teacher said this (Etadavoca satthā). Why say "optionally" (vā)? "Yaṃ abravi." Why say "generally" (pāyena)? That lotus flower born in the water (Yametaṃ vārijaṃ pupphaṃ).

143. Mo itare. In the other two genders (masculine and feminine), the niggahīta following the words 'ya', 'ta', and 'eta' is changed to the letter 'm' when followed by a vowel. Example: Whom among the gods they call the husband of Sujā (Yamāhu devesu sujampatīti). The Blessed One, wishing to clarify that matter (Tamatthaṃ pakāsento). Having known this matter (Etamatthaṃ viditvā). King Siñjaya said that to Maddī (Tamabravi mahārājā maddiṃ). Why say "optionally" (vā)? And that assembly of gods which they call Sudhammā (Sudhammāti ca yaṃ āhu).

144. Samāse do tiliṅge. In a compound (samāsa), in all three genders, the niggahīta following the words 'ya', 'ta', and 'eta' is changed to the letter 'd' when followed by a vowel. Example: That which is immediate to that word or term (Yadanantaraṃ), that which is immediate to that verse (Yadanantaraṃ); it should be analyzed as "yaṃ anantaraṃ." Similarly, that which is immediate to that (Tadanantaraṃ). The meaning of this word or term (Etadattho), the meaning of this verse (Etadattho); it should be analyzed as "etaṃ attho."

145. Sesato mo do ca sare byañjane vā. The niggahīta following words other than the aforementioned 'ya', 'ta', and 'eta' is sometimes changed to either the letter 'm' or the letter 'd' when followed by either a vowel or a consonant. Example: Knowing this matter thus (Evametaṃ abhiññāya), I myself (Ahameva), you yourself (Tvameva), I go to the Buddha for refuge (Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi). Faith (Saddahanā), that benefit (Taddhitaṃ). Why say "optionally" (vā)? Bhikkhunīs are of such conduct (Bhikkhuniyo evācārā), I go to the Buddha for refuge (Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi).
37:
Knowing (that matter) with higher knowledge. I myself, you yourself, I go to the Buddha for refuge. Faith, that benefit. Why say "optionally" (vā)? Bhikkhunīs are of such habit. I go to the Buddha for refuge.

146. Kvaci niggahītāgamo. In some instances, the augmentation of niggahīta occurs when followed by a vowel or a consonant. The eye of wisdom arose. Head downwards. O bhikkhus, it is fit to be extremely weary of this suffering of saṃsāra. Associated with that Dhamma. All faults, small and great. Mental phenomena have mind as their forerunner. Why say "sometimes" (kvaci)? Stay right here for a while. In the next life, one rejoices in the happy heavenly realm.

147. Lopaṃ. In some instances, the niggahīta undergoes elision when followed by a vowel or a consonant. There was a gathering of bhikkhus. From this day forth as long as life lasts.
