I am in their presence. Noble among the wise, the All-Seer. Seeing the Noble Truths. This is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Speech is peaceful, and bodily action is peaceful.
Why say "sometimes" (kvaci)? I am indeed a fool. That Dhamma is the highest blessing for them.

148. Paro saro vā. The vowel following a niggahīta sometimes undergoes elision. They rejoiced. Like pure gold, this also. Why say "optionally" (vā)? To show that the following vowel does not elide in cases like "ahameva," "etadavravi," etc.

149. Lutte byañjano visaññogo. When the vowel following a niggahīta is elided, even if it was a conjunct consonant, it becomes a non-conjunct consonant. Thus those taints (āsavas) (arise) for him. Menstrual blood arises for that woman. If I had eaten, my livelihood would be blameworthy. This matter, however...
38: A juncture (ṭhāna) is the point of connection between the first and second pādas (lines of a verse) without a gap. This juncture is only a place where, due to the elision of a vowel following a niggahīta, a conjunct consonant is made non-conjunct; it is not a juncture formed by the shifting of letters (akkharasaṅkanti). Indeed, in the Tipiṭaka Buddha-vacana, apart from this specific Pali passage where a conjunct consonant becomes non-conjunct due to the elision of a vowel following a niggahīta, there is no other Pali passage where a sandhi (euphonic combination) occurs between the first and second pādas, or the third and fourth pādas, by means of shifting letters or shifting words (padasaṅkanti). However, in the works of poets (kavi), such passages do exist. For example: 'Yatthappatiṭṭhitañceta-metaṃ vatvā vidhintato', 'Upakkamena vā kesa-ñcupacchedakakammunā', 'Sotāpannā ca sakadā-gāmino cāpi puggalā', and 'Nāmaṃ dvidhā catudhā ca-nvatthasāmaññaādito. Vijjamānāvijjamāna-ttādito chabbidhaṃ mataṃ.' This is a Pali passage with shifting letters (akkharasaṅkanti). 'Vadhādipañcaratana-ttayassā guṇavaṇṇanaṃ' is a Pali passage with shifting words (padasaṅkanti). Both types of shifting should be understood as not being found in the Pali Canon, just as a compound (samāsa) starting with a connecting letter is not found between the first and second, or third and fourth pādas. Some teachers might ask: 'In the verse "Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, neka-koṭisataṃ dhanaṃ," are not the first and second pādas connected by sandhi? If so, why say "there is no other Pali passage"?' That is not so, because the first and second pādas are not connected. Here, there is no purpose for a sandhi operation like "cintayitvānānekakoṭisataṃ". Therefore, disregarding the first pāda, only the sandhi operation by means of a compound in "nekakoṭisataṃ" is intended, as in "na arūpāvacarā dhammā".
39: If it is asked, 'How is it known that the two pādas are not connected?', it is known through a variant reading (pāṭhantara). In this context, this variant reading is: 'Nekānaṃ nāgakoṭīnaṃ, parivāretvānahatadā. Vajjanto sabbatūriyehi, lokajeṭṭhaṃ upāgamiṃ.' (At that time, surrounded by many crores of Nagas, and having all musical instruments played, I approached the Buddha, the Supreme in the world.) In this verse, the word 'neka' stands without being connected to the preceding word (as an anupapada). Because it stands thus, it is known that 'the two pādas are not connected'. Just as the words 'alābu' and 'လာဗု' (lābu) appear separately in the Dispensation (Sāsana), so too the words 'aneka' and 'neka' appear separately in the Dispensation in places like 'anekakoṭisannicayo' and 'nekakoṭisataṃ dhanaṃ'. Thus, it should be understood that in the Pali Canon, shifting of letters (akkharasaṅkanti) and shifting of words (padasaṅkanti) are entirely absent in every way. If such shifts existed, the words would become broken and fragmented. If the words were broken and fragmented, the meaning would become unclear. To the veneyya (those to be taught) listening to the Dhamma, the understanding of the meaning would appear as if it were broken and fragmented. Therefore, the Buddha, the Lord of Dhamma, avoiding those two types of shifting, established the textual order (tanti) in the Māgadhi language, the natural linguistics (sabhāva-nirutti) which is the root language of all beings. The Noble Ones, the disciples of the Buddha, also established the Pali tradition following that very method of the Buddha. In the utterances of deities and others, they removed what was to be removed and included only pure grammar (byañjana) in the Pali Canon. 150. When 'ma' follows, the 'i' following a niggahīta becomes 'a' or 'u'. Example: 'taṃ imināpetaṃ' becomes 'tadamina...', 'evaṃ imaṃ' becomes 'evumaṃ'. 151. When 'ha' follows, 'a' becomes 'e'. Example: 'kaṃ ahaṃ' becomes 'kehaṃ' or 'kahaṃ'. 152. When the word 'pati' follows, the letter 'ka' of the word 'sahaka' becomes a niggahīta. Example: 'Brahmā Sahampati'.
40: 153. When a consonant follows, a niggahīta becomes 'aṃ'. Example: 'evaṃ vutte' (when thus said), 'taṃ sādhu' (that matter is good). 154. In words like 'pariya', the letters 'ra' and 'ya' undergo metathesis (vipariyāya) with 'ya' and 'ra'. Example: 'pariyudāhāsi' becomes 'payirudāhāsi' (he preached). 'ariyassa' becomes 'ayirassa' (of the noble one). 'kariyā' becomes 'kayirā' (should be done). 'bahu-ābādho' becomes 'bavhābādho' (having much illness). 'masakā' becomes 'makasā' (mosquito). 'na abhineyya' becomes 'anabhineyya' (not to be led). 'ariyā' becomes 'ayirā' (noble ones). The word 'ariya' also refers to a lord (sāmī). 'ariyo', 'ayiro', and 'sāmī' have the same meaning. 155. In the word 'saṃ', when the following niggahīta is elided due to a following consonant, the preceding 'a' vowel becomes long (dīgha). Example: 'saṃratto' becomes 'sāratto' (intense passion). Similarly, 'sārāgo' (intense passion), 'sārambho' (malice), 'avisāhāro' (concentration, the opposite of distraction). Why say 'in the word saṃ'? To show that lengthening does not occur in 'ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ' and 'kiṃ nu imā va samaṇiyo', etc. 156. In the Scriptures (Pāvacana), the 'i' of the word 'Vāsiṭṭha' becomes 'e'. Example: 'Vāseṭṭho' (the youth Vāseṭṭha). 157. The regulation by the number of syllables is called chanda (meter). The regulation by the sequence of heavy (garu) and light (lahu) syllables is called vutti (rhythm). 158. In verses, elision of letters (akkharalopa) occurs to prevent the meter from breaking. Example: 'adussa me khettapālassa' becomes 'dussa me khettapālassa' (the cloth of that field-guard). 'cando va patito chamāyaṃ' becomes 'cando va patito chamā' (like the moon fallen on the ground). 'pubbe va ca somanassa-domanassaṃ' becomes 'pubbe va ca somanadomanassaṃ' (formerly joy and grief). 'evameva nūna rājānaṃ' becomes 'evameva nu rājānaṃ' (even so surely the king). Thus, elision of initial, middle, and final letters should be understood. It should be applied in other places as well. 159. Deviation (viparītatā) occurs for the sake of protecting the vutti. Here, I shall state the opinion of the teachers. Some teachers say that deviation occurs in verses to protect the vutti, i.e., to maintain the rule of heavy and light syllables. Other teachers say that deviation of letters occurs to protect the 'vats' (observances/meters) such as Gāthā-vatta, Suttanta-vatta, Taraṅga-vatta, etc.
41:
Some teachers say that the transformation of letters occurs for the sake of preserving the observances (vatta) such as Gāthāvatta, Suttantavatta, and Taraṅgavatta. "Akaraṃhase te kiccaṃ, akaraṃhasate kiccaṃ." One should practice with that wise person, being joyful and mindful. Why do you abandon the former appearance?

160. In the Suttas, the elision and transformation of letters occur for the sake of ease of pronunciation. The sixty-two practices, "dwaṭṭhipaṭipadā." Thus, two intermediate eons, "dwantarakappā." Having known and realized by one's own higher knowledge, "sayaṃ abhiññāsacchikatvā." Reflecting appropriately, "paṭisaṅkhā yoniso." Made of gold, "soṇṇamayaṃ." Butter, "nonītaṃ." That bird indeed laments, "vilapatvevaso dijo." Just as the Samantapāsādikā, "samantapāsādikātveva." Well-expounded, "svākkhāto." A forest thicket, "vanappagumbe." Happiness, suffering, life; "sukhe, dukkhe, jīve." Life and these seven aggregates, "jīve ca sattime kāyā." Which Gandhabba deity? "ke gandhabbe." Both fools and the wise, "bāle ca paṇḍite ca." Eight hundred abodes of Nagas, "aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate." The brahmin woman of the Kosiya lineage has lost affection for the brahmin father, "viratte kosiyāyane." This Ariya Dhamma is that very Sappurisa Dhamma and is only one, "esese eke."

Furthermore, teachers desire the change of the vowel 'o' to 'e' in "soyathidaṃ" as "seyyathidaṃ." Those teachers might have seen a variant reading; however, we do not see it. Likewise, they desire the change of the vowel 'ā' to 'o' in "sā itthī" as "sotthī." We, however, do not see the word "sotthī" with the meaning "that woman" (sā itthī); we only see the word "sotthī" with the meaning "good woman" (su-itthī). In this regard, this Aṅguttara Pali is the evidence: "A good woman (sotthī) does not despise her husband with jealous conduct." In that Pali, this is the word-splitting from the euphonic combination (saṃhitā): "su-itthī" becomes "sotthī." Likewise, teachers...
42:
...desire the change of the vowel 'o' to 'ū' in the words "rattañño" and "rattaññū." We, however, as seen in the Pali such as "kālaññū samayaññū ca, sa rājavasatiṃ vase," desire only the state of ending in 'ū' (ū-kāranta) by the power of the 'ū' suffix in the sense of having that habit (of knowing), as in "rattaññū, sabbaññū, kālaññū." Furthermore, as seen in the Pali "rattañño, vaṃsañño," we also desire the state of ending in 'o' (o-kāranta) as in "rattañño, vaṃsañño." However, in the word "sabbaññū," this method (of ending in 'o') cannot be obtained.

## 161. The increase and other changes of letters in words with few letters.
"Sarati" (remembers) becomes "susarati" (remembers well). "Sakehi" (with one's own property) becomes "suvakehi." "Svāmi" (lord) becomes "suvāmi." "Svāminī" (lady) becomes "suvāminī." "Satto" (being) becomes "sattavo." "Macco" (being) becomes "mātiyo." "Dve" (two) becomes "duve." "Taṇhā" (craving) becomes "tasinā." "Pamhaṃ" (eyelash) becomes "pakhumaṃ." And so forth.

## 162. The decrease and other changes of letters in words with many letters.
"Ācariyaṃ" (teacher) becomes "āceraṃ." "Kātiyāno" (Kaccāyana) becomes "kaccāno." "Padumāni" (lotuses) becomes "padmāni." And so forth.

## 163. When certain vowels or consonants follow, the state of ending in 'a' for nouns ending in 'o' is natural (original).
"So eva attho" becomes "sa evattho" (that very meaning). Likewise, "sa sasīlavā" (that person is virtuous), "esa ābhogo" (this reflection), "esa dhammo" (this Dhamma), "tuvañca dhanusekho ca" becomes "tuvañca dhanusekha ca." Likewise, "kakusandha koṇāgamano," "thera vādānamuttamo." In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, since the vowel 'o' is not seen and the sound of the case ending (vibhatti) is not heard, it is said that "kakusandha" is a designation without a case ending, and "thera" is a designation without a case ending. Therefore, in "sa evattho, esa ābhogo," etc., the words "sa" and "esa" may be said to be words without case endings in a figurative sense (pariyāyena). In a literal sense (nippariyāyena), however, "Having practiced the Dhamma in this world..."
43:
"O King, you will go to heaven." In this instance, although it occurs in the vocative sense (ālapana) and the case ending is elided, the words "sa," "esa," and "i" are indeed with case endings, just like the word "rāja" which has a case ending. This is true; if the word "rāja" with its elided case ending is considered as having a case ending, why should "sa," "esa," and "i" be without case endings when the vowel 'o', which is a transformation of the case ending, has become 'a'? Thus, the words "sa" and "esa" are indeed with case endings. In places such as "tuvañca dhanusekha ca," words like "dhanusekha" and "kakusandha" are either without case endings or with case endings. However, words that are strictly without case endings are terms like "sata" (because of sinking and perishing) and "asa" (because of always existing). Therefore, in the phrase "satasmiṃ ti hoti," the word-split should be made as "sata asmi," meaning "I am impermanent (anicca)." In the phrase "asasmiṃ ti hoti," the word-split is "asa asmi," meaning "I am permanent (nicca)."

164. In preserving the meter (vuttirakkhaṇa), when the augment 'ma' follows, the state of ending in 'a' for nouns ending in 'o' is natural. "Maggamatthi" (The path exists, but the traveler does not). "Paccayākārameva ca." "Esa maggaṃ." Why is it said "when the augment 'ma' follows"? In the instance "esa maggo adhammaṭṭha" (This is the path of those not established in Dhamma), because the augment 'ma' does not follow, it remains as 'o'.

165. In preserving the meter, when there is a substitution of 'ma' (from niggahīta), the vowel 'a' becomes long (dīgha). "Nayidaṃ paññavatāmiva" (As this is not the case for the wise). "Dhammo arahatāmiva" (Like the Dhamma of the Arahants). "Nabhaṃ tārācitāmiva" (Like the sky adorned with stars). Why is it said "when there is a substitution of 'ma'"? In the instance "bako kakkaṭakāmiva" (As the heron reaches the state of having its neck cut by the crab), because there is no substitution of 'ma', the vowel does not become long by this rule.

166. In preserving the meter, the vowel 'i' of the word "apica" is elided, and the letter 'p' is changed to 'c'. "Accāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo" (This middle part will be a circle of carp). Why is it said "in preserving the meter"? In places such as "apicāyaṃ tapodā" (This Tapodā river flows), the elision and substitution are prohibited because it is not a verse.
44:
167. The letter "ti" of the word "aticca" should be elided. Alternatively, in places where the metre (vutti) of a verse is to be preserved, the letter "ti" of the word "aticca" is elided. (Example: Accāyaṃ majjhimokhaṇḍo.)

168. In places where the metre of a verse is to be preserved, the niggahīta may leave its own place of dependence and move to another position. (Example: Tatthaṃ asse ayācisuṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ vipassisuṃ.) In this treatise, some characteristics are stated as irregular (aniyama); through these irregular characteristics, various forms are accomplished. Even so, because they are stated as irregular, listeners might become confused in various Pali passages, and there might be an excessive production of forms. To avoid both, I shall state a few regulations (niyama). In stating this, it should not be considered a fault of repetition.

169. The vowel 'i' becomes 'a'; for that reason, the letter 't' should be elided. (Example: In the place of "imā gāthā abhāsittha", it becomes "imā gāthā abhāsatha". In the place of "udakenābhisinciṭṭha", it becomes "udakenābhisincatha".)

170. In some places, the vowel 'a' becomes 'e'. (Example: Navacchannake doṇi diyyati.)

171. In some places, the vowel 'a' becomes 'o'. (Example: Pitā cupahato mano.) Why is "kvaci" (in some places) said? It is to prevent this from occurring in words like "upahatamano".

172. The vowel 'u' becomes 'o'. (Example: Sotattho, sotinto, sovaṇṇamayaṃ, sotthī.)

173. In compounds (samāsa) and derivatives (taddhita), the vowel 'e' of the word "geha" becomes 'a' or 'i'. (Example: Gahakūṭaṃ, gahapati, gahaṭṭho, gihī.)
45:
174. The vowel 'e' is changed to 'i'. In cases like "dummijjhaṃ" or "dummejjhaṃ" (the state of being unwise), it can be done optionally (vā).

175. When an augment (āgama) occurs, the vowel 'a' is also changed to 'e'. This occurs in the sentence "haññayevāpi koci naṃ" (someone might kill him). That sentence should be analyzed as "haññe eva koci naṃ".

176. The vowel 'o' is changed to 'ā' and also to 'u'. This occurs in "vivaṭacchadā" (one who has a roof opened) and "ārugyaṃ" (the state of being free from illness). It also occurs in "na tenatthaṃ abandhi su" (he is not bound by that benefit), "avhāyantu suyuddhena" (let them call with a good fight), and "api nu hanukā santā" (are the jaws weary?). Among those examples, "vivaṭacchadā" is indeed "vivaṭacchado". This is true; in the Sub-commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta, it is stated: "vivaṭacchadā is a designation made by changing the vowel 'o' to 'ā'". In "abandhi su", it is "abandhiso", or the letter 'su' is merely a particle (nipāta).

177. Before a consonant, the vowel 'u' is changed to 'i'. This occurs in "āsīviso" (a snake with poison in its mouth).

178. The vowel 'e' of the word "eva" following "yathā", "tathā", or other words is changed to 'i'. This occurs in "yathā eva" becoming "yathariva", "tathā eva" becoming "tathariva", and "bhusāmiva" (as if very much).

179. When there is a conjunct consonant (saññoga) or when an augment (āgama) occurs, a long vowel (dīgha) is made short (rassa). This occurs in "pageva itarā pajā" (what need to say of other beings?), "mayā samma dakkhātā" (well preached by me), and "diṭṭheva dhamme aññā" (the knowledge of the path of Arahatship occurs in this very life).

180. The letter 's' of the word "āsava" when referring to a person is doubled (dvitta). "Āsavo" is made into "assavo". This occurs in "assavā piyabhāṇinī" (an obedient wife who speaks pleasant words) and "yance puttā anassavā" (those sons who are disobedient). Why is it said "when referring to a person"? Because in the phrase "āsavā dhammā" (the āsava states), the word "āsava" does not refer to a person but only to the Dhamma (therefore doubling is not done).
46:
The words "ca" and "assa" do not occur [in that sense]. This is because a word is established in its meanings by convention. This method should be well-borne in mind.

181. The consonant 'd' of the word "paṭipadā" is elided in some places. In this rule, "paṭipadāya" should be understood as "of the word paṭipadā". This is because, just as there is a designation of meaning, there is also a designation of the word itself. For example, as in the designation "of you all, of us (tumhamhākaṃ tayimayi)". (Examples:) "I have shown the practices (paṭipā), great and small, high and low." "Venerable Sir, please preach your excellent practice (paṭipaṃ)." "By the practice (paṭipāya)," "in the practices (paṭipāsu)." Why is "in some places (kvaci)" said? It is to indicate that elision does not occur in phrases such as "the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā)".

182. When the word "āgāmī" follows, the vowel 'i' of the word "sakiṃ" is changed to the letter 'a' along with the augment 'd'. (Example:) Sakadāgāmī (one who will come to this human world only once).

183. When a vowel-trigger or a consonant-trigger follows, the word "pati" is changed to "pacca". (Example:) "Paccājāto" (born in a low family). "Paccājāyati" (is born). Here, "paccājāto" means "patijāto" (born depending on). Thus, because of the consonant-trigger, the word "pati" occurs with the trigger. Alternatively, "paccājāto" is "pati-ājāto" (born facing towards). This analysis is made based on the Pali: "If they reach the human state, they are born facing (ājāyare) a wealthy family." Thus, because of the vowel-trigger, the word "pati" occurs with the trigger. In those two types, by the former method (consonant-trigger), the lengthening of the vowel 'a' of the word "pacca" and the consonant sandhi (conjunction) should be understood. By the latter method (vowel-trigger), vowel sandhi should be understood.

184. For the sake of euphony (vācāsiliṭṭhattha), words such as "anta" and "gata" are appended at the end of a word. (Example:) Suttanto, kammanto, vanantaṃ, brahmajālasuttantaṃ, gūthagataṃ, mutthagataṃ, disatā, devatā, idappaccayatā.
47:
185. If joining vowels in a usage makes the word difficult to pronounce, Sandhi (euphonic combination) should not be performed. Similarly, there is no Sandhi in instances such as 'ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī' (not perceiving form within oneself), 'yāva ime idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ', and 'imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi'.

186. If joining vowels in a usage ruins the meaning, Sandhi should not be performed. For example, the term 'āyasmā ānando'. (If joined as 'āyasmānando', the name Ānanda is ruined and could be misinterpreted as Elder Nanda.)

187. Vowels separated by consonants in two words do not form Sandhi. There is no Sandhi in instances such as 'akkocchi maṃ, avadhi maṃ' (he abused me, he struck me), 'indriyesu sutaṃvutaṃ' (well-restrained in the faculties), 'ete haṃsā pakkamanti' (these geese fly away), and 'orodhā ca kumārā ca' (the harem ladies and the princes). If it is asked, "Do vowels not form Sandhi in instances such as 'nanu ca bho sa sīlavāti' (O friend, is he not virtuous?)", the answer is that they do not form Sandhi; it is merely because the letter 'a' appears in the place where the letter 'o' was elided. If that is the case, those usages are not Sandhi usages; then why are they taught in the context of Sandhi? It is true; because they are mostly included among Sandhi usages, these usages are considered Sandhi usages, and therefore they are taught in the context of Sandhi. In the world, usage is often seen based on general convention, such as 'ānagarā khadiravanaṃ' (the acacia forest up to the city).

188. Vowels separated by consonants within a single word sometimes form Sandhi. For example, 'ārāmarukkha-cetiyāni' (shrine-gardens and shrine-trees) and 'cetiyāni vandiṃsu' (they worshipped the shrines).

189. The elision of a pure vowel (suddhasara—a vowel without consonant support) does not occur even when followed by the 'ā' of the word 'ādi' or another vowel. Even when followed by the 'ā' of the word 'ādi' or another vowel, because there is no support called a consonant, the elision of unsupported pure vowels does not occur as they would be unable to clearly manifest the meaning. Words beginning with 'a' are called 'a-ādayo'. Similarly, there are 'ā-ādayo', 'i-ādayo', 'ī-iṃnaṃ tthatthaṃ', and 'u āgato'. Why is it said that the elision of a pure vowel does not occur? It is to show that elision can occur in words like 'akārādayo' and 'pabbatādayo' because they have consonant support.
48:
In this rule, even if there is a preceding vowel and the 'ā' of the word 'ādi' follows, because there is a support, it does not exist as a pure vowel (suddhasara) and thus indeed undergoes elision.

190. When there is an upapada (nearby word), even if the 'ā' of the word 'ādi' follows or another vowel follows, both pure and impure vowels indeed undergo elision.

When there is an upapada, even if the 'ā' of the word 'ādi' follows or another vowel follows, both pure and impure vowels indeed undergo elision. In the phrase 'akkharāpi a-ādayo', it becomes 'akkharāpādayo'. In the phrase 'ka a īsā', it becomes 'kesā'. The compound of 'ko ca, a ca, īso ca' is 'kesā'. Here, the word 'ka' refers to Brahmā, the word 'a' refers to Viṣṇu, and the word 'īsa' refers to Īśvara (Lord). Although these usages shown by these two characteristics do not exist in the Pali Canon, these secular usages are mentioned for the sake of comparison with the Pali Canon. Because they are spoken by the power of the Nīti grammar treatises, it should not be considered that they are spoken in an inappropriate place.

191. The letter 'i' of the word 'iti' following a pure vowel should be elided. In this Dispensation of the Buddha, the letter 'i' of the word 'iti' following a pure vowel is elided because it is capable of manifesting the meaning. In the passage 'iti ca danti ca duti ca khanti ca ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti', there is the phrase 'na hevaṃ vattabbe'. Here, by splitting the words as 'i iti ca' and eliding the following letter 'i', the term 'iti ca' is formed. In this instance, the letter 'i' should be recited with a slight pause. Because it is recited in this way, this term is capable of manifesting the meaning. However, in terms like 'a-ādayo', if the letter 'a' is elided, the term 'ādayo' is not capable of manifesting the meaning of 'akārādayo'. This is because there is no recitation with a pause, and the distinguishing letter 'a' has been destroyed. When the distinguisher is destroyed, who will distinguish the thing to be distinguished? Therefore, it is not capable of manifesting the meaning. But the term 'iti ca'...
49:
...is indeed capable [of manifesting meaning] because it is to be recited with a pause. In the convention of poets (kavisamaya), only the term 'i iti' is desired. However, in the word of the Buddha (pāvacana), both methods are desired.

This is because there is a single-intentioned word-junction (saṃhitā-padaccheda). For example, splitting 'tatra ayaṃ' as 'tatrāyaṃ', etc. There is also a double-intentioned word-junction. For example, splitting 'su āgatāṃ' as 'svāgataṃ' or 'su āgataṃ' as 'sāgataṃ', etc. Alternatively, the terms 'du-īhitikā' and 'dvīhitikā', though the word-splitting is similar, have different meanings; they should be known as joined words (saṃhitā-pada) with two intentions in a single form.

Another method: 'anatthada' means one who gives harm (anattha). In that same word 'anatthada', by changing the letter 'd' to 't', it becomes 'anatthato'. Or it is called 'anatthato' because harm comes from this man. Thus, it is a joined word with two intentions. Splitting 'sā ahaṃ' as 'sāhaṃ' by the power of the feminine gender; or splitting 'so ahaṃ' as 'sāhaṃ' by the power of the masculine gender; another method is splitting 'cha ahaṃ' as 'chāhaṃ' by the power of number—these are word-junctions with three intentions. Intentions of four types and so on do not exist. Thus, the Dispensation of the Blessed One has diverse intentions and wonderful methods.

Here are the usages:
"I, that person, shall wander alone."
"I, that person, now know the Dhamma of the Sugata Buddha who teaches."
"They still have a mere amount of food, therefore there might be life for six days."

Here also, because 'cha ahāni' can form a compound as 'chāhaṃ' with the meaning of 'six days', it should be known as a joined word with the word-splitting 'cha ahaṃ' becoming 'sāhaṃ'. The example is like calling 'cha āyatanaṃ' as 'saḷāyatanaṃ'. Thus, the term 'sāhaṃ' has three intentions. The meaning of such words should be applied according to the usage and by the power of the context of the meaning. Furthermore, 'tatrāyaṃ' etc., is called a single-junction double-contraction (ekasandhi-dvisaṅkhepa) joined word. 'Sutā ca paṇḍitātyamha' etc., should be noted as a double-junction triple-contraction (dvisandhi-tisaṅkhepa) joined word.
50:
Furthermore, there are words that are both non-sandhi and sandhi. What are these words? They are "ubhayattha kaliggāho, ubhayattha kaṭaggāho," and so on. Taking defeat in both worlds, or taking defeat in both benefits, is called "ubhayattha kaliggāho"; it means taking a loss. In the word "ubhayattha kaṭaggāho," the same method applies. "Kaṭaggāho" means taking victory (winning).

However, in this treatise, the various distinctions mentioned regarding the preservation of meter (chanda) and rhythm (vutti), etc., will not be fully detailed for fear of making the text too extensive. In this work, statements such as "for the sake of preserving the meter," "for the sake of preserving the rhythm," and "for the sake of ease of pronunciation" should be understood as being spoken merely according to worldly usage.

In reality, the Blessed One does not guard meter or rhythm, nor does He perform the elision of letters, etc., for the sake of ease of pronunciation. A scholar who is apprehensive and fearful might guard meter and rhythm out of fear of the blame that arises from the apprehension of other scholars, and might perform the elision of letters, etc., for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

But the Blessed One is free from apprehension and fear; there is no error in the Blessed One's Pāvacana (Teaching). Why would that Blessed One guard meter and rhythm because of the blame of others? Why would He perform the elision of letters, etc., for the sake of ease of pronunciation?

This matter has been stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā (Mūla-ṭīkā) as follows: "The Blessed One does not count the lightness or heaviness (lahu-garu) of words. However, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be guided (veneyya) who are capable of realization, He determines the teaching in various ways without contradicting the nature of the Dhamma (dhamma-sabhāva). Therefore, the abundance or scarcity of letters should not be criticized anywhere."

Thus, in this treatise, whatever methods of Nīti (rules) we have established to the best of our ability for the benefit of the Sasana, all those Nīti should be learned with respect for the Sasana by sons of good family who are endowed with faith.

## The Section on Mixed Sandhi Rules (Vomissakasandhividhāna) is finished.
51:
Reflecting on the proficiency in the Pāli Dhamma, which is adorned with various methods, and which is joined with the three types of sandhi—vowel, non-vowel (consonant), and mixed—in the presence of vowels and non-vowels.

By exerting effort in the noble Sandhikappa, which is the essence of many kinds of methods, a wise person may attain the noble essence of meaning.

## Thus, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of speech within the Tipitaka together with its commentaries and ninefold limbs, the twentieth chapter called Sandhikappa is finished.

## 2. Nāmakappa (Chapter on Nouns)

After this Sandhi section, I shall speak of the Nāmakappa, which brings benefit to students, for the sake of proficiency in the Tipitaka, which is the noble intention of the Buddha.

192. A word that is endowed with clarity, etc., that makes known the hidden meanings of substance, gender, number, and case (kāraka), and that is formed by the application of case endings, is called a liṅga (stem/gender). A word that is endowed with the state of clarity, etc., that makes known the hidden meaning, and is a completed form, is called a liṅga. Examples: Buddho, Bhagavā, etc. Indeed, it has been said:

"The completed word 'rukkha' is called a liṅga;
The meaning of the liṅga (liṅgattha) is that which is shown by that completed liṅga.
Thus, having known both the liṅga and its meaning,
A wise person should apply them."

193. A clear word is called masculine (pulliṅga). A clear speech is called pulliṅga. Examples: puriso, napuṃsako, āpo, mātugāmo, rājā, etc.

194. An unclear word is called feminine (itthiliṅga). Examples: devatā, ratti, vīsati, etc.

195. A word that is neither clear nor unclear is called neuter (napuṃsakaliṅga). Examples: cittaṃ, rūpaṃ, kalattaṃ, akkhaṃ, etc.

196. A word that possesses meaning but is devoid of roots (dhātu), suffixes (paccaya), and case endings (vibhatti) is called a liṅga. A form that is devoid of roots, suffixes, and case endings, that possesses meaning, that is hidden, that is a component of completed words, and is established first, is called a liṅga. Examples: purisa, citta, mālā, etc.
52:
197. Prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) are also called liṅga. Prefixes and particles are indeed called liṅga. Examples: pati, atthi, sakkā, etc.

198. The fourteen endings starting with 'si' and the eighteen endings starting with 'ti' are called case endings (vibhatti). The words starting with 'si' and the words starting with 'ti' are those named vibhatti. They are called vibhatti because they are variously distributed by the power of the object (kamma), etc., and by the power of the singular (ekatta), etc.

199. The case endings starting with 'si' should be understood in relation to nouns (nāma), and those starting with 'ti' in relation to verbs (ākhyāta).

200. Si, yo, aṃ, yo, nā, hi, sa, naṃ, smā, hi, sa, naṃ, smiṃ, su. Those case endings which are called nominal case endings (nāma-vibhatti) are fourteen in their own nature: si, yo, aṃ, yo, nā, hi, sa, naṃ, smā, hi, sa, naṃ, smiṃ, su. The two words 'si' and 'yo' are named the first case (paṭhamā). 'Aṃ' and 'yo' are the second (dutiyā). 'Nā' and 'hi' are the third (tatiyā). 'Sa' and 'naṃ' are the fourth (catutthī). 'Smā' and 'hi' are the fifth (pañcamī). 'Sa' and 'naṃ' are the sixth (chaṭṭhī). The two 'smiṃ' and 'su' are named the seventh case (sattamī).

201. Of each pair, the former is singular (ekavacana) and the latter is plural (bahuvacana).

202. These case endings follow after the liṅga. These aforementioned various case endings follow after the liṅga which has become a stem; they do not follow after a completed liṅga. Why? Because there is no need to complete again what is already completed.

203. These case endings also follow after conventional words (rūḷhī), imitative words (anukaraṇa), prefixes (upasagga), etc. For example: Viḍūḍabho, yevāpanako, diso, ruco, karotissa, abhissa, patissa, caṇḍoraṇaṃ. Towards the mountain (pati), may there be worship (namo atthu), perform worship (namo karohi), etc., occur with case endings. In the sense of the vocative (ālapaṇa), the 'si' case ending is named 'ga'. Examples: bho purisa, bhoti ayye, etc. They also have the names 'gha' and 'la'.
53: The words such as Pati, Namo atthu, and Namo karohi are formed with case endings (vibhaktis). 204. In the sense of address (ālapana), the suffix 'si' is called 'ga'. In the sense of address, the word 'si' is called 'ga'. Examples: Bho purisa, bhoti ayye. 205. The i-vaṇṇa and u-vaṇṇa are called 'jha' and 'la' respectively. Examples: Isinā, daṇḍino, aggino, bhikkhuno, sayambhuno, vādino. 206. In the feminine gender, those i-vaṇṇa and u-vaṇṇa are called 'pa'. Examples: Rattiyā, itthiyā, vīsatiyā, navutiyā, dhenuyā, vadhuyā. 207. The vowel 'ā' (ā-kāra) in the feminine gender is called 'gha'. Examples: Saddhāya, kaññāya. 208. In the masculine and neuter genders, the augment 'sa' occurs before the suffix 'se'. Examples: Purisassa, aggissa, daṇḍissa, bhikkhussa, sayambhussa, cittassa. 209. In the feminine gender, the augment 'sa' occurs before the singular case endings substituted as 'saṃ' and 'sā'. Examples: Yassaṃ, yassā, amussaṃ, amussā. 210. The final vowel of words such as 'etā' and 'imā' becomes 'i' (ikāra) before the singular case endings substituted as 'saṃ' and 'sā'. Examples: Etissaṃ, etissā, imissaṃ, imissā, aññissaṃ, aññissā, aññatarissaṃ, aññatarissā, aññatamissaṃ, aññatamissaṃ, ekissaṃ, ekissā.
54: ## 211. Tāya vā. The final vowel (ā) of the word 'tā' optionally (vā) becomes 'i' when followed by the singular case substitutions 'saṃ' and 'sā'. Examples: Tissaṃ, tissā. (Due to the word 'vā') Tassaṃ, tassā. ## 212. Tetimāto sassa ssāya. After the words 'tā', 'etā', and 'imā', the suffix 'sa' is optionally (vā) substituted with 'ssāya'. Examples: Tissāya, tissā, etissāya, etissā, imissāya, imissā. ## 213. Rassattaṃ gho. The vowel (ā) called 'gha' becomes short (a) when followed by the singular case substitutions 'saṃ' and 'sā'. Examples: Tassaṃ, tassā, yassaṃ, yassā, sabbassaṃ, sabbassā. ## 214. Dvādito dasantānāgamo namhi. After numerals starting from 'dvi' up to 'dasa', the augment 'na' (nakārāgama) occurs when the suffix 'naṃ' follows. Examples: Dvinnam, tinnam, catunnam, pañcannam, channam, sattannam, aṭṭhannam, navannam, dasannam, ekādasannam, aṭṭhārasannam. ## 215. Ticatuto thiyaṃ issamassaṃ. In the feminine gender, after the words 'ti' and 'catu' (when the suffix 'naṃ' follows), the augments 'issaṃ' and 'assaṃ' occur respectively. Examples: Of the three feelings (Tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ), of the four women (Catassannaṃ itthīnaṃ). ## 216. Pato smiṃsmānaṃ amāvā. After the vowels (i, u) called 'pa', the suffixes 'smiṃ' and 'smā' are optionally (vā) substituted with 'aṃ' and 'ā' respectively. Examples: Matyaṃ, matiyaṃ, matyā, matiyā, pathabyaṃ, pathaviyaṃ, pathabyā, pathaviyā. ## 217. Nāsasmiṃnamā. After the vowels (i, u) called 'pa', the suffixes 'nā', 'sa', and 'smiṃ' are optionally (vā) substituted with 'ā'. Examples: One does not always attain happiness through deceit (Nikatyā sukham edhati). The moon shines by night (Ratyā ruccati cando). Throughout the three watches of the night (Ratyā tiyāmaṃ). The goddess Phussatī with beautiful limbs on the earth (Pathabyā cārupuvvaṅgī). Why say 'optionally' (vā)? An enemy endowed with wisdom is better (Matiyā upeto).
55: ## 218. Ādito aṃso. After the word 'ādi', the suffix 'smiṃ' is optionally (vā) substituted with 'aṃ' and 'o'. Examples: Ādiṃ, ādo, ādismiṃ, ādimhi. ## 219. Aññasmā ā ca. After words other than 'ādi', the suffix 'smiṃ' is optionally (vā) substituted with 'aṃ', 'o', and 'ā'. Examples: Those who bring offerings by day and by night (Divā ca ratto ca haranti ye baliṃ). Whether by day or by night (Divā vā yadi vā rattiṃ). There was a king in Bārāṇasī (Bārāṇasiṃ ahu rājā). Why say 'optionally' (vā)? O Great King, in Bārāṇasī (Bārāṇasyaṃ mahārāja), there is also the reading 'Bārāṇassaṃ'. ## 220. Sare jhalānamiyuvā. When a vowel follows, the vowels called 'jha' (i, ī) and 'la' (u, ū) are optionally (vā) substituted with 'iya' and 'uva'. Examples: Tiyantaṃ, pacchiyāgāre, aggiyāgāre, bhikkhuvāsane, puthuvāsane. Why say 'when a vowel follows'? Timalaṃ. Why say 'optionally' (vā)? Pañcahaṅgehi, cakkhāyatanaṃ. ## 221. Ikārassa ayo ṇānubandhe. When a vowel with the indicatory letter 'ṇa' follows, the vowel 'i' (ikāra) is substituted with 'aya'. Examples: Vatthuttayaṃ, atthadvayaṃ, or atthadayaṃ. ## 222. Passa yo. The vowel (i, ī) called 'pa' is substituted with 'ya' when a vowel substituted from a suffix follows. Examples: Nikatyā, nikatyaṃ, on the earth and on the mountain (Pathabyā pabbate ceva), standing on the earth (Pathabyaṃ ṭhito). ## 223. Pitussulopo nāṃhināssa ca yā vā. The vowel 'u' of the word 'pitu' is elided (lopa) before the suffix 'nā', and the suffix 'nā' is optionally (vā) substituted with 'yā'. Examples: Done by the father (Pityā kataṃ), or pitarā kataṃ. Here, the word 'pityā' should be understood as a masculine form that resembles a feminine form, like 'hetuyo', 'jantuyo', and 'adhipatiyā'. There is also the Pali: 'The marking done by the mother and the father is very good' (Matyā ca pityā ca kataṃ su sādhū).
56:
224. Due to these suffixes: yo, aṃ, nā, sa, smā, sa, smiṃ, and su, the 'o' of the word 'go' is substituted with 'āva' and 'ava'. (For example:) Gāvo, gavo gacchanti—The cows go. Bhonto gāvo, gavo tiṭṭhatha—O cows, stand still. Gāvo, gavo—[To] the cows. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ passati—He sees the cow. Gāvena, gavena—By the cow. Gāvassa, gavassa deti—He gives to the cow; santakaṃ vā—or the cow's property. Gāvā, gavā apeti—He departs from the cow. Gāve, gave—In the cow. Gāvesu, gavesu patiṭṭhitaṃ—It is established in the cows.

225. After the 'o' of the word 'go' has been substituted with 'āva', the suffix 'yo' is substituted with 'ī'. (Example:) Gāvī gacchanti—The cows go. Jano gāvī passati—The person sees the cows.

226. Due to the suffix 'aṃ', the final vowel (a) of the 'āva' substitution for the word 'go' is optionally substituted with 'u'. (Example:) It becomes gāvuṃ or gāvaṃ.

227. Following the word 'go', the suffix 'naṃ' is substituted with 'aṃ', and the 'o' of the word 'go' is substituted with 'ava'. (Example:) Gavañcetaramānānaṃ—Among the cows crossing the river (if the leader bull goes straight).

228. In an unelided (alutta) compound, when the word 'pati' follows, the suffix 'naṃ' following the word 'go' is substituted with 'aṃ', and the 'o' of the word 'go' is substituted with 'ava'. (Example:) Āyasmā Gavaṃpati—The Venerable Gavaṃpati. Muhuttajāto va gavaṃpatī yathā—Just like a newly born bull-king (touches the ground). Why is it said "in an unelided compound"? Because in an elided compound, it exists as Gopati—Lord of the cows.

229. In an elided (lutta) compound, the 'o' of the word 'go' is substituted with 'ava' whether a vowel or a consonant follows. (Example:) Gavassakaṃ—Cows and horses; gaveḷakaṃ—cows and goats; gavājinaṃ—cowhide (or leopard skin); sagavacaṇḍo—a cow that is fierce in its own herd; paragavacaṇḍo—a cow that is fierce in another's herd. Here, if someone asks, "How is the word 'gavapānaṃ' formed?", the answer is: In this word, the milk produced from cows is called 'gavaṃ'; because it is a drink, it is called 'pānaṃ'; when these two are combined, it is formed as 'gavapānaṃ'. If asked about words such as 'Sakyapuṅgavo', since the word 'puṅgava' here signifies 'the best' (seṭṭha), the formation of the word 'gava' should not be considered (by this rule).
57:
How so? In this context, the milk produced from cows is called 'gavaṃ'. Because of the sense of being drinkable, it is called 'pānaṃ'. Since it is both produced from cows and is a drink, it becomes 'gavapānaṃ'. How about in words such as 'Sakyapuṅgavo'? In this case, since the word 'puṅgava' denotes 'the best', the formation of the word 'gava' need not be considered.

230. When the suffix 'naṃ' follows, the entire word 'go' is optionally substituted with 'gu'. (Example:) Gunnaṃ deti (He gives to the cows), gunnaṃ siṅgāni (the horns of the cows).

231. According to the opinion of other teachers, when the suffixes su, naṃ, and hi follow, the entire word 'go' is optionally substituted with 'goṇa'. (Example:) Goṇesu, goṇānaṃ, goṇehi, goṇebhi. Because it says 'optionally' (vā), when the 'goṇa' substitution does not occur, forms like gosu, gonaṃ, gohi, and gobhi also exist.

232. Also when the remaining suffixes starting with 'si' follow (according to other teachers), the entire word 'go' is optionally substituted with 'goṇa'. (Example:) Goṇo, goṇā. Bho goṇa, bhavanto goṇā. Goṇaṃ, goṇe. Goṇena. Goṇassa. Goṇā, goṇasmā, goṇamhā. Goṇasmiṃ, goṇamhi. Because it says 'optionally', when the 'goṇa' substitution does not occur, forms like go and gāvo also exist.

233. Because it is derived from the root 'guṇa', the word 'go' should not be substituted with 'goṇa'. In our view, since it is accomplished by the power of the root 'guṇa āmantane' (guṇa in the sense of addressing), the substitution of 'go' with 'goṇa' is not desired.

234. For stems ending in u and ū, the final vowel is optionally substituted with uva, ava, or ura when the suffixes smiṃ and yo follow. (Example:) Bhuvi (on the earth or in the eyebrow), pasavo (beasts or goats), pasū, garavo (teachers), garū, caturo (four persons), cattāro.
58:
235. The suffix 'aṃ' and the letter 'ma' following the vowels i, ī, u, ū and the letters la, pa must be changed to niggahīta. Examples are: Isiṃ (the sage), mahesiṃ (the Buddha, the great sage), bhikkhuṃ (the monk), sayambhūṃ (the self-enlightened Buddha), aṭṭhiṃ (the bone or the seed), āyuṃ (life), rattiṃ (the night), itthiṃ (the woman), yāguṃ (rice gruel), vadhuṃ (the bride), pulliṅgaṃ (masculine gender), pumbhāvo (manhood), puṅkokilo (male cuckoo).

236. When the suffix aṃ, a substitution (ādesa), a suffix (paccaya), or an augment (āgama) follows, the preceding vowel should be elided in some cases, and that 'aṃ' etc. should remain in their original form (pakati). Examples are: Purisaṃ, purise, pāpaṃ, pāpe, pāpiyo (one more evil than another), pāpiṭṭho (the most evil), paropaṇṇāsa dhammā (dhammas exceeding fifty), saradosataṃ (for a hundred years). Why is it said "when the suffix aṃ, a substitution, a suffix, or an augment follows"? To prevent the elision of the vowel and the remaining in original form in cases like rattiyo, hetunā, etc. Why is it said "in some cases (kvaci)"? To prevent the operation of this rule in cases like bhikkhuṃ, sayambhūṃ, dhenuṃ, yāgu, bhikkhunī, gahapatānī, sammadakkhāto, etc. By the power of mentioning 'original form' (pakati), euphonic combination (sandhi) also occurs. Examples are: Seyyo (one better than another), seṭṭho (the best), jeyyo (one greater than another), jeṭṭho (the greatest).

237. When associated with the suffix aṃ, a substitution, a singular suffix, or the suffix yo, a vowel not termed 'gha' must be made short (rassa). Examples are: Itthiṃ, vadhuṃ, itthiyā, vadhuyā, itthiyo, vadhuyo, bhoti itthi, bhoti vadhu, sayambhūṃ, daṇḍiṃ, sayambhūnā, daṇḍinā, sayambhūmhā, sayambhūmhi, daṇḍino, bho sayambhū, bho daṇḍi.

238. When the suffix yo which is to be elided follows, a vowel not termed 'gha' does not undergo shortening (it remains long). Example: Sayambhū tiṭṭhanti (The self-enlightened Buddhas stand). Likewise, daṇḍī, itthī, vadhū. Bho sayambhū tumhe tiṭṭhatha (O self-enlightened Buddhas, you all stand).

239. Non-neuter stems do not undergo shortening when the suffix 'si' follows. Examples are: Sā itthī (that woman), so daṇḍī (that one with a staff), so sayambhū (that self-enlightened Buddha), sā vadhū (that bride), sā bhikkhunī (that nun).

240. Neuter stems undergo shortening when the suffix 'si' follows. Examples are: Sukhakāri dānaṃ (the gift that produces happiness), sukhakāri sīlaṃ (the virtue that produces happiness), sīghayāyi cittaṃ (the mind that travels swiftly), gotrabhū cittaṃ (the gotrabhū consciousness).
59:
241. After the word *uba*, the suffix *naṃ* becomes *innaṃ*. Example: *ubhinnaṃ*.

242. According to other teachers, after the word *dwi*, the suffix *naṃ* also becomes *innaṃ*. Example: *dvinnaṃ*.

243. After the numeral *ti*, the suffix *naṃ* becomes *iṇṇaṃ* or *iṇṇannaṃ*. Examples: *tiṇṇam*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*.

244. Because of the suffix *naṃ*, the numeral *dwi* becomes *duvi*. Example: *duvinnaṃ*.

245. The final vowel is lengthened (*dīgha*) because of the *yo* suffixes that have been elided, or the *yo* suffixes with the letter *ni*. Examples: *aggī*, *bhikkhū*, *rattī*, *yāgū*, *aṭṭhī*, *aṭṭhīni*, *āyū*, *āyūni*, *sabbāni*, *yāni*, *tāni*, *kāni*, *amūni*, *imāni*.

246. The final vowel is lengthened (*dīgha*) because of the suffixes *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*. Examples: *aggīsu*, *aggīnaṃ*, *aggīhi*, *bhikkhūsu*, *bhikkhūnaṃ*, *bhikkhūhi*, *purisānaṃ*. However, in this context, the lengthening does not occur in cases such as "*sukhettesu brahmacarīsū*" in order to preserve the meter (*vutti*).

247. The final vowel of numerals starting with *pañca* becomes *a* (*atta*) because of the suffixes *yo*, *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*. Examples: *pañca purisā*, *pañca purise*, *pañca itthiyo*, *pañca cittāni*, *cha*, *satta*, *aṭṭha*, *nava*, *dasa*. *pañcasu*, *pañcannaṃ*, *pañcahi*, *chasu*, *channaṃ*, *chahi*, *sattasu*, *sattannaṃ*, *sattahi*, *aṭṭhasu*, *aṭṭhannaṃ*, *aṭṭhahi*, *navasu*, *navannaṃ*, *navahi*, *dasasu*, *dasannaṃ*, *dasahi*. By the power of the word *anta*, the end of the word *cha* sometimes becomes long (*dīgha*) when followed by a consonant. Examples: *chārattaṃ vippavaseyya* (should live apart for six nights); *chāpi pācīnato ninnā vuttā* (six [rivers] are also said to incline towards the east).

248. When followed by the suffix *inī*, the end of the word *pati* becomes *a* (*atta*). Example: *nakulamātā gahapatānī* (the householder-wife who is the mother of Nakula).

249. Because of the suffixes *aṃ*, *yo*, *nā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *su*, *smā*, and *smiṃ*, the end of the suffix *ntu* becomes *a* (*atta*). Examples: *āyasmantaṃ*, *āyasmante*. *guṇavantaṃ*,
60:
*guṇavante*. *guṇavantena*, *guṇavantehi*, *guṇavantebhi*. *satimantena*, *satimantehi*, *satimantebhi*, *guṇavantassa*, *satimantassa*, *guṇavantānaṃ*, *satimantānaṃ*, *guṇavantesu*, *satimantesu*, *guṇavantasmā*, *guṇavantamhā*, *guṇavantā*, *himavantā āgatamha* (we have come from the Himālaya), *guṇavantasmiṃ*, *guṇavantamhi*, *guṇavante*. *himavante vasāmi* (I live in the Himālaya). *guṇavantesu*.

250. In the neuter gender, the end of the suffix *ntu* becomes *a* (*atta*) because of the *yo* suffixes, and the *yo* suffixes themselves become *i* (*itta*). Example: *guṇavanti kulāni* (virtuous families).

251. Because of the suffixes *aṃ* and *sa*, the entire suffix *ntu* optionally (*vā*) becomes *a* (*atta*). Examples: *satimaṃ bhikkhuṃ* or *satimantaṃ bhikkhuṃ*. *bandhumassa rañño* or *bandhumato rañño*.

252. Because of the suffix *si*, in some instances of verse, the suffix *ntu* optionally (*vā*) becomes *a* (*atta*). In this rule, the word "*katthaci*" refers to the context of verse. Examples: *himavanto va pabbato*. *puññavanto jutindharo*. *gatimanto satimanto, dhitimanto ca so isi*. Why is "*vā*" said? To indicate that the change does not occur in cases like *himavā pabbato*.

253. This rule, "It is accomplished in the sense expressed," should be understood as a governing rule for the subsequent rules.

254. When the word *aggi* is expressed, it is accomplished as *agginī* and *ginī*. All subsequent suffixes are obtained, such as *aggini*, *agginī*, *agginayo*, *agginiṃ*, etc. Similarly, *gini*, *ginī*, *ginayo*. The Pali usage of these two words has been shown below.
61:
255. *satte sattavāti*. When a being (*sattavā*) who clings to the aggregates of form, etc., is to be expressed, it is accomplished as '*sattava*'. As in: "You also are a noble being (*sattavo*)." All subsequent suffixes are obtained, such as *sattavā*, *sattavaṃ*, etc. Why is '*satte*' said? To prevent the form '*sattava*' in the sense of merely clinging, being particularly attached, or being stuck to the aggregates of form, etc.

256. *udake dakanti kanti ca*. When the word *udaka* is to be expressed, it is accomplished as '*daka*' and '*ka*'. All subsequent suffixes are obtained, such as *dakaṃ*, *dakāni*, *kaṃ*, *kāni*, etc. As in: "Flowers born on land and flowers born in water," "Ripe mango and cold water," "He has crossed the difficult path devoid of water" (*kantāraṃ*).

257. *udakဿ kvaci kalāpo ca*. In some instances, the letter '*ka*' of the word *udaka* is elided. As in: *udadhi*, *mahodadhi*, "In the middle of the forest, the dark-blue water flows," "One who is heedless while carrying water," "The water-pot also is filled." Why is '*kvaci*' said? To prevent the elision of '*ka*' in cases like: "Desiring to carry water for those parents," "Taking the water-pot." In this rule, although the four words starting with '*udadhi*' should strictly be mentioned in the section on Sandhi (*sandhikappa*), they are brought here to show the distinct appearance of the three words *ka*, *daka*, and *udaka*, and to show that the letter '*ka*' in the word *udaka* is elided in some places.

258. *mūḷhe muddāti*. When the sense of confusion (*mūḷha*) is to be expressed, it is accomplished as '*muddha*'. *muddho*, *muddhā*.

259. *yosvattamakatara sso jho*. Because of the *yo* suffixes, the vowel named '*jha*' (*i*, *ī*) which has not been shortened becomes '*a*'. *aggayo*, *munayo*, *isayo*.

260. *lo ca vevosu*. The vowel named '*la*' (*u*, *ū*) which has not been shortened also becomes '*a*' because of the substitutions '*ve*' and '*vo*'. As in: "Monks, there are these two extremes," "Friends, monks," "Monks, listen to my words," "He addressed the monks, saying 'Monks'," *hetave*, *hetavo*.
62:
## 261. Mātulādīnamanto āno īpaccaye.

Due to the suffix ī, the final part of words such as mātula is substituted with āna. Examples: mātulānī (aunt), ayyikānī (grandmother), varuṇānī (consort of the deity Varuna), and sākiyānī (Sakyan princess). Why is "īpaccaye" stated? It is to indicate that the substitution with āna does not occur in instances such as bhikkhunī, jālinī, and gahapatānī.

## 262. Nadiyā dissa jjā yosuvā.

Before the yo case endings, the ī of the word nadī is optionally substituted with jjā. Example: Najjāyo suppatiṭṭhāyo (The rivers have good landing places). Najjāyo is the same as nadiyo (rivers).

## 263. Yohī saha jjo.

Together with the yo and hi case endings, the ī of the word nadī is optionally substituted with jjo. Examples: Najjo sandanti (The rivers flow), najjo passati (He sees the rivers). Why is "vā" (optionally) stated? To indicate that it does not occur in instances such as nadiyo sandanti and nadiyo passati.

## 264. Nādyekavacanehi jjā smiṃ nā jjañca.

Together with the singular case endings starting from nā, the ī of the word nadī is optionally substituted with jjā. Together with the smiṃ case ending, it is also substituted with jjaṃ. Examples: Najjā kataṃ (done by the river), najjā pupphaṃ dadāti (gives a flower to the river), najjā apeti (departs from the river), najjā nerañjarāya tīre (on the bank of the Nerañjarā river). Najjā, najjaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in the river). Why is "vā" stated? To indicate that the aforementioned rule does not apply in instances such as nadiyā and nadiyaṃ.

## 265. Sabbato hissa bhi vā.

After all genders, the hi case ending is optionally substituted with bhi. Examples: purisebhi, purisehi, itthībhi, itthīhi, cittebhi, cittehi.

## 266. Smāsmiṃnaṃ yathākkamaṃ yathārahaṃ mhāmhi.

After all genders, the smā and smiṃ case endings are substituted with mhā and mhi respectively, in order and as appropriate. Examples: purisamhā, purisasmā, purisamhi, purisasmiṃ. cittamhā, cittasmā, cittamhi, cittasmiṃ. According to the Pāḷi method, the words mhā and mhi are seen following some feminine stems only in verses (gāthā): "Kusāvatimhi nagare" (in the city of Kusāvatī), "yathā balākayonimhi" (as in the womb of a crane). It should be understood that these are letter transpositions for Kusāvatiyaṃ and balākayoniyaṃ.
63:
Why is "yathārahaṃ" (as appropriate) stated? To prevent [this substitution] in instances such as satthārā apeti (departs from the teacher) and satthari patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in the teacher). Alternatively, it should be understood that the word "yathārahaṃ" is intended to show that, according to the Pāḷi method, the words mhā and mhi are not found after feminine stems in prose (cuṇṇiya).

## 267. Katākārehi na timehi.

After the words ta and ima which have been changed to the letter a, the substitutions of mhā and mhi for the smā and smiṃ case endings do not occur. Examples: asmā, asmiṃ. Why is "katākārehi" stated? To allow for forms like tamhā, tamhi, imamhā, imamhi.

## 268. Suhisu liṅgākāro e.

Before the su and hi case endings, the final a of a stem is substituted with e. Examples: sabbesu, yesu, tesu, kesu, purisesu, imesu, kusalesu, tumhesu, amhesu, sabbehi, yehi.

## 269. Sabbakatarādayo sabbanāmāni.

Words such as sabba and katara are pronouns (sabbanāma). Their specific forms have been fully explained in all their varieties below.

## 270. Sabbanāmānaṃ pana naṃmhi.

The final a of pronouns is substituted with e before the naṃ case ending. Examples: sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ, kateresaṃ, kateresānaṃ.

## 271. Ato nāyena.

After an a-kāra stem, the nā case ending is substituted with ena. Examples: sabbena, yena, tena, kena, anena, purisena, rūpena.

## 272. Sissa o.

After an a-kāra stem, the si case ending is substituted with o. Examples: sabbo, yo, so, ko, amuko, puriso.

## 273. So vā ṭhāne.

After an a-kāra stem, the nā case ending is optionally substituted with so in appropriate places. Examples: atthaso (by way of meaning), byañjanaso (by way of phrasing), akkharaso (by way of letters), suttaso (by way of suttas), padeso (by way of parts), yasaso (by way of fame/retinue), upāyaso (by way of means).
64:
Upāyaso (by means). Why say "vā"? To prevent it from occurring in 'atthena' (by meaning), 'byañjanena' (by consonant), etc. Why say "ṭhāne"? To prevent it from occurring in 'purisena' (by the man), 'cittena' (by the mind), etc.

274. Dīghorato smāssa. After the words 'dīgha' and 'ora', the 'smā' suffix is replaced by 'so' in some places. Dīghaso (by length). (In some places) it becomes dīghamā (by length), oraso (from this side), oramā (from this side).

275. Yonam ninañcāe. After an 'a' ending, the nominative 'yo' and accusative 'yo' suffixes are respectively replaced by 'ā' and 'e'. Likewise, the 'ni' which replaces nominative 'yo' and accusative 'yo' are replaced by 'ā' and 'e' in some places. Purisā tiṭṭhanti (The men stand), purise passati (He sees the men), rūpā tiṭṭhanti (The forms stand), rūpe passati (He sees the forms). Why say "vā"? Because there are forms like rūpāni tiṭṭhanti (The forms stand), rūpāni passanti (They see the forms).

276. Smāsmimnaṃ. After an 'a' ending, the 'smā' and 'smiṃ' suffixes are respectively replaced by 'ā' and 'e' in some places. Purisā apeti (He departs from the man), or purisasmā (from the man). Purise patiṭṭhitaṃ (It is established in the man), or purisasmiṃ (in the man).

277. Tiliggato ṭhānesiyoname. After the three genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—the 'si' and 'yo' suffixes are replaced by 'e' in appropriate places and in some instances. Vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge (Like a woodland thicket with blossoming tops). Ke ca chave pāthikaputte (What are the wretched sons of Pāthika like?). Ke paṇḍite sabbakāmadade (Who are the wise ones who give all desired things?). Dīgharattaṃ bhattā me bhavissati (My husband will be for a long time). Tato vātātape ghore, sañjāte paṭihaññati (Moreover, the fierce wind and heat of the sun are dispelled). The meaning should be connected as "Vihāre na paṭihaññati". Rohitā naḷape siṅgu (The carps, the naḷapa fish, and the large fish are many). Bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissanti (Both fools and the wise, having run and wandered on, will make an end of suffering). These words are spoken by way of the masculine singular and plural. Sukhe dukkhe (Happiness, suffering), aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate (Eight hundred abodes of Nagas). These words are spoken by way of the neuter singular and plural. Viratte kosiyāyane (The detached woman of the Kosiya clan). These words...
65:
These terms are spoken by virtue of the singular of the feminine gender. What is the purpose of the word "vā"? It is to prevent the substitution of "e" in cases such as vanappagumbo, sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, and virattā kosiyāyanī. Why is "ṭhāne" said? It is to prevent the substitution of "e" in cases such as rājā, attā, kaññā, and brāhmaṇī.

278. That which is the benefit in actions such as cutting is called tadattha. In the action of cutting, etc., that material object which is the benefit is called tadattha.

279. In the sense of tadattha, the dative singular is substituted with -āya and -atthaṃ. After a stem ending in -a standing in the sense of tadattha, the dative singular is substituted with -āya, and the substitution -atthaṃ also occurs. "Let this many trees be cut for the sake of a sacrificial post (yūpatthāya)." Here, the sacrificial post is the benefit of the action of cutting trees. "For the benefit, for the welfare, for the happiness of devas and humans." For the benefit (attatthaṃ). For the welfare (hitatthaṃ). For the happiness (sukhatthaṃ). For what purpose (kimatthaṃ)? For that purpose (tadatthaṃ). For the purpose of oil, etc., for wiping the bowl. For the purpose of the arising of my merit and the increase of knowledge for completing the text.

280. In some instances, the dative singular occurs after masculine and neuter stems in the sense of the accusative, instrumental, ablative, genitive, and locative cases; that case ending is also substituted with -āya.

281. These three substitutions do not occur after pronouns. After pronouns, the three substitutions -ā, -e, and -āya do not occur for the case endings smā, smiṃ, and sa. Sabbasmā, sabbasmiṃ, sabbassa. Yasmā, yasmiṃ, yassa. Tasmā, tasmiṃ, tassa. Imasmā, imasmiṃ, imassa. Other pronouns should also be applied in this manner.

282. Alternatively, after some pronouns, the case endings smā and smiṃ are substituted with -ā and -e. Those forms are rare. Forms together with the locative such as "sabbe" are seen in various Niddesa Pāḷi and other texts. However, the Great Elder Yamaka taught the locative and ablative forms as "sabbe, sabbā," etc.
66:
283. In the place of the five singular case endings—nā, sa, smā, sa, and smiṃ—after the suffix -ā named Gha, the substitution -āya occurs. (Example) Done by the maiden (kaññāya). Gives to the maiden. Departs from the maiden. The maiden's property. Established in the maiden.

284. After the vowels i, ī, u, and ū named Pa, the substitution -yā occurs (in the place of the five case endings). (Example) Rattiyā (by/because of/to/from/of/in the night). Itthiyā. Deviyā. Dhenuyā. Vadhuyā.

285. After the word sakha, the vocative si-suffix named Ga is substituted with -a or -ā. (Example) O friend (bho sakha). O friend (bho sakhā). Regarding the substitution of -ā for the Ga-suffix after the word sakha, there is this Pāḷi text—
"Hey, friend cobra, why do you abandon me?"

286. In the view of other teachers, the substitutions -i, -ī, and -e occur in the place of the Ga-suffix after the word sakha. (Example) O friend (bho sakhi). O friend (bho sakhī). O friend (bho sakhe).

287. After words such as brahma and muni, the substitution -e for the Ga-suffix occurs optionally. (Example) O Brahma, (preach) the sublime Dhamma among humans. O Great Brahma, this mountain is (Mount Gandhamādana). O Great Sage (Mahāmune), remain for an aeon. O Seer (Ise), let a son be born. O Venerable One (Bhadante), now the trees (are red) like glowing embers, and so forth. What is the purpose of saying "vā" (optionally)? It is to indicate that there are instances where the substitution -e does not occur. (Example) O Great Brahma, I ask you.

288. After the suffix -ā named Gha, the substitution -e for the Ga-suffix always occurs. (Example) O foolish woman (bāle), come and ask for forgiveness. O noble lady (ayye). O maiden (kaññe). O Kharādiya.

289. In the context of a compound (samāsa), the substitution -e for the Ga-suffix also occurs after words such as mātu. (Example) O Mother of Nanda (Nandamāte), it is wonderful. O Mother of Nanda, it is marvelous. O daughter of the wealthy man. O princess. What is the purpose of saying "samāse"? It is to indicate that the substitution -e does not occur if it is not a compound. (Example) O mother (bhooti mātā). O daughter (bhooti dhītā).
67:
290. After words such as amma, the vocative case ending (Ga) never reaches the substitution of -e. O mother (ammā), O mother (annā), O father (or mother/child) (tātā).

291. After the short vowels (i, u, ū) named La, the vocative plural Yo-suffix should be substituted with -ve or -vo. O monks (bhikkhave, bhikkhavo), O causes (hetave, hetavo), O beings (jantave, jantavo).

292. After those named Jha (i, ī) and those named La (u, ū), the Sa-suffix should optionally be substituted with -no. Of the fire (aggino), of the fire (aggissa). Of the staff-bearer (daṇḍino), of the staff-bearer (daṇḍissa). Of the monk (bhikkhuno), of the monk (bhikkhussa). Of the self-become Buddha (sayambhuno), of the self-become Buddha (sayambhussa).

293. After those named Gha (a), Pa (i, u, ū), Jha, and La, the Yo-suffix should optionally be dropped. Maidens (kaññā, kaññāyo), nights (rattī, rattiyo), women (itthī, itthiyo), daughters-in-law (vadhū, vadhuyo), gruels (yāgū, yāguyo), those people (amū, amuyo), fires (aggī, aggayo), monks (bhikkhū, bhikkhavo), self-become Buddhas (sayambhū, sayambhuvο), bones (aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni), lives (āyū, āyūni).

294. After those named La (u, ū), the Yo-suffix should optionally be substituted with -vo or -no as far as possible. Monks (bhikkhavo), monks (bhikkhū). Self-become Buddhas (sayambhuvο), self-become Buddhas (sayambhū). Causes (hetavo), causes (hetū), causes (hetuyo). Beings (jantavo), beings (jantuno), beings (jantū), beings (jantuyo). The inclusion of the word "ca" has the benefit of restricting (establishing) the substitution of -vo and -no in certain u-ending pronouns. Those men stand (amū purisā tiṭṭhanti), look at those men (amū purise passatha).

295. Due to the Sa-suffix, the word amha together with its case ending should be substituted with mamaṃ. It is given to me (mamaṃ dīyate), my retinue (mamaṃ pariggaho).

296. Due to the nominative plural Yo-suffix, the word amha together with its case ending should be substituted with mayaṃ. We go (mayaṃ gacchāma). Why is "amhasse" said? In "purisā tiṭṭhanti" (men stand), the substitution mayaṃ does not occur because it is not the word amha. Why is "yomhi" said? In "ahaṃ gacchāmi" (I go), the substitution mayaṃ does not occur because it is not the Yo-suffix. Why is "paṭhame" said? In "amhākaṃ passasi" (you see us), the substitution mayaṃ does not occur because it is not the nominative case.
68:
In this treatise, the v-kāra and m-kāra of the suffixes -vantu and -mantu are separated from the vowel, and to make pronunciation easier, the vowel 'a' is taken, and it is referred to as the '-antu suffix'. A part of a suffix also receives the name of the suffix itself. The substitution (ādesa) of that -antu suffix is also prescribed according to the usage.

297. Before the first yo-inflection, the substitution of '-nto' as well as the substitution of '-ā' occurs at the end of the -antu suffix along with its inflection. (Example:) Guṇavanto tiṭṭhanti — Virtuous ones stand. Satimanto tiṭṭhanti — Mindful ones stand. Satimā tiṭṭhanti — Mindful ones stand. Cakkhumā andhīkā honti — Those with the eye of wisdom become blind (by following the will of women).

298. When followed by the se-inflection, the substitution of '-ntassa' at the end of the -antu suffix along with its inflection occurs optionally (vibhāsā). (Example:) Sīlavantassa, sīlavato vā — To the virtuous one.

299. When followed by the si-inflection, the substitution of '-ā' for the -antu suffix along with its inflection occurs invariably (niccaṃ). (Example:) Guṇavā, paññavā, satimā, dhitimā — One who has virtue, one who has wisdom, one who has mindfulness, one who has fortitude (effort).

300. In the neuter gender, when followed by the si-inflection, the substitution of '-aṃ' for the -antu suffix along with its inflection occurs optionally. (Example:) Guṇavaṃ cittaṃ tiṭṭhati — The virtuous mind stands. Rucimaṃ pupphaṃ — A flower with a pleasing color. Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? Vaṇṇavantaṃ agandhakaṃ — A flower that has color but no scent (this is to show that the substitution of 'aṃ' does not occur in such cases).

301. According to another opinion of the teachers, the substitution of 'aṃ' occurs when followed by 'ga' (the name for vocative si) for the -antu suffix along with its inflection. (Example:) Bho guṇavaṃ — O virtuous one. Although in the Dispensation (Sāsana) there is no vocative (addressing) with a niggahīta, in the passage 'yassassi naṃ paññavantaṃ visayhā', the niggahīta (anusāra) is added after the word paññavanta to preserve the heavy syllable (garu) of the verse. 'Naṃ' is a particle that completes the verse...
69:
...it is a particle (nipāta). It means 'Bho yasassī paññavanta'. Therefore, in this instance 'Bho guṇava', the niggahīta should not occur.

302. In our opinion, when followed by the si-inflection named 'ga', the substitutions of 'a' and 'ā' (avanna) for the -antu suffix along with its inflection occur as appropriate. (Example:) Bho guṇava, bho guṇavā — O virtuous one. Bho satima, bho satimā — O mindful one. Pāde vandāmi cakkhuma — O Blessed One who possesses the five types of eyes, I pay homage to your feet. Evaṃ jānāhi pāpima — Know thus, O evil Mara. Taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā — O Blessed One, the factors of enlightenment are indeed excellent. Kathaṃ nu bhagavā tuyhaṃ — O Blessed One, why did your disciple die? Āyasmā tissa — The Venerable Tissa.

303. When followed by the nā, smiṃ, and sa inflections, the substitutions of 'tā', 'ti', and 'to' for the -antu suffix occur respectively and optionally. (Example:) Guṇavatā, guṇavantena — By the virtuous one. Guṇavati, guṇavantasmiṃ — In the virtuous one. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa — To/Of the virtuous one. Satimatā, satimantena. Satimati, satimantasmiṃ. Satimato, satimantassa.

304. When followed by the naṃ-inflection, the substitution of 'taṃ' for the -antu suffix occurs optionally. (Example:) Guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ — To/Of the virtuous ones. Satimataṃ, satimantānaṃ.

305. In the neuter gender, when followed by the si-inflection, the substitution of 'imaṃ' for the word 'idaṃ' occurs optionally. (Example:) Imaṃ cittaṃ tiṭṭhati, idaṃ cittaṃ tiṭṭhati vā — This mind stands.

306. In genders other than neuter (masculine and feminine), the substitution of 'ayaṃ' for the word 'idaṃ' occurs invariably. (Example:) Ayaṃ puriso — This man. Ayaṃ itthī — This woman.
70:
## 307. Yo-aṃ-nādīsu ca telingikassimo vā.
For the word 'idaṃ' used in the three genders, the substitution of 'ima' occurs optionally when followed by the inflections yo, aṃ, nā, etc. The inclusion of the word 'ca' is for the purpose of excluding the requirement of the entire word with its inflection (savibhattiggahaṇa). Example: Ime purisā tiṭṭhanti — These men stand; Ime purise passatha — Look at these men. Imaṃ purisaṃ — This man; Imaṃ itthiṃ — This woman; Imaṃ cittaṃ passati — He looks at this mind, or Idaṃ cittaṃ passati. Imā gāthāyo — These verses; imāya — by this woman; imāhi — by these women; imissāya — to this woman; imissaṃ — in this woman; imāsaṃ — to these women; imāsu — in these women; imassa — to this person; imesaṃ — to these persons; imasmā — from this person; imehi — by these persons; imasmiṃ — in this person; imesu — in these persons.

## 308. Amussāduṃ-maṃ-sisu napuṃsake.
For the word 'amu' in the neuter gender along with its inflection, the substitution of 'aduṃ' occurs when followed by the aṃ and si inflections. Example: Aduṃ pupphaṃ passati — He looks at this flower; Aduṃ pupphaṃ virocati — This flower is beautiful.

## 309. Itthipumanapuṃsakasaṅkhyaṃ.
This phrase 'itthipumanapuṃsakasaṅkhyaṃ' should be understood as being for the purpose of governance (adhikāra). This is the original commentary (vutti); what follows is the subsequent commentary (anuvutti) that clarifies the intention. Because they express feminine, masculine, and neuter, the forms of the numerals called feminine-masculine-neuter are now being stated by us. In this statement, both the words for feminine-masculine-neuter and the numerals are governed.

## 310. Yosu dvinnaṃ dve-duve.
For the numeral 'dvi' (two) in the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders along with its inflection, the substitutions of 'dve' and 'duve' occur when followed by the yo-inflections. Example: Dve itthiyo — Two women; dve dhammā — two dhammas; dve rūpāni — two forms; dve napuṃsakā — two neuters; duve kaññāyo — two maidens; duve samaṇā — two recluses; duve cittāni — two minds.

## 311. Ticatunnaṃ tisso-catasso tayo-cattāro tīṇi-cattāri.
For the numerals 'ti' (three) and 'catu' (four) in the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders along with their inflections, these substitutions—'tisso', 'catasso', 'tayo', 'cattāro', 'tīṇi', and 'cattāri'—occur when followed by the yo-inflections. Example: Tisso vedanā — Three feelings; catasso disā — four directions. Three—
71:
People, three people (acc.), four men, four men (acc.). Three bases (āyatana), four noble truths.

## 312. Ubhūbhayato yonemo.
When the pronouns 'ubha' and 'ubhaya' occur in the feminine, masculine, or neuter genders, the 'yo' case endings following them are changed to 'o'. Examples: two princes, two princes (acc.), two women, two feet. Two gods and humans, two women, two minds.

## 313. Suhisu anto ca.
The final letter of the word 'ubha' is also changed to 'o' before the 'su' and 'hi' case endings. Examples: at both ends, in two men, in two women, on both sides, in two minds, with both hands, with both arms, with two minds. The teachers also desire the forms 'ubehi', 'ubebhi', and 'ubesu'; the formation of those forms is not difficult.

## 314. Rājassa savibhattikassase rañño rājino.
For the word 'rāja' together with its case ending, the substitutions 'rañño' and 'rājino' occur before the 'se' case ending. Examples: [He] gave a gift to the king, the king's country, the practice of Dhamma is pleasing to the king, the king's property.

## 315. Naṃ mhi raññaṃ vā.
Before the 'naṃ' case ending, the substitution 'raññaṃ' optionally occurs. Examples: raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ (of the kings).

## 316. Nāmhi raññaā rājinā.
Before the 'nā' case ending, the substitutions 'raññā' and 'rājinā' occur. Examples: by that king, by King Sabbadatta.

## 317. Smiṃmhi raññe rājini.
Before the 'smiṃ' case ending, the substitutions 'raññe' and 'rājini' occur. Examples: established in the king, established in the king.

## 318. Tumhāmhassa tayi mayi.
For the words 'tumha' and 'amha', together with the 'smiṃ' case ending, the substitutions 'tayi' and 'mayi' occur. Examples: in you, in me.
72:
319. When the 'si' case ending follows, the entire word 'amha' together with its case ending is changed to 'ahaṃ' or 'ahakaṃ'. For example: ahaṃ gacchāmi (I go), ahakaṃ gacchāmi (I go), ahakañca cittavasānubhāsitaṃ (There is also the meaning of 'I' which is spoken according to the desire of the mind).

320. When the 'si' case ending follows, the word 'tumha' (which is other than 'amha') together with its case ending is changed to 'tuvaṃ' or 'tvaṃ'. The word 'tumha' is indicated by the term 'itarassa'. For example: tuvaṃ satthā (You are the teacher), tvaṃ senāpati (You are the general).

321. When the 'se' case ending follows, the words 'tumha' and 'amha' together with their case endings are respectively changed to 'tava' and 'mama', or 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ'. For example: tava, mama, tuyhaṃ, mayhaṃ (to you, to me; or of you, of me).

322. When the 'aṃ' case ending follows, the words 'tumha' and 'amha' together with their case endings are changed to 'taṃ' and 'maṃ', or 'tuvaṃ' and 'mamaṃ'. For example: taṃ, maṃ, tuvaṃ, mamaṃ (you [acc.], me [acc.]).

323. When the 'nā' and 'smiṃ' case endings follow, the words 'tumha' and 'amha' together with their case endings are changed to 'tayā' and 'mayā'. For example: tayā, mayā (by you / in you, by me / in me).

324. When the 'aṃ' case ending follows, the entire word 'tumha' together with its case ending is respectively changed to 'tuvaṃ' or 'tvaṃ'. For example: kaliṅgarassa tuvaṃ manye (I think of you as chaff), kaṭṭhassa tvaṃ manye (I think of you as wood), ahaṃ tvaṃ māressāmi (I will kill you)—this is the kind of usage found in the Commentaries.

325. When the second, fourth, or sixth case endings follow the words 'tumha' and 'amha' which stand after another word, they are respectively changed to 'vo' and 'no' together with their case endings. For example: pahāya vo gamissāmi (Having abandoned you, I will go), mā no ajja vikantiṃsu (Let them not cut us today), dhammaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi (O monks, I will teach you the Dhamma), saṃvibhajetha no rajjena (Share with us the kingdom's wealth), tuṭṭhosmi vo bhikkhave pakatiyā (O monks, I am pleased with you by your nature), satthā no bhagavā anuppatto (Our teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived). Why is 'navā' (optionally) said? It is to prevent the substitution in places such as 'eso amhākaṃ satthā' (This person is our teacher). Why is 'tumhamhākaṃ' said? It is to prevent the substitution in places such as 'ete isayo passasi' (Do you see these sages?), because they are not 'tumha' or 'amha'.
73:
For what purpose is the term 'padasmā' (after a word) included? It is to prevent the substitution in places such as 'tumhākaṃ satthā' (where there is no preceding word). For what purpose is the term 'dutiyācatutthīchaṭṭhīsu' included? It is to prevent the substitution in places such as 'gacchatha tumhe' (where the case endings are not the second, fourth, or sixth).

326. Due to the following fourth or sixth singular case endings, the substitutions 'te' and 'me' optionally occur in place of 'tumha' and 'amha' respectively, when they follow a preceding word. (For example:) "I give you (the brahmin) five excellent villages." "Give me an excellent village." "This is your country." "This person is my son."

327. The substitutions 'te' and 'me' do not occur due to the second singular case ending. (For example:) "I wish to see you (Prince Hatthipāla) healthy for a hundred years." "That person speaks to me."

328. Due to the third singular case ending, the substitutions 'te' and 'me' optionally occur respectively. (For example:) "Evil was done by you," "tayā kataṃ pāpaṃ." "Evil was done by me," "mayā kataṃ pāpaṃ."

329. Due to the plural case endings, the substitutions 'vo' and 'no' occur respectively. (For example:) "The deed was done by you (plural)." "The deed was done by us."

330. Due to the first plural (yo) case ending, the substitutions 'vo' and 'no' also occur. (For example:) "You (plural) should go to the village." "We shall go to the village."
74:
331. Due to the si inflection, the substitution of ā along with the inflection occurs optionally at the end of the word Puma. (Example:) "The man stands." Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? Because it is not always present in such places as "Pumo sadā na vijjati."

332. At the end of words such as Maghava and Yuva, the substitution of ā occurs always due to the si inflection. (Example:) "Maghavā (Sakka)", "Yuvā (a youth)".

333. In the view of some teachers, the substitution of aṃ along with the inflection occurs at the end of the word Puma due to the vocative singular inflection. (Example:) "O man!"

334. In a compound (samāsa) also, the substitution of aṃ at the end of the word Puma occurs optionally. (Example:) "A group of women, men, and neuters." Why is 'vibhāsā' (optionally) said? To prevent the substitution of aṃ in places like "itthipumanapuṃsakā".

335. Due to the yo inflections, the substitution of āno along with the inflection occurs at the end of the word Puma. (Example:) "Men", "O men!"

336. Due to the smiṃ inflection, the substitution of āne along with the inflection occurs optionally at the end of the word Puma. (Example:) "Established in the man" (pumāne) or "pume".

337. Due to the hi inflection, the substitution of āne occurs at the end of the word Puma. (Example:) "By men", "From men". Why is the word 'vibhatti' (inflection) mentioned again? It is to exclude the term 'savibhatti' (along with the inflection).

338. Due to the sa, smā, and su inflections, the substitution of u occurs optionally at the end of the words Puma, Kamma, and Thāma. (Example:) "Of the man" (pumuno), "pumassa". "He departs from the man" (pumunā), or "pumasmā". "Of the deed".
75:
Kammassa (kammuno). Freed from the deed (kammunā), or kammasmā. Thāmuno (thāmassa). Freed from strength (thāmunā), or thāmasmā.

339. Ā vā susmiṃ. The substitution of ā at the end of the word Puma occurs optionally due to the su inflection. Pumāsu or pumesu.

340. Nāmhi ca. The substitutions of ā and u at the end of the word Puma occur optionally due to the nā inflection. Pumānā kataṃ, pumunā or pumena.

341. Kammaṃtassa akārukārā. The substitutions of a and u at the end of the word Kamma occur optionally due to the nā inflection. Kammanā kataṃ phalaṃ (The result is produced by the deed), kammunā or kammena.

342. Kvaci yuvādģnamā sunāsu. The substitution of ā at the end of words such as Yuva occurs optionally in some places due to the su and nā inflections. Yuvāsu. Yuvānā kataṃ, or yuvena. Maghavāsu. Maghavānā kataṃ, or maghavena.

343. Sabbāsvāna. The substitution of āna at the end of words such as Yuva occurs optionally in some places due to all inflections. Yuvāno tiṭṭhati (The youth stands), yuvānā tiṭṭhanti (The youths stand). Yuvānaṃ or yuvaṃ passati (Sees the youth). Yuvāne or yuve passati (Sees the youths). The remaining inflections should be completed fully. Maghavāno tiṭṭhati, maghavā tiṭṭhati (Sakka stands). Maghavānā tiṭṭhanti (Sakkas stand). Maghavānaṃ or maghavaṃ passatha (Look at Sakka). Maghavāne or maghave passati (Sees the Sakkas). The remaining inflections should be completed fully. In this context, the method "Maghavā, Maghavanto" is also obtained.

344. Tumhamhehi namākaṃ. After the words Tumha and Amha, the naṃ inflection is substituted with ākaṃ. Tumhākaṃ (of you, to you), amhākaṃ (of us, to us).

345. Aṃānañca appathamoyo. After those words Tumha and Amha, the yo inflection other than the nominative is substituted with ākaṃ, aṃ, and āna. Tumhākaṃ passāmi (I see you), or tumhe passāmi. Amhākaṃ passasi (You see us), or amhe passasi. In this manner, tumhaṃ, tumhānaṃ. amhaṃ, amhānaṃ.
76:
346. Matantare sassa vā aṃ. In another view of the teachers, the sa inflection following the words Tumha and Amha is optionally substituted with aṃ. It is given to you (tumhaṃ), it is given to you (tava). Your possession (tumhaṃ pariggaho), your possession (tava pariggaho). To me/of me (amhaṃ, mama).
