347. Sabbanāmakārato yo-pathamo e. The nominative yo inflection following a pronoun (sabbanāma) ending in a is substituted with e. All (sabbe), those who (ye), they (te), who? (ke), these (ime), you (tumhe). It is said, "Why should we do?" (kathaṃ amhe karomase).

348. Dvande ṭhitā vā. The nominative yo inflection following a pronoun ending in a situated in a dvanda compound is optionally substituted with e. Katarakatame, or katarakatamā.

349. Nāñño sabbanāmavidhi. Except for the substitution of e for the yo inflection following a pronoun ending in a situated in a dvanda compound, no other pronominal rules should be applied. To the front and back (pubbāparānaṃ), to the northeast (pubbuttarānaṃ), to the below and above (adhuttarānaṃ).

350. Tatiyātappurise ca. In a tatiyā-tappurisa compound also, other pronominal rules should not be applied. To the woman who was first by a month (māsapubbāya itthiyā), to the men or women who were first by a month (māsapubbānaṃ purisānaṃ, itthģnaṃ vā).

351. Bahubbģhismiñca. In a bahubbģhi compound also, other pronominal rules should not be applied. To the woman who previously had a dear husband (piyapubbāya itthiyā), to the women who previously had dear husbands or to the men who previously had dear wives (piyapubbānaṃ itthģnaṃ, purisānaṃ vā).

352. Hoti disāsabbanāmānaṃ. For pronouns denoting directions, pronominal rules do indeed apply in a bahubbģhi compound. In the southeast corner (dakkhiṇapubbassaṃ), to the southeast corner (dakkhiṇapubbassā). In the northeast corner (uttarapubbassaṃ), to the northeast corner (uttarapubbassā).

353. Sabbanāmato naṃ saṃsānaṃ. The naṃ inflection following a pronoun is substituted with saṃ and sānaṃ. To whom/of whom? (katamesaṃ, katamesānaṃ). To which women/of which women? (katamāsaṃ, katamāsānaṃ). To all/of all (sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ).
77: Sabbāsaṃ, sabbāsānaṃ. Yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yāsaṃ, yāsānaṃ. Tesaṃ, tesānaṃ. Tāsaṃ, tāsānaṃ. Kesaṃ, kesānaṃ. Kāsaṃ, kāsānaṃ. Imesaṃ, imesānaṃ. Imāsaṃ, imāsānaṃ. Amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ.## 354. Rājassa sunamhisu rāju.Due to the suffixes su, naṃ, and hi, the end of the word rāja is changed to rāju. Rājūsu, rājūnaṃ, rājūhi, rājūbi.## 355. Kvaci samāsuttarapadatthe.In some instances, words such as rāja that stand as the final member of a compound are to be declined according to the method of the word purisa. Mahārājo, cattāro mahārājā (the four great kings). Mahārājaṃ, mahārāje. Mahārājena, Sivirājena (sent by the great King Sivi). Mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, Dhammarājassa satthuno (of the Teacher who is the King of Dhamma). Mahārājānaṃ. Mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ devarājānaṃ, saṅgāmo paccupaṭṭhito (A battle between the two kings of gods has arisen). Nikkhamante mahārāje (When the great king was departing). Mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhi, mahārājesu. O great king (Bho mahārāja), O great kings (Bhavanto mahārājā).In the same way, this applies to phrases such as "Sabbasakho bhāvitatto" (Friend of all, one with a developed self). Even in non-compounds, it should be understood as rājānaṃ by the power of the dative and genitive cases. This is because the Pāḷi text "Ārādhayati rājānaṃ" (He pleases the king) is seen. Why is "kvaci" (in some cases) stated? It is to show that in cases like mahārājūsu, mahārājūnaṃ, mahārājūhi, etc., the purisa declension is not followed.## 356. Idasse sabbassa.Due to the suffixes su, naṃ, and hi, the entire word idaṃ is changed to e in some cases. The original state (pakatibhāva) of the word idaṃ is known through the Pāḷi text: "Idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo" (Dependent origination through this conditionality). Because of the causes of these (effects), it is called idappaccayā; idappaccayā itself is called idappaccayatā. Esu, imesu, esaṃ, imesaṃ, ehi, imehi.
78:
357. Nāmhi animi. When the nā inflection follows, the substitutions ana and imi occur in place of the entire word idaṃ. (Examples:) anena, iminā.

358. Simhāyamanapuṃsakassa. When the si inflection follows, the substitution ayaṃ occurs in place of the entire word idaṃ when it is not in the neuter gender. (Examples:) ayaṃ puriso (this man), ayaṃ itthī (this woman), ayaṃ mātugāmo (this woman), ayaṃ orodho (this harem woman), ayaṃ garūnaṃ dāro (this wife of the teachers), ayaṃ āpo (this water), ayaṃ napuṃsako (this neuter person).

359. Amunomosaṃ. For the word amu when it is not in the neuter gender, the letter ma is changed to the letter sa in some instances when the si inflection follows. (Examples:) asu rājā, amuko rājā, asu itthī, amukā itthī.

360. Tetatatesaṃ. For the words eta and ta when they are not in the neuter gender, the letter ta is changed to the letter sa when the si inflection follows. (Examples:) eso puriso, esā itthī, so puriso, sā itthī.

361. Nattaṃ tassa vā sabbalingesu. In all genders, the letter ta of the pronoun ta is optionally substituted with na. (Examples:) naṃ, taṃ, ne, te, nena, tena, nesu, tesu, namhi, tamhi, nāyā, tāyā, nāhi, tāhi, nābi, tābi. In this context, according to the scriptural logic (sāsanayutti), it should be understood that the substitution of na for ta occurs only when it follows another word. This is seen in the Pali text: "na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandatīti" (Seeing him, he does not smile; nor does he welcome him).

362. Attaṃ sasmāsmimsāṃsāsu. In all genders, the letter ta of the pronoun ta is optionally substituted with a when followed by the inflections sa, smā, smiṃ, or the substitutions saṃ and sā. (Examples:) assa, tassa, asmā, tasmā, asmiṃ, tasmiṃ, assaṃ, tassaṃ. (With the word itthiyā:) assā, tassā itthiyā kataṃ (done by that woman); assā, tassā itthiyā deti (gives to that woman); assā, tassā itthiyā apeti (departs from that woman); assā, tassā itthiyā pariggaho (the property of that woman); assā, tassā itthiyā patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in that woman).
79:
363. Idaṃsaddassa ca. Also for the word idaṃ. In all genders, the entire word idaṃ is optionally substituted with the letter 'a' when followed by the inflections sa, smā, smiṃ, saṃ, and sā. Examples: assa, imassa. Asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ (from this world to the next world). Imasmā. Asmiṃ lokasmiṃ devate (the goddess in this world). Imasmiṃ. Assaṃ, imissaṃ. Assā, imissā kaññāya kataṃ (done by this young woman). Assā, imissā kaññāya ruccati alaṅkāro (the ornament is pleasing to this young woman). Assā, imissā kaññāya nissaṭaṃ (freed from this young woman). Assā, imissā kaññāya santakaṃ (the property of this young woman). Assā, imissā kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in this young woman).

364. Sabbanāmato kakārāgamo yathātanti. According to the scriptures, the augment 'ka' is added after pronouns. Examples: amuko, asuko, amukaṃ, asukaṃ, amuka, asuka. Why is it said "according to the scriptures"? It is to indicate that the augment 'ka' does not occur in instances such as 'yo so bhagavā', 'yā itthī', 'sā itthī', etc.

365. Ghapehi smiṃsānaṃ saṃsā. After pronouns designated as gha (ending in ā) and pa (ending in i, ī, u, ū), the substitutions saṃ and sā occur respectively in place of the inflections smiṃ and sa in some instances. Examples: sabbassaṃ, sabbāyaṃ (established in all). Sabbassā, sabbāya (gives to all, or the property of all). Similarly: imissaṃ, imāyaṃ, imissā, imāya. Amussaṃ, amuyan, amussā, amuyā.

366. Nāsmāsmiṃiccetāniseva. After pronouns designated as gha and pa, these inflections nā, smā, and smiṃ should be regarded as being like the sa inflection along with their own values. Examples: sabbassā itthiyā kataṃ (done by every woman). Sabbassā itthiyā apeti (departs from every woman). Sabbassā itthiyā patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in every woman). Tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ (together with that girl). In the phrase "By which woman and for what reason should I be diminished?", there is 'kassā'. In the phrase "Tassā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati" (He indulges in sexual intercourse with that woman), there is 'tassā'. Aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hoti (His mind is attached to another woman). In the phrase "idha means in this view (imissā diṭṭhiyā)", 'idha' has that meaning. Yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā (in which single world-system).
80:
367. In the feminine gender, when the case ending naṁ follows, the letter ta of a pronoun is optionally changed to sa. (sānaṁ paññāyati - The increase of those sensations is evident.) Why is "optionally" (vā) said? Because tāsaṁ also exists.

368. In the three genders, when the case ending naṁ follows, the letter ta of a pronoun is also optionally changed to ā. (āsaṁ itthīnaṁ - of those women; or tāsaṁ. āsaṁ purisānaṁ - of those men. āsaṁ cittānaṁ - of those minds; or tesaṁ.) In this regard, there are Pali passages: "The wise do not get angry with those women," "All the sorrows of those people vanish," "Neither the hair of those people nor their webbed hands and feet are seen." In those Pali passages, nāsaṁ should be split as na āsaṁ. sabbāsaṁ should be split as sabbe āsaṁ. Here, āsaṁ means "of those two people." Here, since the masculine method has already been seen, and the neuter method follows the same pattern as the masculine, it is considered as already seen; thus āsaṁ cittānaṁ is stated. In some books, the Pali is found as sabbesaṁ sokā vinassanti. There, it should be split as sabbe esaṁ, as in the phrase sutaṁ metaṁ bho gotama.

369. In the view of other teachers, the substitutions āya and yā for the case ending smiṁ do not occur after pronouns named gha and pa. (etissaṁ, etāyaṁ, imissaṁ, imāyaṁ, amussaṁ, amuyaṁ.)

370. In our view, however, those substitutions do occur. (etāya patiṭṭhitaṁ - established in this; imāya patiṭṭhitaṁ, amuyā patiṭṭhitaṁ.)

371. Words such as mana, vaca, etc., are called the manogaṇa group. Their specific forms have been explained below.

372. Words such as bila, pada, etc., are called the manogaṇādi group.
81:
373. After words of the manogaṇa group and others, the case ending smiṁ should be changed to i, and the case endings nā and smā should be changed to ā in certain instances. (For example: manasi, manasmiṁ - in the mind. vacasi, vacasmiṁ - in the speech. ayasi, ayasmiṁ - in the iron. ayasā kataṁ - made of iron; or ayena. ayasāva malaṁ samuṭṭhitaṁ - just as rust arising from iron eats that very iron; or ayasmā. Likewise, there are manasā, vacasā, vayasā.) All words belonging to the manogaṇa group should be expanded and understood in this manner. (For example: bilasi, bilasmiṁ - in the hole. padasi, padasmiṁ - in the place or on the foot. bilasā, bilena - by the hole. padasā, padena - by the foot. mukhasā - by the mouth. vegasā - by speed. rasasā - by taste. āyusā, āyunā - by life.) In this way, other words belonging to the manogaṇa group should also be expanded and understood. Why is "manogaṇādīhi" said? It is to prevent the substitutions of i and ā in words such as purisasmiṁ, purisena, purisasmā, cittasmiṁ, cittena, cittasmā, kaññāyaṁ, kaññāya, etc.

374. After words of the manogaṇa group and others, the case ending sa should be changed to o in certain instances. (For example: manaso, manassa - of the mind. tapaso, tapassa - of the practice. bilaso, bilassa - of the hole.)

375. The final letter of words in the manogaṇa group and others becomes o in certain instances after the case ending is elided (in compounds and derivatives). (For example: manomayaṁ - made of mind. ayomayaṁ - made of iron. tejodhātu - the fire element. tapodhano - one whose wealth is practice. siroruho - hair growing on the head. āpokasiṁaṁ - the water kasiṇa. vāyokasiṁaṁ - the air kasiṇa.) Why is "vā" (optionally) said? It is to prevent the change to o in words such as ayasalākaṁ (iron rod).

376. After words of the manogaṇa group, when a vowel of a case ending or a suffix follows, the letter sa should be inserted in certain instances. (For example: manasā, vacasā - by mind, by speech. manasi, vacasi - in mind, in speech.) abyaggamanaso naro - a man with an undistracted mind. thiracetasaṁ kulaṁ - a family with a firm mind. saddheyyavacasā upāsikā - a female lay follower with trustworthy speech. mānasikaṁ - arising in the mind. vācasikaṁ - arising in the speech. Why is "vā" (optionally) said? It is to prevent the insertion of sa in words such as mano, manā, manaṁ, mane, manena, manaāyatanaṁ, etc.
82:
377. After words of the manogaṇa group, the case ending aṁ should be changed to o in certain instances. (For example: adāne kurute mano - he sets his mind on not giving. kassapassa vaco sutvā - having heard the words of Kassapa. tapo idha krubbasi - you perform practice here. yaso laddhā na mazzeyya - having obtained fame, one should not be intoxicated.) Why is "vā" (optionally) said? It is to prevent the change to o in words such as yasaṁ laddhāna dummedho (the fool, having obtained fame), manaṁ aññāsi (he knew the mind), etc. Why is "manogaṇato" said? It is to prevent the change to o in words such as bilaṁ pavisa jambuka (Jackal, enter the hole), cittamaññāsi, kaññaṁ passati, etc.

378. When the letter bha (the case ending bhi) follows, the entire word santa is changed to sa, and the letter ba should be inserted at the end. (For example: sabbhireva samāsetha - one should associate only with the virtuous. sabbhūto - one who has reached tranquility. sabbhāvo - the nature of being manifest.)

379. When words such as kāra follow, the entire word santa should also be changed to sa. (For example: sakkāro - worship by the virtuous. sakkato - worshipped by the virtuous. sakkatvā - having acted respectfully.)

380. When all case endings starting with si follow, the entire word santa should be changed to sabbhi. (For example: sabbhi, sabbhī, sabbhayo - the virtuous person.) All remaining forms should be expanded and understood in this manner. In this context, it should be firmly believed that the word sabbhi exists respectively in the seven cases, as seen in phrases such as sabbhīhi saddhiṁ, bahupe taṁ asabbhi jātaveda, asabbhirūpo puriso, etc.

381. Alternatively, the formation of the word sabbhi can be understood through the power of the roots sad and bhid. (For example: sabbhinibbānaṁ - Nibbāna which destroys the defilements.)
83:
382. The 'nta' of the word 'santa' occurring in a designation (paññatti) becomes 'aṃ' when followed by the 'si' inflection. (Example:) Saṃ sappuriso (A good person). Why say "in si"? To prevent the 'aṃ' substitution in instances such as "Santo sappuriso loke" (The good are peaceful in the world). Why say "in designation"? To prevent the 'aṃ' substitution in instances such as "Santo danto niyato brahmacārī" (Peaceful, tamed, certain, living the holy life).

383. The 'nta' of words beginning with 'gacchanta' optionally becomes 'aṃ' when followed by the 'si' inflection. (Examples:) Gacchaṃ, gacchanto (one who goes); mahaṃ, mahanto (one who honors), and so forth. Why say "words beginning with gacchanta"? To prevent the 'aṃ' substitution in words such as anto, danto, and vanto.

384. According to another Pali method, in the feminine gender as well, the 'nta' of words beginning with 'gacchanta' optionally becomes 'aṃ' when followed by the 'si' inflection. (Example:) Sā gacchaṃ, gacchanti (She goes). Knowing, she says "I do not know"; seeing, she says "I do not see." Why say "in the feminine"? To prevent the 'aṃ' substitution due to the 'si' inflection in instances such as gacchantaṃ kulaṃ (a going clan) and jānantaṃ cittaṃ (a knowing mind).

385. According to another Pali method, in the masculine gender, the 'nta' of words beginning with 'gacchanta' optionally becomes 'aṃ' when followed by the 'yo' inflection of the first case (nominative). (Examples:) Ye gacchaṃ (Those who go). "O sirs, we shall obtain the eye of wisdom." "Friends, do you indeed live knowing and seeing?" By the decision of this rule, words such as "te gacchanto bhavanto" are prohibited.

386. When followed by the inflections sa, smiṃ, nā, and naṃ, the 'nta' of words beginning with 'gacchanta' should be regarded as the suffix 'ntu'. (Examples:) Gacchato, mahato (to/of the one going, to/of the one honoring). Gacchati, mahati (in the one going, in the one honoring). Gacchatā, mahatā (by the one going, by the one honoring). Gacchataṃ, mahataṃ (to/of those going, to/of those honoring).

387. The 'nta' of words beginning with 'arahanta' should also be regarded as the suffix 'ntu' optionally when followed by the 'yo' inflection of the first case. (Examples:) Arahanto viharanti (Arahants dwell). "Santo sappurisā loke" (In the world, good people are called 'Devadhamma'). "Bhavanto āgacchantu" (May the venerable ones come). Why say "optionally" (vā)? To prevent the treatment as the suffix 'ntu' in instances such as "Mayañcamha anarahantā" (We are not Arahants).
84:
By the mark of this rule (387), words such as "te gacchanto, bhavanto gacchanto" (plural forms ending in -o) are prohibited.

388. Due to the 'aṃ' inflection, the 'nta' of the word 'santa' optionally becomes 'a'. (Example:) He associates with the good, or else with the bad (Saṃ bhajati yadivā-asaṃ). Why say "optionally" (vā)? For forms without the substitution, such as santaṃ and asantaṃ.

389. After the word 'āyasmantu', the 'yo' inflection of the first case is always changed to 'ā'. By the power of the Vinaya terminology prescribed by the Blessed One, when referring to two monks, the 'yo' inflection of the first case following the word 'āyasmantu' is always changed to 'ā'. (Example:) "Let the two venerable ones listen to my (announcement)." Why say "the first case"? To prevent the 'ā' substitution in the second case (accusative), as in "Āyasmante pucchāmi". Why say "referring to two" (dvīsu)? To prevent the 'ā' substitution when referring to many monks, as in "Uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ" (O venerable ones, the introduction has been recited).

By the mark of this rule and by this original example of 'āyasmanta', forms such as "guṇavantā, satimantā" are prohibited. Just as the word "arahantā" is accepted because the word "anarahantā" is found in the Pali texts, words such as "guṇavantā, satimantā" are not accepted because such words do not appear in the Pali texts. Just as the words "āyasmanto, arahanto" are found in the Pali texts, plural forms ending in -o such as "gacchanto, mahanto, caranto" are not found. Just as the words "santo, ayyo" are found in the Pali texts in both singular and plural forms, among thousands of words like "gacchanto, mahanto, caranto", not a single word is found in the plural form.

390. After words such as brahma, atta, sakha, and rāja, the 'si' inflection is changed to 'ā'. (Example:) Brahmā (Brahma) stands. Likewise: attā (self), ātumā (self), sakhā (friend), rājā (king), sā (dog), pumā (man), rahā (evil), daḷhammo (one who draws a strong bow), paccakkhadhammā (one who has realized the Four Truths), vivaṭacchadā (one who has opened the veil of defilements), vattahā (being), yuvā (youth), maghavā (Sakka), addhā (time/duration), and muddhā (head/fool). These words are similar to each other in some inflections and dissimilar in others.
85:
391. The nominative case ending 'yo' should optionally (vā) be changed to 'ā'. After words such as 'brahma', the nominative case ending 'yo' should optionally be changed to 'ā'. Brahmā tiṭṭhanti (The Brahmas stand). Attā tiṭṭhanti (The selves stand). Netādisā sakhā honti [Khu 5-156] (Those lions of such nature [hit by arrows] are not friends). Cattāro mahārājā [Dī 2-206; Dī 3-158] (The four Great Kings). The remaining words should be treated in the same manner. Why is 'optionally' (vā) said? To indicate that the change to 'ā' does not occur in 'Brahmāno tiṭṭhanti'.

392. The case ending 'yo' should be changed to 'āno'. After words such as 'brahma', the case ending 'yo' should optionally (vā) be changed to 'āno'. Brahmāno gacchanti (The Brahmas go), Brahmāno passati (He sees the Brahmas). In the same way: attāno, sakhāno, rājāno, sāno. Why is 'optionally' (vā) said? To indicate that the change to 'āno' does not occur in 'sakhāyo tiṭṭhanti' (the friends stand), 'sakhāyo passati' (he sees the friends), and 'sāne passati' (he sees the dogs).

393. The case ending 'aṃ' should be changed to 'ānaṃ'. After words such as 'brahma', the case ending 'aṃ' should optionally (vā) be changed to 'ānaṃ'. Brahmānaṃ, brahmaṃ; attānaṃ, attaṃ; sakhānaṃ, sakhaṃ; rājānaṃ, rājaṃ. Why is 'optionally' (vā) said? To indicate that the change to 'ānaṃ' does not occur in 'sakhāraṃ passati' (he sees the friend).

394. After the word 'sakha', the case ending 'yo' should be changed to 'āyo' and 'no'. Sakhāyo, sakhino tiṭṭhanti (The friends stand). Sakhāyo, sakhino passati (He sees the friends).

395. After the word 'raha', the nominative case ending 'yo' is changed to 'no', and the final vowel of 'raha' is also changed to 'i'. Rahino tiṭṭhanti (Evils stand). Bhonto rahino tiṭṭhatha (O sirs, let evils stand).

396. Because of the case ending 'nā', the final vowel of the words 'raha' and 'daḷhadhamma' should be changed to 'i'. Rahinā kataṃ (Done by evil). Daḷhadhamminā kataṃ (Done by Daḷhadhammī [King Pīḷiyakkha]). Why is 'because of the case ending nā' said? To indicate that the change to 'i' does not occur in 'rahā apeti' (he departs from evil).

397. After words such as 'vattaha', the 'yo' case ending other than the nominative (i.e., accusative) should be changed to 'āne'. After words such as 'vattaha', the 'yo' case ending other than the nominative (i.e., accusative) should be changed to 'āne'. Vattahāne passati (He sees the beings). Similarly, he sees evils (rahāne), those who hold firm bows (daḷhadhammāne), those who have opened the veil of defilements (vivaṭacchadāne), dogs (sāne), those with shaven heads (vuttasirāne), paths (addhāne), and heads (muddhāne).

398. After the words 'vattaha', 'raha', 'addha', and 'sā', the case ending 'smiṃ' should be changed to 'āne'. After words such as 'vattaha', 'raha', 'addha', and 'sā', the change of the case ending 'smiṃ' to 'āne'...
86:
...occurs. Vattahāne patiṭṭhitaṃ (Established in the being). Similarly, it occurs in the words raha, addha, and sā.

399. Because of the case ending 'su', the end of those words 'vattaha', 'raha', 'addha', and 'sā' becomes 'āna'. For example: vattahānesu, rahānesu, addhānesu, sānesu (in dogs).

400. Because of the case ending 'hi', the end of words such as 'vuttasira' (one with a shaven head) becomes 'āna'. For example: vuttasirānehi, vattahānehi, addhānehi.

401. Because of the case ending 'hi', the end of the word 'raha' becomes 'ina'. For example: rahinehi.

402. Because of the case ending 'sa', the end of the word 'vattaha' becomes 'i'. For example: vattahino dadāti, vattahino devarajjaṃ (the state of the king of gods).

403. Because of the case endings 'nā', 'smā', and 'sa', the end of the word 'addha' becomes 'u'. For example: dīghena addhunā (by a long journey), addhunā paṭinissaṭaṃ (separated from the journey), addhuno ruccati (he delights in the journey), dīghassa addhuno accayena (by the passing of a long journey).

404. The case ending 'smiṃ' following words such as 'addha', 'muddha', 'kamma', 'camma', and 'ghamma' is changed to 'ni' in some places. For example: addhani, addhāne (in the journey); muddhani, muddhāne (on the head); kammani, kammasmiṃ (in the action); cammani, cammasmiṃ (in the skin); ghammani, ghammasmiṃ (in the heat); vesmani, vesmasmiṃ (in the house).

405. The case ending 'smiṃ' following the words 'brahma' and 'atta' is always changed to 'ni'. For example: brahmani (in Brahma), attani (in oneself).

406. The case ending 'smiṃ' following words ending in 'ī' such as 'sasi' (moon) is changed to 'ni' in some places. For example: sasini gaganātalaṃ samupagacchati (when the moon rises to the sky), daṇḍini (in the one with a staff), bhogini (in the one with wealth). By saying 'optionally' (vā), 'sasimhi' also exists.
87:
407. Because of the substitution 'no', and the case endings 'nā', 'naṃ', and 'sa', the end of the word 'sakha' is changed to 'i'. For example: sakhino, sakhinā, sakhīnaṃ, sakhissa.

408. Because of the case ending 'hi', the end of the word 'sakha' is changed to 'āra' in some places. For example: sakhārehi, sakhehi.

409. Because of the case endings 'aṃ', 'su', and 'naṃ', the end of the word 'sakha' is changed to 'āra' in some places. For example: sakhāraṃ, sakhaṃ; sakhāresu, sakhesu; sakhārānaṃ, sakhīnaṃ.

410. Because of the case endings 'sa', 'naṃ', and 'naā', the end of the word 'brahma' becomes 'u'. For example: brahmuno, brahmūnaṃ, brahmunā.

411. Because of the case endings 'si' and 'yo', the end of words such as 'satthu' and 'pitu' becomes 'ā', and those case endings 'si' and 'yo' are elided. For example: satthā tiṭṭhati (the teacher stands). Similarly: pitā (father), mātā (mother), bhātā (brother), kattā (doer), vattā (speaker). Satthā tiṭṭhanti (the teachers stand). Pitā tiṭṭhanti (the fathers stand). Avitakkitā maccumupabbajanti (those who are thoughtless and lazy go to death). Bhonto satthā (O teachers). Bhonto pitā (O fathers). Bhotiyo mātā (O mothers).

412. Because of the case endings such as 'yo' and 'aṃ', the end of words such as 'satthu' and 'pitu' is changed to 'āra' in some places. For example: satthāro, pitaro, mātaro, satthāraṃ, pitaraṃ, mātaraṃ, vattāraṃ, gantāraṃ, satthārā, satthārehi, satthārānaṃ. By saying 'optionally' (vā), 'avitakkitā maccumupabbajanti' and 'tiṇṇannaṃ satthūnaṃ' (of the three teachers) also exist.

413. In compounds, because of the case endings such as 'si', the end of words such as 'pitu' is changed to 'āra' in some places. For example: ekamātarā (having the same mother as this man), nimmātāpitaro (this man is one who has no parents), nimmātāpitaram purisam (to the man who has no parents), ekpitarā (they have the same father)...
88:
People have the same mother. A man with an only daughter. One who is not a nun, one who is not a Sakyan princess (daughter of the Buddha).

414. Satthādīnaṃ tomhi. When the suffix to follows, the end of words such as satthu is changed to āra. Satthārato apeti - he departs from the teacher. In the same way: vattārato, gantārato. Regarding this substitution of āra due to the suffix to, this Pali text is found in the Mahāniddesa: "satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati" (he goes from one teacher to another teacher).

415. Samāsagatanāme kvaci. When a noun that is part of a compound follows, the end of words such as satthu is changed to āra in some instances. Hetusatthāradassanaṃ - the reason for seeing the Buddha. Amātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho - (a chicken) that has grown up without being cared for by parents. Satthāraniddeso - pointing out the teacher. Kattāraniddeso - pointing out the agent. Why is it said "in some instances" (kvaci)? It is to prevent the substitution of āra in instances such as satthudassanaṃ (seeing the Buddha), kattuniddeso (pointing out the agent), etc.

416. Namhi. When the naṃ inflection follows, the end of words such as satthu and pitu is changed to āra in some instances. Satthārānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, bhātārānaṃ. (If āra is not substituted) they remain as satthūnaṃ, pitūnaṃ, bhātūnaṃ.

417. Āttañca. When the naṃ inflection follows, the end of words such as satthu and pitu is also changed to ā in some instances. Satthānaṃ, pitānaṃ, bhātānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, kattānaṃ.

418. U samhi salutti ca. When the sa inflection follows, the change of the end of words such as satthu and pitu to u, and the elision of that sa inflection, also occur in some instances. Satthu (the form with the sa inflection elided), satthussa, satthuno. Pitu, pitussa, pituno. Bhātu, bhātussa, bhātuno. "yāya mātubhato poso" (the son who is supported by which mother). Mātuyā (also exists). "buddhamātussa sakkāraṃ, karotu sugatoraso" (may the son of the Buddha perform the honor and hospitality to the mother of the Buddha). Such Pali usage is very rare. Mandhātu, mandhātussa, mandhātuno.
89:
419. In a compound, the final vowel (u) of the word Mandhātu optionally becomes 'atta' in certain instances. Examples: Mandhātajātaka (The Birth Story of King Mandhātu), Sabbaññumandhātasusīhanāda (The great lion's roar of the Omniscient Buddha and King Mandhātu). Why is "vā" (optionally) stated? To indicate that the substitution does not occur in instances like Mandhātumahārājā (The Great King Mandhātu), even though it is a compound.

420. In a compound, the final vowel of words such as Mātu always becomes 'ā'. Examples: Mātāpitu-upaṭṭhāna (Supporting one's parents), Mātāpitaro (Parents), Mātādhītaro (Mother and daughters), Mātāputtā (Mother and sons). "Adūsakā Pitāputtā" (Innocent father and sons), Dhītābhātaro (Daughter and brothers), Mātā Pitā Bhātā Bhaginī-ādayo (Mother, father, brother, sister, etc.).

421. After the 'āra' substitution, the 'yo' case ending becomes 'o'. Examples: Satthāro tiṭṭhanti (The teachers stand), "Bhonto satthāro tumhe dhammaṃ desetha" (O teachers... may you preach the Dhamma), Pitaro (Fathers), Mātaro (Mothers), Vattāro (Speakers), Gantāro (Goers).

422. After the 'āra' substitution, the 'smiṃ' case ending becomes 'i'. Examples: Satthari (In the teacher), Pitari (In the father), Dhītari (In the daughter).

423. After the 'āra' substitution, the 'nā' case ending becomes 'ā'. Examples: Satthārā (By the teacher), Pitarā (By the father), Mātarā (By the mother).

424. When followed by the 'i' substitution (from the 'smiṃ' case ending), the 'āra' substitution becomes short (rassa). Examples: Satthari, Pitari, Mātari (In the teacher, in the father, in the mother).

425. In case endings other than the 'si' case ending, the 'āra' substitution of words such as Pitu becomes short (rassa). Examples: Pitarā, Mātarā, Bhātarā, Dhītarā, Pitaro. There is also: "Arogā mayha mātaro" (May my mothers be free from illness).

426. In the 'aṃ' case ending, the 'āra' substitution for the final vowel of words such as Gantu optionally does not occur. Examples: Gantaṃ or Gantāraṃ (To the goer), "Ramayanteva āgantaṃ" or "Āgantāraṃ" (Delighting only the one who has arrived), Vattaṃ or Vattāraṃ (To the speaker). Why is "Gantādīnaṃ" stated? To indicate that the 'āra' substitution always occurs in words like Satthāraṃ (To the teacher).
90:
427. When followed by the suffix 'to', the word 'bhara', etc., the final vowel of words such as Mātu becomes 'i'. Examples: Mātito, Pitito, Bhātito, Dhītito, Duhitito. "Mātāpettibharo cassaṃ" — May I be one who supports my mother and father. Mātipakkho, Pitipakkho. Mātisaññā, Pitisaññā. Other words should be applied in the same manner.

428. In a compound, when followed by the vocative 'si' case ending named 'ga', the final vowel of the words Mātu and Dhītu becomes 'e'. Examples: Bhoti Tissamāte, Bhoti Phussamāte, Bhoti Seṭṭhidhīte, Bhoti Rājaduhite. "Aṭṭhahi kho Nakulamāte dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo" — O mother of Nakula, a woman who is endowed with eight qualities. Why is "in a compound" stated? To prevent the 'e' substitution in instances like "He māta" and "He dhīta".

429. In a compound, when followed by the case endings 'nā', 'sa', 'smā', and 'smiṃ', the final vowel of the words Mātu and Dhītu optionally becomes 'ā'. Examples: Rājamātāya, Rājadhitāya, Seṭṭhidhītāya. Why is "in a compound" stated? For instances like Mātu, Mātuyā, and Matyā. Why is "optionally" (vā) stated? For instances like Rājamātuyā and Seṭṭhidhītuyā.

430. After the word 'Nettu', the 'smiṃ' case ending optionally becomes 'e'. "Nette ujuṃ gate sati" — When the leader (or the eye) has gone straight. Why is "optionally" (vā) stated? For the form Nettari.

431. After the word 'Nisā', the 'smiṃ' case ending also optionally becomes 'e'. "Nise aggīva bhāsati" — It shines like fire in the night. Why is "optionally" (vā) stated? For the form Nisāyaṃ.

432. After words such as Kattu, the vocative 'si' case ending named 'ga' optionally becomes 'e'. "Uṭṭhehi katte" — O minister, arise. "Ehi khatte" — O minister, come. Why is "optionally" (vā) stated? For forms like "Bho katta" and "He khatta".
91:
433. When the suffix -sa (sa-vibhatti) follows, the augment 's' (s-āgama) occurs after words such as pitu and bhātu. (Examples:) pitussa, bhātussa, satthussa, vattussa. Why is it said "after pitu, bhātu, etc."? It is to prevent the augment 's' in the case of dhītuyā. Indeed, in the Pali scriptures, among feminine gender words, the letter 's' does not exist in its own form, except for the word "mātussā". The word mātussā is merely a metathesis (akkharavippallāsa); therefore, it should be construed only as mātuyā.

434. When the suffix -aṃ follows, the 'u' of the word dhītu is optionally changed to 'a'. (Example:) "kaṇhājinaṃ dhītaṃ" — the daughter Kaṇhājinā. Alternatively, dhītaraṃ.

435. The letter 't' of the words tayā and tayi is optionally changed to 'tv'. (Examples:) tvayā, tayā; tvayi, tayi. "tvayi gadhitacittosmi" — I am one whose mind is attached to you.

436. The letter 't' of the words tāsu and tamhi is optionally changed to 'ty'. (Examples:) tyamhi purisamhi, tyamhi cittamhi, tyāsu itthīsu. "kathaṃ nu vissase tyamhi" — How indeed could one trust in him (the friend who was once an enemy)? "atha vissasate tyamhi" — Then he trusts in him (the king's servant). "khiḍḍāpaṇihitā tyāsu" — Delight is established in them (those women). "rati tyāsu patiṭṭhitā" — Sensual pleasure is established in them (those women). Why is it said "optionally"? (To allow the forms) tamhi, tāsu.

437. The word taṃ, when it has the meaning of "you" (tumhattha), is optionally changed to tyaṃ. "āturo tyānu pucchāmi" — I, who am afflicted (by the poison of an arrow), ask you. Why is it said "optionally"? (To allow the form) taṃ anupucchāmi.

438. The 'mh' of the words amhākaṃ and amhesu is optionally changed to 'sm'. (Examples:) asmākaṃ, amhākaṃ; asmesu, amhesu. However, in maintaining the rhythm (light and heavy syllables) of a verse, the form "asmisu" is also found, due to the change of the letter 'e' to 'i', as in the word "idha hemantagimhisu".
92:
439. Because of the suffix -hi, the final letter of the word atta becomes 'ana'. (Examples:) attanehi, attanebhi.

440. After the word atta, the suffix -sa is changed to 'no'. (Example:) attano.

441. After the word atta, the suffix -smā is changed to 'na'. (Example:) attanā nissaṭaṃ (freed by oneself).

442. After the designations 'jha' (i, ī) and 'la' (u, ū), the suffix -smā is also changed to 'na'. (Examples:) agginā apeti (departs from the fire). Likewise, daṇḍinā, sayambhunā.

443. After the designations 'gha' (ā) and 'pa' (i, ī, u, ū), the suffix -smiṃ is optionally changed to 'yaṃ'. (Examples:) kaññāyaṃ, kaññāya; rattiyaṃ, rattiyā; itthiyaṃ, itthiya; yāguyaṃ, yāguya; vadhūyaṃ, vadhūya.

444. After neuter gender words, the suffix -yo is changed to 'ni'. (Examples:) aṭṭhīni, aṭṭhī; āyūni, āyū.

445. After neuter gender words ending in 'a', the suffix -yo is always changed to 'ni'. (Examples:) yāni cittāni tiṭṭhanti (which minds remain); yāni kulāni passati (which families he sees); tāni, tāni; kāni, kāni; bhayāni, bhayāni; rūpāni, rūpāni. However, in instances such as "rūpā saddā rasā gandhā" and "rūpe ca sadde ca atho rase ca", the forms "rūpā", "rūpe", etc., are accomplished by changing the suffix -ni to 'ā' and 'e'. This rule should be understood as demonstrating the constancy of the substitution to 'ni'.

446. After neuter gender words ending in 'a', the suffix -si is changed to 'aṃ'. (Examples:) sabbaṃ, idaṃ, yaṃ, taṃ, kaṃ, rūpaṃ.

447. After stems other than those specified in rules such as "sino aṃ" and "sissa o", the following vocative -si (designated as 'ga') and the nominative -si undergo elision (lopa).
93:
The suffix -si also (undergoes elision). (Examples:) O worthy and beautiful Queen Phussatī (bhadde phussati), O lady (bhoti itthi), that woman (sā itthī), O staff-bearer (bho daṇḍi), that staff-bearer (so daṇḍī), O teacher (bho sattha), that teacher (so satthā), O king (bho rāja), that king (so rājā). Why is it said "after others" (sesehi)? To indicate that the suffix is not elided in words like "puriso gacchati" (the man goes). Why is it said "ga and si"? To indicate that the suffix is not elided in words like "itthiyā", "satthussa", etc., because they are not the vocative -si designated as 'ga'.

## 448. Sabbāsamākhyātavajjitopasagganipātādīhi ca yathārahaṃ
Among the four types of words—noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), prefix (upasagga), and particle (nipāta)—all suffixes from the nominative to the locative, both singular and plural, occurring after prefixes, particles, etc. (excluding verbs), undergo elision as appropriate. Grammarians do not desire the elision of plural suffixes after prefixes and particles because they are indeclinable (asaṅkhyā) words. However, the teachers of the Dispensation (sāsanikā) do desire it. Thus, in the Dispensation, the elision of plural suffixes after indeclinable words should be accepted because the meaning must be taken as primary. It is true that the application of a suffix occurs by the power of the meaning. For example: "atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā" (nine in the 'presence' condition, nine in the 'absence' condition). Therefore, no contradiction should be made in forming the definitions: "atthiyā bhāvo atthitā" (the state of being is called atthitā), "natthiyā bhāvo natthitā" (the state of non-being is called natthitā).

Regarding the application of suffixes after such indeclinable words, these are the examples. What are they? "suriyassuggamanaṃ pati" (concerning the sunrise), "sakko brāhmaṇavaṇṇena pāto nesaṃ adissatha" (Sakka, in the guise of a brahmin, appeared to them in the morning). "buddhasmā pati sāriputto" (Venerable Sāriputta is equal to the Buddha). In examples such as "ayaṃ bhikkhu anu sāriputtaṃ paññavā" (this monk is wise, following Sāriputta), there is the elision of the nominative singular suffix. Here, depending on the word "pati", the sense of "uggamana" (rising) becomes the object (kamma). The word "pati" also regards the sense of "sakka" (Sakka). Therefore, the nominative singular suffix is applied after that word "pati", and subsequently, that suffix is elided. This method should be applied as appropriate. In examples such as "ime bhikkhū anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto" (these monks are wise, following Sāriputta), "sādhu buddharakkhitadhammarakkhitā mātaraṃ anu" (Buddharakkhita and Dhammarakkhita are good, following their mother), there is the elision of the nominative plural suffix. Thus, in expanded words (vyāsapada), only certain suffixes after certain prefixes undergo elision, not all. The Venerable [Mahākaccāyana], however...
94: The Venerable Mahākaccāyana, in the Niruttipiṭaka, stated that all twenty prefixes (upasaggas) are without case endings (vibhaktis). Regarding indeclinables (nipātas), however, he stated that some have case endings while others do not. We, however, desire that in analytical forms (vyāsa-pada), some prefixes have case endings and some do not. In all verbal forms such as 'pabhavati' and 'parābhavati', we desire the complete absence of case endings in every way. In compound words (samāsa-pada), however, we desire the presence of case endings in every way. Regarding indeclinables, we desire only the method as previously stated. In the statement, 'Knowing in various ways is called pajānanā' [Abhi-aṭṭha 1.191], there is the elision of the instrumental singular case ending. Things thrown upwards are called ukkhittāni; things thrown inwards are called pakkhittāni; in these instances, there is the elision of the locative singular case ending. This method should be expanded upon. Wealth exists; wealths exist; sons exist; wealths exist [Khu 1.22]. The king is able to conquer enemies; he is able to conquer the enemy; this suffering is obtained by the man [Khu 6.176, 352]. These sufferings are obtained by the man. Come, friend; come, friends; come, venerable sir; come, venerable sirs; come, friend, turn back [Khu 6.153]. Friend, do not speak thus [Khu 6.367]. This is the elision of the nominative singular and plural after an indeclinable. May there be homage; pay homage to the Nāga [Khu 1.196]. This is the elision of the nominative and accusative singular. Thus it is by way of analysis (vyāsa). By way of compound (samāsa), however, in the case of 'atthikhīrā' (a brahmin woman who has milk), meaning 'this woman has milk', the 'si' case ending is elided. In the context of 'How shall my disciples increase through faith?', the instrumental singular is elided. One who desires to give gifts [Aṅ 2.28] is called 'dātukāmo'; here, the dative singular is elided. This method should be expanded upon. Ascetic and brahmin, ascetics and brahmins, ascetic and brahmin (acc.), etc., up to 'among ascetics and brahmins'; this is analysis (vyāsa). Here, the elision of all case endings, nominative, accusative, etc., both singular and plural, after the word 'ca' should be understood. Therefore, it is said 'as appropriate' (yathārahaṃ).
95:
An objection may arise regarding this rule: "O Venerable Sir, since the application of syādi case endings does not even exist in the domain of verbs (ākhyāta), why is it said 'from prefixes, indeclinables, etc., excluding verbs'?" True, but even so, someone might have the view: "Because forms like karotissa, gacchatinno, and hotissā are seen, the application of syādi case endings also occurs from verbal stems." To prohibit that view, the word 'vajjita' (excluded) is stated. In 'karoti dhātu', 'gacchati dhātu', etc., it is to show that the elision of case endings also occurs from conventional terms (rūḷhī-sadda) such as 'karoti-dhātu', which is formed from 'karoti' and 'dhātu'. And to show that the elision of case endings also occurs from these nouns: "It is called asa because of the meaning 'exists'; it is called sata because of the meaning 'sinks'" [Abhi-aṭṭha 2.496], the word 'ādi' is used in 'nipātādīhi'. In this place, although the specific forms of the twenty prefixes and the indeclinables should be mentioned, they are not shown here because they will become clear in the analysis of the four types of words later on.

449. In a compound, before a following word such as a gender-marker, the final letter of the word 'puma' is elided. Pullingaṃ. Pumbhāvo. Puṅkokilo.

450. After a word ending in i-vanna (i, ī), the 'aṃ' case ending is optionally changed to 'yaṃ'. Bodhiyaṃ, Bodhiṃ. Dāsiyaṃ, Dāsiṃ. Itthiyaṃ, Itthiṃ. "May you realize the omniscience of the Buddhas" [Khu 4.320]. "Like a maidservant born in the house" [Khu 6.355].

451. After a word ending in 'jha' (i, ī) that has been made short (katarassa), the 'aṃ' case ending is optionally changed to 'naṃ'. "If one should see a person who habitually sees faults" [Khu 1.24]. Vajja-dassiṃ, Verinaṃ [Khu 1.123]. Daṇḍinaṃ. Bhoginaṃ.

452. After that same word ending in 'jha' that has been made short, the 'yo' case endings are optionally changed to 'no'. Daṇḍino, Daṇḍī. Bhogino, Bhogī. He Daṇḍino, He Bhogino.
96:
453. By another method, the end of words such as 'vajja-dassī' optionally becomes 'ina' before the case endings aṃ, yo, smiṃ, and su. (For example:) Sees the one who sees faults. If one should see a person who habitually sees faults [Khu 1.24]. Sees those who see faults. Stands in the one who sees faults; stands in those who see faults. Sees the living being (pāṇinaṃ). Sees the living beings. Living beings are oppressed [Saṃ 1.102]. Stands in the living being; stands in the living beings. Sees the famous one (yasassinaṃ); sees the famous ones; stands in the famous one. "In the famous one named Mātaṅga" [Khu 6.61]. Stands in the famous ones. The enemy (acc.); sees the enemies. Stands in the enemy. "Among those who have enemies, they (live) without enmity" [Khu 1.42]. Sees the one with a staff; sees those with a staff. In the one with a staff; stands in those with a staff. Sees the wealthy one (or the hooded snake); sees the wealthy ones. In the wealthy one; stands in the wealthy ones. In this way, in the masculine gender, many hundreds of words ending in 'ī' such as 'sikhī' (fire or peacock) and 'karī' (elephant) should be applied. This rule is a 'pajjuṇṇagatika' rule, following the method previously established. Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? (When not applied by the 'vā' rule:) Vajja-dassiṃ, Vajja-dassino (sees the fault-seer, sees the fault-seers). Vajja-dassimhi, Vajja-dassīsu (stands in the fault-seer, stands in the fault-seers).

454. In verse (gāthā), the 'smiṃ' case ending after the word 'puṇṇamā' is changed to 'āye'. (Example:) On the full-moon Uposatha day [Khu 4.392]. Like the moon on a full-moon day [Khu 4.320]. Why is 'in verse' said? Because in prose, it exists as 'visākhā-puṇṇamāya rattiyā' (on the night of the full moon of Visākhā) [Udāna-aṭṭha 46].

455. In verse, the word 'tabba' together with its case ending after the word 'lajji' is changed to 'tāye'. In this rule, the word 'lajji' also includes 'alajji'. They are ashamed of what is not shameful (such as a rice bowl); they are not ashamed of what is shameful (such as the genitals) [Khu 1.58]. In this instance, the 'smiṃ' case ending is applied after the words 'alajjitabba' and 'lajjitabba', and then 'tabba' together with that 'smiṃ' is changed to 'tāye'.
97:
In this context, 'alajjitāye' means 'in the fear of what is not shameful.' 'Lajjitāye' means 'in the fear of what is shameful.'

## 456. Kissa ve ka.
When the suffix 'va' follows the word 'kiṃ', 'kiṃ' is changed to 'ka'. Where is the dance? Where is the song? O Tissa, beloved of the gods, where have you gone?

## 457. Thaṃ haṃ syādīsu ca.
Even when the suffixes 'thaṃ', 'haṃ', and 'syādi' (case endings) follow, the word 'kiṃ' is changed to 'ka'. How shall we know that? Where will he see me? Who is worthy to blame him? Who are you? Knowing what special benefit do you strive? What woman? 'Kathaṃ' means 'in what manner', 'kathaṃ' means 'to what manner', 'kathaṃ' means 'by what manner', and so forth. Here, 'ko pakāro', 'kaṃ pakāraṃ', etc., are taken as the analytical sentences (atthavākya) and as examples of the word 'kathaṃ', not merely as analytical sentences. Indeed, here, by the sentence 'ko pakāro kathaṃ' and so forth, two applications are shown at once. This is like how with a single water pot, watering a mango tree and bathing a monk can be done. The Pāli verse here is: "I have watered the mango tree, and the monk has been bathed. I have also accumulated no small amount of merit." The teachers, however, bring the metaphor that with a single water pot, watering a mango tree and bathing the teacher are accomplished.

## 458. Napuṃsake aṃsisu vā.
When the case endings 'aṃ' and 'si' follow the word 'kiṃ' in the neuter gender, 'kiṃ' is optionally changed to 'ka'. What mind? What form? (If 'ka' is not substituted:) Kiṃ cittaṃ, Kiṃ rūpaṃ.

## 459. Ko iti samāse nāme.
In the context of a compound, when the word 'nāma' follows, 'kiṃ' is optionally changed to 'ko'. What named man? Or 'kiṃnāmo'. What named...
98:
...woman? Or 'kiṃnāmā'. What named family? Or 'kiṃnāmaṃ'. What is the name of your preceptor? Why say 'in a compound' (samāse)? "What is the name of this woman?" (Here, although the word 'nāma' is present, it is not a compound, so 'ko' is not substituted). Why say 'before nāma' (nāme)? Of what clan are you? What man (kinnara)? What family?

## 460. Ku hiṃ haṃ hiñci hiñcanaṃ tratotho dācanaṃdāsu.
When the suffixes 'hiṃ', 'haṃ', 'hiñci', 'hiñcanaṃ', 'tra', 'to', 'tha', 'dācanaṃ', and 'dā' follow, the word 'kiṃ' is changed to 'ku'. Where? (kuhiṃ, kuhaṃ). In some place (kuhiñci, kuhiñcanaṃ). Where? (kutra). From where? (kuto). Where? (kuttha). At some time (kudācanaṃ). When? (kudā).

## 461. Sabbassetattatṃ tothesu vā.
When the suffixes 'to' and 'tha' follow, the whole word 'eta' is optionally changed to 'a'. From this place (ato). In this place (attha). (If 'a' is not substituted:) Etto, ettha.

## 462. Niccaṃ tre.
When the suffix 'tra' follows, the whole word 'eta' is always changed to the letter 'a'. In this place (atra).

## 463. Idဿိ thaṃဒါနိဟတောဓေသု.
When the suffixes 'thaṃ', 'dāni', 'ha', 'to', and 'dha' follow, the whole word 'idaṃ' is changed to 'i'. In this way (itthaṃ). Now (idāni). Here (iha). From here (ito). Here (idha).

## 464. Dhunāmhattaṃ.
When the suffix 'dhunā' follows, the whole word 'idaṃ' is changed to 'a'. Now (adhunā).

## 465. Rahimheta.
When the suffix 'rahi' follows, the whole word 'idaṃ' is changed to 'eta'. Now (etarahi).

## 466. Avaṇṇantitthiyā āpaccayo.
After feminine stems ending in the letters 'a' or 'ā', the suffix 'ā' is added. Kaññā, saddhā, sālā, sabbā, yā, sā, kā, katarā, sabbaññutā, janatā, devatā.
99:
467. The suffix 'ī' is added in the feminine gender after words beginning with 'nada' and words other than those beginning with 'nada'. Nadī (river), mahī (earth), kumārī (maiden), taruṇī (young woman), sakhī (female friend), itthī (woman), yakkhī (female ogre), nāgī (female nāga).

468. The suffix 'ī' is added in the feminine gender after the suffixes 'ṇava', 'ṇika', 'ntu', and 'ṇeyya'. Māṇavī (daughter of Māṇava), paṇḍavī (daughter of Paṇḍu), nāvikī (woman who travels by boat), gotamī (daughter of Gotama), guṇavatī (virtuous woman), satimatī (mindful woman), venateyyī (son of Vinatā), konteyyī (son of Kuntī).

469. The suffix 'inī' is added after stems ending in 'i' (such as 'pati'), stems ending in 'u' or 'ū' (such as 'bhikkhu'), stems ending in 'a' (such as 'rāja'), and stems ending in 'ī' (such as 'daṇḍi'). Gahapatānī (housewife), isinī (female sage), kapinī (female monkey), kiminī (female insect), arinī (female enemy), bhikkhunī (nun), paracittavidunī (woman who knows others' minds), utunī (menstruating woman), rājinī (queen), yakkhinī (female ogre), nāginī (female nāga), khattiyānī (noble lady), sākiyānī (Sākyan lady), araññānī (great forest), pokkharaṇī (lotus pond), sīhinī (lioness), tāpasinī (female ascetic), daṇḍinī (woman with a staff), bhoginī (concubine), sukhinī (happy woman), sikhinī (woman with a husband/crest), hatthinī (female elephant), medhāvinī (wise woman), tapassinī (lonely/ascetic woman), piyabhāṇinī (woman of pleasant speech). Other words should also be joined in this manner.

470. The suffix 'inī' is also added after the word 'iddhimantu' in the feminine gender. Iddhimantanī (woman with psychic power), iddhimantiniyo (women with psychic powers).

471. When the suffix 'ī' follows, the entire part of the suffix 'ntu' is changed to the letter 't'. Guṇavatī (virtuous woman), satimatī (mindful woman), cakkhumatī (woman with the eye of wisdom), bhikkhunī (nun), bhāvitindriyā (one with developed faculties). A woman should be beautiful (rūpavatī). Iddhimatī (woman with psychic power), mahatī (great), naṅgalasīsā (like a plow-head). The teachers, however, desire the change of the suffix 'ntu' to 't' optionally in some cases. In their view, forms such as guṇavatī, guṇavantī, kulavatī, kulavantī, satimatī, satimantī, mahatī, mahantī, etc., occur. Among them, varieties like 'guṇavantī' are rarely found in the Dispensation (Sāsana).

472. When the suffix 'ī' in the feminine gender follows, the whole word 'bhavanta' is changed to 'bhota'. Bhoti ayye (Noble lady), bhoti kaññe (O maiden), bhoti kharādiye (O Kharādiya).

473. Bho ge. Due to the vocative case ending ge, the entire word bhavanta is changed to bho. Examples: O man, O fire.

474. Athavekabahvatthēsu bho nipāto. Alternatively, it should be known that the particle bho occurs in both singular and plural meanings. Examples: O man, stand; O men, stand; O mind, O minds. O man, know thus. That chaplain said to those king's men, "O you, if you wish to kill me, kill me only after showing me to the king." O yakkhas, O drunkards. O great stone slab, emerge upon the water. O housewives, go. In the direct address of the Dhamma, the word bho has a singular ending: "O, how wonderful! O, how marvelous!"

475. Matantarē akārapitādīnamā. In another teacher's view, due to the ge ending, the short a and the endings of words such as pitu become long ā. Examples: O man, stand; O father, O brother, O mother, O teacher, etc.

476. So rassaṃ vā. In another teacher's view, that substituted ā optionally becomes short a due to the ge ending. Examples: O king, O king (long), O self, O self (long), O teacher, O teacher (long), etc., are stated in the singular sense according to another teacher's view.

477. Pa-jha-lā niccaṃ. These letters called pa, jha, and la always become short due to the ge ending. Examples: O woman, O daughter-in-law, Phussatī of noble complexion, O one with a staff, O Self-become (Sayam-bhū).

478. Rājādisatthāditō gassattaṃ. After the rāja group and the satthā group, the ge ending must always be changed to a. "O great king, practice the Dhamma." "O king, I am not a helpless person." O self, O teacher, O father.

479. Brahmādikattāditō vā. After words beginning with brahmā and kattū, the ge ending should optionally be changed to a. (Examples:) O Brahmā, O friend, O minister, O minister. Why is "optionally" said? (Examples where the change to a does not occur:) "O Brahmā, (preach) the sublime Dhamma among men", "O Mahābrahmā, flee", "Hey friend, why do you abandon me?", "O minister, arise", "O minister, if so". Here khattā refers to a minister who manages all affairs. Both the words kattā and khattā have no difference in meaning (they are synonymous).

480. Matantarē bhavantassa bhōnta-bhantē-bhōntō-bhaddē ge galōpō. In another teacher's view, due to the ge ending, the word bhavanta is changed to bhōnta, bhantē, bhōntō, or bhaddē, and the ge ending is also elided. (Examples:) bhōnta, bhantē, bhōntō, bhaddē.

481. Bhōntīti appasiddhaṃ. In this Dispensation of the Blessed One, among those four forms, it should be known that the form bhōnta is not well-known (rarely used).

482. Bhantē-bhaddēti ekaputhuvacanantamabyayaṃ. The two words bhantē and bhaddē should be regarded as indeclinables (particles) ending in both singular and plural, just like the word āvuso. (Examples:) "Venerable sir, come." That person made those monks forgive him, saying, "Venerable sirs, please forgive." "O lady, you are a queen." "O good ladies, go."

483. Ayyatō ālapana-ekavacana-bahuvacanānamō vā. After the word ayya, the vocative singular and plural endings should optionally be changed to o. (Examples:) "O noble one, go", "O noble ones, go", "O friend, do not do such a thing", "O noble ones, come to the royal residence." Why is "optionally" said? (Examples where the change to o does not occur:) "O noble one", "O noble ones".
102:
484. Savibhattikassa bhōntō paccattālapana-atthe yōsu. Due to the yo endings occurring in the nominative sense and vocative sense, the word bhavanta together with its case ending should optionally be changed to bhōntō. Example: "May the venerable wanderers be silent." Thus in the nominative sense: "May the venerable wanderers not make a sound", "O three hundred disciples, listen to these words of the Buddha." It is also thus in the vocative sense. Why is "optionally" said? To prevent the change in places such as: "Those venerable ones come", "Venerable ones, come".

485. Nā-smā-sēsu bhōtā-bhōtō. Due to the nā, smā, and sa endings, the word bhavanta together with its case ending should optionally be changed to bhōtā or bhōtō. Examples: "With the Venerable Gotama", "Departing from the venerable one", "Is the venerable one well?", "The property of the venerable one". Why is "optionally" said? To allow the forms: bhavantēna, bhavata, bhavantassa, bhavatō.

486. Matantarē vassōbhāvō kvaci yōsu. In the view of other teachers, due to the yo endings, the letter va of the word bhavanta should sometimes be changed to o. Examples: "Venerable ones, stand", "He sees the venerable ones". Why is "sometimes" said? To prevent the change in places such as: "If these three matters are acceptable to the venerable ones' reflection, they should be taken."

487. Bhaddantassa vā bhadantē ge. When the ge ending follows, the word bhaddanta should optionally be changed to bhadantē. Examples: "Venerable sir, now the trees flowering at the tips of the vines are like glowing embers", "O great king, we are five wise men". Why is "optionally" said? To allow the form: "He bhaddante".

488. Matantarē bhadanta-bhantē yōsu ca. In the view of other teachers, when the ge and yo endings follow, the word bhaddanta should also be changed to bhadanta or bhantē. Examples: bhadanta, bhantē. Why is "sometimes" said? To prevent those changes in places such as: bhaddanta, bhaddantā.

## 489. Saddaniddesova atthaniddeso.
In some places, the ancient commentators have indicated the meaning in the same way as indicating the word. What is that? The word "Bhagavā" is noble. It is called "vacana" because it is spoken; it conveys the meaning. "Bhagavā" is the meaning; "noble one" is the meaning. Why is it said "in some places"? Having heard the words of that king, the King of Devas (Sakka) said this.

## 490. Atthaniddesova saddaniddeso.
In some places, the grammarians (akkhara-cintaka) have indicated the word in the same way as indicating the meaning; it is not only we who do this now. For example: "Tumhamhākaṃ tayimayī".

## 491. Amhatumhānaṃ tomhi mamatava.
When the suffix -to follows, the substitutions mama and tava always occur in place of the words amha and tumha. [Examples:] He departs from me (mamato apeti); he departs from you (tavato apeti). There is no one more excellent than I (mamato uttaritaro natthi). This person is superior to you (tavato ayaṃ adhiko). This person is inferior to you (tavato ayaṃ hīno). In this regard, there is this Pali: "By [her] power, she created a woman more beautiful than even me (mamato)". Here, by seeing the occurrence of the Pali word "mamato", it should be noted that the word "tavato", which is not seen, is also included. This is because those wise ones who know the method must take the unseen method that follows the same rule as the seen method. Why is it said "when the suffix -to follows"? [Examples with -yā:] He departs from me (mayā apeti); he departs from you (tayā apeti); there is no one superior to me; this person is inferior to you.

## 492. Tvādayo ekabavhatthesu vibhattisaññā.
The suffixes starting from -to and ending with -dācanaṃ, when occurring in the singular and plural senses as appropriate, are called vibhatti (case endings). [Examples:] sabbato, yato, tato, kuto, ato, ito, sabbadā, yadā, tadā, idha, idāni, and so on.

## 493. Tatiyapañcamīchaṭṭhīsattamīyatthesu to kvaci.
In some places, the suffix -to is applied in the senses of the instrumental (tatiyā), ablative (pañcamī), genitive (chaṭṭhī), and locative (sattamī) cases. [Examples:] aniccato (by way of impermanence), dukkhato (by way of suffering), rogato (by way of disease), and so on, occur in the instrumental sense.
104:
[Examples:] "Well-born from both sides, from the mother's side (mātito) and from the father's side (pitito), of pure descent." And, "In this world, no destruction of wealth comes from the king (rājato), or from thieves (corato), or from fire (aggito)." Such examples occur in the ablative sense. "I do not desire that wealth obtained through the support of another's gift (parato dānapaccayā)." Thus it occurs in the genitive sense. The meaning is "because of the support of another's (parassa) gift." [Examples:] ekato, purato, pacchato, passato, piṭṭhito, pādato, sīsato, mūlato, heṭṭhato, and so on, occur in the locative sense. [Examples:] sabbato, katarato, yato, tato, and so on, occur in the instrumental, ablative, and locative senses as appropriate. Why is it said "in some places"? [Because of forms like] sabbeṇa, sabbasmā, sabbasmiṃ.

## 494. Sattamiyā tratha sabbanāmato.
After pronouns (sabbanāma), the suffixes -tra and -tha occur in the locative sense. [Examples:] sabbatra, sabbattha (also occurs as sabbasmiṃ), yatra, yattha, tatra, tattha, amutra, amuttha.

## 495. Yamhā paṭhamatthe.
In some places, after the word "ya", the suffixes -tra and -tha occur in the sense of the nominative case (paṭhamā). [Examples:] "Even which (yatra) disciple." "Where (yattha) such a teacher exists." Why is it said "in some places"? [Because of forms like] yo hi nāma, yo etādiso.

## 496. Itinā niddisitabbe to.
In some places, the suffix -to occurs in the nominative sense when it is to be indicated by the word "iti". [Examples:] Those of wrong view regard form as self (attato). The fool regards that object as beautiful (subhato). They contemplate as impermanent (aniccato). In that context, "attato upagacchanti" means they take it as "self" (attā). This same method applies in other cases as well.

## 497. Yတေဟိ ပစ္စတ္တဝစနဿ တော နိဒါနာဒီသု.
When words such as "nidāna" follow, the nominative case (paccattavacana) after the words "ya" and "ta" is in some places replaced by the substitution -to. [Example:] yatonidānaṃ (because of which cause).
105:
(Page-105) That thing has that cause (tatonidānaṃ). Because of which reason (yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ) [he is oppressed]. Why is "kvaci" (in some places) said? Because there is the evidence "yaṃnidānaṃ" (because of which cause).

498. When the vibhattis -smiṃ and -sa follow, the niggahīta of the word "kiṃ" must be elided. The forms are: "Why (kismiṃ) are the Sivi people angry with me?", "Of what (kissa) well-practiced [deed] is this the result?"

499. In the locative sense, the suffix -va must be applied after the word "kiṃ". The forms are: "Where (kva) is the dance? Where (kva) is the song?", "O King Devānampiyatissa, where (kva) are you going?"

500. After the word "ku", the suffixes -hiṃ, -haṃ, -hiñcanaṃ, and -hiñci must be applied. [Examples:] kuhiṃ, kuhaṃ, kuhiñcanaṃ, kuhiñci. These suffixes are not applied in the case of "kismiṃ me sivayo kuddhā".

501. After the word "ta", the suffixes -hiṃ and -haṃ must be applied. [Examples:] tahiṃ, tahaṃ. Alternatively, it can also be "tasmiṃ".

502. After the word "sabba", the suffix -dhi must be applied. [Example:] sabbadhi. Alternatively, it can also be "sabbasmiṃ".

503. After the word "idaṃ", the suffixes -ha and -dhā must be applied. [Examples:] iha, idha. Alternatively, it can also be "imasmiṃ".

504. After the word "ya", the suffix -hiṃ must be applied. [Example:] yahiṃ. Alternatively, it can also be "yasmiṃ" or "yesu".

505. When the sense of time (kāla) is intended, the suffixes -dā and -dācanaṃ must be applied after the words kiṃ, sabba, añña, eka, ya, and ku. The forms are: kadā, sabbadā, aññadā, ekadā, yadā, kudā, kudācanaṃ. The evidence is: "I have never seen (kudācanaṃ) your Dhamma or Adhamma at any time", "When (kudā) will that matter happen?"

506. After the word "ta", the suffixes -dā and -dāni must be applied. [Examples:] tadā, tadāni.

507. After the word "idaṃ", the suffixes -rahi, -dhunā, and -dāni must be applied. [Examples:] etarahi, adhunā, idāni. Some teachers explain the sense of time by associating it individually with the four words: "yadā, tadā, sadā, idāni".
106:
Some teachers say 'yadā kāle' and so forth, by combining the word 'kāle' with each of these four words: yadā, tadā, sadā, and idāni. This should not be accepted. The reasons are: because the suffixes -dā and -dāni already denote time (kāla); because it would result in a redundant expression similar to saying 'yasmiṃ kāle' (at which time); and because such a method is not found in the Buddha's words of the Tipiṭaka along with the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

However, the method of using synonyms (vevacana) is found in the Buddha's words specifically taught as: 'Appaṃ vassasataṃ āyu, idānetarahi vijjati' (Life is less than a hundred years; it exists now, at this present time).

Similarly, some say 'yasmā kāraṇā' and so forth, by combining the word 'kāraṇā' with each of the words 'yasmā' and 'tasmā'. This also should not be accepted. The reasons are: because the causal meaning is already made clear by the indeclinable words 'yasmā, tasmā, kasmā' themselves; and because such a method, occurring by way of common usage (lokavohāra), is not found in the Pali Canon or the ancient Commentaries. Therefore, seeing such a method in any particular place is not an authority for the wise.

In the Commentaries, however, it is found as: 'yasmā means for which reason (yaṃ kāraṇā), yasmā means by which reason (yena kāraṇena), tasmā means for that reason (taṃ kāraṇā), tasmā means by that reason (tena kāraṇena), kasmā means for what reason (kiṃ kāraṇā), kasmā means by what reason (kena kāraṇena)'. In texts such as the Netti, 'kiṃ kāraṇaṃ' is also found: 'Among those persons' practices, for what reason (kiṃ kāraṇaṃ) does one with a craving temperament emerge through the painful practice with sluggish direct-knowledge or with swift direct-knowledge?'

When a cause such as ignorance (avijjā) is to be spoken of in the context of ultimate reality (paramattha), then 'tasmā kāraṇā' is said; it means 'tato hetuto' (from that cause). Indeed, even in the Commentary, a place where 'tasmā kāraṇā' is said with this very meaning in mind is found; we shall not show that place here. Let those wise persons who are capable of grasping the method search for that place. Thus, in the context of common usage, 'yasmā kāraṇā' etc. should not be said; but in the context of ultimate reality, it is said based on the aforementioned meaning—this system should be well borne in mind.

508. Sabbassa dāmhi so vā. When followed by the suffix -dā, the end of the word 'sabba' is optionally (vā) changed to the letter 'sa'. (Example:) 'Sadā ramati paṇḍito' (A wise person always delights). Why is 'vā' (optionally) said? It is to indicate that the word 'sabba' is not changed in places such as 'Sabbadā sīlasampanno' (One endowed with virtue always crosses the flood).

In this matter, this is said: In some Paritta books, the reading 'sabbabuddhānubhāvena, sabbadhammānubhāvena, sabbasaṅghānubhāvena sabbadā sadā sotthi bhavantu te' is found. That reading is improper. This is because the word 'sabbadā' and the word 'sadā' cannot be combined together. Therefore, only the phrase 'sadā sotthi bhavantu te' should be said.

Here, there might be an objection: 'O teacher, just as in the Pali passage "Appaṃ vassasataṃ āyu, idānetarahi vijjati", the words idāni and etarahi, though having the same meaning, are seen combined as synonyms, so too can the words sabbadā and sadā be combined as synonyms, can they not?' That is not so, because such a method is illogical in the books carefully considered by the teachers, and because there would be an excess of syllables in the verse foot (gāthāpāda).

In this matter, the following decision should be understood: In that reading, the word 'sabba' alone, excluding the suffix -dā, should be regarded as being stated by way of the method of ellipsis (peyyāla). This is true: in ancient books, the word 'sabba' is found without the suffix -dā as 'sabbasaṅghānubhāvena sabba sadā sotthi bhavantu te'. By such an ellipsis of the word 'sabba', the teachers stated the reading 'sabba sadā sotthi bhavantu te' to show that, just like the phrase 'sadā sotthi bhavantu te' in the fourth foot of the three verses beginning with 'Yaṃkiñci ratanaṃ loke', the verse 'Bhavatu sabbamaṅgalaṃ' should be divided into three parts, and the phrase 'sadā sotthi bhavantu te' should be appended at the end of each foot in the fourth foot position for each of the phrases 'sabbabuddhānubhāvena' and so forth. This is true. In this case, with the word [sabba] which is without case ending...
108:
The method of ellipsis (peyyāla) is shown by the word 'sabba' (all). Therefore, it should be understood that this phrase "sadā sotthi bhavantu te" (may you always be well) must be connected in all places. For those who, without considering such a method, think that the syllable 'dā' has been omitted (lost) in this place and insert the word 'dā' to recite "sabbadā sadā sotthi bhavantu te," their reading should not be accepted. The reading should be recited only according to the method of expansion.

In that context, the method of ellipsis (peyyāla-naya) refers to the method of expansion (vitthāra-naya). Stopping here, three types of ellipsis methods are stated. They are: the ellipsis indicated by the word 'iti' by taking the initial and final words/syllables and omitting the middle; the ellipsis indicated by the word 'ādi'; and the ellipsis indicated by the word 'sabba'. Here, for the ease of understanding for the listeners, I shall provide an illustration (payoga). What is that illustration? A wise person, endowed with the wisdom of rebirth-linking, being ardent and prudent, establishing himself in virtue (sīla), develops concentration (samādhi) and insight (vipassanā). That person, having cut through the tangle of craving, attains Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Establishing in virtue... he untangles this tangle."

In this place, the word 'āha' (said) should be joined with the word 'iti' as "iti āha" (thus he said). This is called the ellipsis indicated by the word 'iti', taking the beginning and the end while omitting the middle. Where it is not indicated in this way but shown as "tenāha bhagavā sīle patiṭṭhāyāti ādi," the method of expansion is shown by the word 'ādi' joined with the nominative case. This is called the ellipsis indicated by the word 'ādi'. In this place, because there is no word 'iti' alone, the word 'āha' cannot obtain a connection (sambandha) with 'iti' as "iti āha." Similarly, because the word 'āha' is not stated by the power of the accusative case of the word 'ādi', it cannot obtain a connection with the word 'iti ādi' as "iti ādimāha." Therefore, separating the phrase "tenāha bhagavā," it is shown by the word 'ādi' together with 'iti' in the phrase "sīle patiṭṭhāyāti ādi." The verse ending with the words "so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ" is shown in its complete form. The ellipsis by the word 'sabba' has already been mentioned. There are three types of ellipsis: middle ellipsis (majjhe-peyyāla), initial ellipsis (ādi-peyyāla), and all-inclusive ellipsis (sabba-peyyāla). This system should also be well-reflected upon.

509. Avaṇṇo yamhi lopaṃ. Before the suffix 'ya', the 'avaṇṇa' (a, ā) undergoes elision. Examples include bāhussaccaṃ, etc.

510. Pasatthassa sattho niccaṃ. The word 'pasattha' must always be substituted with 'sattha'. This is the original commentary (mūla-vutti). This is the explanatory commentary (anuvutti) that makes the meaning known. The root 'saṃsa' occurs in the sense of praising. By the power of the suffix 'ta' prescribed in the sense of the object (kamma) following this root 'saṃsa', all 'pasattha' words that arise must always be substituted with 'sattha'. Because people praise that person, he is called 'sattho'. Similarly, he is also called 'pasattho'. In this context, it should be noted that these words 'sattho' and 'pasattho' differ only by the absence or presence of a prefix (upasagga), just like the words 'takko' and 'vitakko', or 'cāro' and 'vicāro', but there is no distinction in their meaning. Why is 'pasatthassa' said? (The answer is) for the words 'viddhasthā' (destroyed) and 'vinalīkatā' (uprooted).
109:
The verse ending with the words "so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ" is shown in its complete form. The ellipsis by the word 'sabba' (sabba-sadda-peyyāla) has already been mentioned.

There are three types of ellipsis:
Middle ellipsis (majjhe-peyyāla),
Initial ellipsis (ādi-peyyāla),
And all-inclusive ellipsis (sabba-peyyāla).
This method should also be well-reflected upon.

## 509. Avaṇṇo yamhi lopaṃ.
Before the suffix 'ya', the 'avaṇṇa' (a, ā) undergoes elision. Examples: bāhussaccaṃ (great learning), paṇḍiccaṃ (wisdom), vepullaṃ (abundance), kāruññaṃ (compassion), kosallaṃ (skillfulness), sāmaññaṃ (asceticism), sohajjaṃ (friendship).

## 510. Pasatthassa sattho niccaṃ.
The word 'pasattha' is always substituted by 'sattha'. This is the original commentary (vutti). This is the explanatory commentary (anuvutti) that makes the meaning known. The root 'saṃsa' occurs in the sense of praising (pasaṃsana). By the power of the suffix 'ta' prescribed in the sense of the object (kamma) following that root 'saṃsa', all 'pasattha' words that arise are always substituted by 'sattha'. People praise that person (saṃsiyati pasaṃsiyati), therefore he is called 'sattho'. Similarly, he is called 'pasattho'. In this context, it should be noted that these words 'sattho' and 'pasattho' are distinguished only by the absence or presence of a prefix (upasagga), just like the words 'takko' and 'vitakko', or 'cāro' and 'vicāro'. In terms of meaning, however, there is no distinction. Why is 'pasatthassa' said? (For the words) viddhasthā (destroyed), vinalīkatā (uprooted). When the dawn has risen (aruṇe uddhatte).

## 511. Satthassa so tame.
The word 'sattha', which expresses 'praised' (pasattha-vācaka), is substituted by 'sa' before the suffix 'tama'. This person is praised, and this person is also praised; this person is praised specifically more than these others—thus he is called 'sattamo'. It means 'the most praised' (pasatthataro). For that reason, the word 'sattamo' is found by way of extracting the meaning both in the sense of an ordinal number (saṃkhyā-pūraṇa, i.e., the seventh) and in the sense of a virtuous person (sādhu-jana). The Blessed One (Isisattamo), who is more specifically praised than the group of seers (isi) who have seen the Four Noble Truths (or who is the seventh when counting from Vipassī), preached the Paṭṭhāna treatise (Sattamaṃ), which is more specifically praised than the earlier treatises (or which is the seventh). In this context, the former word 'Sattamaṃ' is stated only by the power of the ordinal sense. However, this word 'Isisattamo' is stated both by the power of the ordinal sense and by the power of a virtuous person who is said to be specifically praised. For that very reason, the treatise named Paṭṭhāna is the seventh, following the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and other treatises. The Blessed One, who is noble among the Sakyan kings, is the seventh Buddha, following Vipassī and the other Buddhas. Of the person who is specifically praised...
110:
...is also seen. In the phrase "Sattamaṃ isisattamo," the word *sattama* is found in the sense of completing the number seven (the ordinal sense) and in the sense of a virtuous person (one who is praised). Here, the word "sattamaṃ" is spoken only by way of the ordinal sense (the seventh). However, the word "isisattamo" is said to be spoken both by way of the ordinal sense and especially by way of the sense of a virtuous person, meaning a most praiseworthy individual.

This is because the treatise named Paṭṭhāna is the seventh book when taking the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and others in order. The Blessed One, who is like a lion among the Sakyans, is also the seventh Buddha when taking Vipassī and the other Buddhas in order. He is also called "sattama" by virtue of being a most praiseworthy person.

Therefore, it is stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: "'Isisattamo' means one who is most especially praised among the praiseworthy sages (*isi*) who have reached the designation of 'sages' due to their path of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. When taking Vipassī and the other Buddhas in order, the Blessed One is called the seventh (*sattama*)." Here, the phrase "catusaccāvabodhagatiyā" is spoken by taking the meaning of the root "*isu gatiyaṃ*" according to the method of grammar.

The word-analysis (*vigraha*) here is: "Isīnaṃ sattamo" (the most excellent among sages) or "Isīsu sattamo" (the most excellent in sages). Alternatively, Noble Ones such as the Buddha are called "isi" because they seek (*esana*) virtues such as morality (*sīla*) in their own continuums and the continuums of others. He is called "Isisattama" because he is both a sage (*isi*) and especially praiseworthy (or the seventh). Thus should the meaning be understood here.

512. Pasatthassa iyiṭṭhesu. When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the entire word *pasattha* is substituted with *sa*. (Examples:) *Seyyo*, *seṭṭho*.

513. Jo vuḍḍhassa. (When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow,) the word *vuḍḍha* is substituted with *ja*. (Examples:) *Jeyyo*, *jeṭṭho*.

514. Nedantikassa. (When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow,) the word *antika* is substituted with *neda*. (Examples:) *Nediyo*, *nediṭṭho*.

515. Sādho bāḷhassa. (When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow,) the word *bāḷha* is substituted with *sādha*. (Examples:) *Sādhiyo*, *sādhiṭṭho*.

516. Khuddakassa kaṇo. (When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow,) the word *khuddaka* is substituted with *kaṇa*. (Examples:) *Kaṇiyo*, *kaṇiṭṭho*.
111:
517. Matantare yuvassa ca. In the opinion of other teachers, the word *yuva* also (becomes *kaṇa*). In the other opinion of teachers, when the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the entire word *yuva* is substituted with *kaṇa*. Examples: *Kaṇiyo*, *kaṇiṭṭho*.

518. Lutti vantumantuvīnaṃ. When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the suffixes *vantu*, *mantu*, and *vī* are elided. Examples: *Guṇiyo*, *guṇiṭṭho*, *satiyo*, *satiṭṭho*, *medhiyo*, *medhiṭṭho*.

519. Nidāne kissa kuto samāse. In a compound (*samāsa*), when the word *nidāna* follows, the word *kiṃ* is substituted with *kuto*. The word *kiṃ* existing in a compound is substituted with *kuto* when the word *nidāna* follows. In the sense of "What is the cause of these dhammas?", it becomes *kutonidānā*.

520. Idassa ito. The word *idaṃ* existing in a compound is substituted with *ito* when the word *nidāna* follows. In the sense of "This existence (*attabhāva*) is the cause of these [dhammas]", it becomes *itonidānā*.

521. Itthañca nāme. When the word *nāma* follows, the substitution *itthaṃ* also occurs. When the word *nāma* follows, the word *idaṃ* existing in a compound is substituted with *ittham*. In the sense of "The name of this person is thus," it becomes *itthan-nāmo*. It means "one having such a name." However, in places such as "The Venerable Puḷinathūpiya Thera spoke these verses in this manner (*itthaṃ*)," the suffix *thaṃ* should be understood as being applied in the sense of manner (*pakārattha*) in the word *itthaṃ*.

522. Kvaci kvassa ko iti. In some instances, the word *kva* is substituted with *ko*. In some contexts, the word *kva* becomes *ko*. "O Great King, where is your strength? Where is your array of chariots?" Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? To prevent the substitution in "*kva naccaṃ*."

523. Sossa su. The word *so* is substituted with *su* in some instances. The word *so* becomes *su* in some instances. "Like a beast that cannot achieve its purpose with gold, he could not achieve his purpose with that Dhamma." Why is "kvaci" said? To prevent the substitution in "*evaṃ so nihato seti*."
112:
524. Nossa nu amhatthe. In the sense of "our" (*amhākaṃ*), this word *no* is substituted with *nu* in some instances. The example is: "*api nu anukā santā*" (the young of the crows are indeed weary). Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? To prevent the substitution of *nu* in places such as "*api no*." Why is "no" said? To prevent the substitution of *nu* in places such as "*sāni maṃsāni*" (the flesh of dogs).

525. Kitake antato sissu vā. In a *kitaka* (derivative) word, the vowel *u* is optionally substituted for the *si* inflection following the suffix *anta*. The example is: "*avhāyantu suyuddhena*" (challenging me with a good fight). Why is "vā" (optionally) said? To prevent the substitution of *u* in places such as "*avhāyanto aṭṭhāsi*" (he stood calling).

526. Ācariyassācero. The word *ācariya* is optionally substituted with *ācera*. The forms are *ācero* or *ācariya* (teacher). Illustrative examples are: "*āceramiva māဏavo*" (as a young student serves his teacher), and "*ñatvā ācerakaṃ mataṃ*" (knowing the teacher's view).

527. Saṃsaddassa niggahītaṃ mattamīkāre saro dīghaṃ me. The *niggahīta* of the word *saṃ* is substituted with the letter *ma* when followed by the suffix *ī* which has the possessive sense (*assatthi*). Because it is followed by that letter *ma*, the vowel *a* of the preceding *sa* is lengthened. "*Saṃ assa atthīti sāmī*" (He has wealth, therefore he is called *sāmī*). This name *sāmī* is a designation for a ruler (lord). If that *ī* is shortened, it becomes *sāmi*. In the feminine gender, it is formed as *sāminī* by means of the suffix *inī*.
