After they have been made to face one, they are later connected with an action such as "Go" or "Eat." Therefore, because there is no connection with an action at the time of addressing, this Vocative does not receive the designation of kāraka. In the case of what is to be performed now, there is no designation of Āmantana. For how can one address that which does not clearly exist? For that very reason, the designation of the address "Buddha" is seen only after the Blessed One had attained Buddhahood.
145:
The vocative address "Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero" (Namo te buddha vīratthū) (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.48) does not apply to a Bodhisatta who has not yet become a Buddha; it applies only to a person who has attained Buddhahood. Similarly, the address "O Great King, practice the Dhamma" (Dhammañcara mahārājā) (Khuddaka Nikāya 6.4) is not found for one who is not yet a king, but only for a king who has been consecrated. Therefore, such an address does not exist for something that is yet to be established, as in "May you become a king." Although one might address something that is not currently established or does not exist by nature as "O non-existence," "O rabbit's horn," or "O son of a barren woman," such addresses are not authoritative.

577. Liṅgatthe paṭhamā.
The first (nominative) case ending occurs in the mere expression of the meaning of the stem (liṅga).
Examples: Puriso, purisā, itthī, kulaṃ, pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, phasso, vedanā, nibbānaṃ, doṇo, khārī, āḷakaṃ, eko, dve. All prefixes (upasagga) such as pa, parā, etc., should also be joined. There are also some particles (nipāta) such as atthi, sakkā, labbhā, ha, aha, etc. The particles divā, bhiyyo, namo occur in both the nominative sense and the accusative sense. Particles like ca, vā, pana, etc., occur in the senses of all seven case endings starting from the nominative.

In this context, the word itself is intended as the "stem" (liṅga) because it makes known or indicates the meanings—such as the conceptual meanings of woman, man, etc., or the ultimate meanings of hardness, touching, etc.—which are expressed by the three types of gender and are free from clarity, lack of clarity, or both; or because it indicates meanings like "variety" (pakāra) of prefixes, etc., which are free from those three characteristics.

The "meaning of the stem" (liṅgattha) refers to the conceptual meaning of terms like "pot" or "cloth," known as derivative concepts (upādā-paññatti), which are designated based on form, etc., arising in a particular continuity and which cannot be said to be identical to or different from those forms, and which are divided into groups, continuities, etc. It also refers to the general characteristic such as "hardness," known as an appropriate concept (tajjā-paññatti), which is common to its own class and distinct from other classes of natural phenomena like the earth element or contact, which are differentiated by time, place, etc., and which is established by metaphorical attribution according to convention.

That stem-meaning is of two types: mixed with the object (kamma), etc., and pure (suddha). Among these, since the second (accusative) case endings, etc., are prescribed for the object, etc., the term liṅgattha in this rule refers to the meaning of a pure word—one that is unmixed with the object, etc., and is associated with gender, number, and quantity, or the meaning of words like prefixes that are free from those. It should be understood that the meaning mixed with the eight entities like the object, as expressed by verbs, primary derivatives (kita), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa), also falls within the scope of the nominative case because it is not the domain of the accusative, etc., and because only the stem-meaning is prominently present.

Regarding this, the summary verse (saṅgaha-gāthā) beginning with "Paṭhamā vibhāveti" will be cited:
The nominative case alone occurs in the sense of prefixes, in the sense of certain particles, in the sense of the object, etc., as expressed by the four types of expressors (vācaka), and in the pure, unmixed meaning of the stem.

32. Ālapane ca.
The nominative case ending also occurs in the sense of address (ālapaṇa). When the sense of address exceeds the mere expression of the stem-meaning...
146:
In this sutra, the term 'liṅgattha' (meaning of the stem) refers to the pure meaning of a word that is associated with gender (liṅga), number (saṅkhyā), and measure (parimāṇa), or the meaning of words such as prefixes (upasarga) and particles (nipāta) which are free from those, and is not mixed with the object (kamma) and so forth. Even the meaning mixed with the object, etc., expressed by verbs (ākhyāta), primary derivatives (kita), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa), should be understood as the domain of the first case (paṭhamā vibhatti) only, because there is no special meaning to be further expressed by the second case (dutiyā) and so forth, and because only the 'liṅgattha' is evident. In this regard, it is said:
"The first case occurs in the sense of a prefix, in the sense of certain particles, even when the sense of the object (kamma) etc. is expressed (by the word-form), and in the pure sense of the stem (liṅga) etc."

578. Ālapane ca. The first case occurs in the sense of the stem (liṅgattha) when there is the additional sense of address (ālapana). (Examples) O man, O men. Friend, come here; (to the father) please call him back. Friends, know the place. O king of golden deer, make an effort. Friend cobra, why do you abandon me? Hey, vile thief! Maid, take this child; lady, do not be angry, and so forth.

579. Hetumhi. The first case also occurs in the sense of cause (hetu). (Examples) They do not speak untruth for their own sake. Why do you not delight in birth? and so forth.

580. Kammatthe dutiyā. The second case occurs in the sense of the object (kamma). (Examples) He makes a chariot. He milks a cow.

581. Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge. When time (kāla) and distance (addhāna) are continuously associated with a substance (dabba), quality (guṇa), or action (kriyā), the second case occurs after the stems expressing that time and distance. Regarding time—(He partakes of) milk-rice for seven days; (He partakes of) meat-rice for a month. The river is pleasant throughout the autumn (sarada); the Nandana garden is pleasant at all times. He recites for a month; he studies for a month; he taught the Abhidhamma for three months. Regarding distance—There is a forest range for a yojana; the mountain is long for a yojana; he recites for a kosa; for a yojana...
147:
He goes while quarreling. Why is it said "in accantasaṃyoga" (continuous connection)? He eats month after month; he establishes a monastery at every league (yojana).

582. Prefixes (upasagga) such as anu and particles (nipāta) such as dhi are called kammapavacanīya. Prefixes such as anu and particles such as dhi receive the name kammapavacanīya. Those prefixes and particles which have a kamma (action) such as lakkhaṇa (characteristic) expressed in various ways are called kammapavacanīya.

583. The word anu is called kammapavacanīya in the senses of lakkhaṇa (characteristic), sahattha (association), and hīna (inferiority). Among those prefixes and particles, the word anu is called kammapavacanīya in the senses of lakkhaṇa, sahattha, and hīna. They go forth (become monks) following the Bodhisatta who went forth (or imitating the state of a monk). The city of Bārāṇasī is established along the river. The wise man is inferior to the Venerable Sāriputta.

584. The words pati, pari, and anu are called kammapavacanīya in the senses of lakkhaṇa (characteristic), itthambhūtakkhāna (state of being), bhāga (portion), and vicchā (repetition). In the sense of lakkhaṇa—May divine foods appear to me following the rising of the sun. The moon shines towards the tree; (pari) towards the tree; (anu) towards the tree. In the sense of itthambhūtakkhāna—Devadatta is good towards his mother; (pari) towards his mother; (anu) towards his mother. In the sense of bhāga—In this distribution, let whatever would be my portion be given; give the portion intended for me (pari). In the sense of vicchā—In every meaning, the name-word enters. The moon shines on every tree; (pari) on every tree; (anu) on every tree.

585. The word abhi is called kammapavacanīya in the senses of lakkhaṇa, vicchā, and itthambhūtakkhāna. This excellent sound of fame has spread abroad concerning that Venerable Gotama. The moon shines on every tree. Devadatta is good towards his mother. In the sense of a particle (nipāta)—I, the Buddha, rebuke the one who strikes (or kills) a Brahmin. Let there be reproach for the intense shooting with a piercing arrow. Let there be reproach for that vomited poison. And so forth.
148:
586. Kammapavacanīyayutte. In a construction connected with particles (nipāta) or prefixes (upasagga) having the sense of a kammapavacanīya, the second (accusative) case occurs. The examples are exactly as shown previously.

587. Gatibuddhibujapaṭhaharakarasayādīnaṃ kārite vā. In the construction of roots having the meanings of going, knowing, eating, reciting, carrying, doing, sleeping, etc., when connected with a causative (kārita) suffix, the second case optionally occurs. A man causes a man to go to the village, or [he causes to go] by means of a man. Likewise: causes to know, causes to eat, causes to recite, causes to carry, causes to do, causes to sleep; thus it occurs in all causative forms.

588. Kvaci chaṭṭhīnamatthe antarādiyogae. In connection with antarā, etc., the second case occurs in some instances in the sense of the sixth (genitive) case. This second case also occurs in connection with antarā, abhito, parito, pati, and paṭibhāti. He is one who has entered upon a long journey between Rājagaha and Nālandā. In the grammar of Saddattha, however, only one word antarā is used, as in "antarā nadiñca gāmañca" (between the river and the village). He dwells inside the village. He dwells around the village. Near the Nerañjarā river. Aggivessana, three similes indeed appeared in my mind.

589. Tatiyāsattamīnañca. The second case also occurs in some instances in the sense of the third (instrumental) and seventh (locative) cases. If the Ascetic Gotama greets me first. You also do not speak to me. Without the True Dhamma, where is happiness? Without the means, the goal is not accomplished. This is for the sense of the third case. For the sense of the seventh case, the second case occurs in terms of time and direction, in the construction of the root vasa preceded by upa, anu, or adhi, in the construction of the roots si, ṭhā, or vasa preceded by adhi, and in the sense of drinking or wandering therein. In time—Having adjusted the lower robe in the morning. At one time, the Blessed One... He benefits by way of the pre-existence condition (purejāta-paccaya) for a short time. In this night, the four Great Kings... In the eastern direction, the Great King Dhataraṭṭha... In the construction of the root vasa preceded by upa, etc.—He dwells depending on the village, dwells along [the village], dwells presiding over [the monastery].
149:
In the usage of the root vasa: he dwells depending on the village, dwells along the village, dwells presiding over the monastery, dwells in the village, dwells governing the house. In the usage of the roots si, ṭhā, and vasa preceded by adhi: he will sleep pressing upon the earth, he stands firmly in the village, he dwells governing the village. In the sense of drinking and wandering: he drinks from the river, he wanders in the village, and so forth.

590. Bhāvanapuṃsake dutiyekavacanaṃ. In an adverbial modifier (kriyāvisesana), also known as bhāvanapuṃsaka, the second case singular occurs. Here, bhāvanapuṃsaka is a term used in the Dispensation (Sāsana), while kriyāvisesana is a term used in grammatical treatises. Although ancient teachers said: "Since the standing of the agent in the sense of the object (kamma) for adverbial modifiers is established by logic, no separate rule is needed for that purpose," this rule was nevertheless commenced to provide a definition so that listeners would not be confused in usage. Because an action, being non-substantial, has an indistinct gender, lacks a specific number, and has the nature of being accomplished, its modifier is also used in the neuter gender, singular number, and second case ending. (Example:) The moon and the sun move unevenly (visamaṃ). He stood at one side (ekamantaṃ). Listen to that Dhamma well (sādhukaṃ) and attend to it. In that context, visamaṃ means "in an uneven manner." Ekamantaṃ means "another place" or "to one side," or it is the use of the second case in the sense of location (locative).

591. Karaṇe tatiyā. The third case occurs in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa). (Example:) He burns the hut with fire. He shoots with a bow.

592. Sahādiyogae ca. The third case also occurs in connection with saha, etc. The third case occurs when connected with words such as saha, saddhiṃ, samaṃ, nānā, vinā, and alaṃ. Among those, connection with the word saha occurs in the coexistence of action, quality, or substance. For example: It exists together with thought (vitakka). Together with the son...
150:
It is plump. It is the gain of the teachers and preceptors together with the resident pupils and those living with them. The Blessed One dwelt together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. It is compared as equal to a thousand [pieces of] wealth. There is separation and dissociation from all my dear and pleasing beings and formations. The Saṅgha may perform the Uposatha even without Gagga. There is no benefit for you by living here. Being a man who has seen strength, what benefit is there for me by crossing alone? O witless ascetic, what use have you for these matted locks? O Vakkali, what use have you for looking at this foul body? and so forth.

593. Sahatthe. The third case ending also occurs in the sense of "together with" (saha). Devadatta entered the city of Rājagaha together with Kokālika, the junior monk. Living together with fools is suffering.

594. Kattari paṭhamā tatiyā ca. The first case ending occurs for the agent expressed by a verb (ākhyāta). The third case ending occurs for the agent not expressed by a primary derivative (kita) or a verb (ākhyāta). The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma. The Dhamma is taught by the Blessed One. A snake bites a man. A man is bitten by a snake.

595. Dutiyatthe tatiyā. The third case ending occurs in the sense of the second case (accusative). He sows sesame in the field. Divide the kingship for us. Here, "tilehi" means "sesame" (accusative plural). Or, "hi" is merely a particle, and "tile" is a word ending in the accusative case, like the word "rūpe" in the passage: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises."

596. Pañcamiyatthe. The third case ending also occurs in the sense of the fifth case (ablative). We are well-freed from that Great Ascetic.
151:
Better than sole sovereignty over the earth,
Better than going to heaven,
Better than lordship over all the worlds,
Is the fruit of Stream-entry.

597. Paccatte. The third case ending also occurs in the sense of the agent (paccatta). As in: "I have need of a gem" (maṇinā me attho). However, the teachers also accept the usage: "He himself designates himself" (attanāva attānaṃ sammanni). That view is not appropriate. In this example, the bhikkhu is the agent; therefore, the word "attanāva" is a qualifier (visesana), and that qualifier excludes designation by others. Just as in this Aṅguttara passage: "He himself is a killer of living beings, and he encourages others in killing living beings," where the nominative sense "the person himself is a killer" is not appropriate, but rather the instrumental sense "the person by himself is a killer" is appropriate; likewise, in the phrase "He himself designates himself," the nominative sense "the bhikkhu himself designates himself" is not appropriate, but rather the instrumental sense "the bhikkhu by himself designates himself" is appropriate. This word "sayaṃ" (self/by oneself) functions in the instrumental sense, and the fact that the word "attanā" has the same meaning as the word "sayaṃ" is very well-known in the Dispensation. Therefore, it should be understood that the word "attanā" has the third case ending in the instrumental sense and qualifies the act of designating. Another method: this word "attanā" is an indeclinable (avyaya) that resembles a word with a case ending.

598. Itthambhūtalakkhaṇe. The third case ending occurs in the sense of a characteristic mark (lakkhaṇa) of a person who has reached such a state (itthambhūta). That servant girl named Kāḷī, with her broken head and with blood trickling down, caused the neighbors to despise [her mistress]. If one should have another new bowl exchanged for a bowl with fewer than five mends. In that example, "with a broken head" (bhinneṇa sīsena) means "having a broken head"; this method applies to other examples as well. Thus, in the Buddha's Dispensation, when two words with the same meaning (apposition) exist...
152:
...it is a characteristic mark of such a state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). In grammatical treatises, however, a word that does not have the same locus (vināsamanādhikaraṇa) is called itthambhūtalakkhaṇa. "He saw a wanderer [marked] by a triple staff" (tidaṇḍakena paribbājakaṃ adakkhi) means he saw a wanderer characterized by a triple staff. Similarly, in the case of "He saw the king [marked] by a white parasol" (setacchattena rājānaṃ adakkhi).

599. Kriyāpavagge. The very rapid completion of an action is called kriyāpavagga; in that sense, the third case ending occurs. For example: He set out for Bārāṇasī in just one day; he completed the monastery in nine months.

600. Pubbasadisasamūnakalahanipuṇamissakasakhilādiyoge. The third case ending also occurs in connection with words such as pubba (before), sadisa (similar), sama (equal), ūna (less), kalaha (strife), nipuṇa (clever/subtle), missaka (mixed), and sakhila (amiable). For example: earlier by a month (māsena pubbo); similar to the father (pitarā sadiso); equal to the mother (mātarā samo); less by a kahāpaṇa (kahāpaṇenūno); strife because of a sword (asinā kalaho); strife by words (vācāya kalaho); subtle in conduct (ācārena nipuṇo); gentle and subtle in speech (vācāya nipuṇo); mixed with molasses (guḷena missako); mixed with sesame (tilena missako); amiable in speech (vācāya sakhilo), and so forth.

601. Hetutthappayoge. The third case ending occurs in the sense of cause (hetu) and in connection with words having the sense of cause. For example: He lives because of food (annena vasati); one crosses the flood by faith (saddhāya tarati oghaṃ). For whatever purpose one should approach the Blessed One, for that purpose he approaches (yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami). One does not become an outcast by birth (na jaccā vasalo hoti). A man bound because of a hundred [coins of debt] (satena baddho naro); these are examples of the sense of cause (hetuttha). For what reason? (kena nimittena); by what appearance/reason? (kena vaṇṇena); by what cause? (kena hetunā); in what sense? (kenaṭṭhena); by what condition? (kena paccayena); these are examples of connection with words having the sense of cause (hetutthappayoga).

602. Sattamiyatthe. The third case ending also occurs in the sense of the seventh case (locative). This occurs in contexts of time, distance, direction, place, and so forth. For example: at that time (tena samayena); at that time (tena kālena); hearing the Dhamma at the proper time (kālena dhammasavanaṃ). That [Dhamma-Vinaya] is your...
153:
When I have passed away, (the Dhamma and Vinaya) shall be your teacher. He eats in a month; he runs in a yojana; King Virūḷhaka is in the southern direction. Where the Blessed One is, there he approached, and so forth.

603. Yenaṅgavikāro. The third case (tatiyā vibhatti) occurs with the part of the body by which a deformity of the person (the possessor of the part) is characterized. (Examples) Blind in the eye, crooked in the hand, lame in the foot, hunchbacked in the back.

604. Visesane pakatiādīsu ca. That which distinguishes is called an attribute (visesana), such as lineage, etc. The third case occurs in the sense of an attribute consisting of lineage, name, caste, craft, age, quality, or ornament, and also in the sense of nature (pakati), etc. The Protector (Buddha) is called Gotama by lineage. He is famous by the name Sāriputta, and he is wise. The Blessed One is a Khattiya by birth. He is seven years old by birth (age). He is a reed-maker by craft. Subhadda, he is twenty-nine years by age. He is good by knowledge. He is noble by practice. He is very beautiful with a golden complexion. Queen Maddī was beautiful with those ornaments. She is beautiful by nature. For the most part, the brahmins and householders of Campā approached to see the Blessed One. He runs unevenly. He buys grain with two measures (doṇa). He sells horses for a thousand, and so forth.

605. Sampadāne catutthī. The fourth case occurs in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna). He gives a gift to the Buddha. He is a giver to a recluse or a brahmin.

606. Namossotthisvāgatādiyoge ca. The fourth case also occurs in association with words such as namo, sotthi, and svāgata. O heroic Buddha, may there be homage to you. Pay homage to the Naga (Arahant). Welfare...
154:
May there be safety and welfare for all beings. Great King, welcome to you; moreover, your coming is not unwelcome. My coming was indeed a welcome one.

607. Apādāne pañcamī. The fifth case occurs in the sense of the ablative (apādāna). One should restrain the mind from evil. Like the moon freed from clouds. That man will be released from fear.

608. Kāraṇatthe ca. The fifth case also occurs in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). Due to not understanding, not penetrating, and not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they really are (one wanders in Saṃsāra). Conditioned by ignorance, formations (saṅkhāra) arise.

609. Chaṭṭhī sāmimhi. The sixth case occurs in the sense of the owner (sāmī), whether recognized by literal meaning (anuvattha) or by conventional usage (rūḷhī). The wealth of the king; Indra, the lord of the gods; not far from the mango grove; a heap of gold. Other genitive usages should also be applied by comparison. In the sutra 'Yassa saṃ, yassa vā pati, taṃ sāmī', all genitive usages are included by the word 'vā', which has the sense of options (vikkappana).

610. Kriyākārakajāte assedamitibhāvahetumhi. The sixth case occurs in the sense of the cause (bhāvahetu) expressed as 'this is of him', which arises from the action (kriyā) and the factor (kāraka). Alternatively, the sixth case occurs in the sense of the cause of the relationship between attribute and substantive, expressed as 'this is of him', arising from the action and the factor. The king's man; the king of the gods, and so forth.

611. Bhāvahetumatte. The sixth case occurs in the sense of mere cause (bhāvahetumatta) expressed as 'this is of him'. The monk's portion; the monk's face; the shadow of the mountain peak; the offering to Kuvera, and so forth.

612. Sambandhasambandhīsambandhesu. The sixth case occurs in the sense of connection (sambandha), the thing connected (sambandhī), and connection. The sixth case occurs in pure connection and in the connection that has reached the state of being the thing connected. The slave of the king's chaplain; the house of the king's son.
155:
I was once the horse Kaṇṭhaka, born at the same time as the son of King Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu, the noble city of the Sakyans.

613. The connection between the qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesitabba/visesya) is called sambandha (relationship). Alternatively, the mutual connection between the qualifier and the qualified is to be known as sambandha.

614. The genitive case (chaṭṭhī) occurs in a relationship based on two related substances. For example: "The king's man" (rañño purisa), etc.

615. The genitive case occurs in a sense qualified by a part or portion (bhāga). For example: "In the last month of the summer months," "In the third month of the rainy months," "One-third of an aeon (kappa)," etc.

616. The genitive case occurs in metaphorical distinction where there is no actual difference in nature (abhede bhedopacāra). For example: "The body of a stone statue," "As if you were digging into the heart of a stone with kaṇikāra wood," etc.

617. The genitive case occurs when a human skull is used as a bowl. For example: "The bowl of a human skull."

618. The genitive case occurs in the sense of separation (visilesa). For example: "The loosening of a joint."

619. The genitive case occurs in connection with the word rujati (to ache/be in pain). For example: "Devadatta is in pain."

620. The genitive case occurs in connection with measurement or counting. For example: "A handful of sesame seeds," "There are not a hundred shells," etc.

621. The genitive case occurs in connection with indeclinables (avyaya) and words indicating direction (disā). For example: "Because of doing to the low-born," "It appeared in front of him," "Behind him," "Only far from those who know," "To the south of the city," etc.
156:
622. The genitive case is also employed in connection with *pada* (path/reason). "Heedlessness is the path to death." "Virtue is the foundation (path) of all wholesome states."

623. The genitive case is employed in connection with the sense of *bhāva* (state/nature). "The state of being sharp in wisdom" or "the manifestation of wisdom." "The lightness of matter."

624. The genitive case is employed in connection with *hetu* (cause). "He dwells because of the Buddha." "Because of me alone, many people might harm one another."

625. The genitive case is employed in connection with *ujjhāpana* (complaining/reproaching) and so forth. "One should complain to the great generals; one should speak out; one should cry out." "He complained to the neighbors." In some instances, it does not occur. In such places as "Having complained to the deities, he departed from that place," [the accusative is used instead of the genitive].

626. The genitive case is employed in connection with *bhāvasādhana* (abstract nouns of action) and so forth. "The accumulation of matter." "The aging and dissolution of the aggregates." "The passing away of various beings." "There is no regrowth of a [severed] nose." "The movement of elements." "The exhaustion of eye-drops." "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful." "The dyeing of clothes by one who is not a dyer is wonderful." "The drinking of milk by Yaññadatta is indeed good." "The destruction of lust and so forth is called Nibbāna." "This renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is the escape from sensual pleasures." "The preparation of seeds." "The attainment of the Noble Dhamma." "The flow of merit." "The offering to the fire." "The enactment of training rules," and so forth.

627. The genitive case is employed in the sense of the object (*kamma*) of the suffixes *yu*, *ṇvu*, and *tu*. "Delusion obstructs the knowable (*ñeyya*)." "Oil causes the flesh to grow over the wound." "An axe is the means for cutting a tree." "The lifting of the foot." "One who does not deceive the world."
157:
"One who scratches the earth." "There is no doer of the deed." "Those who perform a deed hastily and without reflection," and so forth.

## 628. Bhīrutāyogē dutiyātatiyāyō ca
In connection with fear (*bhīrutā*) [in the sense of the object], the genitive case is employed, and the accusative and instrumental cases are also employed. This rule (*lakkhaṇa*) is stated according to the method of the Pali [texts] for the purpose of excluding the ablative case. However, teachers [of grammar] desire only the ablative case in connection with fear. Where the ablative case is not evident in a usage, they explain it as having the sense of the ablative through case substitution (*vibhattivipallāsa*).

"Bhikkhus, do not fear meritorious deeds." "Being afraid of the four poisonous snakes." "Dreading false speech (unable to dread)." "All tremble at the rod; all fear death." "Fear the end of suffering." "Friend, I do not fear." "Not even a single bird or beast frightens me." "One dreads what should be dreaded." Thus, the genitive, accusative, and instrumental cases occur in connection with fear. In this regard, it is said:

"In connection with fear, the genitive, as well as the accusative and instrumental—only these three occur in the Pali [texts]; the ablative, however, is not possible."

Why is it said "in the Pali [texts]"? It is to show that the ablative case occurs in non-Pali contexts, such as "Fear arises because of a thief" (*corā bhayaṃ jāyati*). Here, one might ask: "Venerable sir, is it not seen in the Pali also that the ablative case is used in connection with fear, as in 'From whom there is safety, from him fear arises'?" That is not so, because that usage has the sense of 'arising' (*uppatti*) as its scope. In that context, the word 'arisen' (*uppannaṃ*) should be supplied and connected. For this reason, another similar Pali passage is seen where the word 'arisen' (*jāta*), which is the cause of that fear, is expressed: "Fear has arisen from the protector." Furthermore, in the phrase "Fear arises because of a thief," it should be understood that the ablative case is certainly obtained by the power of the word "arises" (*jāyati*).

## 629. Āgamiṭṭhānito
The genitive case also follows the word *putha* which has an augment, and the word *ava* which is in a position to be changed to *o*. Examples include the augment of the letter 'ga' at the end of *putha* as *puthassa*, and the change of the prefix *ava* to *o* as *o avassa*.

## 630. Okāsē
The locative case (seventh case) is employed in the sense of location (*okāsa*). "He finds a footing (support) in deep water." "The mind delights in evil." "A clansman lives the holy life under the Blessed One." "He stays in a bronze dish."
158:
629. The genitive case also follows the word that has an augment and the word that is in a position to be substituted. Examples include the augment of the letter 'ga' at the end of the word *putha* as *puthassa*, and the change of the prefix *ava* to *o* as *o avassa*.

630. The locative case (seventh case) is employed in the sense of location (*okāsa*). "He finds a footing (support) in deep water." "The mind delights in evil." "A clansman lives the holy life under the Blessed One; he eats from a bronze dish."

631. The genitive and locative cases are employed in connection with words such as *sāmi* (lord), *issara* (ruler), *adhipati* (chief), *dāyāda* (heir), *sakkhi* (witness), *patibhū* (surety), *pasuta* (intent on), and *kusala* (skilled). "Lord of cows" (*goṇānaṃ sāmi*), "Lord among cows" (*goṇesu sāmi*). In the same way, they are used with *issara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sakkhi*, *patibhū*, *pasuta*, and *kusala*. "One skilled in meanings" (*atthānaṃ kovido*, *atthesu kovido*). "Dear son, recognize the wise ministers who are skilled in welfare."

632. The genitive and locative cases are also employed in the sense of specification or selection (*niddhāraṇa*). In this context, *ubbāhana* is the term used in the Dispensation (*sāsana*), while *niddhāraṇa* is the term used in grammar (*saddasattha*). *Ubbāhana* refers to taking out and carrying away from a group based on birth, quality, or action. *Niddhāraṇa* refers to setting apart and identifying one from a group based on those same factors of birth, etc. Although these two differ in name, they do not differ in meaning. When the sense of specification (*niddhāraṇa*) is clear, the genitive and locative cases are used after the noun expressing the group. "Among men, the khattiya is the bravest" (*manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo*, *manussesu khattiyo sūratamo*). "Among cows, the black cow gives the most milk" (*kaṇhāgāvīနံ sampannakhīratamā*, *kaṇhāgāvīsu sampannakhīratamā*). "Among women, the golden-complexioned one is the most beautiful" (*sāmā nārīနံ dassanīyatamā*, *sāmā nārīsu dassanīyatamā*). "Among travelers, the one who runs is the fastest" (*pathikānaṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo*, *pathikēsu dhāvanto sīghatamo*), and so forth. Although the plural is generally used, the example "In the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), the state called conascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) is a part of the mental phenomena" is a locative specification ending in the singular.
159:
633. Anādaraṃhi ca. When the sense of disregard (anādara) is to be conveyed, the genitive and locative cases occur after a noun that expresses an action. (Example) While the child was crying (disregarding the child's crying), he went forth; while the child was crying, he went forth. While King Sivi was watching, he took them away by beating them. While the great crowd was watching, Death took (beings) away.

634. Kvaci tatiyāsattamiyatthe chaṭṭhī. In some instances, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental (tatiyā) and locative (sattami) cases. In this context, there is a rule that the genitive case must be used when connected with a primary derivative (kita) suffix having the sense of the agent (kattar). (Example) Done by Buddhaghosa, or done by Buddhaghosa (instrumental). Likewise, done by Kaccāyana, or done by Kaccāyana. Approved by the king, or by the king. Likewise, honored by the king, well-treated by the king, respected by the king, esteemed by the king. Monks, those who do not enjoy mindfulness of the body do not enjoy the Deathless (Nibbāna). Teachers also desire the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental in the passage: "Many good deeds have been performed by me." This desire is appropriate because it is found in the passage: "Friends, at that time, kamma was performed by me and by you."

635. Tatiyatthe vā tatiyā. The instrumental case also occurs in the sense of the instrumental. Therefore, usage that conveys both meanings is seen. For example: "The wise one gives the best gift."

636. Yajassa karaṇe. The genitive case occurs in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) of the root yaj (to sacrifice/worship). (Example) He worships the fire with ghee, or with ghee (instrumental). Likewise, he worships the Buddha with flowers.

637. Pūritatthayoghe. The genitive case occurs when connected with the sense of being full. (Example) The wise one is full of merit. It means "by merit." Having filled the bowl with rice. One contemplates this very body full of various impurities.

638. Tulyatthaki'malamādiyoghe. The genitive case occurs when connected with words meaning "equal" (tulya), and with words like kiṃ, alaṃ, etc. (Example) Equal to the father, or equal to the father (instrumental). Equal to the mother, or equal to the mother.
160:
Or, "What is the use of that pleasant thing?" It means, "What is the use of that pleasant thing?" (instrumental). In instances like "That pleasant thing is of no use; my hermitage is well-made," the genitive case occurs in the sense of the instrumental. Thus, the genitive occurs in the sense of the instrumental.

639. The genitive case occurs in the sense of the locative (sattami) when connected with words like kusala (skilled). "Women who are skilled in dancing and singing, who are trained, and who are elegant (will entertain you)." "Are you not skilled in the parts of a chariot?" "Skilled in the path, skilled in what is not the path." "Venerable sir, there are noble yakkhas who are devoted to the Blessed One." "Three times a day" (divasassa tikkhattuṃ or divase tikkhattuṃ), "Three times a month." "Great King... from where do you come at midday?" etc. Thus, the genitive occurs in the sense of the locative.

640. The genitive case also occurs in some instances in the sense of the accusative (dutiyā) and the ablative (pañcamī). There, in the sense of the object (kamma) connected with a primary derivative (kita): "There are those who speak ill of him." "Those who do work quickly," "The giver of the Deathless (Nibbāna)." "Clarity (pasāda) based on the four great elements," etc. Likewise, in the sense of the object of remembering, etc.: "He remembers his mother" (mātu sarati or mātaraṃ sarati). "No one remembers those petas; beings (exist) because of their own kamma." "He desires a son" (puttassa icchati or puttami'cchati).

When the root kar is in the sense of preparing or refining (patiyatana), the genitive case also occurs. Preparing means abhisankhāra. "He refines the water (makes it clear)" (udakassa patikurute or udakaṃ patikurute). "He straightens the arrow" (kaṇḍassa patikurute or kaṇḍaṃ patikurute). Thus, the genitive occurs in the sense of the accusative.

The genitive case also occurs when connected with the senses of the ablative, such as distinction (vibhatta) and decline (parihāni). "The discipline of the Sugata is superior to the ninety-six heretical doctrines" (meaning it is superior to the ninety-six heretical doctrines). "Outside of this dispensation (Sāsana)..."
161:
The Pali word "Pāsaṇḍā" is found (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya). Due to not hearing the Dhamma, they decline from the supramundane Dhamma. In this context, in the sentence "If I should be angry with that person... I will decline from virtue (sīla)," the Genitive case does not occur. Thus, the Genitive case occurs in the sense of the Ablative case.

Teachers, however, also desire the Genitive case when associated with words expressing fear, which is an Ablative sense. Examples include: "Why should I fear that happiness?", "All beings tremble at punishment; all fear death," "Afraid of the four venomous snakes," and so on. In those instances, "tassa sukhassa" means "tasmā sukhā" (from 그 happiness). The decision here is: just as two usages are seen in the Pali regarding association with decline (parihāni) through the Genitive and Ablative cases—namely "dhammassa parihāyanti" and "parihāyissāmi sīlato"—two such usages are not seen regarding association with fear (bhaya). In phrases like "jātaṃ saraṇato bhayaṃ," the Ablative ending in "saraṇato" is due to its association with the word "jāta" and others, not because of the sense of fear. In the phrase "yato khemaṃ tathā bhayaṃ," the word "tato" is an Ablative ending due to the implied sense of the word "uppannaṃ" (arisen), not because of the sense of fear. Therefore, a separate rule is established below.

Why is "kuci" (sometimes/somewhere) mentioned? He speaks profound words. He speaks Dhamma at the proper time. He rejoices in the merits of others. He knows the Truths. A maker of a mat. A killer of beasts. Similarly, in the past participle (niṭṭhā) and others: One who desires happiness has built a monastery. Those who have made a chariot; one who has made a chariot. One who is also skilled in elephant-craft. A maker of a mat. One who is making a mat, one who is making a mat, one who is making a mat, and so on.

641. The Locative case (Sattamī) is used in the senses of object (kamma), instrument (karaṇa), and cause (nimitta). "Friends, these Ājīvakas are good; they pay homage to the monks (bhikkhus)." Thus...
162:
In the sense of the object (the locative case is employed). They wander for alms with their hands. They wander for alms with their bowls. They go by the paths; thus, in the sense of the instrument as well (the locative case is employed). The leopard is killed for its skin; the elephant is killed for its tusks. Thus, in the sense of the cause (nimitta), (the locative case is employed).

## 642. Sampadāne ca.
In the sense of the recipient (sampadāna) as well, the locative case occurs. An offering given to the Saṅgha has great fruit. Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I too shall be honored.

## 643. Pañcamiyatthe ca.
In the sense of the ablative (pañcamī) as well, the locative case occurs. They ward off elephants from the banana groves.

## 644. Kālabhāvesu ca.
In the sense of time (kāla) and in the sense of state (bhāva), which serves as a marker for another action, the locative case occurs after a stem. In this rule, 'time' refers to occasions such as a moment (khaṇa), laya, muhutta, morning, and so on. Therein, the duration of time equal to ten finger-snaps is called a khaṇa. A duration of ten khaṇas is called a laya. A duration of ten layas is called a khaṇa-laya. A duration ten times that of a khaṇa-laya is called a muhutta. A duration ten times that of a muhutta is called a khaṇa-muhutta; thus should the divisions be understood. 'Bhāva' means action (kriyā); that action is also called 'the meaning of the root' (dhātvattha). And in this rule, that action is intended only as a marker (lakkhaṇa) for another action.

Among those instances of time and state, in the sense of time: He went in the morning; he came in the evening. For that king, it rains out of season; it does not rain in season. Three months after the month of Phussa, it is the month of Visākha. One hundred thousand aeons (kappa) from now, the Visionary One (the Buddha Padumuttara) arose.

In the sense of state (bhāva): While the monks were being served food, he went. After they had eaten, he came. While the cows were being milked, he went. After they were milked, he came, and so forth. Therein, 'bhikkhūsu' is the locative of state (bhāva-sattamī). If it is asked, 'How does it become a locative of state?', it is because it is a locative obtained by way of the action. Here, 'bhāva' refers to the action of eating or the action of going. In truth, the action of going (by another) is marked by the action of eating of a certain monk; the locative case occurs in the monk who possesses that action of eating which is the marker of the action of going. This is the intended meaning. The locative case is found in that monk who possesses the preceding action, by whose action the action of another person is well-marked or known. This rule clarifies that aforementioned meaning.

Then the wicked Māra, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, approached the Blessed One.
163:
The term 'locative of state' (bhāva-sattamī) is a designation used by the power of the meaning. Here, 'bhāva' refers to action (kriyā). When the marker of an action (bhāva-lakkhaṇa) arises through the action of someone, the locative case occurs in that person. The intended meaning is this—when the marking, well-noting, or knowing of another's action occurs by the action of someone, the locative case is found in that person who possesses the first action. This rule illuminates that meaning. In the passage: "Then the wicked Māra, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, approached the Blessed One" [D. ii, 87; S. v, 228; Khp. 153], the action of Māra approaching the Blessed One is marked by the action of the Venerable Ānanda departing from the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, the locative case occurs in the Venerable Ānanda who possesses that action of departing. In this context, generally, the term 'locative of state' (bhāva-sattamī) is applied to a word that is co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) only when an action-denoting word (bhāva-vācaka-pada) is clearly present. However, the teachers, in some places where a co-referential action-denoting word is absent, supply words such as 'sati' (being) and so on, making them co-referential, and call it a locative of state. Accordingly, those teachers supply terms like 'sati', 'gammamāne' (while going), 'vattabbe' (when it should be said), etc., as appropriate.

Here, a question may arise: "If in the phrase 'bhikkhūsu bhojiyamānesu', the word 'bhikkhūsu' is called a locative of state because it is a locative obtained in connection with an action, then what kind of locative is 'bhojiyamānesu', and by which rule is it established?" It is called a co-referential locative (tulyādhikaraṇa-sattamī), and it is established by this very rule. Should it not be called a locative of state according to its literal meaning (anvattha), since this locative itself exists in the action? True, however, the ancient teachers did not apply the term 'locative of state' to such co-referential [participle] words; it should be understood that they applied it only to the other word [the noun].
164:
For example, in the phrase "Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ" (We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, who is endowed with clear vision and virtuous conduct), the word "buddhaṃ" is established by the rule "Kammatthe dutiyā" (The accusative case in the sense of an object). The words "vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ" and "gotamaṃ" are also established by that same rule. Similarly, in the context of bhāvasattami (the locative absolute), the application of case endings to samānādhikaraṇa (appositional) words is established by the aforementioned method. Even so, in places such as "Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ," one should not desire multiple objects, such as two, three, or four objects. Only a single object is desired because a single meaning is expressed by many words.

In this same way, in places such as "Bhikkhūsu bhojiyamānesu" (While the monks are being fed) and "Acirapakkante āyasmante ānande" (Soon after the Venerable Ānanda had departed), one should not desire multiple locative absolutes, such as two, three, or four locative absolutes. Only a single locative absolute is desired because a single meaning is expressed by many words. It should be understood that this method is the same for samānādhikaraṇa dative (sampadāna) and others.

## 645. Upādhīyoge adhikiissaravacane.

Because these words "upa" and "adhi" occur in the senses of excess (adhika) and lordship (issara), the locative case (sattami) is employed when associated with "upa" and "adhi" to express the sense of excess or the sense of lordship. In this rule, the term "issaravacana" is taken in two ways: as the expression of a lord (issarassa vacanaṃ) and as an object that has the expression of a lord (issaravacanaṃ yassa vatthuno taṃ). Therefore, the locative case is employed to express the lord, or to express the existence of a lord as in saying, "This person is the lord of that person."

"Upa khāriyaṃ doṇo" — The meaning is that a doṇa is in excess of a khārī basket. "Upa nikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ" — The meaning is that a kahāpaṇa is in excess of a nikkha. "Adhi brahmadatte pañcālā" — The meaning is that the people of Pañcāla are the lords over King Brahmadatta. "Adhi nacce gotamī" — The meaning is that Gotamī is the mistress over the dancers. "Adhi devesu buddho" — The meaning is that the Buddha is the Lord over the gods, such as conventional gods (sammuti-deva). Some teachers, however, taking the sense of excess for the word "adhi," state the meaning as: the Buddha is superior to the three types of gods.
165:
Some teachers, taking the sense of superiority for the word 'adhi', state the meaning as: 'The Omniscient Buddha is superior to the three types of gods.'

In this context, a question may arise: Are the phrases 'Adhi Brahmadatte' and 'Adhi devesu' compound words (samāsapada) or analyzed phrases (vyāsapada)? They should be understood only as analyzed phrases. For if they were compound words, it would lead to an undesirable meaning such as 'The Pañcālas exist in King Brahmadatta who is the lord' or 'The Buddha exists in the gods who are the lords.' Therefore, by way of analysis, just as in the phrase 'lord over cows' (gosu issaro), the meaning should be understood as 'The Pañcālas are the lords over Brahmadatta' and 'The Buddha is the Lord over the gods.' This same method applies to 'Adhi nacce gotamī' (Gotamī is the mistress over the dance). However, in phrases such as 'Upa khāriyaṃ doṇo', the meaning should be understood by way of connecting with the genitive sense (chaṭṭhī): 'The doṇa is more than the khārī (basket).'

## 646. Ussukkamaṇဍitesu tatiyā ca.

The instrumental case (tatiyā) and the locative case (sattami) occur in the senses of ussukka (exertion) and maṇḍita (delight). In this rule, the word 'ussukka' expresses the sense of exertion (seha), and the word 'maṇḍita' expresses the sense of being pleased or devout (pasanna). For example: A virtuous man who exerts himself through wisdom (ñāṇena ussukko), or exerts himself in wisdom (ñāṇasmiṃ vā ussukko); one who is pleased through wisdom (ñāṇena pasīdito), or is pleased in wisdom (ñāṇasmiṃ vā pasīdito). Here, although the aforementioned case endings do not occur directly in the senses of ussukka and maṇḍita but rather in another sense, their occurrence in that other sense is due to the senses of ussukka and maṇḍita. Therefore, it should be understood that the rule says 'ussukkamaṇḍitesu' by making those senses primary. This method is the same in other similar instances.

## 647. Akkhātari upayoge pañcamī.

'Akkhātā' refers to the instructor or expositor (paṭipādayitā). 'Upayoga' refers to the systematic acquisition of knowledge after undertaking precepts (sīla) and so forth.

Exertion, attendance, the desire to listen, service, and the respectful acquisition of arts and sciences are called 'niyama' (systematic discipline).
166:
When one wishes to indicate systematic learning (upayoga), the Ablative case (Pañcamī) occurs after [the word denoting] the speaker (akkhātā). According to the statement that since the sense cannot exist [in the abstract], the rule must be applied to the word, the Ablative case occurs after the word expressing that speaker. For example: He learns from the preceptor (upajjhāyā adhīte). He hears from the preceptor (upajjhāyā suṇoti). From whomsoever one may learn the Dhamma (yamhā dhammaṃ vijāneyya). Why is it said 'in systematic learning' (upayoga)? To prevent the Ablative from occurring in instances such as 'He listens to the words of a dancer' (nāṭakassa suṇoti), where it is not systematic learning. However, in the Mukhamattadīpanī, it is stated: 'These examples are established by the inclusion of the term apādāna and the inclusion of the term disāyoga.' Whether they are so established or not, we shall demonstrate the rules in detail both to make known the pervasive nature of the rules, like rain, and to produce proficiency in the listeners regarding the various distinctions of usage. Therefore, it should not be said that there is the fault of tautology (punaruttidosa) in those various places. Indeed, great effort has been made in this work for the benefit of the Sasana.

## 648. Yaṃtaṃkiṃyoge kāraṇato kvaci.
In connection with the words 'yaṃ', 'taṃ', and 'kiṃ', the Ablative case sometimes occurs after the word 'kāraṇa'. For example: For which reason (yaṃkāraṇā), for that reason (taṃkāraṇā), for what reason do you cause me suffering? (kiṃkāraṇā me na karosi dukkhaṃ). Why is 'kvaci' (sometimes) said? To prevent the Ablative in instances such as 'What is the reason?' (kiṃ kāraṇam).

## 649. Kāraṇatthe hetukimyatehi paṭhamā.
The Nominative case (Paṭhamā) sometimes occurs after the words 'hetu', 'kiṃ', and 'yata' (ya) when they are used in the sense of cause. For example: One should not speak a lie for one's own sake (na attahetū alikaṃ bhaṇāti). For what reason do we revile the Blessed One? (kiṃkāraṇaṃ bhagavantaṃ nindāma). Why do you not delight in birth? (kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi). For which reason I do not see my son (yañca putte na passāmi). I ask the venerable Gotama about those various reasons (taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmi). Here, although it is generally indicated by the sequence of meaning as 'Therefore I ask the Blessed One', those words 'taṃ taṃ' are understood to express the distant sense and the personal sense respectively. In this regard, some teachers say that the word 'kiṃ kāraṇaṃ' is in the Accusative case (Dutiyā); that is not appropriate, because the Nominative is seen in the passage 'na attahetū alikaṃ bhaṇāti'.
167:
650. Kiṃsmā chaṭṭhī rule. The Genitive case (Chaṭṭhī) sometimes occurs after the word 'kiṃ' when it is used in the sense of cause. (Example:) "Taṃ kissa hetu" (For what reason is that?). "Kissa tumhe kilamatha" (Why are you weary?). Why is it said "in some places"? (Examples where the Genitive does not occur:) "Kena kāraṇena āgatosi" (For what reason have you come?). "Kasmā vadesi" (Why do you speak?).

651. Some teachers say that the Genitive case after the word "hetu" should be elided. Some great masters of grammar, seeing the Genitive case occurring after the word 'hetu' which expresses the sense of cause, and favoring that view, wish to elide the Genitive case after the word 'hetu' when it is used in the sense of cause within the Sasana. "Annassa hetu vasati" (He lives for the sake of food) is their view. In this way, in places such as "buddhassa hetu" and "taṃ kissa hetū", the Genitive case is also elided. If this were so, it might be possible that in some sutta passages of the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka along with the Commentaries, the Genitive case after the word 'hetu' would remain without being elided. However, such usage is not seen anywhere. The commentators should also explain the Pali as "kissa hetussa" for "kissa hetū" by way of the Genitive case. But those teachers did not explain it in that way. Therefore, in places such as "annassa hetu vasati", the meaning should be understood only as "annassa kāraṇā vasati" and so forth.

652. "Yathātaṃ" refers to the Pali text which follows the sequence of the Genitive and Nominative cases. The word 'pāḷi' signifies sequence (paṭipāṭi). The sequence of the Genitive and Nominative cases used in the sense of cause is in accordance with the Pali. (Example:) "Taṃ kissa hetu". "Taṃ" is an indeclinable particle used as a verse-filler (pudapūraṇa). "Kissa hetū" means "for what reason". Alternatively, it should be explained by the power of the Ablative case (Pañcamī) as "kasmā".

653. The sequence of the Nominative and Ablative cases. The sequence of the Nominative and Ablative cases used in the sense of cause is in accordance with the Pali. (Example:) "Yaṃkāraṇā" and so forth.
168:
654. And the sequence of those Nominative and Ablative cases standing in inversion, when used in the sense of cause, is also in accordance with the Pali. For example: "That person might reach death because of that cause, or reach suffering equivalent to death" (so tato nidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ), and so forth.

655. Alternatively, the group of words such as "yaṃkāraṇā" should be understood as a collection of indeclinables (nipātasamudāya). Because the methods of the Pali are difficult to understand, by another method, words like "yaṃkāraṇā" should be noted as a collection of indeclinables. Therefore, in those words, one should not perform an analysis of the case as Nominative, Ablative, or Genitive. For example: yaṃkāraṇā, kiṃkāraṇā, kissahetu, tatonidānaṃ, and so forth.

656. Words such as "yebhuyyena" should be known as indeclinables (nipāta-avyaya) that resemble words ending in case-terminations. For example: Beings are mostly (yebhuyyena) reborn in the lower realms. Between (antarena) the pair of Sal trees. Having set aside the instructions of others, he himself (sāmaṃyeva) fully realized the Truths, and so forth.

657. In connection with the words 'saha' and 'saddhiṃ', the Ablative case (Pañcamī) sometimes occurs in the sense of the Instrumental case (Tatiyā). When the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, simultaneously with the Parinibbāna (saha parinibbānā), Brahma Sahampati addressed with a verse. Along with the words (saha vacanā) of the Blessed One, the Koliyan princess Suppavāsā, being free from illness, gave birth to a son free from illness. Together with the community of disciples (saddhiṃ sāvakasaṅghato), I shall attain Parinibbāna right here. In this context, the suffix '-to' is called the Ablative case by virtue of its name, as it has already received the designation of a case-ending. Therein, "saha parinibbānā" means exactly together with the attaining of Parinibbāna. "saha vacanā" means exactly together with the speech. In such instances, because there is the benefit of exclusion (vivaccheda), the word "eva" should be applied by interpolation even if it is not explicitly stated. Why is "kvaci" (sometimes) said? Because in instances such as "together with a great community of monks" (mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ) and "he delights together with his sons" (puttehi saha sammati), only the Instrumental case occurs.
169:
658. The locative case (sattami) is used in the sense of the instrumental case (tatiya) when associated with the word 'saha'. (Example:) "Saha sacce kate mayhaṃ". It means "simultaneously with my act of truth". Here, the verb "kate" expresses the sense of action (karaṇa), just as in the sentence "bhikkhussa kālaṅkate saṅgho pattacīvarassa sāmī" (when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes).

659. The instrumental case (tatiya) and the locative case (sattami) are used in the sense of the nominative case (pathama). (Example:) "Maṇinā me attho" (I have need of a gem). "Idampissa hoti sīlasmiṃ" (This practice also pertains to his virtue).

660. The nominative case (pathama) is used in the sense of the instrumental case (tatiya). (Example:) "Ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyaṃ" (Practicing the holy life with intention). "Anāgārehi cubhayaṃ" (Not mixing with both householders and monks). Here, "ubhayaṃ" means "ubhayehi", where there is a change in case and number. Similarly, in the Theragāthā, regarding the verse of Venerable Upasena, "Appiccho ceva santuṭṭho", it is stated that the word "ubhayaṃ" is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa).

661. The locative case (sattami) is used in the sense of the instrumental case (tatiya). (Example:) "Maṇimhi passa nimmitaṃ" (See what is created by the gem); it means created by the gem. "Khīyethakappo ciradīghamantare" (The eon would be exhausted through the passing of a long duration of time); it means through the passing of a long duration.

662. The word "samaya" (occasion/time) is used with the instrumental (karaṇa), accusative (upayoga), and locative (bhumma) cases according to the order of the Piṭakas. In the three Piṭakas—Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma—the word "samaya" is used with the instrumental, accusative, and locative cases respectively. "Tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharati naḷerupucimandamūle" (At that time, the Blessed Buddha was staying at Verañjā at the foot of the Naḷeru Neem tree). This is the use of the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) in the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ addhānamaggappaṭipanno hoti" (On one occasion, the Blessed One was traveling along the main road between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā). This is the use of the accusative case (upayoganiddesa) in the Sutta Piṭaka. "Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti" (At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen). This is the use of the locative case (bhummavacana) in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
170:
In this context, it is asked: "Why is the word 'samaya' referred to differently using the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) and others in the three Piṭakas?" It is done so because of the existence of specific meanings to be shown.

How so? Firstly, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there exist the meanings of cause (hetu) and means (karaṇa). This is because the Blessed One, while prescribing the training rules (sikkhāpada) which are difficult to understand even for those like Venerable Sāriputta, stayed in various places (such as Vesālī, Rājagaha, etc.) by means of that occasion (samaya) which was the cause (hetu) and the means (karaṇa) for prescribing the rules, and while considering the cause for the prescription of training rules. Therefore, to illuminate that causal meaning, the reference is made in the Vinaya using the instrumental case (karaṇavacana).

In the Sutta Piṭaka, there exists the meaning of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). This is because for as long as the Blessed One taught the suttas such as the Brahmajāla Sutta, throughout that entire duration, He dwelt in the abiding of compassion (karuṇāvihāra). Therefore, to illuminate that meaning of continuous duration, the reference is made in the Sutta using the accusative case (upayoganiddesa).

In the Abhidhamma, however, there exist the meanings of locus (adhikaraṇa) and the marking of an occurrence by another occurrence (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa). Indeed, the 'samaya' which has the meaning of time and collection (samūha) is the locus (adhikaraṇa) for the phenomena such as contact (phassa) taught in the Abhidhamma. By the occurrence of 'samaya'—which is called the moment (khaṇa), the combination (samavāya), and the cause (hetu)—the occurrence of those phenomena such as contact is marked (bhāvalakkhaṇa). Therefore, to illuminate those meanings of locus and marking of occurrence, it should be understood that the reference is made in the Abhidhamma using the locative case (bhummavacana). 

There is a summary verse (saṅgahagāthā) here:
"Considering various meanings, the word 'samaya' is expressed in the Vinaya and other Piṭakas through the instrumental, accusative, and locative cases."

However, the ancient commentators (porāṇā) explain: "Whether it is said 'taṃ samayaṃ', 'tasmiṃ samaye', or 'tena samayena', this is merely a difference in expression; in all instances, the meaning is only the locative (bhumma)." Therefore, according to their view, even when it is said "tena samayena", the meaning should be understood as "tasmiṃ samaye", and even when it is said "ekaṃ samayaṃ", the meaning should be understood as "ekasmiṃ samaye".
171:
Standing at this point, I shall describe the varieties of the instrumental (karaṇa). Just as greed and so on, and non-greed and so on, are called root-causes (hetu-hetu), other phenomena that exist as supporting conditions are called conditional causes (paccaya-hetu). In this way, the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) occurring in the sense of instrument is called karaṇa-karaṇa (instrumental-instrumental). The instrumental case occurring in the sense of the agent and so on is also given names in this text such as kattu-karaṇa (agentive-instrumental), hetu-karaṇa (causal-instrumental), and so on. Having understood this, those names should be known along with their examples.

"Cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati" (One sees a form with the eye). This is karaṇa-karaṇa.
"Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo" (The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One). This is kattu-karaṇa.
"Sāriputtoti nāmena vissuto" (Known by the name Sāriputta). This is visesana-karaṇa.
"Annena vasati" (One lives by means of food). This is hetu-karaṇa.
"Bhinnena sīsena āgato" (He came with a broken head). This is itthambhūta-karaṇa.
"Bhuñja puttehi khattiya" (O King, enjoy [the meal] together with your children). This is sahattha-karaṇa.
"Maṇinā me attho" (I have need of a gem). This is paccatta-karaṇa.
"Saṃvibhajetha no rajjena" (Divide the kingdom for us). This is kamma-karaṇa.
"Sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena" (We are well-freed from that Great Ascetic). This is nissakka-karaṇa.
"Tena kho pana samayena" (At that time). This is bhumma-karaṇa.
"Pakatiyā abhirūpo" (Beautiful by nature), "Yebhuyyena campeyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā" (Mostly the brahmins and householders of Campā). Such examples are called tadanya-karaṇa. Thus, there are eleven types of karaṇa.

When that tadanya-karaṇa is further divided, there are many varieties: instrumental associated with particles (nipātayoga-karaṇa), instrumental of prohibition (paṭikkhepa-karaṇa), instrumental of a defective limb (kucchitaṅga-karaṇa), instrumental of the completion of an action (kriyāpavagga-karaṇa), instrumental of time and distance (kāladdhāna-karaṇa), instrumental of effort in decoration (maṇḍitu-ussukka-karaṇa), instrumental associated with 'saha' and so on (sahādiyoga-karaṇa), instrumental associated with words like 'pubba' (former), 'sadisa' (similar), 'samūna' (equal), 'kalaha' (quarrel), 'nipuṇa' (skilful), 'missaka' (mixed), 'sakhila' (friendly), and so on, and the instrumental of non-association (ayoga-karaṇa). Thus, it should be noted that tadanya-karaṇa is of many kinds.

## 663. Saṅkhyāliṅgatthāvikaraṇatthamuppattivibhattīnaṃ.

The occurrence of inflections (vibhatti) is for the purpose of making the number (saṅkhyā) clear and for making the meaning of the gender/base (liṅgattha) clear. "Puriso tiṭṭhati" (The man stands), "Purisā tiṭṭhanti" (The men stand). "Ekaṃ, dve, tīṇi" (One, two, three).
172:
664. When a single meaning is to be expressed, the singular number (ekavacana) is used. (Examples:) woman, man, mind.

665. Just as in the case of a single meaning, the singular number is also used when multiple meanings are to be expressed. (Examples:) "That army was great." "Many people are confident." A group of people, a group of monks, a group of fish, and so forth.

666. When multiple meanings are to be expressed, the plural number (bahuvacana) is used. (Examples:) women, men, minds.

667. Just as in the case of multiple meanings, the plural number is also used for a single meaning. (Example:) "The phenomena (Nibbāna) which are without conditions," and so forth.

668. The singular number is used in the sense of a collection (samudāya), genus (jāti), metonymy based on dependence (nissaya), and the characteristic of unity (ekattalakkhaṇa).

In the sense of a collection (samudāya): A group of devas, all people, and so forth.

In the sense of genus (jāti): "One should not intentionally deprive a living being (pāṇa) of life." "The crop is abundant," and so forth.

In the sense of metonymy based on dependence (nissaya): "The people of Sāvatthī had faith and were confident." "Venerable Sir, this Nāḷandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and deeply devoted to the Blessed One," and so forth. The meaning should be applied as: "The inhabitants of Sāvatthī had faith and were confident," etc.

In the sense of the characteristic of unity (ekattalakkhaṇa): Wholesome and unwholesome, calm and insight, the three characteristics, death and rebirth, coming and going, and so forth.

669. The plural number is used for multiple collections. (Examples:) "Honored by groups of relatives." "Groups of devas have assembled." "These sixty are the groups of devas," and so forth.
173:
## 670. Kvaci jātiattagarūsu ca.
The plural number is also sometimes used in the sense of genus (type), self, and respected persons.

(Examples:) The barleys are abundant; the barley is abundant. The rices are abundant; the rice is abundant. It is our nature; it is my nature. I gave seats to the venerable ones who arrived at my presence. The meaning is: I gave a seat to the monk who arrived at my presence.

## 671. Aparicchedamātikānusandhinayapucchānusandhinayapucchāsabhāgaputhucittasamāyoga-puthuārammaṇatannivāsatamputtekābhidhānatannissitāpekkhaārammaṇakiccabhedesu ca.
The plural number is also used in the following cases: lack of delimitation, the method of connection with the matrix (mātikā), the method of connection with a question, the answer corresponding to a question, association with many minds, having many objects, the place of residence, their sons, a single designation for many, metonymy based on dependence, diversity of objects, and diversity of functions.

To first illustrate the lack of delimitation (apariccheda): "The phenomena which are without conditions," "The phenomena which are unconditioned." This is plural due to an indefinite number.

In the method of connection with the matrix (mātikānusandhinaya): "Which are the phenomena that are without conditions?" and so forth.

In the method of connection with a question (pucchānusandhinaya): "These phenomena are those without conditions," and so forth.

In the answer corresponding to a question (pucchāsabhāga): "Which are the phenomena without resentment? Excluding those phenomena, the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena..." and so forth.

In the association with many minds and having many objects: "Monks, there are other phenomena, deep and hard to see (omniscience)..." and so forth.

In the place of residence (tannivāsa): "He dwells among the Sakyans," and so forth.

In the sense of their sons (tamputta): "The sons of the Videhans (Prince Dīghāvu) exist," and so forth.

In the sense of a single designation (ekābhidhāna): "You, Sāriputtas (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), go." "Tigers (tigers and lions), return from here," and so forth.

In the sense of metonymy based on dependence (tannissitāpekkha): "The beds make a noise (cry out)," and so forth.

In the diversity of objects (ārammaṇabheda): "The four foundations of mindfulness."

In the diversity of functions (kiccabheda): "The four right efforts."
174:
## 672. Interchange (Vipallāsa) of Gender, Case, Number, Time, Person, and Syllable.

In this Dispensation (Pāvacana) of the Buddha, there are six kinds of interchange: interchange of gender (liṅgavipallāsa), interchange of case (vibhattivipallāsa), interchange of number (vacanavipallāsa), interchange of time (kālavipallāsa), interchange of person (purisavipallāsa), and interchange of syllable (akkharavipallāsa).

Among these six, the interchange of gender comes first. For example: "Siviputtāni cāvhaya" (Call also the son Jāli and daughter Kaṇhājinā of the Sivi kingdom). "Evaṃ dhammāni sutvāna, vippasīdanti paṇḍitā" (Having heard the Dhamma thus, the wise are especially confident), and so on.

The interchange of case has already been made clear through various characteristics. Nevertheless, to prevent confusion for listeners in matters where they might be greatly bewildered, I shall again speak specifically on the interchange of case.

What is this interchange of case? For example: "Ayaṃ puriso mama atthakāmo, yo maṃ gahetvāna dakāya neti" (This man desires my welfare; he who, having taken me, leads me to the water). "Appo saggāya gacchati" (Few go to heaven). Here, the dative case (catutthī) is used in the sense of the accusative (dutiyā). The meaning should be understood as "dakaṃ neti" (leads to the water) and "saggaṃ gacchati" (goes to heaven). "Asakkatā casma dhanañjayāya" (They were also not well-treated by King Dhanañjaya). Here, the dative is used in the sense of the instrumental (tatiyā); the meaning is "dhanañjayena" (by Dhanañjaya).

"Puññāya sugatiṃ yanti, cāgāya vipulaṃ dhanaṃ" (Because of merit, they go to a happy destination; because of generosity, they obtain great wealth). This is also the dative used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "puññena" (by merit) and "cāgena" (by generosity). That meaning should be understood specifically through the sense of cause (hetu), as "by means of merit as a cause" and "by means of generosity as a cause." In that context, the word "puññāya" is a neuter form, not a feminine form. The word "cāgāya," however, is a masculine form.

Other teachers, however, desire these two words "puññāya cāgāya" to be feminine words ending in the suffix -ā and in the ablative case (pañcamī). If that were so, in the instances "dakāya neti," "appo saggāya gacchati," and "asakkatā casma dhanañjayāya," the three words "dakāya, saggāya, dhanañjayāya" would also have to be feminine words ending in the suffix -ā. But these three words are neither feminine nor do they end in the suffix -ā. Rather, they are forms produced by the substitution of "-āya" for the dative singular in the neuter and masculine genders respectively. They are forms that cause great wonder to listeners, are not common to secular grammars, and are wonders within the Dispensation.
175:
They are forms of extraordinary wonder within the Dispensation. For instance, the dative form "Namo Buddhāya," which follows the rules of secular grammar, becomes only the form "Namo Buddhassa" when it enters the Dispensation. The teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) also place only such forms, which are in accordance with the Pāḷi, in the domain of grammatical composition. It has been explained in detail below that a form similar to "Namo Buddhāya" is seen in the Dispensation only in the interchange of case (vibhattivipallāsa) involving the sense of the infinitive (tumattha), and not in associations such as dāna (giving) or namo (homage).

In the passage "Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāya" (Venerable ones, desist from my words), "vacanāya" is the dative case used in the sense of the ablative (pañcamī); the meaning is "mama vacanato" (from my words). In the phrase "Bhiyyoso mattāya," the word "matta" is only neuter. Through the power of case interchange and the substitution of "-āya" for the dative singular, it is the dative case used in the sense of the ablative. If it were feminine, as in the passage "Mattā sukhapariccāgā," then it would be the ablative case used in the sense of the ablative, and there would be no function of case interchange. The fact that "mattāya" has an ablative sense is clear from its association with the word "bhiyya" (more), as in the passage "Tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati." "Bhiyyoso mattāya" means "more than the measure" (mattato bhiyyo). Having thus understood it as the ablative sense, the meaning should be established through the power of the instrumental sense as "excessively beyond the measure" (atirekappamāṇena).

In the passage "Mahāgaṇāya bhattā me," "mahāgaṇāya" is the dative case used in the sense of the genitive (chaṭṭhī); the meaning is "lord of the group" (gaṇassa bhattā). In the passage "Ko nu kho bhante hetu, ko paccayo bhagavato sitassa pātukammāya?" (Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the manifestation of the Blessed One's smile?), "pātukammāya" is the dative case used in the sense of the locative (sattamī); the meaning is "in the manifesting" (pātukaraṇe). Or, it is the dative in the sense of the genitive, meaning "What is the cause and reason of the manifestation of the smile?" In the passage "Sā nuna kapaṇā ammā, cirarattāya rucati" (That poor mother will surely weep for a long night), "cirarattāya" is the dative case used in the sense of the accusative of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga-dutiyā); it means "cirarattaṃ" (for a long time).
176:
The meaning is indeed "for a long time" (cirakālaṃ). Thus, the interchange of case (vibhattivipallāsa) accompanied by the substitution of "-āya" for the dative singular by the power of masculine and neuter genders should be specifically noted. However, in passages such as "Mā iti kirāya," "Samamessanti cirāya subbatā," and "Cirassaṃ vata passāmi," words like "kirāya" should be understood as indeclinable words (avyaya) that resemble words ending in case-terminations. In these, the method of case interchange should not be considered because the words "kira" and "cira" have indistinct genders.

Interchange of number (vacanavipallāsa) is as follows:

"Nagā nagaggesu susaṃvirūḷhā, udaggameghena navena sittā.
Vivikakāmassa araññasaññino, janeti bhiyyo usabhassa kalyataṃ."
(The trees, well-grown on the mountain peaks and sprinkled by the fresh clouds of the early rainy season, produce greater well-being for the bull-like seeker of seclusion who perceives the forest.)

"Janeti" (singular) means "janenti" (plural: they produce); or this itself is the original reading. Here, some might say: "If an alternative plural reading 'janenti' is seen, the teachers of the Commentaries should have spoken by taking only that as the standard, saying 'janenti bhiyyo usabhassa kalyataṃ'." True, but even so, because the alternative singular reading "janeti" is also seen and because the method of the Pāḷi is difficult to know, the teachers of the Commentaries, out of respect for the True Dhamma, did not say this singular reading is improper, but instead showed the method of number interchange (vacanavipallāsa) as "janenti."

In "Najjo ca anupariyāti, nānāpupphadumāyutā" (The river also flows surrounding it, endowed with various flowering trees), there is also an interchange of number. There, "najjo" (plural form) refers to a single river (ekā nadī).

Interchange of time (kālavipallāsa): "Chabbassāni nāma muggayūsakulatthayūsakalāyayūsahareṇuyūsādīnaṃ pasatapasatamattena yāpessati" (For six years, he sustained himself [literally: will sustain] on a mere handful of green gram soup, horse gram soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup, etc.). In that context, "yāpessati" means...
177:
One should bring forward the preceding noun-sound (nāmasadda) and connect it. Indeed, due to the association with the noun-sound, it becomes an usage like that of the future. "Yāpesi" is just such an usage of the past tense. Interchange of person (purisavippallāsa) refers to such instances as "Puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ" (May she obtain a son who grants noble boons), etc. In that context, "labhetha" has the meaning of "labheyyaṃ" (I would like to obtain).

Another method is "Mā tvaṃ bhāyi mahārāja" (O Great King, do not fear), etc., which is the interchange of case-ending and person (vibhattipurisavippallāsa). In truth, the meaning is "Mā bhāyassu" (Do not fear).

Interchange of letters (akkharavippallāsa) is found only in verses (gāthā) in the Pāḷi Canon, and not in prose (cuṇṇiyapada). Furthermore, that interchange of letters occurs only in the context of the feminine gender and the i-vowels (i, ī). In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is also found in some prose passages. Here is the Pāḷi Canon for this:
"Just as in the womb of a female crane (balākayoni), there is never a male," and,
"At which time in the city of Kusāvatī, there was a monarch (Mahāsudassana)."

In those instances, "balākayonimhi" means "balākayoniyaṃ" (in the womb of a female crane). "Kusāvatimhi" means "Kusāvatiyaṃ" (in the city of Kusāvatī). Indeed, the letter "mhi" is commonly seen in the masculine and neuter genders in both prose and verse; likewise, the letter "yaṃ" is common only in the feminine gender. In "Yathā balākayonimhi" etc., this letter "mhi" appears in the feminine gender. If one considers the reason why it appears so, since it is not found in the prose of the Pāḷi Canon, it should be understood by logic consistent with the Teaching (Sāsana) that the letter "mhi" occurs by way of interchange of letters (akkharavippallāsa). In the Commentaries, however, having stated the verse "Dvidhā sandhimhi vattati" (It occurs in two ways in rebirth), the reading of the letter "mhi" as "sandhimhi" is found even in a prose position. Here are these characteristics:

## 673. Gāthāsu itthiyaṃ mhikāro.
In both the Pāḷi Canon and the Commentaries, the letter "mhi" appears in the place of the feminine gender in the context of verses. (Example:) In the city of Kusāvatī (Kusāvatimhi nagare); it occurs in two ways in rebirth (dvidhā sandhimhi vattati).
178:
674. Kvaci aṭṭhakathāsu cuṇṇiyapade. In some prose (cuṇṇiyapada) of the Commentaries, the letter "mhi" is found in the place of the feminine gender. (Example:) Sandhimhi, paṭisandhimhi. Why is it said "kvaci" (some)? Because in instances such as sandhiyaṃ, paṭisandhiyaṃ, sugatiyaṃ, dugatiyaṃ, etc., (the letter "mhi" is not present).

Thus, the classification of Kāraka has been stated along with its connections and the determination of case-endings and so forth.
In this treatise, let those men who strive in the scriptural study (pariyatti) apply themselves to the Kāraka.
The wise person who strives here in this treatise becomes skillful in words (grammar) and in the scriptures.
Just as the ancient sages were very skillful in the Pāḷi Canon, in its words, its meanings, and in both, (so too will he be skillful).

## Thus ends the twenty-second chapter named the Classification of Kāraka (Kārakavibhāga) in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of speech of the ninefold Tipitaka together with its Commentaries.

## 4. Samāsakappa
Following this, I shall properly explain Compounds (samāsa) in brief, which bring about welfare and prosperity, and which clarify the meaning of compound words.
