In that context of compounding (samasana), there are two kinds: compounding of words (saddasamasana) and compounding of meanings (atthasamasana). Among those two, compounding of words is found in elided compounds (luttasamāsa) where the case-ending is dropped, such as "samaṇabrāhmaṇā" (ascetics and brahmins), etc. Compounding of meanings is found in unelided compounds (aluttasamāsa) where the case-ending is not dropped, such as "dūrenidānaṃ", "gavaṃpati", "urasilomo", "devānaṃpiyatisso", etc. Or, both kinds are found in elided compounds such as "Sahāyo te mahārāja, mahārājā maruppiyo" (He is your friend, O Great King; the Great King is beloved of the gods), etc. Here, "maruppiya" refers to King Devānaṃpiyatissa.

675. Nāmopasagganipātānaṃ yuttattho samāso. The combined meaning of nouns, prefixes (upasagga), and particles (nipāta) is called a compound (samāsa). Whatever combined meaning there is of those nouns, prefixes, and particles whose word-meanings are employed, that meaning is named "samāsa". (Example:) Kaṭhinadussaṃ (the cloth offered for the purpose of spreading the Kaṭhina robe), etc. Why is it said "nāmopasagganipātānaṃ"? In "Devadatto pacati" etc., by means of the finite verb (ākhyāta)...
179:
In the term "Samāsa" (compound), unification (samasana) is of two kinds: unification by word and unification by meaning. Among these two, unification by word is found in compounds where the case endings are dropped, such as "Samaṇabrāhmaṇā." Unification by meaning is found in compounds where the case endings are not dropped, such as "Dūrenidānaṃ," "Gavaṃpati," "Urasilomo," "Devānaṃpiyatissa," and so on. Both kinds are found in compounds where the case endings are dropped, such as "Mahārāja." Here, "Maruppiyo" refers to King Devānaṃpiyatissa.

675. A word with a connected meaning consisting of nouns, prefixes, or particles is called a Samāsa (compound). That connected meaning of those nouns, prefixes, and particles which are combined is called Samāsa. Examples include "kathiṇadussaṃ" (cloth offered for the Kathina ceremony). Why is it said "nāma-upasagga-nipātānaṃ" (of nouns, prefixes, and particles)? It is to show that compounds do not form with verbs (ākhyāta) in phrases like "Devadatto pacati" (Devadatta cooks). Why is it said "yuttattho" (having a connected meaning)? It is to show that compounds do not form in instances like "bhaṭo rañño, putto devadattassa" (the king's servant, Devadatta's son) because there is no mutual expectation, or in "bakassa setāni pattāni" (the white feathers of a crane) because there is expectation of another word; thus, they lack a connected meaning. What is the benefit of the name "Samāsa"? The benefit is the occurrence of certain changes at the end of words that have become part of a compound.

Why is the verb (ākhyāta) not included here? Is it not true that compounds are seen with verbs? For instance, the word "Pātimokkha" is seen with its definition: "He who guards the virtue (sīla), it releases him from sufferings such as the four states of misery, therefore it is called Pātimokkha." (If one says this), it is not so. In that definition, the word "Pātimokkha" is formed through a derivative (taddhita) process, not through a compound (samāsa) process, just like the word "Ehipassiko." (If one says), "Venerable Sir, in the word 'Ehipassiko,' the derivative suffix 'ṇika' is found in the sense of 'worthy of this procedure: Come and see (ehi passa)'; however, in the word 'Pātimokkha,' no derivative suffix is found." It is indeed found; in the word "Pātimokkha," the suffix "ṇa" occurs in its own sense (sakattha). (If one says), "Venerable Sir, is the suffix 'ṇa' not found only in the sense of lineage (apacca)?" It is not found only in the sense of lineage, as it is also seen in senses such as "tena rattaṃ" (dyed with that color). The rule is stated: "Ṇa occurs in the sense of dye, possession, and other meanings." Let it be so. (If one says), "Venerable Sir, is it not seen that a compound is formed with a verb in the word 'Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ'?" True, although a verbal form is seen here, because it is connected with the particle "iti," that word falls into the category of particles (nipāta) and thus attains the status of a compound word.

676. In some places, the case ending must be elided. The case endings of those nouns, prefixes, and particles that are fit to be compounds reach elision in some places. Examples: "kathiṇadussaṃ" (cloth offered for the Kathina ceremony), "āgantukabhattaṃ" (food offered to visiting monks), and "pabhaṅkaro" (the sun/light-maker).
180:
It is not completed in connection with the second Tappurisa compound. It is like the word 'Ehipassiko'. This is the answer. Venerable Sir, in this word 'Ehipassiko', in the sense of 'Come and see this practice', the taddhita suffix 'ṇika' is evident. In the word 'Pātimokkho', however, one might object that the taddhita suffix is not evident. In 'Pātimokkho', the suffix 'ṇa' occurs in its own sense (sakatttha). This is the answer. Venerable Sir, one might object: 'Is it not true that the suffix ṇa is only evident in the sense of lineage (apacca)?' It is not evident only in the sense of lineage. Why? Because it is also seen in other senses such as 'tena rattaṃ' and so on. It is true that the rule 'ṇa rāgā tassidamanyatthesu ca' has been stated. This is the answer. Let it be so. Venerable Sir, one might object: 'In this word Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ, we see a compound with the verbal form ssāmi.' True, although the verbal form is evident here, because it is connected with the word 'iti', that verbal form 'ssāmi' becomes part of the group of particles (nipāta) and thus enters into a compound. (This is according to the paribhāṣā that a word delimited by the word iti is a particle).

676. Kvacī vibhattilopaṃ. The case endings of those nouns, prefixes, and particles that are fit for compounding and associated with meaning are elided in some instances. Examples: Cloth offered for the purpose of spreading the kaṭhina robe (Kaṭhinadussaṃ); food offered to visiting monks (Āgantukabhattaṃ); one who makes light or the sun (Pabhaṅkaro).

677. Samāsataddhitākhyātakitakānaṃ paccaya padakkharāgamā ca. Not only are case endings elided, but indeed, the suffixes, words, letters, and augments of compounds (samāsa), secondary derivatives (taddhita), verbs (ākhyāta), and primary derivatives (kitaka) are also elided in some instances. Examples: The son of Vasiṭṭha (Vāsiṭṭho); the son of Vinatā (Venateyyo); the side of the Himavant (Himavantapassaṃ), and so on.

678. Na padānaṃ vippakatenuttarena samāso. Words do not form a compound with a following word that expresses an action in progress (incomplete). Examples: One going to the path (Maggaṃ gacchanto); one hearing the Dhamma (Dhammaṃ suṇamāno); one practicing the Dhamma (Dhammaṃ caranto), and so on. Why say 'action in progress'? To show that compounding occurs in cases like: One who has entered upon the long road (Addhānamaggappaṭipanno); one great in virtue (Guṇamahanto). Here, the fact that words like gacchanta express an action in progress is known from such Pāḷi passages as: "That Bhāradvāja, while going (gacchanto), saw the hermit Accuta."

679. Tvāpaccayantādīhi ca. Words do not form a compound with following words ending in the suffix -tvā etc. that express an action in progress. Examples: Not having done (Akatvā); having descended into the battlefield (Saṅgāmaṃ otaritvāna); King Kusa, having mounted the elephant's back, let out a lion's roar (Sīhanādaṃ nadī); in order to give gifts (Dānāni dātuṃ), and so on. Why say 'with following words'? To show that compounding occurs in: Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādo); derived matter (Upādāyarūpaṃ); one desiring to go (Gantukāmo); one desiring to give (Dātukāmo).

680. Ānatatavantutāvīhi ca. Words do not form a compound with words ending in the suffixes -āna, -ta, -tavantu, and -tāvī. Examples: One making a chariot (Rathaṃ kubbāno); one doing work (Kammaṃ karāno); one who has eaten rice (Odanaṃ bhutto); one who has eaten food (Bhattaṃ bhuttavā); one who has eaten food (Bhattaṃ bhuttāvī).
181:
681. When pronunciation is difficult or the meaning is not clear, only a sentence (vākya) occurs. In a place where, if a compound (samāsa) were made, there would be no ease of pronunciation and the meaning would not be clearly known, a compound does not occur; in such a place, it remains only a sentence. (Examples:) "(River water) to be drunk by crows," "(Defilements) to be abandoned by insight-knowledge," "The Elder Puṇṇa, who is the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāṇī," and so on.

682. When there is an upapada (dependent word), words formed from roots (dhātumaya) always form a compound. Words formed from roots that stand with an upapada always form a compound with the preceding words. He performs work (kamma), therefore he is called 'kammakāra' (worker). Because he is born from oneself (atta), he is called 'attaja' (son), and so on.

683. Words ending in the suffix -tvā, etc., being the preceding words, always form a compound (with the following words). Matter that arises depending on the great elements (mahābhūta) is called 'upādāyarūpa' (derived matter). Alternatively, it exists as 'upādārūpa' by eliding the letter 'ya'. It brings about states that arise together depending on mutual causes; therefore, it is called 'paṭiccasamuppāda' (dependent origination). Matter that arises due to a cause that has been performed is 'kaṭattārūpa'; it is also called kamma-produced matter (kammajarūpa). Other examples should also be applied in this manner.

684. A compound also occurs with the word 'iti'. Words form a compound together with the word 'iti' as the preceding word. The faculty (indriya) that arises in one who practices thus: "I shall know the four noble truths not yet known," is called 'anaññātaññassāmītindriya'. The name "Jotipāla" is called 'jotipāloti-nāmaṃ', and so on.

685. A compound also occurs with a finite verb (ākhyāta) where the word 'iti' is elided. Words form a compound together with a finite verb as the preceding word where the word 'iti' is elided. The state of being a monk obtained by the words "Come hither" (ehi) is called 'ehi-upasampadā', and so on. In the term "ehisāgatavādī," however, the compound is formed only with the word 'sāgata', not with the word 'ehi'. This is because the word 'ehi' stands as a part of the sentence. Because he is one who habitually says, "Come hither, may your coming be good (sāgata)," the compound 'ehisāgatavādī' is formed. Why is it said, "with a finite verb where the word 'iti' is elided"? (To show that a compound does not occur if 'iti' is absent:) "Devadatto gato" (Devadatta has gone), and so on.
182:
686. Words also form a compound with a word whose case ending (vibhatti) is not elided (alutta). There is compounding of words together with a word that has an unelided case ending. Examples: Devānaṃpiyatissa, manasikāra, kaṇṭhekāḷa, kutojo, tatojo, itojo, itonidāno, vanejo.

As in the Pali:
"Just as a young monkey born in the forest (vanejo)
Would deceive an old monkey born in the forest (vaneja)."

687. Words also form a compound with conventional names (rūḷhī-nāma). There is compounding of words together with conventional names. Examples: yevāpanakadhammo, yevāpanakadhammā, yaṃvāpanakarūpaṃ, gacchati-dhātu, pacati-dhātu, karoti-dhātu, gami-dhātu, gamu-dhātu, kara-dhātu, si-vibhatti, ā-paccayo, and so on.

688. When there is a qualification of a qualified word (visesanīya), a word that lacks a semantic connection (ayuttattha) due to being separated by another word should be regarded as if it has a semantic connection (yuttattha). A word which, by the power of being separated by another word, lacks a semantic connection, should be regarded as if it has a semantic connection when it qualifies a qualified word. For example: "Monks, just as a pure gold nugget (nikkha) from the Jambu river, which has been very skillfully and well-beaten in the mouth of a furnace by a skilled goldsmith's son... glows, shines, and is brilliant," as in this sentence.

Here, this is the compound formation: That which is well-beaten by one who is very skillful is 'sukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ'; that which is very skillfully beaten in the mouth of a furnace is 'ukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ'; a skilled goldsmith's son is 'dakkhakammāraputto'; that which is very skillfully beaten in the mouth of a furnace by a skilled goldsmith's son is 'dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ'. The meaning is: it is well-beaten after being melted in the mouth of a furnace by a skilled and very proficient goldsmith's son. Here, although it becomes a single word due to being a compound, it should be known that the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya) have made the word-connection (padayojanā) by extracting the terms from time to time according to the sense. This is because the teaching of the Teacher (the Buddha) has diverse methods.
183:
689. Compounding also occurs in the negation of an action (bhāvanisedha), transcending substance (satta) and non-substance (asatta). 'Satta' refers to substance (dabba). 'Asatta' refers to non-substances such as particles (nipāta), etc. 'Bhāva' refers to action (kriyā). Among three words, a word which lacks a semantic connection through the power of the first and second words should be regarded as if it has a connection when there is a negation of action (bhāvanisedha), transcending substance or non-substance. (Examples:) Faces that do not look at the sun (asūriyapassāni), faces that do not look at the moon, one who does not eat kumbhasa-rice, one who does not eat salt, verses that are not to be recited again.

690. Because a word that is dependent (sāpekkha) on another word cannot make its meaning known, it does not form a compound with the immediately following word. Among three words, because the dependent word which is separated cannot make known the meaning that it should convey, it does not form a compound with the immediately following word. (Examples:) Devadatta's teeth are black (devadattassa kaṇhā dantā), the crane's wings are white.

691. Because a single distinct meaning is made known by two similar words, a compound always occurs. Taking the term 'samāsa' (compound) again is for the purpose of removing the prohibition. Among three words, when a single meaning is to be expressed as distinguished by two similar words, a compound always occurs with the immediately following word because the dependent word, even though separated, can make known the meaning it should convey. (Examples:) The divine power of the gods (devānaṃ devānubhāvo), the majesty of kings. In this regard, there is this Pali: "An immeasurable, grand radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine power of the gods (devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ)."

692. In some cases, a dependent word that is not separated (anantari-sāpekkha) forms a compound with the subsequent word. Among three words, because the meaning of the dependent word that is not separated can be known, a compound occurs in some cases with the subsequent word. (Examples:) The king's slave-son (rañño dāsiputto), or the son of the king's slave-woman. In that context, 'samāsa' means compounding (samasana), the condensation of words (padasaṅkhepa). Alternatively, it is called 'samāsa' because it is compounded by making multiple words into one, whether by the power of the sound or the power of the meaning, and whether by eliding the case ending or not eliding it. The characteristic of a compound is the becoming one of various different words. Some teachers, however, say that of words having different meanings...
184:
It is called a compound (samāsa) because it is condensed into a single word (ekapadatta) either by the power of the meaning, or by eliding or not eliding the case endings. It is a word that has been joined together. The characteristic of a compound is the attainment of single-word status by various words. However, some teachers say: "The characteristic of a compound is the state of having a single meaning for words with different meanings."

That compound is of two types by power of function: the elided compound (lutta-samāsa) and the unelided compound (alutta-samāsa). Likewise, it is of two types by nature: the obligatory compound (nicca-samāsa) and the non-obligatory compound (anicca-samāsa). By power of name, there are six types: Avyayībhāva, Kammadharaya, Digu, Tappurisa, Bahubbīhi, and Dvanda. By way of subdivision, there are 27 or 28 types. The two benefits of those compounds are single-word status and having a single case ending.

693. Vibhattilope sarantassa liṅgassa pakati. When the case endings of the words in a sentence are elided, the gender-stem ending in a vowel remains in its natural form (pakati). Examples: Cakkhusotaṃ, Rājaputto. In the sense of "the causes (such as ignorance) of these (effects such as formations)", there are forms like "Idappaccayā" and so on. In this context, the natural form (pakati-rūpa) should be understood either by bringing back the elided vowel or by the word "idaṃ" (which has the substitution "tima") remaining in its own original natural state.

694. Kvaci byañjanantassa. When the case ending is elided, the gender-stem ending in a consonant remains in its natural form in some instances. In the analysis (viggaha) of "What cause does this Dhamma have?", it becomes "Kiṃsamudayo". Why say "kvaci" (in some instances)? In the context of "Venerable Sir, what is the name of this Dhamma-discourse?", even though the analysis is "kiṃ nāmaṃ etassa", it becomes "Konāmo"; because the word "kiṃ" is substituted with "ko", it does not remain in its natural form. Here, the extraction of meaning is as follows: The word "ko" occurs as an interrogative pronoun in the sense of the nominative case (paṭhamā) in such phrases as "ko puriso". It occurs as an interrogative pronoun in the sense of the locative case (sattamī), having the meaning of the word "kva", in such phrases as "Great King, where is your army (ko te balaṃ)?". It should be noted that it occurs in the sense of an inquiry as a component of a compound word in such phrases as "What is the name of your preceptor (konāmo te upajjhāyo)?".
185:
## 695. Upasagganipātā Avyayā.
Prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) are called avyaya (indeclinables). Prefixes and particles are called avyaya because, apart from some euphonic (sandhi), compound (samāsa), and derivative (taddhita) operations, they do not deviate and are not destroyed in all genders, case endings, and numbers. The detailed explanation of their forms will be made clear in the Padavibhāga. These are the usages of those indeclinables when they form an avyayībhāva compound in euphonic operations etc. For example: "Monks, the eye is overwhelmed (by birth, aging, etc.)" (addhabhūtaṃ). "The designation of name occurs overwhelming all" (addhabhavi). "That Bodhisatta lived ruling in the palace" (ajjhāvasī). "The Great Sage Dīpaṅkara Buddha admonished" (ovadeti). Kadannaṃ (a little rice), kāpuriso (a contemptible man), pātayāgu (gruel to be drunk in the morning), pātarāso (morning meal), āvusovādo or āvusovāda (addressing as "āvuso"), ābhidhammiko (one who studies Abhidhamma), "this of a liar" is mosavajjaṃ (the property of a liar), meaning musāvādo (lying), and so forth.

Those words which do not undergo change in the three genders and in all case endings are called avyaya.

## 696. Avyayapubbako Avyayībhāvo.
A compound with an indeclinable at the beginning is an avyayībhāva. A compound that is preceded by an indeclinable and where the meaning of the indeclinable is predominant is an avyayībhāva compound. It is called avyayībhāva because it expresses, specifically expresses, or clearly expresses the meaning of the indeclinables. Indeed, this compound is called "avyayībhāva" because it specifically expresses the meaning of the prefixes and particles named avyaya which are joined with words like "nagara" in words such as "upanagaraṃ". For instance, the meaning of the word "upanagaraṃ" is "nagarasamīpaṃ" (near the city). However, in the passage "Just as a spider follows the web it has made itself, so do beings infatuated with passion follow the stream of craving they have made themselves", the compound "sayaṃkataṃ" is not an avyayībhāva because the meaning is taken according to the order of words and there is no specific expression of an indeclinable's meaning. Indeed, in an avyayībhāva, the meaning of the indeclinable is predominant.

Some teachers say: "Because it is preceded by the meaning of an indeclinable, a noun that is not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable; therefore it is called avyayībhāva." Our view, however, is: In this compound, because it is preceded by the meaning of an indeclinable, even a word that is not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable in part; therefore it is called avyayībhāva. Here, taking "in part" completes this Pali: "ko yaṃ majjhesamuddasmiṃ". In the middle of the ocean is "majjhesamuddaṃ"; in that "majjhesamuddaṃ", the analysis should be made as "majjhesamuddasmiṃ". The meaning, however, should be applied only as "in the middle of the ocean". Now, to prevent confusion for the listeners, I shall show examples expressing the meaning of indeclinables along with the decisions (vinicchaya). "Near the city" is called "upanagaraṃ". This is an analysis with a word for "near" (samīpa) other than "upa". After eliding the nominative singular after the word "upa" and the genitive singular after the word "nagara", the nominative singular occurs at the end of the word. According to some teachers, the genitive and nominative singular occur respectively from the words "nagara" and "samīpa". Then, when the case ending is elided, the word "nagara"...
186:
The term "majjhesamuddaṃ" means in the middle of the ocean. It is analyzed as "majjhesamuddaṃ is in the middle of the ocean; in that majjhesamuddaṃ." However, the meaning should be applied simply as "in the middle of the ocean."

Now, in order that the listeners may not be confused, I shall state the examples illustrating the meanings of indeclinables (avyaya) along with their determinations (vinicchaya). Proximity to a city is called "upanagaraṃ." This analysis (vigga-ha) is an analysis made with another word (other than 'upa'). The nominative singular case follows the word 'upa', and the genitive singular case follows the word 'nagara'. When the case endings are elided, the nominative singular occurs at the end of the compound. According to the opinion of some teachers, the genitive and nominative singular cases occur respectively after the words 'nagara' and 'samīpa'. Then, when the case ending is elided, the word "nagarasamīpa" is formed. Subsequently, in the place of the word 'samīpa', the prefix (upasagga) "upa," which expresses the meaning of proximity, is placed. Thus, it should be understood that in the word standing as "nagaraupa," the reversal of the preceding and following letters is seen through the inversion of the lower and upper positions.

In the sense of absence (abhāva): The absence of distress (daratha) is "niddarathaṃ"; the absence of mosquitoes and gnats is "nimmasakaṃ." Here also, one can obtain an anyapadattha-samāsa (a compound referring to an external object) such as "niddaratho" referring to a man, analyzed as "one for whom there is no distress," or "nimmasakaṃ" referring to a place, analyzed as "a place where there are no mosquitoes." Phrases like "he is without distress, without sin," "the Dhamma without impurity," and "the honeycomb without flies" are due to the illustration of the scope of anyapadattha. Some, however, desire that even by merely expressing absence, as in "the absence of flies is nimmakkhikaṃ," it refers to the substance (dabba), such as the honeycomb. That is not appropriate. For, just as the word "sāmañña" (the state of a recluse), by expressing the state (bhāva), does not refer to the recluse (samaṇa), so also by expressing absence (abhāva), it cannot refer to those respective substances.

In the sense of after (pacchā): "anurathaṃ" (after the chariot); likewise "anuvātaṃ" (with the wind/after the wind). In the sense of suitability (yogyatā): "anurūpaṃ" (suitable to the form); it means suitable to the form. In the sense of repetition (vīcchā): "paccattaṃ" (individually/each to oneself); "anvaddhamāsaṃ" (every half-month/fortnightly); likewise "anusaraṃ" (every sound). This is for the grammarians...
187:
According to the opinion of the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariya), it should be understood thus: 'paccattaṃ' means each to oneself (individually), and 'anvaddhamāsaṃ' means every half-month (fortnightly). 'Anugharaṃ' means house to house; it means according to the order of houses. In the sense of succession (anupubbiya), the order of the elders is called 'anujeṭṭhaṃ'. In the sense of reverse (paṭiloma), the reverse of the current is called 'paṭisotaṃ' (upstream). Here also, turning back and facing upwards is called 'paṭiloma'. This is true; this prefix 'pati' occurs in the sense of turning back; likewise 'paṭipathaṃ' (facing the path/oncoming) and 'paṭisotaṃ' (upstream).

In the sense of concerning or based upon (adhikaccapavatti), that which occurs based on oneself, such as the eye and so forth, is called 'ajjhattaṃ'. The collection of mental states occurring based on the mind is called 'adhicittaṃ'. Although it is indicated in a general sense, it refers only to concentration (samādhi) because the meaning must be taken by way of conventional designation (saṅketa), and because of the saying: "A word expressing a general sense remains fixed in a specific sense." Alternatively, by way of the kammadhāraya compound "the superior mind is adhicittaṃ," it refers only to concentration because that concentration is indicated with the mind as the head (chief). Indeed, the three trainings are higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Some teachers, however, say that this word 'adhicittaṃ', when spoken in reference to concentration, is not an avyayībhāva compound. If it were an avyayībhāva compound, the word-analysis would be "adhicittaṃ is that which occurs based on the mind." In that case, the sense of 'concerning' (adhikacca) alone would not be the meaning of the word 'citta'. In the Adhicitta Sutta and others, concentration is indicated with the mind as the chief; that concentration is called "the superior mind is adhicittaṃ." Therefore, those who wish to establish it as an avyayībhāva compound must search for the meaning; thus they desire the search for another meaning.

What is the use of searching for another meaning here? For even by the definition "adhicittaṃ is that which occurs based on the mind," concentration is illustrated in another manner. This is true; the teachers, when explaining the meaning of this Pali passage "cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ" (developing the mind and wisdom), refer to concentration and insight (vipassanā)...
188:
...while developing. Regarding the explanatory statement "Here, concentration is indicated with the mind as the chief," the sub-commentator (Ṭīkākāra), desiring only the sense of concentration for the word 'citta', stated four definitions such as "It is called citta (concentration) because it thinks upon or closely contemplates the object," and thus the synonym of 'citta' for that concentration is obtainable even without the instruction of others. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, because the word 'citta' is well-established in the sense of consciousness (viññāṇa), it was said: "In this sutta, concentration is indicated with the mind as the chief."

This is true; in the passage "The word (vacana) 'Bhagavā' is noble," the teachers take the word (sadda) by the term 'vacana' and then take the meaning again. The intended meaning is: "It is called vacana (meaning) because it is spoken; the meaning expressed by the word 'Bhagavā' is noble." Knowing this, one should not engage in disputes over the texts that should be taken by way of double intention and so forth in various places. Whatever meaning is appropriate should be taken by those who are expert in methods (nayaññū). In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, the plural definition "The states that occur based on the mind are adhicittaṃ" should be understood as being made in reference to concentration together with its concomitant states (sampayutta-dhamma).

In the senses of limit (mariyādā) and pervasion (abhividhi): In the term "āpāṇakoṭiyaṃ" (until the end of life), the suffix 'ka' is changed to 'ya'. The fame of Kaccāyana, which pervades from childhood, is called "ākomāraṃ." In the sense of prosperity (samiddhi): The abundance of alms-food is "subhikkhaṃ." In the sense of lack of prosperity (asamiddhi): The scarcity of alms-food is "dubbhikkhaṃ." In the sense of proximity (samīpa): Near the river is "anunadaṃ"; near the Ganges is "upagaṅgaṃ"; near the water-pot is "upamaṇikaṃ"; near the wife is "upavadhu"; near the cows is "upagu." In the sense of concerning (adhikata): A talk occurring concerning one woman among women is called "adhitti." Likewise, "adhikumāri" and others should be applied. Thus should the avyayībhāva compound with a prefix at the beginning be understood.
189:
What is the Avyayībhāva compound with a particle (nipāta) as the first member? In the sense of sequence (paṭipāṭi) and repetition (vicchā), the sequence of seniors is 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ' (according to seniority). Whichever seniors there are, they are called 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ' (those who are seniors). Similarly, the sequence of those who are beautiful, or whichever beautiful ones there are, is called 'yathābhirūpaṃ'.

Some teachers say: "The word yathā is designated as Avyayībhāva in the sense of dissimilarity (asadisabhāva). Whichever seniors there are whose days, months, and years are not the same, they are called 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ'. Whichever beautiful ones there are whose complexions—dark, golden, or fair—are not the same, they are called 'yathābhirūpaṃ'. Why is it said in the sense of dissimilarity? It serves the purpose of showing that in cases such as 'yathā devadatto' (like Devadatta) and 'yathā yaññadatto' (like Yaññadatta), the name Avyayībhāva does not apply."

Furthermore, some teachers say: "Whatever sequence of seniors exists, such a sequence is called 'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ'. Indeed, this particle yathā occurs in the sense of similarity (sadisattha); therefore, a sequence of seniors that is like the sequence of seniors is called 'vuḍḍhapaṭipāṭi'."

But we say that the word yathā expresses sequence, and it is a word occurring in repetition (vicchā) expressing the meaning of the pronoun 'ya'.

In the sense of not exceeding the meaning of the member (padatthānatikkama): occurring without exceeding the order is called 'yathākkamaṃ'. Similarly, there are 'yathāsatti' and 'yathābalံ'. Thus, 'yathābalaṃ karoti' means he acts without exceeding his strength.

In the sense of limitation (pariccheda): whatever the extent of life's limit is, it is called 'yāvajīvaṃ'. Similarly, 'yāvatāyukaṃ'.

In the sense of the other side (parabhāga): the other side of the mountain is 'tiropabbataṃ'. Similarly, the other side of the enclosure wall is 'tiropākāraṃ'; the other side of the wall is 'tirokuṭṭaṃ'. The inside of the palace is 'antopāsādaṃ'. Similarly, the inside of the city is 'antonagaraṃ'; the inside of the rainy season is 'antovassaṃ'. Outside the city is 'bahinagaraṃ'. Above the palace is 'uparipāsādaṃ'. Below the couch is 'heṭṭhāmañcaṃ'. Similarly, below the palace is 'heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ'. Before the mealtime is 'purebhattaṃ'. Similarly, after the mealtime is 'pacchābhattaṃ'.

In the sense of totality (sākallattha): being together with flies is called 'samakkhikaṃ'. Similarly, being together with grass is 'satiṇaṃ'. In that context, 'samakkhikaṃ ajjhoharati' means he swallows it together with flies, without excluding even a little bit. In the case of 'satiṇaṃ ajjhoharati', it also means he swallows it without excluding even a little bit.

The side on this side of the Ganges river is called 'oragaṅgaṃ'. The middle of the ocean is 'majjhesamuddaṃ'. Others should also be applied accordingly. Thus, the Avyayībhāva compound with a particle as the first member should be understood.

## ၆၉၇။ တံသဒိသော စ။
Because it has the nature of being preceded by an indeclinable meaning (avyayatthapubbaṅgama), a compound similar to that Avyayībhāva compound is also designated as Avyayībhāva.
190: ...is. Examples are Tiṭṭhagu, Vahagu, Khaleyavaṃ, etc. What is the benefit of the name 'Avyayībhāva'? It serves the purpose of completing tasks such as the elision of case endings after Avyayībhāva compounds ending in 'a'. ## 698. Napuṃsako va so. That Avyayībhāva compound is only of the neuter gender. That Avyayībhāva compound should be understood as only neuter. For example: Adhikumāri (speech concerning a maiden), Upagaṅgaṃ (near the Ganges), Majjhesamuddaṃ (in the middle of the ocean), Upagu (near the cow). ## 699. Ekattaṃ digussa. A Digu compound is singular (and neuter). A Digu compound becomes singular and takes the neuter gender. For example: the three worlds are called Tilokaṃ, the three eyes are called Tinayanaṃ, the four directions are called Catuddisaṃ, the ten directions are called Dasadisaṃ, and the five faculties are called Pañcindriyaṃ. ## 700. Dvande pāṇitūriyayoggasenāṅgakhuddajantukavividhaviruddhavisabhāgatthādīnañca. In a Dvanda compound, parts of living beings, parts of musical instruments, parts of vehicles, parts of an army, small creatures, things with various opposite meanings, things with various dissimilar meanings, etc., are singular and neuter. In a Dvanda compound, parts of living beings, parts of musical instruments, parts of vehicles, parts of an army, small creatures, things with various opposite meanings, and things with various dissimilar meanings, etc., become singular and take the neuter gender. The eye and the ear are called Cakkhusotaṃ; the mouth and the nose are called Mukhanāsikaṃ; the skin, flesh, and blood are called Chavimaṃsalohitaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of parts of living beings (pāṇyaṅga). The conch and the drum are called Saṅkhapaṇavaṃ; singing and playing music are called Gītavāditaṃ; the large drum and the small drum are called Daddaridiṇḍimaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of parts of musical instruments (tūriyaṅga). The ploughshare and the goad are called Phālapācanaṃ; the yoke and the plough are called Yuganangalaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of parts of vehicles (yoggaṅga). The sword and the shield are called Asicammaṃ; the bow and the quiver are called Dhanukalāpaṃ; elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry are called Hatthiassarathapattikaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of parts of an army (senaṅga). Gadflies and mosquitoes are called Ḍaṃsamakasaṃ; small ants and large ants are called Kunthakipillikaṃ; insects and reptiles are called Kīṭasarīsapaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of small creatures (khuddajantuka). The snake and the mongoose are called Ahinakulaṃ; the cat and the mouse are called Biḷāramūsikaṃ; the crow and the owl are called Kākolūkaṃ; the wholesome and the unwholesome are called Kusalākusalaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of various opposites (vividhaviruddha). Virtue and wisdom are called Sīlapaññāṇaṃ. The two Pali passages, 'Indeed, venerable sir, such is the virtue and wisdom of the Blessed One' and 'The man possessed of wisdom is excellent,' serve as evidence for the existence of the word paññāṇa. Calm and insight are called Samathavipassanaṃ; knowledge and conduct are called Vijjācaraṇaṃ; the pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, is called Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ. Thus it is in the sense of various dissimilar things (vividhavisabhāga). By the word 'ādi' (etc.), terms such as maidservant and manservant (Dāsidāsaṃ), woman and man (Itthipumaṃ), bowl and robe (Pattacīvaraṃ), a group of three and a group of four (Tikacatukkaṃ), basket-maker and chariot-maker (Veṇarathakāraṃ), bird-hunter and deer-hunter (Sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ), and long and medium (Dīghamajjhimaṃ) should be included.
191: 701. The formation of the singular neuter in Dvanda compounds of words such as trees, grass, animals, wealth, grain, districts, etc., is optional (vibhāsā). Examples are: Assatthakapitthaṇaṃ or Assatthakapitthanā (the sacred fig and the wood-apple tree); Usīrabīraṇaṃ or Usīrabīraṇā (vetiver and birana grass); Ajeḷakaṃ or Ajeḷakā (goats and sheep); Hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ or Hiraññasuvaṇṇā (silver and gold); Sāliyavaṃ or Sāliyavā (rice and barley); Kāsikosalaṃ or Kāsikosalā (the Kāsi and Kosala kingdoms); Sāvajjānavajjaṃ or Sāvajjānavajjā (blameworthy and blameless states); Hīnapaṇītaṃ or Hīnapaṇītā (the low and the excellent); Kaṇhasukkaṃ or Kaṇhasukkā (black and white).## 702. Two words having the same referent (tulyādhikaraṇa) are combined; that compound is called Kammadhāraya. In a usage where two words of the same referent are combined, that compound receives the name Kammadhāraya. The occurrence of two words with different reasons for application (pavattinimitta) in a single sense, in the relationship of qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesitabba), is called tulyādhikaraṇatā. Just as 'action' (kamma) carries two things—the act (kriyā) and the purpose (payojana)—this compound is called 'Kammadhāraya' because it carries two names for a single meaning. Since the act and the purpose can exist when there is an action, so too, two nouns expressing a single meaning can exist when there is this compound; thus it is said, "It is Kammadhāraya because, like an action, it carries two."## That Kammadhāraya compound is of nine types: (1) Visesanapubbapada, (2) Visesanuttarapada, (3) Visesanobhayapada, (4) Upamānuttarapada, (5) Sambhāvanāpubbapada, (6) Avadhāraṇapubbapada, (7) Nanipātapubbapada, (8) Kupubbapada, and (9) Pādipubbapada.## Among those nine, Visesanapubbapada is: Mahāpuriso (a great man), Nīluppalaṃ (a blue lotus), etc. Visesanuttarapada is: Sāriputtatthero (the Elder Sāriputta), Buddhaghosācariyo (the Teacher Buddhaghosā), Ācariyaguttilo (the Teacher Guttila), etc.
192: Mahosadhapaṇḍito (the wise Mahosadha), Sattaviseso (a special being), etc. What is Visesanobhayapada (a compound with two adjectives, before and after)? One who is both sick and has arisen from the sickness is called Gilānavuṭṭhito. It means a person who, having been sick, has recovered from the illness. A place that is both sprinkled with water and swept is called Sittasammaṭṭhaṃ. Likewise, Andhabadhiro (one who is both blind and deaf), Khañjakhujjo (one who is both lame and hunchbacked), etc.## What is Upamānuttarapada (a compound with a comparison as the last member)? He is called Sīho because he is like a lion; because the Buddha is both [the Buddha] and like a lion, he is called Buddhasīho, etc. What is Sambhāvanāpubbapada (a compound with the sense of 'iti' or 'thinking' in the first member)? The knowledge [thinking] "this is the Dhamma" is called Dhammabuddhi. Likewise, Dhammasaññā (the perception of "this is the Dhamma"), etc. What is Avadhāraṇapubbapada (a compound with the word 'eva' [only/itself] in the first member)? Because the Buddha alone is excellent, he is called Buddhavaro. That same Buddhavaro can also be Visesanuttarapada because he is both the Buddha and excellent. Because it shines like the light of the sun, moon, or fire, it is called Pajjoto; because wisdom itself shines like that light, it is called Paññāpajjoto. Likewise, Paññāpāsādo (wisdom itself is like a palace). Because of the sense of being cherished, it is like wealth, hence Dhanaṃ; because faith itself is like wealth, it is called Saddhādhanaṃ. Likewise, Sīladhanaṃ (the wealth of virtue), etc.## However, the teachers (the authors of Rūpasiddhi) state the etymological definition with emphasis (avadhāraṇa) as: "Because the eye itself is the faculty, it is Cakkhundriya." Does such a statement not seem to exclude the faculty-nature of the ear and so forth? If one asks, "Is there not this same fault in 'Because faith itself is wealth, it is Saddhādhana', etc.?"—there is no fault. It is because faith alone is the wealth of the Noble Ones (ariyas), and gold, silver, clothes, etc., are not the wealth of the Noble Ones. It is because virtue alone is the wealth of the Noble Ones, and gold, silver, clothes, etc., are not; thus, the wealth recognized by worldly people is excluded by the emphasis (avadhāraṇa).## What is Nanipātapubbapada (a compound with the particle 'na' first)? One who is not a Brahmin (or a barber who resembles a Brahmin) is called Abrāhmaṇo. Likewise, Amanusso (a non-human, such as an ogre), Alobho (the opposite of greed), Amitto (an enemy), Akusalā dhammā (unwholesome states), Abyākatā dhammā (indeterminate states), Apunageyyā gāthā (verses that should not be recited again), Asūriyapassā rājadārā (royal consorts who do not see the sun), Acandamullokikāni mukhāni (faces that do not look up at the moon), etc. What is Kupubbapada (a compound with the particle 'ku' first)? A contemptible view is called Kudiṭṭhi. Likewise, Kadannaṃ (disgusting food), Kāpuriso (a contemptible man), a little salt is called Kālavaṇaṃ, etc. Here also...
193:
Because it is a nicca-samāsa (permanent compound), its resolution (viggaha) must be made using words other than its own members. A compound where the first member is 'pa-' or similar prefixes is also a nicca-samāsa. Noble speech is called pāvacana (the Buddha's word). Excessive growth is called pavaḍḍha (the body). Placing evenly or properly is called samādhāna. Knowing in various ways is called vimati (doubt). Thinking in various ways is called vikappa, or it is called vikappa due to distinguished thinking. Dhamma that is superior to or more distinguished than the Suttas is called Abhidhamma. It is called 'Abhidhamma' because of its sense of being superior to and more distinguished than the Sutta texts. A superior deity is called atideva; likewise, adhideva. Superior virtue is called adhisīla. A beautiful man is called sappurisa.

In this context, taking the meaning of 'beauty' (sobhana) for the word 'saṃ', it is interpreted as 'a beautiful man'. In this word 'sappurisa', the niggahīta changes to 'p' because of the following letter 'p'. This is similar to the usage in passages such as 'cirappavāsiṃ' and 'hatthippabhinnaṃ viya aṅkusaggaho'. Just as in 'saddhā saddahanā' etc., the niggahīta changes to 'd' because of the following 'dh' and 'd', so too in this word 'sappurisa', the niggahīta changes to 'p' because of the following 'p'. Alternatively, a peaceful man is called sappurisa; the interpretation as 'a man with a peaceful mind' is appropriate according to the grammatical attribute (guṇa-liṅga). This is because the singular passage 'santo danto niyato brahmacārī' is found. However, interpreting it according to the gender of the object denoted (abhidheyya-liṅga) is not appropriate. This is because the plural passages 'santo sappurisā loke' and 'santo have sabbhi pavedayanti' are found. An action performed beautifully is called sukata, or an action performed well is called sukata. An action performed not beautifully is called dukkaṭa, or an action performed badly is called dukkaṭa, and so forth.

Now, I shall speak of the compound that has two intended meanings. Rice that is both cold and hot is called sītuṇha. Alternatively, cold and heat together are called sītuṇha. As in the phrase 'it dispels cold and heat', it refers to the quality of cold and the quality of heat. In words such as 'katākata', the resolution should be made according to either kammadhāraya or dvanda compounds.
194:
Contemptible wives are called kudārā. Similarly, there are kuputtā (bad sons), kudāsā (bad slaves), and duputtā (bad sons). Alternatively, those who have contemptible wives are called kudārā; thus it can also be a bahubbīhi compound, and so on. A small amount of salt is called kālavaṇaṃ. Similarly, kāpupphaṃ (a small flower). Alternatively, in this meat/fish, salt is little; therefore, it is called kālavaṇaṃ (meat/fish). In this forest, flowers are few; therefore, it is called kāpupphaṃ (forest). In this compound, only the former meaning is intended. Pakāra, parābhava, vihāra, āhāra, upahāra, etc., are also kammadhāraya compounds.

Teachers have also shown other examples. They are: the Buddha who was seen before (diṭṭhapubbo tathāgataṃ), similarly, the Dhamma that was heard before (sutapubbo dhammaṃ), the heaven that was gone to before (gatapubbo saggaṃ). In the passive voice (kammavācaka): the deities who were seen before by him (diṭṭhapubbā devā), similarly, the directions that were heard before or reached before (sutapubbā, gatapubbā disā). In these words like diṭṭhapubba, the state of being tulyādhikaraṇa (co-referential) is not clear. The reason why these are called kammadhāraya compounds should be investigated.

## 703. Saṅkhyāpubbo digu.

A kammadhāraya compound preceded by a numeral is called digu. A collection of two cows is called digu. Because it is similar to the word 'digu', this compound is called 'digu'. Just as the word 'digu' is preceded by a numeral and is in the neuter singular, so too this compound is preceded by a numeral and is mostly in the neuter singular. Therefore, because of its similarity to the word 'digu', it is called 'digu'.

Why is it said 'mostly'? To show that in the usage of scholars (kavi-samaya), it can appear as masculine singular as in 'tibhavo' in the verse 'At that time, the three worlds appear', and as neuter plural as in 'tibhavesu' in the text 'Having bowed to the Buddha, the supreme in the three worlds'. Alternatively, it is called digu because it is understood or known by two characteristics. The two characteristics of digu are: being preceded by a numeral is one characteristic, and being in the neuter singular is another characteristic. Because it is understood by these two characteristics, it is called 'digu'. Or, it is called digu because it proceeds or functions through two factors. In a digu compound, the meaning of the first member is predominant. That digu is of two types: samāhāra-digu and asamāhāra-digu. Among those two, first is the samāhāra-digu—
195:
Because the four truths are brought together as one, it is called Catusaccaṃ (the collection of the four truths). Similarly, Dvipadaṃ (the collection of two words), Timalaṃ (the collection of three impurities), Tidaṇḍaṃ (the collection of three staffs), Tiphalaṃ (the collection of three fruits), Trikaṭukaṃ (the collection of three pungent substances), Catuddisaṃ (the collection of the four directions), Pañcindriyaṃ (the collection of the five faculties), Pañcagavaṃ (the collection of five cows); and because the seven Godāvarī rivers are brought together as one, they are called Sattagodāvaraṃ, and so forth. Examples of Asamāhāra-digu (non-collective numeral compounds) are: Ekapuggala (a single person), Tibhavā (the three worlds), Catuddisā (the four directions), Dasasahassacakkavāḷāni (ten thousand world-systems), and so forth.

704. The case endings such as aṃ (accusative) and others are joined with subsequent words; that compound is called Tappurisa. In whatever usage the case endings like aṃ are joined together with subsequent words, in that usage, that compound bears the name Tappurisa. Because it is similar to the example "Tassa puriso tappuriso" (His man is Tappurisa), this compound is also called "Tappurisa". Just as the word Tappurisa transcends its attribute (qualifier), so too this entire compound transcends its attribute. Therefore, it is called "Tappurisa". In a Tappurisa compound, the meaning of the subsequent word is predominant. That Tappurisa compound is of six kinds, such as Dutiyā-tappurisa (accusative determinative), etc. Because of 'having gone to the ground', it is called Bhūmigata. Similarly, 'having gone to the forest' is Araññagata, and so forth.

In some places, the accusative case does not occur, and it becomes Saraṇagata with the meaning "known as a refuge." In the passage, "Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple approaches the Buddha as a refuge," the word "Buddhaṃ" indicates the object (kamma). "Saraṇaṃ gato" means "saraṇaṃ iti gato" (known as a refuge); due to the elision of the word iti, the word "saraṇaṃ" becomes the nominative case (paccatta-vacana). Therefore, the word gata is joined with the word iti. If the word "saraṇaṃ" were in the nominative case here, why is it seen in the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) in such passages as "They approached that Teacher Dīpaṅkara as a refuge" and "My faithful parents approached the Buddha as a refuge"?

It is not the accusative case; as in "I go to the Buddha as a refuge" (Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi), where the word iti is elided, it is indeed the nominative case. Indeed, by virtue of the transformation of the case, they approached that Teacher Dīpaṅkara "as a refuge," the Buddha "as a refuge"...
196:
...'gone' (gatā) is the meaning. In passages such as "I go to the Buddha as a refuge" (Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi), "I approach the Buddha as a refuge" (Upemi saraṇaṃ Buddhaṃ), and "Whoever have gone to the Buddha as a refuge" (Ye keci Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse), although it is the domain of a transitive verb, the nominative status (paccatta-vacana) of the word "saraṇaṃ" is understood from the observation of the elision of the word iti in such phrases as "The Fully Enlightened One acknowledges [himself as such]" (Sambuddho paṭijānāti), and from the words spoken by the teachers.

One who depends on the Dhamma (Dhammanissita), one who has transcended existence (Bhavātīta), that which exceeds measure (Pamāṇātikkanta), one who has attained happiness (Sukhappatta), one who has entered the stream (Sotāpanna), one who has attained the attainment of cessation (Nirodhasamāpanna), one who has set out on the path (Maggappaṭipanna), one who has mounted a chariot (Rathārūḷha), that which is beautiful throughout the three watches of the night (Sabbarattisobhana), happiness for a moment (Muhuttasukha), and so forth. In an Upapada-samāsa (dependent determinative compound with a verbal derivative), the compounding process is mandatory; there is no separate sentence (analysis). For example: because of 'performing a task', one is called a Kammakāra. Similarly, Kumbhakāra (potter), Atthakāma (one who desires welfare), Dhammadhara (one who upholds the Dhamma). One who habitually practices the Dhamma is called Dhammacārī. Or, because practicing the Dhamma is his habit, he is called Dhammacārī. This compound is a Dutiyā-tappurisa compound.

Made by a lord (Issarakata), pierced by an arrow (Sallaviddha), rice mixed with molasses is called Guḷodana. Similarly, Khīrodana (milk-rice). A chariot yoked with horses is Assaratha. Similarly, Ājaññaratha (a chariot of thoroughbreds). Consciousness associated with the Path is Maggacitta. The island known by the Jambu tree is Jambudīpa. Association with the word tumha is Tayyoga. Similarly, association with the word amha is Mayyoga. Ten exceeded by one is Ekādasa (eleven). This compound is a Tatiyā-tappurisa (instrumental determinative) compound.

Cloth for the purpose of spreading the Kaṭhina is Kaṭhinadussa. It means cloth for the Kaṭhina ceremony. The intention is cloth prepared or brought for the sake of the Kaṭhina robe. Cloth for the sake of a robe is Cīvaradussa. Similarly, the price for a robe (Cīvaramūlya), food for the Saṅgha (Saṅghabhatta), materials for a palace (Pāsādadabba). In this context, the sentence "cloth for the Kaṭhina" (kaṭhināya dussaṃ) is appropriate. Discipline for the sake of the Dhamma is Dhammavinaya. The teachers of the Commentaries establish the definition by virtue of the 'purpose' (tadattha), stating that this Vinaya exists for the sake of the faultless Dhamma (Nibbāna), and not for the sake of worldly existence or enjoyments. Now, to make that 'purpose' clear, I shall speak by way of the Genitive and Dative cases in meanings expressed through plural and singular forms. Thus: food for the sake of guests is Āgantukabhatta.
197:
In the word "yāgubhatta", the meaning is "rice for the sake of gruel" by the power of the dative case (catutthī-vibhatti). In this way, rice for the sake of guests is called "āgantukabhatta", and rice-grains for the sake of gruel are called "yāgutandulā". It should be understood that the meaning of each compound word (samāsa-pada) is formed respectively by the power of the genitive and dative cases. The same applies to "bhattatandulā" (rice-grains for the sake of rice), "gamikabhatta" (rice for the sake of travelers), and so on. This compound is a Dative Determinative Compound (catutthī-tappurisa samāsa).

One who has departed from sexual intercourse is called "methunāpeto". Likewise, "piṇḍapātapāṭikkanto" (one who has returned from the alms-round). Fear caused by the king is called "rājabhaya". Likewise, "corabhaya" (fear of thieves), and so on. In the word "rājato", the suffix "-to" is the ablative case (pañcamī-vibhatti) in the sense of cause (hetu). This method is the same in other words as well. Because of this, the Commentators, keeping the causal sense in mind, made this explanation of the meaning. "Jātibhaya" means fear that arises because of birth (jāti). This method is the same in "rājabhaya" and others. "Attānuvādabhaya" means fear that arises due to blaming oneself repeatedly. "Parānuvādabhaya" means fear that arises due to the blame and censure of others. Thus, in the explanation made by the Teachers, when using the word "bhaya" with the word "uppajjanaka" (arising), those noble Teachers showed the specific action extracted as the scope of the ablative (apādāna). Therefore, we also say, "Fear arising because of the king is rājabhaya." It means fear that arises depending on the king. This method is the same in "corabhaya" and others. This compound is an Ablative Determinative Compound (pañcamī-tappurisa samāsa).

The king's son is called "rājaputto". Likewise, "rājapuriso" (the king's man). The king's slave is called "rājadāso". The son of the king's slave is called "rājadāsaputto". In this way, "rājadāsaputtadhanaṃ" (the wealth of the son of the king's slave) and so on should be taken by the power of mere relation (kevala-sambandha). "Ācariyapūjako" (one who honors the teacher), "maraṇassati" (mindfulness of death), and so on are taken by the power of object relation (kamma-sambandha). "Kāyalahutā" (the state of lightness of body) and so on are taken by the power of state relation (bhāva-sambandha). "Buddharūpaṃ" (the form of the Buddha), "dhanyarāsi" (a heap of grain), and so on are taken by the power of dependent relation (tannissita-sambandha). "Rukkhasākhā" (the branch of a tree), "rukkhamūlaṃ" (the root of a tree), and so on are taken by the power of part-whole relation (avayava-sambandha). "Ayopatto" (an iron bowl), "suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ" (a golden bowl), and so on are taken by the power of modification relation (vikāra-sambandha). "Telakumbho" (a pot of oil) ...
198:
Words like "sappikumbho" (a pot which is the container for ghee) are taken by the power of the relation of being situated there (tatraṭṭhaka-sambandha). "Sasavisāṇaṃ" (hare's horn), "udumbarapupphaṃ" (fig flower), "vañjhāputto" (son of a barren woman), and so on are taken by the power of the relation of that nature (taddhamma-sambandha). "Khapupphaṃ" (sky-flower), "natthiyā bhāvo" (the state of non-existence), and so on are taken by the power of the relation of mere non-existence (asabhāvamatta-sambandha). "Atthiyā bhāvo" (the state of existence) and so on are taken by the power of the relation of existing meaning (vijjamānattha-sambandha).

In this context, according to the method of the Commentaries, "rājapuriso" (king's man) should be understood as a man directed by the king. For it is said in the Commentary: "The aggregates directed by grasping are the grasping-aggregates (upādānakkhandhā), just like a king's man (rājapuriso)." Seeing the Teacher is called "satthāradassanaṃ". Describing the agent is called "kattāraniddeso". Likewise, describing the Teacher is "satthāraniddeso". The daughter of the Sakyan Blessed One is "sakyadhītarā". One who has grown up with his parents is "mātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho", meaning grown up in the presence of his parents. The Genitive Determinative Compound (chatthī-tappurisa) named "Dukkaramagga" is finished.

The front part of the body is called "pubbakāyo". Likewise, the back part of the body is "pacchākāyo". This should be known as the Genitive Determinative Compound named "Durājānamagga", which is spoken of by placing the latter word in the front (pubbanipāta). "Adakkhi" means having seen before. If one asks what was seen, it is a woman, a man, or any phenomenon or matter. If one asks when it was seen, it was seen before. Knowing this connection of meaning, according to usages such as "diṭṭhapubbo tathāgataṃ" (having seen the Tathāgata before), the compound analysis (samāsa-viggaha) should be made as "pubbe diṭṭho diṭṭhapubbo" (one seen before is diṭṭhapubbo).

"This man has seen the Tathāgata before" (tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbo ayaṃ puriso). "This woman has seen the Tathāgata before" (tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbā ayaṃ itthī). "This family has seen the Tathāgata before" (tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ idaṃ kulaṃ).

In this context, the word "diṭṭha" (seen), like the word "dinna" (given) in phrases such as "tassa dinno mayā putto" (the son was given by me to him), mostly occurs in the passive sense (kamma). However, sometimes it also occurs in the active sense (kattu), like the word "dinna" in "dānaṃ dinno devadatto" (Devadatta gives a gift). Because of this, these six great elders—Sabbakāmī Thera, Sāḷha Thera, Revata Thera, Khujjasobhita Thera, Yasa Thera, and Sāṇasambhūta Thera—who performed the Second Council and were also well-known and proficient in the First Council, were co-residents of Ānanda Thera and had seen the Tathāgata before (tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbā). Here, it is seen used in the active sense. Likewise, there are "dhammaṃ sutapubbo" (one who has heard the Dhamma before) and "saggaṃ gatapubbo" (one who has gone to heaven before). In the passive sense, there are "purisena devā diṭṭhapubbā" (gods were seen before by the man), "tena dhammo sutapubbo" (the Dhamma was heard before by him), and "tena disā gatapubbā" (the direction was gone to before by him). Here also, the occurrence of the word "gata" in the passive sense should be known from the Pali text spoken by the Buddha himself: "agatapubbaṃ disaṃ patthayāno sacittaṃ anurakkhe" (one aspiring for the direction never reached before, Nibbāna, should constantly guard his own mind). The Genitive Determinative Compound named "Durājānamagga" is finished.

Perception of form is called "rūpasaññā". Likewise, suffering in Saṃsāra (saṃsāradukkhaṃ), a flower blooming in the forest (vanapupphaṃ), drying in the heat of the sun (ātapasukkhaṃ), cooking in hot coals (aṅgārapakkaṃ), and being bound in prison (cārakabaddho) are Locative Determinative Compounds (sattamī-tappurisa).
199:
"Those Great Elders who chanted (at the Second Council) and were renowned in the (First) Council: Sabbakāmī, Sāḷha, Revata, Khujjasobhita, Yasa, and Sāṇasambhūta. These elders were co-residents (pupils) of the Elder Ānanda and had previously seen the Tathāgata."

In this context, (the term 'diṭṭhapubbā') is found in the agentive sense (kattari). Similarly, there are 'dhammaṃ sutapubbo' (one who has heard the Dhamma before) and 'saggaṃ gatapubbo' (one who has gone to heaven before). In the objective sense (kammani), however, it is: 'diṭṭhapubbā devā purisena' (the gods were previously seen by the man), 'sutapubbo dhammo tena' (the Dhamma was previously heard by him), and 'gatapubbā disā tena' (the direction was previously gone to by him). Here also, by the words of the Buddha himself, "One should constantly guard one's own mind; one who desires the region of Nibbāna which has not been reached before (agata-pubbaṃ)," the occurrence of the word 'gata' in the objective sense is to be understood. The Saṭṭhītappurisa (Genitive Tappurisa) compound 'durājānamaggo' (a path difficult to know) is completed.

'Rūpasaññā' (perception of form) is 'rūpe saññā'. Similarly, 'saṃsāradukkhaṃ' (suffering in saṃsāra), 'vanapupphaṃ' (flower in the forest), 'ātapasukkhaṃ' (dryness in the heat), 'aṅgārapakkaṃ' (cooked on embers), 'cārakabaddho' (bound in prison), and so forth. This is Sattamītappurisa (Locative Tappurisa).

705. When the word 'iti' is elided, a word ending in the nominative case is joined with another word ending in the nominative case; that compound is also designated as Tappurisa. 'So buddhaṃ saraṇagato' (He has gone to the Buddha as a refuge). Here, the analysis of the compound (vigraha) is: 'saraṇam iti gato'. It means he approaches, associates with, serves, or understands the Buddha as "This Blessed One is my refuge." And here, just as 'ājanyaratho' (a chariot joined with thoroughbred horses) and 'pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ' (medicine infused with fermented urine) are Tatiyātappurisa (Instrumental Tappurisa) through the elision of the middle term, so 'saraṇagato' is Paṭhamātappurisa (Nominative Tappurisa) through the elision of the middle term 'iti'. There is no occasion for it to be a Dutiyātappurisa (Accusative Tappurisa) here, because a construction with two objects—as in 'ajaṃ gāmaṃ neti' (he leads the goat to the village) where the objects have different referents—is not desired, and because in 'buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi', the object of the subsequent word is desired in the sense of having the same referent (samanadhikarana), as in "The Buddha is my refuge."
200:
This is also because the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariya) do not desire the subsequent word to be an object when it is intended to have the same referent (samānādhikaraṇa).

706. In another tradition (of the Rūpasiddhi), the nominative is also joined with the genitive. The repetition of the word 'paṭhamā' (nominative) is for the purpose of excluding the elision of 'iti'. In the specific view of the teachers, a word ending in the nominative is joined with a word ending in the genitive; that compound is designated as Tappurisa. 'Aḍḍhapippalī' (half of a long pepper), 'aḍḍhakosātakī' (half of a luffa), 'pubbakāyo' (the front part of the body). This is Paṭhamātappurisa.

Some might say here: "If such a Paṭhamātappurisa exists, then 'sadevako' (together with the devas) should also be a Paṭhamātappurisa." It is not so; because the meaning of another word (anyapadattha) is predominant, it is only a Bahubbīhi, not a Tappurisa. For here, the meaning of the other word is predominant: "That world which exists together with the devas is called 'sadevaka'." In cases like 'aḍḍhapippalī', it should be understood that when 'half of a long pepper' is taken as 'aḍḍhapippalī', it is a Saṭṭhītappurisa.

If that is so, would 'sadevako loko' also be a Tatiyātappurisa when taken as 'sadevaka with the devas'? It would not. Because this 'sadevaka' refers to "that world which exists together with the devas," and thus, because the meaning of the other word is predominant, it is only a Bahubbīhi, not a Tappurisa. Likewise, 'antopāsādaṃ' (inside the palace) and 'upanagaraṃ' (near the city) are Avyayībhāva compounds because the indeclinable meaning is predominant, not Tappurisa.

707. Both of those (Digu and Kammadhāraya) are also designated as Tappurisa. 'Apañcavassaṃ' (not five years), 'asattagodāvaraṃ' (not seven Godāvarī rivers), 'apañcapuli' (not a group of five), 'abrāhmaṇo' (a non-brahmin), 'avasalo' (not an outcast), 'asakyadhītarā' (not a Sakyan princess), 'mātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho' (reared by parents). Here, whether the derivation is "one who is not a Sakyan princess is 'asakyadhītarā'" or "that which is not a Sakyan princess is 'asakyadhītarā'"...
201:
...the definition is stated. These compounds, while remaining in the state of Kammadhāraya or Digu, are called 'Tappurisa' because they are parts of Tappurisa, acting as indicators (jotaka) of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent word over the word 'na' (not). They are not called so by way of exceeding the quality, as in 'rājapūjito' (honored by the king) and so forth. Some teachers, however, name this compound 'Ubhayatappurisa' and, along with this name, desire seven types of Tappurisa starting from Dutiyātappurisa. Since the state of Ubhayatappurisa does not exist for each individual compound in Digu like 'apañcavassaṃ' or Kammadhāraya like 'abrāhmaṇo', that name is not appropriate. This is our preference: briefly, there are three Tappurisas—Sudda-tappurisa, Kammadhāraya-tappurisa, and Digu-tappurisa. In detail, however, there are seven Tappurisas: Paṭhamātappurisa and the six starting from Dutiyātappurisa. What is the benefit of designating them as Tappurisa? The benefit is the completion of the task by the designation 'Tappurisa' according to the rule 'nassattaṃ tappurisabahubbīhīsu'.

708. In the sense of another word (anyapadattha), names are joined. Names are joined in the sense of words ending in nominative and other cases that are external to the words being joined; that compound is designated as Bahubbīhi. He who has many rices (vīhi) is 'Bahubbīhi'. Because of its similarity to the word 'bahubbīhi', this compound is also called 'Bahubbīhi'. Just as the word 'bahubbīhi' resides in the possessor of the quality (substance), so all these compounds reside in the possessor of the quality. Because they reside in the possessor of the quality, they are called 'Bahubbīhi' due to their similarity to the word 'bahubbīhi'. Bahubbīhi is that in which the meaning of another word is predominant. It is of nine types: dvipada, bhinnādhikaraṇa, tipada, nanipātapubbapada, sahapubbapada, upamānapubbapada, saṅkhyobhayapada, disantaraḷattha, and vyatihāralakkhaṇa.

Among them, Dvipada-bahubbīhi occurs in the sense of the six cases starting from the accusative (kamma). Among those six, first in the sense of the accusative: "There are monks who have come to this monastery (saṃghārāma), therefore this monastery is called 'āgatasamaṇa'." Likewise, 'āgatasamaṇā sāvatthī' (Sāvatthī to which monks have come), 'āgatasamaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ' (Jetavana to which monks have come). This Bahubbīhi is called 'atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa'. This is because it is of two kinds.
202:
There are two types of Bahubbīhi compounds: Tagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi and Atagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. Among these, when the analysis (viggaha) is made by a part and the meaning of the external word (aññapadattha), which is the whole, is the meaning of the compound, it is called Tagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. Examples are "lambakaṇṇo" (one with hanging ears) and "samalā akusalā dhammā" (unwholesome states accompanied by stains such as lust, etc.). In the case where the analysis is made by the whole and the whole itself is the meaning of the compound, it is called Atagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. Examples are "pabbatādīni khettāni" (fields bounded by mountains, etc.), "bahudhano" (one with much wealth), and "amalo lokuttaradhammo" (the stainless supramundane Dhamma).

Another method: In a Bahubbīhi where the meaning of the qualifier (visesana) is taken together with the meaning of the external word, it is Tagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. For example, when saying "lambakaṇṇamānaya" (bring the long-eared man), the man is brought along with his long ears. Similarly, when saying "samale akusale dhamme pajahati" (one abandons unwholesome states accompanied by stains), one abandons the unwholesome states along with the stains. However, in a Bahubbīhi where the meaning of the external word is taken alone, excluding the meaning of the qualifier, it is Atagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. For example, when saying "pabbatādīni khettāni kassati" (he plows the fields bounded by mountains, etc.), he plows only the fields and not the mountains. Similarly, when saying "bahudhanamānaya" (bring the man with much wealth), one brings only the man and not the wealth. When saying "amalaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ sacchākāsi" (he realized the stainless supramundane Dhamma), he realized only the supramundane Dhamma and not the stains.

Some teachers, however, thinking that the supramundane Dhamma should be known together with its stainless nature, say that in the phrase "dhammaṃ amalaṃ," the word "amala" is a Tagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi. This view should not be accepted, because stains such as lust are not parts of the supramundane Dhamma. If, however, the expression "sanimmalabhāvo lokuttaradhammo" were used in the sense of "existing together with a stainless nature," then it should be regarded as Tagguna-saṃvijñāna Bahubbīhi.

This monk has conquered the faculties; therefore, he is called "jitindriya" (one with conquered faculties). This Bahubbīhi is Tagguna-saṃvijñāna because the substance called "monk" is taken together with the faculties which are its parts. The designation "monk," etc., arises only in dependence on states such as the faculties. Living with this person is pleasant; therefore, that wise man is called "sukhasaṃvāsa" (one with whom living is pleasant). "Dinnasuṅko rājā" (a king to whom tax is given). "Niggatajano"...
203:
Village. A man with a severed hand, or one whose hand is severed. A district with abundant crops. Other Bahubbīhi compounds should also be applied in the sense of the accusative case and so on. Thus, the two-word Bahubbīhi has been explained in brief.

What is Bhinnādhikaraṇa Bahubbīhi? One who stays for a single night is called "ekarattivāsa." A man who lives with his equals is called "samānavāsa." One who has both signs (both female and male organs) is called "ubhatobyañjanaka." The world that has business at the [right] moment is called "khaṇakicca." In the Pāḷi, it is said: "One who has business only when there is an opportunity." In the Commentary, however, by the power of the intended meaning, it is said: "He is called khaṇakicca because he performs duties at the [right] moment; the meaning is that he performs duties only after obtaining an opportunity." A man with an umbrella in his hand is called "chattapāṇi." One who has an intense desire for giving is called "dānajjhāsaya," and so forth.

What is a three-word Bahubbīhi? Those who have attained success through effort are called "parakkamādhigatasampadā," referring to Great Men (mahāpurisa). Likewise, one who has wealth acquired righteously (dhammādhigatabhoga). One who has removed the hand from the bowl is called "oṇitapattapāṇi." One whose body is [full] like the front half of a lion is called "sīhapubbaddhakāya." A forest that has many rutting elephants is called "mattabahumātaṅga," and so forth.

What is a Bahubbīhi with the particle 'na' as the first member? Because there is no one equal to that Blessed One, He is called "asama" (the peerless). Because there is no communal living with that person, he is called "asaṃvāsa." Because there is no wisdom in this district, it is called an "abuddhika" district, and so forth.

A Bahubbīhi with the word 'saha' as the first member is found in the sense of the nominative case. What is it? That state which exists together with a cause is called "sahetuka."
204:
In the Pali, it is 'sahetu'. However, in the Commentary, it says: 'That Blessed One [knows] this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans.' In this context, the teachers did not employ the relative-demonstrative pronouns 'yaṃ-taṃ' because the gender (liṅga) was not clearly evident in relation to the word 'world' (loka) and so forth. Indeed, those teachers formulated the definition (nibbacana) without the words 'yaṃ-taṃ', such as: 'The world together with devas is sadevaka.' However, since the word 'saha' (together with) does not denote a substance (dabba), it cannot clearly manifest the gender. Therefore, to clarify the gender and remove doubt for the listeners, we shall state the determination by employing the words 'yaṃ-taṃ'. Whatever world exists together with devas, that world is called 'sadevaka'. In this manner, one should understand 'samāraka' and so forth. Whatever generation exists together with recluses and brahmins, that generation is called 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī'.

Another method: Whatever earth exists together with devas, that earth is called 'sadevikā'. What is that earth? It is simply the earth (pathavī). In this manner, an assembly with a king is 'sarājikā parisā'; a chief queen with a king is 'sarājikā mahādevī'. Whatever tree is uprooted together with its roots is 'samūluddhaṭo'. Whatever mind is accompanied by stinginess is 'samaccheraṃ'. These examples should be understood either by changing 'saha' to 'sa' or by the elision of the letter 'ha'. In the form where it remains as originally placed, it should be understood thus: Whatever thief is caught with stolen goods is 'sahoḍḍho'. Lamentation and grief accompanied by stinginess are 'sahamaccharā', and so forth.

A compound with a comparison as the first member (upamānapubbapada) is found in the sense of the nominative case and the genitive case. In such instances, the words 'iva' or 'viya' (like/as) are also used to establish the relationship between the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameyya). Because of the symmetry of his physical proportions, whatever prince is round like a banyan tree is 'nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo'. Whatever cloth is white like a conch shell is 'saṅkhapaṇḍaraṃ'. Because it is said, 'This person is brave like a crow,' he is called 'kākasūro'. In this context, there is also another meaning: 'Because he is braver than a crow, he is called kākasūro.' In this sense...
205:
...it is an ablative tatpurisa compound (pañcamītappurisa). Because the Blessed One sees the ultimate truth (paramattha), He has become like an eye for all; therefore, He is called 'cakkhubhūto' (one who has become an eye). There is also another meaning: because He has reached the eye consisting of wisdom, He is 'cakkhubhūto'. In this sense, it is an accusative tatpurisa compound (dutiyātappurisa). Thus, the upamānapubbapada-bahubbīhi compound is found in the nominative sense. In the genitive sense: the Blessed One whose complexion is like the color of gold is 'suvaṇṇavaṇṇo'. Likewise, there are 'nāgagati', 'sīhagati', 'nāgavikkamo', and 'sīhahanu'. Because He has calves like those of an antelope (eṇī), He is called 'eṇijaṅgho'. Likewise, there is 'usabhakkhandho'. Because He has a voice endowed with eight factors like the voice of Brahmā, He is called 'brahmassaro'. Thus, the upamānapubbapada-bahubbīhi compound is found in the genitive sense.

A compound with numbers on both sides (saṅkhyobhayapada) is seen in the sense of the word 'vā' (or). For example: bowls that are either two or three are 'dittipattā'. Staying for either two days or three days is 'dvīhatīhaṃ'. Words that are either five or six are 'chappañcavācā'. Likewise, there are 'sattaṭṭhamāsā' and 'ekayojanadviyojanāni'. Thus, a compound with numbers on both sides is seen in the sense of the word 'vā'. In this context, the sense of the word 'vā' is indeed the external meaning (aññapadattha). Therefore, because the external meaning is predominant, this compound is called 'bahubbīhi'.

The example showing the sense of the interval between directions: the direction that is the interval between the East and the South is 'pubbadakkhiṇā'; it is called an intermediate direction (vidisā). Likewise, there are 'pubbuttara', 'aparadakkhiṇā', and 'pacchimuttara'.

The example characterized by reciprocal action (byatihāra): this fight proceeds by grabbing each other's hair; therefore, it is called 'kesākesī'. This fight proceeds by striking each other with sticks; therefore, it is called 'daṇḍādaṇḍီ'. This is the bahubbīhi compound in the nominative sense.
206:
Now, in order to produce supreme proficiency for the wise in the Dispensation (Sāsana), I shall describe the tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compounds that are embedded within dvanda, kammadhāraya, etc., along with bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi.

Sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā, tāpasā. (Ascetics whose food consists of naturally fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water.) A leaf, a flower, and a fruit are called paṇṇapupphaphalāni. Those that have fallen by themselves are called sayaṃpatitāni. Those leaves, flowers, and fruits that have fallen by themselves are called sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalāni. Wind and water are called vāyutoyāni. Naturally fallen leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as wind and water, are called sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāni. Only those things are the food for certain ascetics; those ascetics are called sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā. This is a tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi with dvanda and kammadhāraya embedded within. Alternatively, those ascetics for whom there is food consisting of naturally fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water are called sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā. This is a bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi.

Nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu. (A mountain having plateaus fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees.) Trees of various kinds are called nānādumā. Those that have fallen from those various trees are called nānādumapatitāni. Flowers that have fallen from those various trees are called nānādumapatitapupphāni. Those that are made fragrant by those flowers are called nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā. A mountain that has level plateaus (sānu) fragrant with such flowers is called nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu. This is a tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi with kammadhāraya and tappurisa embedded within. Alternatively, fragrant plateaus are called vāsitasānū. Although the word vāsita is dependent (sāpekkha) on the word puppha, it forms a compound because it conveys the meaning. A mountain that has plateaus fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees is called nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu. This is a bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi.

Byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo. (A mountain whose peak is touched by the raindrops of hanging clouds.) A hanging cloud is called byālambambudharo. The raindrops of that cloud are called byālambambudharabindūni. That which is touched (kissed) by those raindrops is called byālambambudharabinducumbito. A mountain that has such a peak is called byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo. This is called a tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi with kammadhāraya and tappurisa embedded within. Alternatively...
207:
A peak that is touched is called cumbitakūṭa. Although it is dependent (on the word bindu), it forms a compound because it has the power to convey the meaning. A mountain that has a peak touched by the raindrops of hanging clouds is called byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo. This is a bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compound.

Amitabalaparakkamajuti. Those that are immeasurable are called amita. Strength, effort, and radiance are called balaparakkamajutiyo. The Blessed One who possesses immeasurable strength, effort, and radiance is called amitabalaparakkamajuti. This is a tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compound contained within kammadhāraya and dvanda. Hereafter, the resolution of compounds (viggraha) should be performed in this manner for compound words.

(The Buddha) who has a full chest, shoulders, and arms. This is a dvanda-gabbha tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compound. A woman who has full cheeks, face, breasts, thighs, and hips. This is also a dvanda-gabbha tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compound. The Blessed One whose feet are touched by the gems set in the crests of the crowns of the noble devas, asuras, garuḍas, humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas. This is a dvanda-kammadhāraya-tappurisa-gabbha tulyādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi compound.
