(The Buddha) who has an immeasurable and solid body; (The Buddha) who has attained immeasurable strength and effort; (A forest) having blooming flowers touched by groups of intoxicated bees; (A mountain) having valleys beautified by flowers fallen from various trees and grasses; the army of Māra holding various pestles, ploughshares, mountains, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and spears in their hands, and so forth—all these should be resolved according to the method.

Because there is no end or limit to that (concept of space), it is called ananta (infinite). Infinite space is called ākāsānanta. Ākāsānanta itself is called ākāsānañca. That ākāsānañca is called ākāsānañcāyatana because it is the base (āyatana) in the sense of a dwelling place for the meditative absorption (jhāna) along with its associated states, like the celestial abode for the devas. This is a bahubbīhi, kammadhāraya-gabbha bahubbīhi compound. In this context, just as bhisakya is the same as bhesajja, so ākāsānanta is the same as ākāsānañca. It is formed by changing the letter 'ta' to 'ca' before a conjunct. Because there is no end to that (consciousness), it is called ananta. Ananta itself is called ānañca. Without saying viññāṇānañca for infinite consciousness...
208: It is called 'Viññāṇañca'. This is because the word viññāṇañca is a rūḷhī term (a term established by usage). That viññāṇañca is called Viññāṇañcāyatana because it is the base (āyatana) for the meditative absorption (jhāna) along with its associated states, in the sense of being a dwelling place, like the divine abode of the gods. This is also a bahubbīhi compound containing a kammadhāraya within a bahubbīhi. Here, by the phrase 'rūḷhī-saddo', it is shown that the word viññāṇañca is established (nirūḷha) in the meaning of the term 'viññāṇānañca'. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: the aforementioned consciousness is perceived (añciyati) or taken as an object (ālambiyati) by the second formless jhāna in the manner described; thus it is 'Viññāṇañca'. The Blessed One for whom seven days have passed since his parinibbāna is called 'Sattāhaparinibbuta'. This compound is a bahubbīhi compound known as bāhirattha (having an external meaning). For in this case, the second member (uttarapada) is in the same grammatical relation (samānādhikaraṇa) with another word (aññapada) other than the word being approached. The other word (aññapada) also draws that second member and, by being in the same grammatical relation, becomes connected with it; therefore, this compound is called 'bāhirattha'. A bahubbīhi that is otherwise is called abāhirattha. Or rather, every bahubbīhi compound is called bāhirattha because it must be understood through the meaning of another word (aññapadattha). However, compounds such as dvanda are called abāhirattha because their meaning does not go outside [the members]. The Blessed One for whom it has not been long since his parinibbāna is called 'Aciraparinibbuta'. Similarly, there is 'Acirapabbajita'. Alternatively, just as in the word 'ṭhitavā', the action of standing (ṭhāna) is called 'ṭhita', so too here, the action of going forth (pabbajana) is called 'pabbajita'. Therefore, the analysis (viggaha) should be: he whose going forth was not long ago is 'Acirapabbajita'. One is called 'pakkanta' because he has departed. He for whom it has not been long since he departed is called 'Acirapakkanta'. Alternatively, as in the phrase 'This is their footprint (padakkanta), like that of elephants on a mountain,' where the word 'padakkanta' occurs in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) meaning the act of treading (padakkamana), so too, keeping in mind the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) where the act of departing (pakkamana) is called 'pakkanta', the departing which was not long ago...
209:
...for that person, there is a departing not long ago"—thus the compound *acirapakkanta* should be formed. In this way, the word *acirapakkanta* is both a *bāhirattha* compound and an *abāhirattha* compound. This method should be applied to other terms as well, as appropriate.

He who has such a name is called *itthannāma*. It means a man of such a name. She who has such a name is called *itthannāmā*. It means a woman of such a name. Similarly: a clan (*kula*) of such a name; "he has such a name" is *evaṃnāma* or *evaṃnāmaka*; of such a lineage (*evaṃgotta*); of such a complexion (*evaṃvaṇṇa*); of such food (*evaṃāhāra*); of such a lifespan (*evaṃāyupariyanta*); of such conduct (*evaṃācāra*); of such fame (*evaṃsiloka*). A man who has such food is *yathānno puriso*. A deity who has such food is *yathānnā devatā*. A man who has his mother as his deity (object of devotion) is *mātudevatā puriso*. One who has virtue of various kinds is *taṃtaṃvidho sīlavā*. One who has virtue of that kind is *tathāvidho sīlavā*. Of the same nature (*sarūpa*); of whatever nature (*yathārūpa*); of that nature (*tathārūpa*); of such nature (*evarūpa*).

He for whom there is a coming according to the truth is *tathāgata*. Likewise, *sugata*. Other terms should be applied in this way. For that king, it has been one month since he was consecrated—thus he is *ekamāsābhisitta*. For that *Āsāḷhī* (full moon), one month has passed—thus *māsagatā Āsāḷhī*. A child for whom it has been one month since birth is *māsajāta*. Likewise, one year old is *saṃvaccharajāta*. All *bahubbīhi* compounds other than *bāhirattha-bahubbīhi* should be known as *abāhirattha*.

He in whom desire has arisen is *chandajāta*. Likewise: one in whom effort has arisen (*ussukkajāta*); one in whom joy and gladness have arisen (*pītisomanassajāta*); one who has well-arisen joy and gladness (*sañjātapītisomanassa*). He whose hands are cut off is *hatthacchinna* or *chinnahattha*. However, in the Blessed One's teaching, words like *chinna* and *jāta* usually become the second member (*uttarapada*) when forming a compound. Words like *paripuṇṇa* and *nipphanna* are always the first member (*pubbapada*). For example:
210:
Words such as "Paripuṇṇavīsativasso" (one who has completed twenty years) and "Nipphannasaṅkappo" (one whose intention is accomplished) are found. That which has a half to complete the eighth is called "aḍḍhaṭṭhamāni" (seven and a half). For that elephant, the measure of seven and a half cubits is its height; therefore, it is called "aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratano" (an elephant seven and a half cubits tall). This is the Bahubbīhi compound known as Dukkaramagga (the difficult-to-form path).

Similarly, in the sentence "The monk enters the village for alms, himself being the fourth," for that monk who is the fourth along with three other monks, he is called "Attacatuttho" (himself as the fourth). Or, he who completes the fourth position for those three is called "Attacatuttho." This is also the Dukkaramagga. Other words should also be applied in this manner.

Because of the meaning "I am the island (refuge) of these people," they are called "Maṃdīpā" (those who have me as their island). This is the Bahubbīhi compound known as Durājānamagga (the difficult-to-understand path). Similarly, because of the meaning "I am the shelter of these people," they are called "Maṃleṇā." Because of the meaning "I am the resort of these people," they are called "Maṃpaṭisaraṇā." Because of the meaning "I am the object of dedication for this Saṅgha," it is called "Mamuddesiko" (the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha dedicated to me). Because of the meaning "The Blessed One is the root of these teachings," they are called "Bhagavaṃmūlakā" (teachings rooted in the Blessed One). In this manner, there is also "Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā" (teachings resorting to the Blessed One).

Mother and father are called "Mātāpitaro." For one who has no mother and father, he is called "Nimmātāpitaro" (a man without parents). There is also "Nimmātāpitarā" (a girl without parents). For one who has a father the same as this man, he is called "Ekapitero" (a man having the same father). There is also "Ekapitarā" (a woman having the same father). For an action that has a single doer (agent), it is called "Ekakattāraṃ" (an action with one agent). In this manner, there is also "Bahukattāraṃ" (an action with many agents). For one who has two teachers, he is called "Dvisatthāro" (a man with two teachers). There are also "Dvisatthāra" (a woman with two teachers) and "Dvisatthāraṃ" (a family with two teachers).

For one who has respect for the Teacher, he is called "Satthāgaru." This is a Lutta-samāsa (elided compound) where the case ending is dropped. In the Aṅguttara Pali, it is found as "Satthāgaru dhammagaru." If it is asked, "Venerable sir, is this not an Alutta-samāsa (non-elided compound) like 'Gavaṃpati' and others?", the answer is no. This is because it is an elided compound like "Mātāpitaro" and others. If it is asked, "Venerable sir, should it not be the reading 'Satthugaru'?", the answer is no. This is because the meaning must be taken according to the non-compound sentence structure. The Durājānamagga Bahubbīhi is completed.
211:
Now, for the sake of generating supreme proficiency for the wise, the two-syllable Bahubbīhi is spoken. He who has good wisdom or good splendor is called "Sudhī." If the analysis is "good wisdom is sudhī," it becomes a Kammadhāraya compound. There are also compounds with two meanings. He who has a good wife is called "Sudo." It means one with a good wife. One with a despised wife is called "Kudo." He who has good wealth is called "Suso." It means one with good wealth. One with a despised wealth is called "Kuso." "Kaṃ" refers to happiness. Because it is the opposite of that happiness, that which is not happiness is "Akaṃ," meaning suffering. Because there is no suffering (akaṃ) in this place, it is called "Nāko," referring to heaven. Other two-syllable Bahubbīhi compounds should also be applied. Three-syllable Bahubbīhi compounds are such as "Sudāro," "Kudāro," etc. Compounds with four syllables and more are well-known. To complete the syllables of a verse (pāda), a Bahubbīhi compound with the syllable "ve" in the middle is also seen, as in "Vuṭṭhiveparamā sarā." With the meaning that for those lakes and rivers, rain alone is the highest measure, it becomes the compound "Vuṭṭhiveparamā." A Bahubbīhi compound with the syllable "eva" in the middle is also seen. With the meaning that he alone is the foremost for this person, it becomes "Etāvaparamo." The Pali is found: "The monk who has reached the further shore would have him (Sāriputta) as the foremost."

Taking the methods from the scriptures and so forth,
For the expansion of the Sasana,
I have extensively elaborated this Bahubbīhi compound.

What is the benefit of the name "Bahubbīhi"? In the Bahubbīhi compound, it serves the purpose of usage in discourse and the completion of grammatical formation.

## 709. A collection of various nouns having the same case ending is called a Dvanda compound.

Whether by gender or by number, the collection of many words associated with one of the eight case endings, which reaches the state of being a single word through the elision of case endings, is called Dvanda. In the Niruttipiṭaka, it is also said: "How does a Dvanda occur? Dvanda is the name for two words having the same case ending but different genders, where the preceding word has fewer syllables and the following word has either an equal or a greater number of syllables..."
212:
It is said, "It is called Dvandva (copulative compound) because it reaches a state of union in a single term." In this context, taking the meanings of the word 'ca' (and) known as itaretarayoga and samāhāra, the formation of a single term through the elision of case endings is called "samuccaya" (aggregation).

In truth, samuccaya means grouping together. This samuccaya is of four types according to meaning: kevalasamuccaya, anvācaya, itaretarayoga, and samāhāra. Among these four, compounds do not form in kevalasamuccaya and anvācaya because they depend on a verb and because the nouns do not have a mutually connected meaning. For example: "Cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca, paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ adāsi" (He gave robes, alms-food, requisites, and bedding); "Dānañca dehi, sīlañca rakkhāhi" (Give gifts and guard virtue).

However, in itaretarayoga and samāhāra, compounds do form because the nouns have mutually connected meanings. Since a Dvandva compound cannot exist with only a single word but requires two or more, the state of becoming non-dual (a single term) through the connection of case endings of at least two words is called Dvandva. It is called Dvandva because pairs of words reach a state of union together. That Dvandva is a compound where the meanings of both members are primary (ubhayapadatthappadhāna).

If the meanings of both members are primary, how can there be a single term? It is said: Since words can occur in meanings such as 'similarity' (sadisa), etc., and because words can indicate two meanings at the same moment, they can exist as a single term. This indication of two meanings is specifically the domain of the Dvandva compound. Just as the root 'bhū' indicates meanings like 'experience' (anubhava) or 'defeat' (abhibhava) only when combined with prefixes like anu or abhi and not alone, so too in words like "gavassakaṃ", words like "go" (cow) indicate two meanings only when combined with other words like "assa" (horse). A single word cannot indicate two meanings. Therefore, it should be understood that this is the domain of the Dvandva compound and not applicable everywhere.

When Sāriputto ca Moggallāno ca are combined, it becomes "Sāriputtamoggallānā". However, when one intends to use it in reference to the word "yuga" (pair), usages such as "Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ" (the pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna) occur. When samaṇa (ascetic) and brāhmaṇa (brahmin) are combined, it becomes "samaṇabrāhmaṇā". Whether it is many ascetics and many brahmins, one ascetic and many brahmins, or many ascetics and one brahmin, it remains "samaṇabrāhmaṇā".
213:
In such instances as "a monk and brahmins" or "monks and a brahmin" or "a monk and a brahmin", four types of definitions (nibbacana) should be made according to the logical fitness of the meaning. The eye and the ear are called "cakkhusotaṃ". What is the benefit of designating it as a Dvandva compound? The benefit is the usage and the accomplishment of the grammatical function in the domain of Dvandva compounds.

710. When followed by a term of the same grammatical relation (tulyādhikaraṇa), the substitution of 'mahā' occurs in place of the words 'mahanta' and 'mahita'. He is a man who is great due to virtues such as morality, etc., and he is that man—thus "Mahāpurisa" (Great Man). He is a man who is honored by people, and he is that man—thus "Mahāpurisa" (Honored Man). Because of being the chief among all queens, she is a queen who is great, and she is that queen—thus "Mahādevī"; or, because she is a queen honored by the people—"Mahādevī". Because it is the cause for attaining the noble Omniscient Wisdom, it is a Bodhi that is great, and it is that Bodhi—or, because it is a Bodhi tree honored by the people—"Mahābodhi". Because of the greatness of the pond, it is a lotus grove that is great—thus "Mahāpadumavanaṃ", and so forth.

711. Also in a Tappurisa compound, the substitution of 'mahā' occurs in place of those words 'mahanta' and 'mahita'. In accordance with the Dhamma heard, the Bodhi of the great or honored Buddha is called "Mahābodhi". One who is attached to the great Omniscient Wisdom is called "Mahāsatta". However, if the definition is "he is a being who is great", then it is a Kammadhāraya compound.

712. The substitution of 'mahā' occurs in place of the word 'mahanta'. The repeated mention of 'mahanta' is to prevent the restriction to Tappurisa and Tulyādhikaraṇa (Kammadhāraya) compounds. The substitution of 'mahā' occurs even in the context of an analytical sentence (vyāsa) of the word 'mahanta'. "Lay follower, your renunciation (pariccāga) is indeed great (mahā)". "The kingship of Bārāṇasī is indeed great". "A great army is seen".
214: 713. In compounds, in some places, the word 'mahanta' is substituted with 'maha'. Examples include: a man of great strength (mahabbalo puriso), virtue of great fruit (mahapphalaṃ sīlaṃ), a woman of great wealth (mahaddhanā itthī), and great fear (mahabbhayaṃ). Why is 'kvaci' (in some places) said? Because in cases like mahāphalaṃ, mahābalaṃ, mahādhanā, a man of great strength (mahābalော puriso), and a householder of great wealth (mahādhanော gahapati), the substitution to 'maha' does not occur, and it remains as 'mahā'. 714. If the preceding word in a coordinate compound (tulyādhikaraṇa) stands in the feminine gender and is a word that can also be expressed in masculine or neuter genders (bhāsitapunnapuṃsaka), then that word should be regarded as masculine or neuter as appropriate. According to the method of this Dispensation, when there is a preceding word in a coordinate compound standing in the feminine gender, if that feminine-expressing word can also be expressed in masculine and neuter genders, it should be seen (regarded) as masculine or neuter as appropriate. The path which has pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā) is the path called 'sukhapaṭipado'. Similarly, there is 'dukkhapaṭipado'. Alternatively, the jhana of the earth-kasina which has painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā) is called 'dukkhapaṭipadaṃ'. Similarly, there is 'dandhābhiññaṃ sukhapaṭipadaṃ'. One who has a painful livelihood (dukkhā jīvikā) is called 'dukkhajīviko'. A man who has long calves (dīghā jaṅghā) is a man called 'dīghajaṅgho'. A family (kula) that has long calves is a family called 'dīghajaṅghaṃ'. Similarly, there are: a man with a good wife (kalyāṇabhariyo puriso), men with good wives (kalyāṇabhariyā purisā), a family with a good wife (kalyāṇabhariyaṃ kulaṃ), and families with good wives (kalyāṇabhariyāni kulāni). One who has great wisdom (mahatī paññā) is called 'mahāpañño'. Or else, because the word 'mahā' is seen in the feminine gender in the Pāli Canon as "senā padissate mahā" (the army is seen as great), the analysis for one who has great wisdom is made as 'mahāpañño'. Similarly, there is 'mahāpaññaṃ kulaṃ'. Why is 'itthivācako' (feminine-expressing) said? In cases like a man whose wealth is wisdom (paññādhanော puriso), a man whose jewel is wisdom (paññāratanော puriso), and a family whose wealth is faith (saddhādhanāṃ kulaṃ), although there is a preceding word in a coordinate compound standing in the feminine gender and the following words are masculine or neuter, there is no transfer to masculine or neuter status because they are not feminine-expressing (itthivācaka). This is because in this context...
215:
The masculine or neuter status of subsequent members is known only through their proximity to another word.

Why is it said "bhāsitapunna-pumsaka" (previously masculine or neuter)? Examples are: "a long-legged woman" (dīghajaṅghā itthī), "a woman of great wisdom" (pahūtapaññā nārī). In these examples, although there is a prior member that is co-referential (tulyādhikaraṇa) occurring in the feminine, and although the subsequent members are feminine, the extension (atidesa) of masculine or neuter status does not occur because those subsequent members do not have a masculine or neuter form expressed in the sentence. Here, the fact that the subsequent members do not express masculine or neuter status is known only through their proximity to another word in the feminine.

Why is it said "yathārahaṃ" (as appropriate)? Examples are: "a district with many rivers" (bahunadiko janapado), "a man with many female slaves" (bahudāsiko puriso), "a family with many girls" (bahukumārikaṃ kulaṃ), "a royal capital with many rivers" (bahunadikā rājadhānī). In this text, as in the Bahubbīhi compound, the meaning is taken as: a feminine word that has a masculine form expressing the meaning of another word in the sentence is called bhāsitapumā; a feminine word that has a neuter form expressing the meaning of another word in the sentence is called bhāsitanapuṃsakā. In that rule, the word "thī" refers to a feminine word. Otherwise, one should not say "bhāsitapunna-pumsaka". In this text, the absence of a feminine suffix in the subsequent member is intended.

## 715. Matantare itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthipumāva ce ti pubbapade.

In the opinion of some teachers, if there is a feminine word that has a previously expressed masculine form, followed by a co-referential subsequent member in the feminine, that word should be regarded as masculine; thus, the absence of a feminine suffix in the prior member is intended.

Example: "a long-legged man" (dīghajaṅgho puriso). Why is it said "itthiyaṃ" (in the feminine)? Example: "one whose wealth is patience" (khamādhano). Here, although the subsequent member is co-referential, the extension of masculine status does not occur because that subsequent member does not occur in the feminine, and the prior member did not have a previously expressed masculine form. Thus, this is a counter-example (paccudāharaṇa) lacking two factors. A counter-example should ideally lack only one factor.

Why is it said "bhāsitapumā"? Examples: "one who has faith as his lead" (saddhādhuro), "one whose nature is faith" (saddhāpakatiko), "one whose nature is wisdom" (paññāpakatiko), "one whose purity is through wisdom" (paññāvisuddhiko). Why is it said "tulyādhikaraṇe" (in co-reference)? Examples: "one who is devoted to a nun" (samaṇibhattiko), "one who is devoted to a girl" (kumāribhattiko).
216:
Kumāribhatti. This masculine-like transformation (pumbhāvātidesa) occurs only in the preceding member of a compound. Because it occurs only in the preceding member, this masculine-like transformation does not take place in these examples: bahudāsiko puriso (a man who has many slave-women), bahukumārikaṃ kulaṃ (a family that has many maidens)—so say some teachers.

## 716. Kammadhāraye ca pubbabhāsitapumā pumāva.
In a Kammadhāraya compound, when there is a following member (uttarapada) in the feminine gender and in apposition (tulyādhikaraṇa), a word that was previously spoken as masculine but now expresses the feminine should be regarded as masculine, as appropriate.

Because of the meaning "That woman is both a Brahmin and a girl," it becomes Brāhmaṇadārikā (a Brahmin girl). Similarly, Vessadārikā (a Vessa girl), Suddadārikā (a Sudda girl). Because of the meaning "That woman is both a princess and a maiden," it becomes Khattiyakaññā (a Khattiya maiden), and so on.

Why is it said "itthiyaṃ" (in the feminine)? Consider: paññāratanaṃ (the jewel of wisdom), samaṇīpadumaṃ (a nun who is like a lotus). In these cases, although they are Kammadhāraya compounds and there is a following member in apposition, the masculine-like transformation does not occur because these words are fixed in their respective genders.

Why is it said "bhāsitapumā" (previously spoken as masculine)? Consider: Gaṅgānadī (the River Ganges), taṇhānadī (the river of craving). In these cases, although they are Kammadhāraya compounds and there are following members in apposition, the removal of the feminine suffix (nivatti) in the preceding member does not occur because words like Gaṅgā are inherently feminine, and the word nadī is not a word that was previously spoken as masculine.

In the Kaccāyana treatise, however, to the question "Why bhāsitapumā?", the example Khattiyabandhudārikā is given, stating that the feminine suffix in the following member is not removed.

Why is it said "yathārahaṃ" (as appropriate)? Consider: Candādevī (Queen Candā), Nandādevī (Queen Nandā). Here, although they are Kammadhāraya compounds and there are following members in apposition, and although words like Canda are seen in the masculine gender as in "Candakumāro, Nandakumāro, Nandatthero," the words Candā etc. in the terms Candādevī etc. are not fixed feminine words. Nevertheless, in accordance with scriptural usage (sāsanānurūpa), the word "yathārahaṃ" is used, and thus the feminine suffix in the preceding member of terms like Candādevī is not removed. In some places, however, the feminine suffix is removed, resulting in "Nandadevī" and "Candadevī," while in other places it is not removed, resulting in "Nandādevī" and "Candādevī." Therefore, we have said "yathārahaṃ."

Alternatively, the terms "Nandādevī" and "Candādevī" are not compounds (samāsa) but are analytical expressions (vyāsa). Indeed, this is seen in the Buddha's teachings.
217:
In many Pali passages, uncompounded (vyāsa) terms such as "paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ" and "paṭhamassa jhānassa, dutiyassa jhānassa" are found. At other times, compounded terms like "paṭhamajjhānaṃ, dutiyajjhānaṃ" are also seen. Therefore, terms like "Nandā devī, Candā devī" should be understood as uncompounded phrases. Their status as uncompounded phrases is extremely clear from verses and prose such as:

"If you should cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose; even so, King Videha will have the hands, feet, ears, and nose of Queen Nandā cut off."

This is very evident from such verses and prose. In the case of being uncompounded phrases, the declension (padamālā) is as follows: Nandā devī (Queen Nandā - Nom.), Nandāṃ deviṃ (Queen Nandā - Acc.), Nandāya deviyā (by/of/in Queen Nandā), Nandāyaṃ deviyaṃ (in Queen Nandā). In the case of being compounds, however, it would be: Nandādevī, Nandādeviṃ, Nandādeviyā, Nandādeviyaṃ; and also Nandadevī, Nandadeviṃ, Nandadeviyā, Nandadeviyaṃ. Among these three types of declension, the first and the third should be accepted as essential, as they mostly conform to the methods of the Pali language. In this treatise, however, in this compound, the meaning of "bhāsitapumā" is taken as: that woman for whom the masculine form was spoken first.

Here is the explanation: For a woman who is the relatee (sambandhī), the related masculine form was spoken either by the grammarians (akkharacintaka) or by the general public. How was it spoken by the grammarians? Prior to feminine terms such as "Brāhmaṇī, Khattiyī, Khattiya, Vessī, Suddī, Caṇḍālī," the masculine was first spoken as "Brāhmaṇo, Khattiyo, Vesso," etc. After that, those words with their case endings were made into words without case endings and placed in their original form (pakati) as "Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, Vessa," etc. Then, keeping in mind the meaning such as "The wife of a Khattiya is a Khattiyā, the wife of a Brahmin is a Brāhmaṇī," the suffixes -ā and -ī were applied as appropriate...
218:
The feminine gender is established later in words such as khattiyā, khattiyī, brāhmaṇī, and vessī. In this way, the grammarians first spoke of the masculine gender.

If it is asked how the common people of the world first spoke of the masculine gender: At the beginning of the first aeon (kappa), there was neither the male gender nor the female gender. To show this absence, it is said: "In the former time, at the beginning of the aeon, which woman was whose wife? In the past, the mind alone produced human beings." As those humans gradually came into existence and gazed intently at one another, the female and male genders appeared on the very same day, and the terms "woman" and "man" came into use. Among those genders, it should be understood that the female gender appeared first, and the male gender appeared thereafter. To show this, it is said in the Haṃsa Jātaka: "In the world, women of great benefit first arose." In this context, the Commentary states the first appearance of the female gender.

Even though this is so, due to the diversity of kamma, among the four classes such as the ruling class (khattiya) and the priestly class (brāhmaṇa) designated by the people, the term for a noblewoman (khattiyā) was designated based on the nobleman (khattiya), and the term for a priestess (brāhmaṇī) etc., was designated based on the priest (brāhmaṇa) etc. Thus, because words like khattiyā and brāhmaṇī have a previously spoken masculine form, it is appropriate to say that the common people first spoke of the masculine gender. Considering these two reasons, we have stated this rule: "Kammadhāraye ca pubbe bhāsitapumā pumā vā" (In a kammadhāraya compound, that which was previously spoken as masculine remains masculine), qualifying it with the word pubbe (previously).

In this place, this point should also be noted: among the words dārako and dārikā, the word dārikā is a word that always denotes the feminine gender. It is not like the word dāsī in "dāsī, dāso, dovāriko puriso, dovārikā itthī," which does not always denote the feminine gender. This is because the word dārikā has the previously spoken masculine form dāraka. Because the masculine form was not previously spoken for dāsī and kumārikā. Here, we shall explain the difference between the two rules (suttas) based on the instructions received from wise men who know the traditional lineage of decisions.
219:
This meaning should be noted because the masculine gender was not spoken. Here, we shall explain the difference between the two rules, like oil and water, based on the instructions received from wise men who know the traditional lineage of decisions. In a bahubbīhi compound, the fact that the masculine etc. was spoken in the subsequent feminine gender is stated only in relation to the aññapada (external referent). However, in the compound called kammadhāraya, referring to the fact that the masculine was previously spoken, the wise should perform the function of making the feminine in the preceding member similar to the masculine.

717. Nassattaṃ tappurisabahubbīhīsu. In tappurisa and bahubbīhi compounds, the sound na becomes a when followed by a subsequent member. Examples: abrāhmaṇo (one who is not a brahmin), anuttaro (one who has no superior).

718. Sare an. In tappurisa and bahubbīhi compounds, the entire word na becomes an when followed by a vowel. Examples: na asso = anasso (a donkey, not a horse), anantaṃ ñāṇaṃ (infinite knowledge).

719. Kussa kad. In tappurisa and bahubbīhi compounds, the particle ku becomes kad when followed by a vowel. Examples: jigucchaṃ annaṃ = kadannaṃ (contemptible food), jigucchaṃ asanaṃ = kadasanaṃ (contemptible meal), kucchitaṃ annaṃ etassāti kadanno (one who has contemptible food); likewise kadasano (one who has a contemptible meal). Why is it said "when followed by a vowel"? It is for the purpose of knowing that the change to kad does not occur in places like kudārā janā (people who have contemptible wives).

720. Appatthe kā. The particle ku becomes kā in the sense of "a little" or "small." Examples: kālavaṇaṃ (a little salt or food with a little salt), kāpupphaṃ (a little flower, a small flower, or a forest with few flowers).

721. Kvaci kucchitatthe ca. In the sense of "contemptible," the particle ku sometimes becomes kā. Examples: kāpuriso or kupuriso (a contemptible man).

722. Samāsantagatānamanto avaṇṇikārukārattaṃ. The endings of nouns that have reached the end of a compound sometimes change to a, ā, i, or u. Examples: sabbesaṃ sakhā = sabbasakho (friend of all). Or, because all people are friends to that Blessed One, He is called sabbasakho. Devānaṃ rājā = devarājo (king of gods). Likewise, devasakho (friend of gods). He who has developed his mind is called bhāvitatto (bhāvitacitta - one with a developed mind). This is the meaning of bhāvitacitta. Not (na)...
220:
Because evil (akusala) does not exist for that person, he is called 'Nāga'. It means 'Nāga' because he does not commit evil. In this context, an Arahant is called 'Nāga'. Because the four truths are brought together, it is called 'Catusacca' (the collection of the four truths). Examples include: five days (Pañcāha), five cows (Pañcagava), umbrella and sandals (Chattupāhana), and near the autumn season (Upasarada).

One who has wide eyes is called 'Visālakkha' (wide-eyed). One who has an unattractive face is called 'Vimukha' (distorted-faced). One who has realized the truths is called 'Paccakkhadhammā' (one who has realized the Dhamma). The scent of Surabhi is called 'Surabhigandhi'. A good scent is called 'Sugandhi'. A contemptible scent is called 'Duggandhi'. A putrid scent is called 'Pūtigandhi'.

Half of the night is called 'Aḍḍharatta' (midnight). The first part of the night is called 'Pubbaratta'. The latter part of the night is called 'Apararatta'. A long night is called 'Dīgharatta'. A family that possesses brindled cows is called 'Citragu'. A place or time where cows stand is called 'Tiṭṭhagu'. Two cows are called 'Digu'.

723. The suffixes -a and -ka occur after nouns that have reached the end of a compound. Because five cows are collected, it is called 'Pañcagavaṃ'. The Dispensation (Sāsana) which has a Teacher (the Buddha) who has not passed away is called 'Anatītasatthuka'. A region that has many ministers is called 'Bahukattuka'. A monastery that is void of (has no) monks is called 'Abhikkhuka'. One who exists together with a cause is called 'Sahetuka'. These are examples.

724. The vowels -ī and -ū standing in the feminine gender are called 'Nadī'. A man who has many female slaves is called 'Bahudāsika'. A family that has many women is called 'Bahuvadhuka'.

725. The suffix -ka occurs after terms named 'Nadī'. A country that has many rivers is called 'Bahunadika'. A forest that has many rose-apple trees is called 'Bahujambuka'.

726. When certain suffixes like -ā are elided, the vowel that was elided reappears when those suffixes are absent. One who has long shanks (lower legs) is called 'Dīghajaṅgha'. A young brahmin girl is called 'Brāhmaṇadārikā'.
221:
727. In the context of treating as masculine or neuter, when the suffix -ka follows, the vowel 'a' becomes 'i'. In the context of the masculine or neuter state, when the suffix -ka follows, 'a' reaches the state of 'i'. Examples: A man with many female slaves (Bahudāsika). A family with many female slaves (Bahudāsikaṃ). A country with many rivers (Bahunadika). A city with many rivers (Bahunadikaṃ).

728. In contexts other than the masculine or neuter state, when the suffix -ka follows, the vowels -ī and -ū become short (rassa) for ease of pronunciation. Examples: A capital with many rivers (Bahunadikā). A woman with many female slaves (Bahudāsikā). A capital with many rose-apples (Bahujambukā).

729. A feminine word excluding those ending in -ā and -ī should not be regarded as masculine or neuter, even if it has a masculine sense due to the meaning "a male spoken of in that female". A country in which there are many rose-apple trees is called 'Bahujambuko'. Likewise, a city with many rose-apples (Bahujambukaṃ). A family with many women (Bahuvadhukaṃ). A king with many armies (Bahucamuko).

730. In an Avyayībhāva compound, the feminine gender should not be regarded as masculine even if it has a masculine sense, because that Avyayībhāva has the characteristic of an indeclinable and because it lacks the expressed gender and number. A region where the red Ganges river exists is 'Lohitagangā', and so forth.

731. When the word 'pati' follows, in some instances, the word 'jāyā' (wife) is substituted with 'tudaṃ' or 'jāni'. One who is both wife and husband is 'Tudaṃpati'; likewise 'Jānipati'. Also 'Jāyampatikā'.

732. In some instances, the suffix -ā is added after words like 'dhanu' at the end of a compound. A person who has a bow with arrows is called 'Kaṇḍivadhanvā'. Likewise, one who has realized the truths (Paccakkhadhammā). One who has the covering opened (Vivaṭacchadā). Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? It is to indicate that the suffix -ā is not applied in cases like 'Kaṇḍivadhanu', 'Paccakkhadhammo', and 'Vivaṭacchado'.
222:
733. After an Avyayībhāva compound ending in 'a', the case endings are sometimes substituted with 'aṃ'. For example: Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, Upakumbhaṃ. Why is "kvaci" (in some instances) said? Because it is not substituted in the example 'ko yaṃ majjhesamuddasmiṃ'.

734. The vowel of an Avyayībhāva compound occurring in the neuter gender is always short (rassa). For example: Adhitthi, Adhikumāri.

735. Case endings following other Avyayībhāva compounds that do not end in 'a' are elided. For example: Adhitthi, Adhikumāri, Upavadhu.

Now, for the sake of generating supreme skill in those who listen to the Dispensation of the Buddha:

I shall speak from the science of grammar (Saddasattha) regarding the name of the Avyayībhāva, its rule (sutta), the commentary (vutti) on that rule, and these three together, as well as the extensive meanings of their applications (payoga).

In the science of grammar, this is stated regarding: the meaning of case endings (vibhattyattha), the meaning of proximity (samīpattha), the meaning of prosperity (samiddhattha), the meaning of abundance and lack (viddhi), the meaning of perpetual absence (sabbadā attābhāva), the meaning of the passing of what exists (vijjamānassa accaya), the meaning of the current unavailability of an object that is free from both existence and passing due to the lack of a cause (anupaladdhi), the meaning of the manifestation of sound (saddapātubhāva), the meaning of 'after' (pacchāttha), the meaning of 'yathā' (yathāttha), the meaning of 'in order' (anupubbattha), the meaning of simultaneity (apubbācarimattha), the meaning of similarity (sadisattha), the meaning of fulfillment (sampannattha), the meaning of entirety (sākalya), and the meaning of 'until the end' (antavacana).

Furthermore, it is stated regarding: the meaning of the word 'yathā' in other senses such as distributive (vicchā) excluding similarity; the meaning of the word 'yāva' in the sense of limitation; the noun with 'pati' occurring in the sense of 'a little'; the words 'akkha' and 'salāka' ending in the instrumental singular; the numbers one, two, three, and four; the word 'pari' in the sense of "this word is not spoken as it was spoken before" in gambling with dice, etc.; the words 'apa', 'pari', 'bahi', 'udicca', etc., together with words ending in the ablative case; the meanings of the prefix 'ā' in limitation (mariyādā) and pervasion (abhividhi); the prefixes 'abhi' and 'pati' together with words indicating a sign in the sense of 'towards' (ābhimukhya); the word 'anu' in the sense of proximity; and the same word 'anu' in the sense of length (āyāma)...
223:
It is stated that the Avyayībhāva compound occurs respectively for words such as Tiṭṭhagū etc., in the sense of another word's meaning [referring to] place or time; for the words pāra and majjha together with words ending in the sixth case (genitive); for numerical words together with words expressing lineage (vaṃsa); or for those [numerical words] together with words expressing rivers; and for words expressing rivers in the sense of a name (saññā) [which is] another word's meaning.

Among those Avyayībhāva compounds, in the sense of a case ending (vibhattyattha): Adhitthi etc., occur in the sense of 'governance over women'. In the sense of proximity (samīpa): Upakumbhaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'near the pot'. In the sense of prosperity (samiddhi): Sumagadhaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'the prosperity of the Magadhans'. In the sense of lack of prosperity (viddhi): Viddhiyaṃ means 'devoid of prosperity'. Dussaddhiyaṃ means 'lack of faith among those with faith'; Dubbhojanaṃ means 'lack of food', and so on. In the sense of absence (abhāva): Nimmakkhikaṃ means 'absence of flies'; Niddarathaṃ means 'absence of distress', and so on. In the sense of the passing of something existing (accayatthā): Nihimaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'the frost has passed'.

In the sense of unavailability at present (sampati anupalabdhi) due to the lack of causes, being free from the two modes: Abhikosumbhaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'at present, cloth dyed with safflower is not obtainable'. In the sense of the manifestation of sound (saddapātubhāva): 'The story in which the voice of the Venerable Kaccāyana was manifested' is called Iti Kaccāyanaṃ. Here, the word 'iti' illuminates the aforementioned specific meaning. In the sense of 'after' (pacchā): Anurathaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'after the chariots'. In the sense of 'according to' (yathā): Anurūpaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'according to the form'. In the sense of 'succession' (anupubba): Anujeṭṭhaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'according to seniority'. In the sense of 'simultaneity without before or after' (apubbācarima): Sacakkaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'bearing [something] together with the wheel in a single moment'. In the sense of 'similarity' (sadisa): Sarūpaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'similar in form'.

In the sense of 'abundance' (sampanna): Sakhettaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'an abundant field'. Here, the word 'saha' expresses the sense of abundance. In the sense of 'totality' (sākalya—including parts): Samakkhikaṃ etc., occur. Here, the word 'kalā' expresses a 'part'; sakalaṃ means 'together with parts', i.e., the meaning of 'with parts'. The state of being 'with parts' is called sākalya; in that sense of totality: Samakkhikaṃ means 'rice entirely with flies'. Alternatively, the word sākalya has the meaning of 'entirety' (kasiṇa). In that case, rice mixed with all the flies is called Samakkhikaṃ.
224:
In the sense of expressing the end (learning): Uṇādyantaṃ means 'studied up to the end of the Uṇādi [text]', because of the sense 'studied starting from the Soṇa etc. texts'. In senses other than similarity, the word yathā [is used]: Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'according to those respective elders who exist'. Here, the word yathā expresses vicchā (repetition/order).

In the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇa), the word yāva [is used]: Yāvajīvaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'as long as the extent of life exists' (until the end of life).

When the word pati in the sense of 'a little' (matta) is combined with a noun: Sākapati occurs in the sense of 'a very little vegetable'. Likewise, Sūpapati (a little curry), etc.

The word pari in the sense of 'it was said thus, but not as before' is combined in games of dice etc., with the words akkha and salāka ending in the third case (instrumental), and with the numerical words one, two, three, and four. Akkhapari means 'it was said thus by the die, but not as before'. Salākāpari means 'it was said thus by the peg, but not as before'. Ekapari, Dvipari, Tipari, Catupari, etc., occur in the sense of 'not as before by one, two, three, or four'.

When apa, pari, bahi, udicca, etc., are combined with a word ending in the fifth case (ablative): Apapāṭaliputtaṃ, Paripāṭaliputtaṃ, Bahipāṭaliputtaṃ, Udiccapāṭaliputtaṃ, etc., occur in the sense of 'it rained away from the city of Pāṭaliputta'.

The word ā is used in the senses of limit (mariyādā) and inclusion (abhividhi): Āpāṭaliputtaṃ occurs in the sense of 'it rained up to the city of Pāṭaliputta'. Ākumāraṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'the fame of the Venerable Kaccāyana is pervasive even unto the children'.

When the words abhi and pati are combined with a word expressing a sign (lakkhaṇa) in the sense of 'towards' (ābhimukhya): Abbhaggi, Paccaggi, etc., occur in the sense of 'moths fall facing the fire'.

The word anu in the sense of 'near' (samīpa): Anuvanaṃ etc., occur in the sense of 'near the forest'. That same word anu in the sense of 'lengthwise' (āyāma): Anugaṅgaṃ Bārāṇasī occurs in the sense of 'the city of Vārāṇasī situated along the Ganges river'.
225:
The words *Tiᙩᙩhagu* and others occur in the sense of place or time as the meaning of another word (*a!!apadattha*). The place where, or the time when, cows stand is called *Tiᙩᙩhagu*. The place where, or the time when, cows are carried is called *Vahagu*. The time when there is barley on the threshing floor is called *Khaleyavaṁ*. This is how they should be understood.

The words *pāra* and *majjha* form compounds with words ending in the genitive case (*chaᙩᙩhī*). On the other bank of the Ganges is *Pāregaṅgaṁ*. In the middle of the Ganges is *Majjhegaṅgaṁ*. This is how they should be understood.

Numeral words form compounds with words expressing lineage (*vaṁsa*). In his lineage, there are three successive Kosala generations; therefore, it is called *Tikosalaṁ*. This is how they should be understood.

Those numeral words also form compounds with words expressing rivers. Seven Godāvarī rivers are combined; therefore, it is called *Sattagodāvaraṁ*. This is how they should be understood.

Words expressing rivers that are well-known as names form compounds in the sense of another word (*a!!apadattha*). The place where the Ganges river flows like a madman is called *Ummatttagaṅgaṁ*. *Tuṇhīgaṅgaṁ* (the place where it flows silently), *Lohitagaṅgaṁ* (the place where the water flows red like blood). This is how they should be understood.

## 736. Mātādīnamā dvandepitādīsu.
In a *Dvanda* compound, the final vowel of words such as *mātu* becomes *ā* when followed by words such as *pitu*. The repetition of this rule is to prohibit the change to *ā* in a *Tappurisa* compound. Mother and father are *Mātāpitaro*. In this manner, the words with the following meanings should be understood: *Mātābhātaro*, *Mātādhītaro*, *Pitābhātaro*, *Pitādhītaro*, *Bhātāmātaro*, *Bhātāpitaro*, *Bhātādhītaro*, *Dhītāmātaro*, *Dhītāpitaro*, *Dhītābhātaro*, *Mātāputtā*, *Mātābhaginī*, *Pitāputtā*, *Pitābhaginī*, *Mātāpitābhātādhītaro*, *Mātāpitādhītāputtā*, *Mātāpitābhātādhītā*, and *Dhītābhaginiyo*. Thus, in a *Dvanda* compound, the end of words such as *mātu* changes to *ā* when followed by words such as *pitu*. Such a word formation is seen in the *Mahāparinibbānasuttanta Aᙩᙩhakathā* as "*mātāpitābhātābhaginīādikēhī*". Why is it said "in *Dvanda*"? The father's brother is called *Pitubhātā*.
226:
737. In both *Bahubbīhi* and *Dvanda* compounds, there is the 'single remainder' (*ekasesa*) of words having the same form (*sarūpa*). The color of gold is 'gold-color' (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇa*). Because the color of the Blessed One is like the color of gold, He is called '*Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*'. In the same way, '*Brahmassaro*' and others are formed. However, in this case, when the analysis (*vigga-ha*) is made as "one whose color is like the color of gold," there is no function of *ekasesa*. But it does occur according to another specific intention. This is how *ekasesa* occurs in a *Bahubbīhi* compound. In a *Dvanda* compound, however, that which is both name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*) is '*Nāmarūpaṁ*'. One who is both the deity Citta and the deity Sena is '*Cittaseno*'.

738. In a compound ending with a *taddhita* suffix, there is the 'single remainder' (*ekasesa*) of words having the same form. Because he has a complexion like that of Brahmā (or of excellent gold), he is called '*Brahmavaṇṇī*'.

739. In a *Dvanda* compound, there is the 'single remainder' (*ekasesa*) of identical syllables (*akkhara*). The state of being a deity and the state of being a human is '*Devamanussattaṁ*'. In this manner, '*Nāgasupaṇṇatā*' and '*Itthipumbhāvo*' are also formed. Here too, if the analysis is made as "the state of those who are both deities and humans is *devamanussattaṁ*," there is no function of *ekasesa*. But it does occur according to another specific intention.

740. When it is said "*Puriso ca Puriso ca*," some grammarians (*akkharacintaka*) with unstable intellect claim that the word '*Purisā*', which is taken by making a single remainder of identical forms, is a "*Dvanda* compound." That statement should not be accepted because there is no identical form for a collection of various dissimilar words.

741. In my own view, the singular word '*Puriso*' is a compound (*samāsa*). Without taking the plural word '*Purisā*', which has already undergone *ekasesa*, as a compound word, only the singular word '*Puriso*' is taken as a compound according to another intention. It is called '*Puriso*' because it means 'one who dwells in a secluded place'. Or, it is called '*Puriso*' because it means 'one who dwells in an exalted place'. Just as '*Vanajo*' is a *kitaka* compound because it means 'born in the forest', so too '*Puriso*' is a compound. Just as '*Urago*', '*Pādapo*', '*Aṇṁajo*', '*Kutojo*', and '*Itojo*' are compound words, so too '*Puriso*' is a compound word. Just as '*Migāsahābhi*' and others are not compound words, so too *ekasesa* words like '*Purisayo*' are not compound words. If analyzed according to the other mentioned intention, the plural words '*Purisā*' are compounds. They are called '*Purisā*' because they mean 'those who fulfill their own lineage'. When analyzed in this way, it should be noted that it is not a compound. In this regard, the statement "*Puriso pi visesato*" is said. In both the word '*Puriso*' and the word '*Purisā*', they can be both compounds and non-compounds depending on the specific analysis.
227:
In our view, the word "Purisa" should be regarded as a compound (samāsa). It is called "Purisa" because it dwells in a high place (uccē ṭhāne). Just as "Vanaja" is a compound because it is born in the forest, "Purisa" is a compound because it dwells in a high place. Just as "Uraga" (snake—going by the chest), "Pādapa" (tree—drinking by the feet), "Atraja" (born from oneself), "Kutojo" (born from where?), and "Itojo" (born from here) are compound words, this word "Purisa" is also a compound word. While "Migā" (deer) and "Sīhā" (lions) are not compounds, "Purisā" (men) and "Itthiyo" (women) are words formed by elision (ekasesa). However, if the derivation (viggaha) is made with a different intention as mentioned, the singular form "Puriso" and the plural form "Purisā" are indeed compounds. If the derivation is "He is called Purisa because he fulfills his own lineage (attano kulaṃ pūreti); they are called Purisā because they fulfill it," then they are not compounds.

In this regard, it is said:
Both the word "Puriso" and the word "Purisā" can be compounds or non-compounds, depending on the specific derivation.

742. In the word "Saḷāyatana", there is elision (ekasesa) of words and letters that are similar or dissimilar in sound. While "Saḷāyatana" is the base (ādhāra), elision occurs for dissimilar (virūpa) and similar (sarūpa) words and letters. The five bases (Cakkhāyatana, etc.) and the sixth base (Manāyatana) together are called "Saḷāyatana".

Excluding the word "Saḷāyatana" entirely, the elision of dissimilar sounding words is not desired (does not occur) in other compounds or in words ending in secondary derivatives (taddhita).

743. When the word "Nadī" follows, "Khudda" is substituted with "Kun". It is called "Kunnadī" (small river) because it is both small and a river.

744. When the word "Pipāsā" follows, "Khuddā" is substituted with "Khu". "Khuppipāsābhibhūto" (one overcome by great, or base, or solitary thirst).
228:
745. According to the rule "Kvacī samānassa so", in some instances, the word "Samāna" is changed to "Sa". The Buddha, who has a complexion like Siṅgīnikkha gold, is called "Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo". The sun, which has a complexion like gold, is called "Harissavaṇṇo". The Buddha, who has a kinsman of the Gotama lineage similar to the kinsman of the sun because of being of the Gotama lineage, is called "Sādiccabandhu"; because He is both Buddha and Sādiccabandhu, He is called "Buddhasādiccabandhu". This meaning should be understood according to the Commentary on the Pali text "Buddhasādiccabandhuno". This compound is said to be one whose meaning is extremely difficult to demonstrate or understand. An owl, which has a lineage similar to that of Sakka (Indra) because of being of the Kosiya lineage, is called "Indasagotto". It is evident in the Pali: "Of the owl named Indasagotto, who is hooting...". Why is "Kvacī" (in some cases) said? It is to prevent the change of "Samāna" to "Sa" in places like "Gajo yathā indasamānagottaṃ".

746. According to the rule "Sahassa hassa ca lopo vā", in some instances, the word "Saha" is changed to "Sa", or the letter "ha" is elided. A person with gods is called "Sadevako"; a person with wealth is called "Sadhano". The Blessed One who exists with the name Dīpaṅkara is called "Dīpaṅkarasanāmako". Likewise, there are "Candasavhayo" (the prince named Canda) and "Saṅkhasavhayo" (the brahmin named Saṅkha). The teachers of the Commentaries, however, explained "Candasavhayo" as one who is called by the word "Canda". In this context, it should be noted as if the "dda" of the word "Sadda" is elided. Our view, however, is: "Avhātabbaṃ" means "Avhayaṃ" (name); the prince who exists with the name Canda is meant by "Candasavhayo". Why is "Kvacī" said? It is to prevent the change of "Saha" to "Sa" or the elision of "ha" in places such as "Sahamaccharā ca" and "Sahoḍḍhaṃ coraṃ".
229:
747. In appropriate places, the letters "ve" and "ta" are inserted in the middle of nouns within a compound. For example: "Vuṭṭhiveparamā sarā" (rivers, oceans, and lakes with abundant raindrops), "Kuhiṃ vaṅkatapabbato" (Where is the Vaṅkata mountain?), and "Saḷaṅgatamantaṃ vyākariṃsu" (The wise ones who possess the six factors [or Vedic knowledge] reflected on the signs from the Vedas and answered). The letter "ta" in "Saḷaṅgata", etc., should be understood in the sense of possession (atthi-attha) or in its own sense (sak-attha). Why is "ṭhāne" (in appropriate places) said? It is to prevent the insertion of "ve" and "ta" in phrases like "Ārogyaparamā lābhā" (Health is the highest gain) and "Sinerupabbatuṭtamo" (The noble Mount Sineru).

748. In some instances within a compound, the word "Dinna" is substituted with "Datta". For example: "Buddhadatto" (given by the Buddha), "Paradattupajīvī" (one who lives depending on what others give). Why is "Kvacī" said? It is to prevent the substitution with "Datta" in cases like "Dhammadinnā bhikkhunī", "Dinnādāyī" (one who habitually takes what is given), and "Dinnapāṭikaṅkhī" (one who desires what is given). Why is "Samāse" said? It is to prevent the substitution with "Datta" in the sentence "Dānaṃ dinnaṃ" (The gift is given). In truth, the word "Datta" as a separate subordinate attribute (guṇa-pada) does not exist in the Dispensation (Sāsana). In Sanskrit, however, it exists as "Dattaṃ yenapi apādānaṃ dattaṃ", meaning "That which is given by someone is indeed taken". Although the word "Datta" exists separately in the Dispensation, it is not a subordinate attribute because it exists only as a designation (paṇṇatti/name). For example, the name of "Bhūridatta" is "Datta".

749. After the word "Sakka", etc., the word "Dinna" is always substituted with "Dattiya" in a compound. For example: "Sakkadattiye assame vasiṃsu" (They lived in the hermitage given by Sakka), "Brahmadattiyaṃ cīvaraṃ" (the robe offered by a Brahmā), and "Devadattiyaṃ paṃsukူlacīvaraṃ" (the rag-robe offered by a deity). In these words, the compound "Sakkadattiya" is formed because it was given by Sakka. The same method applies to "Brahmadattiya" and "Devadattiya". However, some members of the Order who grew up familiar with Sanskrit, without looking at the Pali method, composed words like "Brahmadattaṃ cīvaraṃ" and "Devadatto patto". Such compositions are inappropriate when compared with the Dispensation. This is because such qualitative attributes do not exist in the Dispensation and because the teachers of the Commentaries have rejected them.
230:
750. Dviditinamisse. In a compound, the vowel 'i' of the words 'dvi', 'di', and 'ti' is sometimes changed to 'e'. Examples: Dvebhāvo, manaso advejjho (undividedness of mind), tecattālīsaṃ (forty-three), dvecattālīsaṃ (forty-two). That king of swans who has two wings with a color like that of gold is called Kañcanadepiñcho. Why is 'kvaci' (sometimes) said? To indicate that the change to 'e' does not occur in cases such as dvibhāvo, dvirattaṃ (two nights), tirattaṃ (three nights), ticattālīsaṃ (forty-three), and dvicattālīsaṃ (forty-two).

A mindful person should always and repeatedly apply this Saddanīti eye-ointment, which purifies the eye of wisdom and removes the film of delusion.

## Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, named Samāsakappa, in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the modes of expression of the Tipitaka along with its Commentaries and the ninefold Dispensation.

## 5-Taddhitakappa

Henceforth, I shall continue to teach this chapter named Taddhita, which brings benefit to the listeners; listen to it with a concentrated mind.

Taddhita is the name of suffixes starting with 'ṇa' that occur in meanings such as apacca (offspring), etc. It is also the name of the method (rule) to be accomplished through mental construction (parikappa), etc. In this way, words without suffixes such as the ekasesa word 'purisā' (formed by the mental construction 'puriso ca puriso ca'), the word 'vīsatī' (formed by 'dasa ca dasa ca'), the word 'cuddasā' (formed by 'catūhi adhikā dasa'), and the word 'aḍḍhuḍḍho' (formed by 'aḍḍhena catuttho') must also be regarded as Taddhita words, and not otherwise. However, some people, holding that 'Taddhita is only the name of suffixes such as ṇa', say that the ekasesa word 'purisā' is not a Taddhita word because it lacks a suffix, but is merely a pure noun (suddhanāma). That view should not be accepted, because even though it lacks a suffix, the meaning is to be grasped by the power of mental construction (parikappa). Indeed, to make known that the word 'purisā' denotes many men, [one says] 'puriso ca puriso...'
